notes.narrative: On the I degree, freely interchange C6 and Cmaj7 almost all the time. 'We can replace C6 by Cmaj7 or vice-versa almost all the time.' (Ch. 6, p. 200). Use C6 instead when the melody is the octave to avoid a b9 conflict between melody and chord.

references.source: Ch. 6 — How to Study the Harmonic Fields

notes.narrative: 'We can replace C6 by Cmaj7 or vice-versa almost all the time. The only exception is when the melody is the octave. In this case we must use C6, in order to not create a conflict between the melody and the chord (a b9 interval).' (Ch. 6, p. 200). The maj6 voicing is the preferred choice specifically when the melody sits on the octave of the root.

references.source: Ch. 6 — How to Study the Harmonic Fields

notes.narrative: 'We do not have to put the (#4) in the chord all the time, but in a few cases it might work. In theory, G/F can be considered an F Lydian chord, including G7(13) or G7(9).' (Ch. 6, p. 209). The #4 (augmented 11th) is optional on the IV Lydian maj7 chord and need not appear in every voicing.

references.source: Ch. 6 — How to Study the Harmonic Fields

notes.narrative: For major chords functioning in a Lydian context, the augmented 11th (#4) is the characteristic note of the mode. 'For major chords and dominant 7th chords, most of the time we use the #11th (#4) to prevent unwanted dissonance with the major 3rd.' (Ch. 4, p. 126). Apply #11 freely on major chords to preserve Lydian modal color.

On the IIIm (Phrygian) degree, recast Em7 as the slash voicing Cmaj7/E or C/E. 'Em7 can be replaced by Em7(b6), Cmaj7/E or even C/E, which are the same chords.' (Ch. 6, p. 207). This slash approach reinterprets the maj7 chord as an upper structure over the phrygian bass.

references.source: Ch. 6 — How to Study the Harmonic Fields

notes.narrative: On the VIm (Aeolian) degree, every Fmaj7/A can be considered an Aeolian chord. 'In theory, every Dm7/A or Fmaj7/A can be considered as an Aeolian chord.' (Ch. 6, p. 217). Use the Fmaj7/A slash voicing to supply an aeolian color over the vi bass note.

references.source: Ch. 6 — How to Study the Harmonic Fields

notes.narrative: 'Cm(b6) is exactly the same as Abmaj7 first inversion.' (Ch. 4, p. 83). When a Cm(b6) voicing appears, recognize it as Abmaj7 in first inversion and choose the label that best fits the harmonic context.

Extended notes on the Ionian (I) chord include the major 9th, perfect 11th, and major 13th as tensions, but 'not all extended notes of a chord must be in it. Many of them should only be played as the passing tones of a melody on the chord.' (Ch. 5, p. 182). Add the major 9th to the I voicing for color, but treat it as a melodic option rather than a required component.

On the IIm (Dorian) degree, the base min7 voicing can be freely replaced with its Dorian extensions. 'We can replace Dm7(9) dorian by Dm7(11) or even Dm7(13).' (Ch. 6, p. 204). Begin from the Dm7 shape and add the 9th, 11th, or 13th depending on the melodic context.

references.source: Ch. 6 — How to Study the Harmonic Fields

notes.narrative: On the IIIm (Phrygian) degree, Em7 can be enriched or replaced with a flat-6 addition or equivalent slash voicings. 'Em7 can be replaced by Em7(b6), Cmaj7/E or even C/E, which are the same chords. However, as a phrygian chord, Em7 can also be replaced by Esus(b9).' (Ch. 6, p. 207).

references.source: Ch. 6 — How to Study the Harmonic Fields

notes.narrative: On the VIm (Aeolian) degree, replace Am7 with Am7(9), Am7(11), or Am7(b6) for extended color, or use the slash voicings Dm7/A or Fmaj7/A. 'We can replace Am7(9) Aeolian with Am7(11) or even Am7(b6). But just like any degree, the characteristic notes do not have to be in the chord all the time.' (Ch. 6, p. 217).

references.source: Ch. 6 — How to Study the Harmonic Fields

notes.narrative: The 9th is a standard Dorian extension on the IIm degree. 'We can replace Dm7(9) dorian by Dm7(11) or even Dm7(13).' (Ch. 6, p. 204). Dm7(9) is the primary Dorian voicing recommended as the starting point before adding the 11th or 13th.

references.source: Ch. 6 — How to Study the Harmonic Fields

notes.narrative: 'In theory, we could also use Dm6, but minor 6th chords are more complex than they look, so we will come back to them later. For now, let us consider that they can sometimes replace a minor 7th chord.' (Ch. 6, p. 204). Defer the min6 on the IIm degree until the simpler Dorian extensions are mastered.

references.source: Ch. 6 — How to Study the Harmonic Fields

notes.narrative: On the V degree, the dominant 7th can always be replaced with a sus chord. 'We can replace the V chord (dominant) with a sus chord. Example: G7 can be replaced by Gsus9 or Gsus13.' (Ch. 6, p. 213).

references.source: Ch. 6 — How to Study the Harmonic Fields

notes.narrative: 'For major chords and dominant 7th chords, most of the time we use the #11th (#4) to prevent unwanted dissonance with the major 3rd. Only in some specific cases do we use the major 3rd and the perfect 11th (4th) together.' (Ch. 4, p. 126). On dominant 7th chords prefer #11 over natural 11 except in deliberate cases.

The perfect 11th (natural 4th) is listed as an avoid note for the Mixolydian (V) chord: 'Avoid notes: perfect 4th' (Ch. 5, p. 182). For dominant chords, avoid placing the natural 11th in the voicing because it clashes with the major 3rd; use #11 instead on major and dominant qualities.

Prefer the #11 on dominant chords functioning as the V or in a Lydian Dominant context. 'For major chords and dominant 7th chords, most of the time we use the #11th (#4) to prevent unwanted dissonance with the major 3rd.' (Ch. 4, p. 126). The Lydian Dominant scale (IV of Melodic Minor) is the primary source for this color on the V chord.

'Notice that in this type of chord, the 5th is almost always omitted.' (Ch. 4, p. 126). When voicing a 13th chord on guitar, drop the 5th to keep the voicing practical; the essential tones are the root, 3rd, 7th, and 13th.

A G7(13) or G7(9) voicing over an F bass implies F Lydian. 'In theory, G/F can be considered an F Lydian chord, including G7(13) or G7(9).' (Ch. 6, p. 209). Use the dom13 chord as an upper-structure slash to evoke the Lydian color on the IV degree.

references.source: Ch. 6 — How to Study the Harmonic Fields

notes.narrative: 'Every dominant chord with more than one altered extended note is called an altered chord.' (Ch. 4, p. 126). When applying alterations to a dominant chord, ensure at least two altered extensions (e.g., b9 and b5, or #9 and #5) are present to qualify it as altered; a single alteration simply modifies the dominant without crossing into the altered category.

The VII Altered Scale (Root/min 2nd/aug 2nd/maj 3rd/aug 4th/min 6th/min 7th) from Melodic Minor is the primary theoretical source for altered dominant voicings. 'We cannot use the chord families derived from these three groups of scale modes to guide us through songs, we can only use them to add more colors to the chords.' (Ch. 7, p. 224). Apply Altered Scale colors on top of an existing dominant chord rather than as a structural replacement.

references.source: Ch. 7 — Leading Tone & How Other Scales Appeared
references.citation: p. 224, 'Function of derived chord families'; p. 251, 'Altered Scale intervals'

notes.narrative: 'For major and minor chords, we should avoid intervals of a flat 9th between the bass note and the top note of the chord.' (Ch. 4, p. 77). This prohibition applies broadly to any voicing where the interval from bass to top note spans a minor 9th, so when building dom7b9 shapes take care not to position the b9 as the top note against the bass.

references.citation: p. 77, 'Flat-9 between bass and top to avoid'

notes.narrative: 'The VII degree cannot use the 9th in the chord, because it would be flat 9th, which does not work properly for this type of chord. Remember that the flat 9th is an avoid note on locrian chord.' (Ch. 6, p. 221). Never add the 9th to the half-diminished VII chord when reinterpreted as a dominant-7 slash voicing over the leading tone.

references.source: Ch. 6 — How to Study the Harmonic Fields

notes.narrative: 'We can replace the V chord (dominant) with a sus chord. Example: G7 can be replaced by Gsus9 or Gsus13.' (Ch. 6, p. 213). The sus4 substitution for the V dominant is a primary Mixolydian color move; keep the perfect 4th in place of the 3rd and leave the minor 7th intact.

references.source: Ch. 6 — How to Study the Harmonic Fields

notes.narrative: 'Suspended chords are those where the 3rd is replaced by the 4th or 2nd. We call these chords sus2 and sus4. Although the two instances exist, the most common is to replace the 3rd by the 4th.' (Ch. 4, p. 108). Always treat the sus4 as a 3rd-replacement voicing, not as an added-tone chord.

'In order to visualize this type of chord properly, it is recommended to consider them as dominant 7th chords using some different tension notes. In other words, for the sus chords visualization, we will use the simple dominant 7th chord shapes we already know to guide us.' (Ch. 4, p. 109). Build every sus4 shape by starting from a known dominant-7 shape and replacing the 3rd with the 4th.

'As a phrygian chord, Em7 can also be replaced by Esus(b9) and sometimes Em7(b9), which was often used by composers such as Antonio Carlos Jobim and also Heitor Villa Lobos.' (Ch. 6, p. 207). On the IIIm Phrygian degree the sus(b9) voicing is a characteristic coloristic substitution with a strong Brazilian art-music precedent.

references.source: Ch. 6 — How to Study the Harmonic Fields

notes.narrative: 'Bø can be replaced with G7/B or even G/B. This happens frequently because we consider the Bø as being G7(9)/B.' (Ch. 6, p. 221). The half-diminished VII chord should routinely be recast as a slash voicing of the dominant a minor 7th below, making its locrian function explicit through the bass note alone.

references.source: Ch. 6 — How to Study the Harmonic Fields

notes.narrative: The minor 2nd (b9) is the primary avoid note for Locrian: 'Avoid notes: minor 2nd' (Ch. 5, p. 182). On the half-diminished VII chord, 'the VII degree cannot use the 9th in the chord, because it would be flat 9th, which does not work properly for this type of chord.' (Ch. 6, p. 221). Never voice the 9th on a Locrian half-diminished chord.

references.source: Ch. 6 — How to Study the Harmonic Fields

notes.narrative: 'There is no inversion to diminished or augmented chords, because they are symmetric. Symmetric chords are those that repeat themselves in a predetermined intervallic cycle. The diminished chord, for example, repeats itself each minor 3rd.' (Ch. 4, p. 75). Do not apply root/first/second inversion analysis to dim7 shapes; instead navigate them via their enharmonic minor-3rd equivalences.

Dominant 7th chords 'have a strong relationship with diminished, half diminished and major 7th (#4) chords.' (Ch. 4, p. 128). Use the dim7 as an enharmonic substitute for a dominant-7 chord a half-step above any of its chord tones, exploiting the four-way symmetric identity to access distant tonal regions.

The Harmonic Major VIIm Locrian (bb7) mode (Root/min 2nd/min 3rd/perf 4th/dim 5th/min 6th/dim 7th) is the theoretical source for diminished 7th colors including o7(b13) and (11) textures (Ch. 7, p. 277). 'We cannot use the chord families derived from these three groups of scale modes to guide us through songs, we can only use them to add more colors to the chords.' (Ch. 7, p. 224). Apply these dim7 colors as tension layers over existing chords, never as structural substitutes.

references.source: Ch. 7 — Leading Tone & How Other Scales Appeared
references.citation: p. 277, 'Harmonic Major VIIm Locrian bb7'; p. 224, 'Function of derived chord families'

notes.narrative: 'The diminished triad will use a left shape using 3 consecutive strings. Actually this type of diminished shape is not as common as the real diminished chord. We use this shape to create phrases (licks) when improvising, or even when we play a solo guitar piece.' (Ch. 4, p. 64). Reserve the triadic diminished left-side shape for melodic/improvisational use rather than comping.

'There is no inversion to diminished or augmented chords, because they are symmetric... the augmented chords repeat themselves every major 3rd.' (Ch. 4, p. 75). Do not label augmented chord shapes as root, first, or second inversions; treat the three enharmonic positions as equivalent.

The bIII Lydian Augmented scale from Melodic Minor (Root/maj 2nd/maj 3rd/aug 4th/aug 5th/maj 6th/maj 7th) is the primary color source for augmented dominant tones (Ch. 7, p. 251). Apply the augmented color over a dominant chord as a tension device, not as a structural harmonic move. 'We can only use them to add more colors to the chords.' (Ch. 7, p. 224).

references.source: Ch. 7 — Leading Tone & How Other Scales Appeared
references.citation: p. 251, 'bIII Lydian Augmented intervals'; p. 224, 'Function of derived chord families'

notes.narrative: The Im Harmonic Minor mode yields a min-maj7 chord (Root/min 3rd/perf 5th/maj 7th). Its characteristic note is the major 7th and its avoid note is the minor 6th when the chord is Am(maj7): 'Avoid notes: minor 6th when the chord is Am(maj7). Characteristic notes: major 7th.' (Ch. 7, p. 226). Emphasize the major 7th as the defining tension and keep the minor 6th out of the voicing when holding on the chord.

references.source: Ch. 7 — Leading Tone & How Other Scales Appeared

notes.narrative: 'It is important to understand that we cannot use the chord families derived from these three groups of scale modes to guide us through songs, we can only use them to add more colors to the chords.' (Ch. 7, p. 224). The min-maj7 voicing sourced from Harmonic Minor is a coloristic tension device layered over an existing minor chord, not a progression-guiding substitution.

references.source: Ch. 7 — Leading Tone & How Other Scales Appeared

notes.narrative: When voicing Am(maj7), avoid the minor 6th as a chord tone: 'Avoid notes: minor 6th when the chord is Am(maj7).' (Ch. 7, p. 226). The minor 6th is usable as a passing tone in the melody over the chord but must never land as a resting note within the voicing.

references.source: Ch. 7 — Leading Tone & How Other Scales Appeared

notes.narrative: 'For major and minor chords, we should avoid intervals of a flat 9th between the bass note and the top note of the chord.' (Ch. 4, p. 77). This voicing prohibition also applies to inversions and slash voicings: check that the outer-voice interval between bass and melody is never a minor 9th when the chord is major or minor.

references.citation: p. 77, 'Flat-9 between bass and top to avoid'

notes.narrative: 'For major and minor chords, we should avoid intervals of a flat 9th between the bass note and the top note of the chord.' (Ch. 4, p. 77). When building maj7 voicings in any inversion, verify that the interval spanning from the lowest sounding note to the highest is not a minor 9th.

references.citation: p. 77, 'Flat-9 between bass and top to avoid'

notes.narrative: 'For major and minor chords, we should avoid intervals of a flat 9th between the bass note and the top note of the chord.' (Ch. 4, p. 77). On min7 shapes the most common trigger is a 3rd-inversion voicing where the b7 bass sits a minor 9th below the root on top; revoice to eliminate that span.

references.citation: p. 77, 'Flat-9 between bass and top to avoid'

notes.narrative: 'C6 is exactly the same as Am7 first inversion and Cm(b6) is exactly the same as Abmaj7 first inversion. We can call them by both names, but depending on the harmonic situation one of them will work better.' (Ch. 4, p. 83). Choose the C6 or Am7/first-inversion label that best fits the harmonic context; neither is universally preferable.

'C6 is exactly the same as Am7 first inversion.' (Ch. 4, p. 83). When encountering Am7 in first inversion, recognize it as functionally equivalent to a C6 voicing; select whichever label serves the local harmonic analysis.

'It is very important to understand that drop chord voicings can only be used with tetrads, leaving behind the tensions 9th, 11th and 13th that will be used later with the extended chords.' (Ch. 4, p. 84). Apply Drop 2 and Drop 3 transformations only to four-note dominant 7th shapes; never apply them to extended (9, 11, 13) voicings.
'Drop chord voicings can only be used with tetrads.' (Ch. 4, p. 84). Drop 2 and Drop 3 apply to the four-note maj7 chord exclusively; do not carry these transformations into maj9 or maj7#11 voicings.
'Drop chord voicings can only be used with tetrads.' (Ch. 4, p. 84). Use Drop 2 / Drop 3 on the four-note min7 chord shape only, not on min9 or min7(11) extensions.

'It is important to understand that some chords using the left side shape might not work properly because they are almost impossible to play. The 5th string/left side shape works better than the 6th string/left side shape, which we do not use with a minor chord.' (Ch. 4, p. 58). When building Chord Skeleton shapes for any quality on the 6th string, avoid the left-side shape; prefer 5th-string or right-side alternatives.

'The 6th string/left side shape... we do not use with a minor chord.' (Ch. 4, p. 58). For minor chord skeletons rooted on the 6th string, always use the right-side or 5th-string skeleton rather than the left-side shape.

'It is important to remember that many of the chords on the guitar have to be edited. This is totally different from the piano which is a complete harmonic instrument, where we can have many chord voicing possibilities without having to omit any note.' (Ch. 4, p. 112). On guitar, freely omit chord tones — especially the 5th — to make voicings physically playable; this is not a compromise but the instrument defining constraint.

references.citation: p. 112, 'Guitar must omit notes; not piano'

notes.narrative: 'Many of the chords on the guitar have to be edited... unlike the piano which is a complete harmonic instrument.' (Ch. 4, p. 112). For maj7 voicings, omit the 5th when needed to make the shape playable; the root, major 3rd, and major 7th carry the essential identity.

references.citation: p. 112, 'Guitar must omit notes; not piano'

notes.narrative: 'However, for minor chords the perfect 11th (4th) can be used freely.' (Ch. 4, p. 126). Unlike major and dominant chords where the natural 11 clashes with the major 3rd, the minor 11th is an unrestricted tension on any minor 7th voicing and may be added at will.

'The choice of notes for a chord sequence, most of the time must keep the smallest possible movement between the notes from one chord to another. Certainly, sometimes there may be deliberate leaps, but the smallest movement will almost always be the best way.' (Ch. 4, p. 84). When moving between dominant 7th voicings (or any chord pair), choose the inversion and string set that minimizes total voice movement.

'The choice of notes for a chord sequence, most of the time must keep the smallest possible movement between the notes from one chord to another.' (Ch. 4, p. 84). Select maj7 inversions (root, 1st, 2nd, 3rd position) to minimize melodic step size when moving to or from the chord.

'The extended chords will be learned by rooting them on the 5th and 6th strings. The 4th string will be used to play the 6th and 5th string chords without the bass note. Usually, a 4th string chord is derived from a 6th string chord. It will start from the 7th or 6th of the chord.' (Ch. 4, p. 127). When moving a dominant 7th voicing to the 4th string, begin from the shape 7th or 6th degree rather than attempting an independent fingering.

'We rarely use the perfect 4th over an Ionian chord. However we have some exceptions, where we can find chords with 4ths and 3rds or even omitted 3rd chords.' (Ch. 6, p. 200). On a maj7 Ionian chord, treat the natural 4th as an avoid note except in specific open-voicing or quartal contexts.

references.source: Ch. 6 — How to Study the Harmonic Fields

notes.narrative: 'Avoid notes: perfect 4th' on the Mixolydian (V) chord (Ch. 5, p. 182). The natural 11th/4th creates a characteristic half-step clash with the major 3rd in dominant 7th voicings; use #11 instead or omit the 11th entirely.

'Drop chord voicings can only be used with tetrads.' (Ch. 4, p. 84). The half-diminished (min7b5) is a tetrad and may be subjected to Drop 2 / Drop 3 transformations; do not apply these to any extension-bearing version of the chord.

A dominant chord carrying both a #9 and any other alteration qualifies as an altered chord: 'Every dominant chord with more than one altered extended note is called an altered chord.' (Ch. 4, p. 126). Apply the #9 in combination with at least one other alteration (b5, b9, #5, or b13) and source the resulting color from the VII Altered Scale of Melodic Minor.

Dominant 7th chords 'have a strong relationship with diminished, half diminished and major 7th (#4) chords.' (Ch. 4, p. 128). The dom7b5 participates in this web of enharmonic identities; use the relationship to navigate between a dom7b5 and a diminished or half-diminished voicing on the same set of strings.

'VERY IMPORTANT: Not all extended notes of a chord must be in it. Many of them should only be played as the passing tones of a melody on the chord.' (Ch. 7, p. 227). The major 9th on a maj9 chord is primarily a melodic passing-tone resource; omitting it from the voicing is standard practice and does not undermine the chord identity.

references.source: Ch. 7 — Leading Tone & How Other Scales Appeared

notes.narrative: 'Not all extended notes of a chord must be in it. Many of them should only be played as the passing tones of a melody on the chord.' (Ch. 5, p. 182). On a min9 chord the 9th belongs primarily to the melody line over the chord; it need not appear in the comping voicing.

'Not all extended notes of a chord must be in it. Many of them should only be played as the passing tones of a melody on the chord.' (Ch. 5, p. 182). On a dom13, the 9th and 11th layers in particular serve as melodic ornaments rather than mandatory voicing components; voice only the root, 3rd, 7th, and 13th on the guitar.

'To make visualization easier, choose chords that are close to each other, using only the 6th and 5th string chords. The 4th string chords should be studied only after you are comfortable with the others.' (Ch. 6, p. 187). Master all dominant 7th voicings rooted on the 6th and 5th strings before attempting 4th-string positions.

references.source: Ch. 6 — How to Study the Harmonic Fields

notes.narrative: 'To make visualization easier, choose chords that are close to each other, using only the 6th and 5th string chords. The 4th string chords should be studied only after you are comfortable with the others.' (Ch. 6, p. 187). Learn all maj7 voicings rooted on the 6th and 5th strings as a prerequisite to studying 4th-string maj7 positions.

references.source: Ch. 6 — How to Study the Harmonic Fields

notes.narrative: 'To make visualization easier, choose chords that are close to each other, using only the 6th and 5th string chords. The 4th string chords should be studied only after you are comfortable with the others.' (Ch. 6, p. 187). Build min7 fluency first on the 6th and 5th strings in a single key before moving to 4th-string positions or modulating.

references.source: Ch. 6 — How to Study the Harmonic Fields

notes.narrative: 'Gsus9: means that we have chord tones: root, perfect 4th, minor 7th and major 9th. Gsus13: means that we have chord tones: root, perfect 4th, minor 7th and major 13th. (It can also mean: root, perfect 4th, minor 7th major 9th and major 13th).' (Ch. 4, p. 108). Always decode sus9/sus13 symbols by stripping the 3rd and substituting the 4th within the dominant-7 parent shape before adding the named extension.

Bruno prescribes a three-rule directional picking system applicable to any chord quality or melodic context: use a down-stroke when crossing to a higher string, an up-stroke when crossing to a lower string, and alternate strokes when staying on one string. As stated in Chapter 1 (p. 4): "When going to a higher string, use a down-stroke. When going to a lower string, use an up-stroke. When playing on one string, use alternate strokes."

Bruno justifies the directional picking system on economy-of-motion grounds applicable across all chord qualities and melodic lines: "I found one concept or rule that causes the pick to travel the least amount of distance" (Chapter 1, p. 4). The pick is always positioned where it next needs to be, eliminating wasted reverse travel.

Bruno prescribes a free-floating right hand for all picking contexts regardless of chord quality: "Do not touch the strings, bridge or any other part of the guitar with the fingers of your right hand" (Chapter 1, p. 5). This no-anchor posture — reinforced in Chapter 2 (p. 8–9) to include the pick guard — is a physical precondition for the directional system to work across any texture.

Bruno prescribes elbow-driven picking motion as a mechanical requirement for all strokes: "The right hand, wrist and elbow should always be relaxed and never tense or tight. The wrist should not move or tilt. The movement should come from the elbow" (Chapter 1, p. 5). Chapter 2 (p. 7) reinforces: "Practice keeping your wrist straight but not stiff. Remember: the movement is from the elbow."

Bruno prescribes practicing every exercise starting with both a down-stroke and an up-stroke, regardless of chord quality or texture: "I recommend that you practice all the exercises starting with both strokes. There should be only a very slight difference in sound" (Chapter 1, p. 6). This is restated for arpeggios (Chapter 5, p. 24) and string skipping (Chapter 6, p. 28).

Bruno prescribes a tempo range of MM 60–120 as the starting bracket for all exercises regardless of chord quality: "I recommend you practice these exercise at MM 60 to 120, then increase your speed from there" (Chapter 1, p. 6).

Bruno prohibits skipping around the book: "The exercises are designed to take the student from point A to Z. It is not a good idea to skip around in this book" (Chapter 1, p. 6). This applies globally regardless of the chord quality or technique the student wants to target.

Bruno prescribes strict muting for the in-between stroke across any adjacent-string double-stop: "This stroke is difficult to master. It involves going between two adjacent strings... Apply to any two adjacent strings using the double-stop of your choice. Do not let notes ring!" (Chapter 2, p. 10). The no-ringing requirement is equally in force for consecutive strokes (Chapter 3, p. 5).

Bruno prescribes rhythmic evenness as a prerequisite to tempo for consecutive-stroke drills: "It is necessary to play the above exercises evenly. At this stage, precision of the 8th notes is more important than speed" (Chapter 3, p. 5).

For repeating triplet arpeggio patterns across three adjacent strings (drill context only), Bruno prescribes breaking the alternation rule in favor of three consecutive down-strokes followed by three consecutive up-strokes: "use three 'down-strokes' followed by three 'up-strokes'. Apply to any three note chord on any three adjacent strings" (Chapter 3, p. 6). Bruno explicitly states: "when playing triplets with a repeating pattern such as a triad or some other pattern, it is better to break the rule."

The three-down / three-up triplet exception is scoped to drill technique only; in real melodic lines, strict alternation returns. Bruno states: "however, if I had to play a triplet phrase in the context of a line and not in an exercise, I would adhere to the rule" (Chapter 3, p. 6). Do not carry the consecutive-down triplet pattern into actual bebop phrase playing.

Bruno prescribes uniform application of the directional rule across all six major-scale fingerings (6V2, 5V2, 6V4, 5V4, 6H2, 5H2): "Below are the six basic fingerings for the major scales. This will give you an idea how the rule works on any scale or scale type passage" (Chapter 4, p. 9). String-crossing notation (asterisks) makes the higher/lower-string rule visible at every transition.

For arpeggio playing across any chord quality, Bruno prescribes articulation (note separation) as the primary challenge, not speed: "The difficulty with any arpeggio exercise, is keeping the notes from ringing. Articulatioin is more important han speed" (Chapter 5, p. 15).

Bruno designates the major triad arpeggio exercise as a foundational warm-up for developing note separation across all arpeggio work: "Major triad exercises: This makes a great warm-up exercise. It is very difficult to play with clean articulation. The result is well worth the time. This exercie alone will facilitate the separtion of notes with any phrase that contains an arpeggio or arpeggio fragment" (Chapter 5, p. 19).

Bruno proscribes treating sweep picking as a separate technique distinct from directional picking: "I have seen this referred to as sweep picking. I see no reason to make any distinction. Everything follows the rule: Higher string = 'down stroke' Lower string = 'up stroke'" (Chapter 5, p. 21). The directional rule subsumes what others call sweep picking.

For minor 11 arpeggios, Bruno prescribes a fingering that places notes on adjacent strings to enable consecutive same-direction strokes and thereby unlock sextuplet velocity: "Minor 11 arpeggios: Because of the fingering it is possible to play 6 notes in one beat (sextuplet). The fingering sets up the consecutive down and up strokes to go across four strings" (Chapter 5, p. 22). Saxophone players and pianists use phrases like this.

For minor 9th arpeggios, Bruno prescribes adjacent-string fingerings as the design principle that makes two-octave spans playable: "By using fingerings that place notes on adjacent strings, either higher or lower, these large two octave arpeggios become possible" (Chapter 5, p. 25). The fingering—not picking aggression—makes the speed possible (Chapter 5, p. 24).

When a rest separates phrases, Bruno licenses breaking the directional rule for the phrase start: "I have found when there is a rest between phrases, it is possible to break the rule and use whatever stroke you please to start the phrase" (Chapter 5, p. 24). This is the one codified exception to starting-stroke determination.

Bruno prescribes a hierarchy in which musical intent governs fingering and picking choices — the reverse is proscribed: "You have to be careful to NOT let the fingerboard make the music. The music comes from inside; the picking mechanism described in this book is designed to make it easier for the music to be realized" (Chapter 5, p. 25). This aesthetic axiom governs arpeggio vocabulary and melodic line construction equally.

Bruno prescribes applying the same directional rule to non-adjacent string skips: "When skipping strings the same rule applies: When going to a higher string use a down-stroke; when going to a lower string, use an up-stroke" (Chapter 6, p. 26). Applied across string pairs (4 and 2), (5 and 3), (6 and 4).

For the specific combination of up-stroke accent, in-between stroke, and string skip, Bruno pragmatically overrides his own directional rule and prescribes standard alternate picking: "I find that when playing exercises like this it is easier to play them with alternating 'down' - 'up' strokes" (Chapter 6, p. 30). This is the master's sanctioned personal exception for the hardest combined technique.

Bruno prescribes re-working picking patterns when a phrase is relocated to a different fingerboard position: "Here's the same phrase in the 7th position. This changes the picking considerably" (Chapter 7, p. 34). The same melodic idea in a different position may require a completely different stroke sequence.

In bebop phrase contexts, Bruno prescribes slurred triplets over fully picked triplets for horn-like articulation: "I prefer the 2nd example; it sounds more horn-like" (Chapter 7, p. 36). Slurred triplets must be mastered starting from both a down-stroke and an up-stroke (Chapter 7, p. 36).

Bruno prescribes thinking of articulations as inflections analogous to speech accent, realized by slurring: "These inflections are accomplished by slurring notes. Pick one note and play two notes" (Chapter 8, p. 38). Shifting the slur placement to a different beat within an identical phrase changes its inflection (Chapter 8, p. 40).

Bruno prescribes a long-short rhythmic gesture for bebop phrase endings: "make sure you play these last two notes, long, short" (Chapter 8, p. 39). This is a recurring cadential articulation applied in bebop phrase contexts.

Bruno prescribes that hammer-on and pull-off slurs must be placed on notes sharing a single string: "Try moving the slur over any two notes that are on the same string" (Chapter 8, p. 41). This is not a stylistic preference but a physical constraint of the technique.

Bruno prescribes treating slur placement as a creative decision the player must internalize, not a fixed score: "I've added a few slurs. Experiment adding your own slurs at different places" (Chapter 8, p. 42). The method provides exemplars but requires the student to self-direct slur experimentation.

Bruno licenses consecutive down-strokes as a sanctioned rule-break to emulate big-band horn-section accent emphasis: "I use consecutive down strokes to emphsis certain notes. This type picking is useful when you are trying to emulate a big band type phrase" (Chapter 9, p. 49). Slurs are presented as an equivalent alternative for the same phrase (Chapter 9, p. 50).

Bruno prescribes consecutive down-strokes as preferable to strict alternation when a rhythmic break separates notes: "When there is a rhythmic break between notes, you may want to use to down strokes" (Chapter 9, p. 50). This is the second codified exception to the alternation rule.

Bruno prescribes repetition over analysis as the meta-practice rule for internalizing the picking system: "The key is repetition. Do not overanalyze your right hand movements. After a short time, these strokes will become second nature" (Chapter 10, p. 51). Advanced players who have long-established habits will struggle most and must be patient with the process.

For a minor tonic chord (e.g., Dm as the I chord of a minor-key song), Bernstein prescribes the min6 voicing as the default -- the major 6th replaces the minor 7th -- unless the melody forces a different choice. Chapter 4, p.7.

When the melody explicitly plays the minor 7th of a minor tonic chord, Bernstein prescribes switching from min6 to a min7-type voicing -- specifically using quartal voicings to emphasize both the 7th and the 11th. As he taught: 'the melody plays the minor 7th of the chord, so he suggested playing more of a Dm7-type chord, possibly using quartal voicings to emphasize the 7th and the 11th.' Chapter 4, p.7.

Do not default to min6 when the melody note is the minor 7th of the chord -- the major 6th in a min6 voicing conflicts with the melody's b7. Bernstein's worked example: in a song where 'the melody plays the minor 7th of the chord,' the default Dm6 is overridden and Dm7 (quartal) is prescribed instead. Chapter 4, p.7.

For dom7 (and all chord qualities), Bernstein prescribes beginning with shell voicings -- root, third, and seventh only -- before any extensions or alterations. 'He stopped me and advised me to start with basic chords first--just the root, third, and seventh of each chord ... before making more informed decisions about incorporating chord extensions.' Chapter 5, p.9.

When a melody note risks being doubled by the bass (making it feel weak), Bernstein prescribes voicing the dominant as dom7#11 so the melody note becomes the #11 -- giving it a distinct harmonic 'outfit.' The worked example: 'he prefers to play a B7#11 chord, where the F becomes the #11, allowing the melody note to have a different outfit that enhances its impact and makes it feel good.' Chapter 5, p.9.

On dominant chords that resolve, Bernstein prescribes playing the ii-V a tritone up or down from the original -- 'like playing the related ii chord of the tritone substitution' -- to add harmonic interest during the resolution. Rhythmic placement within the bar is critical: 'playing it in the incorrect position within the bar can create a sense of awkwardness.' Chapter 7, p.13.

Bernstein prescribes a two-phase approach to comping across a tune: start with conservative shell voicings and signature runs only where reliable, then progressively explore extensions and substitutions from the third or fourth chorus onward, after the melody-chord relationships are mapped. 'After playing the third or fourth chorus, he would begin to explore further.' Chapter 4, p.6.

Do not play the root of the I (major tonic) chord. Demonstrated on 'Ornithology': Bernstein showed 'his preference for not playing the roots of the I (one) chords,' choosing instead an I69 derived from the V of that I, which 'adds a unique tension and flavor to the I (one) chord, not resolving the tension fully.' Chapter 6, p.12.

Instead of rooting the I chord, Bernstein prescribes voicing it as an I69 derived from the V chord of that I, deliberately leaving tension partially unresolved. This preserves forward momentum: 'avoiding an excessive emphasis on the I chord is a wonderful way to maintain a sense of forward momentum.' Chapter 6, p.12; Chapter 7, p.13.

Do not overemphasize the I (major tonic) chord. Bernstein teaches: 'when the I chord is overemphasized, it can give the impression that the song is being dragged or held back.' Forward momentum depends on treating the I with restraint -- under-resolve rather than settling. Chapter 7, p.13.

When the I (major tonic) chord is sustained over 2 or 4 measures, Bernstein prescribes actively exploring tension and resolution internally rather than holding a static voicing: 'it becomes essential to explore the play between harmonic tension and resolution within that chord.' Space and rhythm are also key tools within this internal motion. Chapter 6, p.12.

For minor chords as for all chord qualities, Bernstein prescribes starting with root, third, and seventh only before adding extensions. The student is directed to 'focus on listening to the melody and understanding the relationship between the basic chords and the melody before making more informed decisions about incorporating chord extensions.' Chapter 5, p.9.

O'Rourke classifies maj7 (and its extensions such as C6, CMaj9) within the Major harmonic family -- one of three families that every chord must belong to. The Major family is the I chord of the ii-V-I progression and drives the selection of major-cadence voicings from the chord dictionary. Chapter 2, p. 33.

For major chords, O'Rourke prescribes selecting a voicing from the Major ii-V-I chord collection, indexed by three inputs: the melody string (1st or 2nd), the chord type (major), and the melody note's interval relative to that chord. The collection covers every diatonic interval as the top note so any melody note can be harmonized: 'Which means: no matter which note is in the melody line, you can harmonize it by referring to the chord collection.' Chapter 2, p. 35; Chapter 4, p. 114.

O'Rourke prescribes dropping notes from major voicings in priority order when the full shape is unplayable: 'Intervals most commonly omitted include the 5th, the root (1st), the 11th, and the 9th. Note though that even the 3rd and the 7th can be omitted for more complex chords in certain situations as well.' The 5th is the first candidate to cut because its absence does not destroy the chord's essential character. Chapter 2, p. 79.

O'Rourke provides Major ii-V-I chord collections in two string-set variants -- string set 4321 and string set 5432 -- to match wherever the melody sits on the top two strings. The arranger selects the variant whose highest string corresponds to the string carrying the melody note at that moment. Chapter 8, pp. 266-269.

O'Rourke codifies the Tritone Substitution Rule universally: 'You can replace any chord with another whose root is a tritone away from the root of the original chord.' This applies to major chords, justified by shared guide tones (3rd and 7th swap places between the two chords). Chapter 7, p. 220.

O'Rourke prescribes that the I major chord can be replaced by the vi chord of the key: 'Rule: you can replace the I chord of a key with the vi chord of the key.' This is grounded in the relative-key relationship -- shared key signature means shared harmonic context. Chapter 7, p. 224.

O'Rourke prescribes a second major-to-minor substitution: 'Rule: you can substitute a major chord for chord iii of its key.' Together with the I-to-vi rule, this pair gives two licensed major-to-minor reharmonization moves for the I chord. Chapter 7, p. 225.

O'Rourke's fifth substitution rule applies to all chord qualities including major: 'Melodic common tone substitution rule: substitute any chord for another chord, as long as the new chord has a note in common with it that you use as the melody note on top.' The melody note on top of the replacement chord must be a note the original chord also contains. Chapter 7, p. 247.

O'Rourke prescribes that major (and all) chord voicings are placed on the first melody note of each bar and at chord changes, not on every melody note: 'In fact, less is more -- placing chords at key places "here and there" is easier on the hands and is usually more than enough to imply the harmony beneath the melody line.' Chapter 4, pp. 113, 122.

For solo-guitar arranging, O'Rourke prescribes the shell voicing as the irreducible minimum for major chords: root, 3rd, and 7th only, with the 5th dropped first: 'These are called shell voicings -- i.e. the "bare bones" of what you need to define the sound of the chord: the root, 3rd, and 7th.' The 6th may substitute for the 7th for a warmer, more resolved color. Chapter 5, pp. 145-147.

O'Rourke prescribes using substitutions and color additions to major chords only occasionally, not as a default density: 'Keeping things simple most of the time and just adding a substitution occasionally to brighten up the arrangement is the approach I find works best -- a good arrangement is all about subtlety!' Chapter 7, p. 222.

O'Rourke classifies min7 within the Minor harmonic family, specifically the 'm7 sub-family' (as distinct from the m7b5 sub-family): 'Minor: "m7" sub-family -- e.g. Cm7, Cm9, Cm13.' The m7 sub-family functions as the ii chord in the major ii-V-I progression and drives selection of major-cadence minor voicings. Chapter 2, pp. 33-34.

O'Rourke prescribes that min7 voicings (as the ii chord in a major context) are selected from the Major ii-V-I chord collections on string sets 4321 and 5432, indexed by melody string, chord type, and melody-note interval relative to that chord. The collection is structured so every diatonic interval can appear on top. Chapter 2, p. 35; Chapter 8, pp. 266-269.

For min7 voicings, O'Rourke prescribes the same omittable-notes priority as all chord types: drop the 5th first, then root, 11th, 9th, with 3rd and 7th as last-resort omissions in complex voicings. Chapter 2, p. 79.

O'Rourke prescribes using a min7 chord built from the 5th of any dominant chord as a substitution for that dominant: 'You can use a minor 7 chord from the 5th of any dominant chord (which is like using the iim7 that belongs to the dominant chord). For example: an F7 chord's 5th interval is C. So you could play Cm7 over F7 to get an interesting sound.' This is borrowed from Pat Martino's minor conversion concept. Chapter 7, p. 230.

For solo-guitar arranging, O'Rourke prescribes the shell voicing as the primitive for min7 chords: root, 3rd, and 7th only, built on the 6th string root, with the 5th omitted. Shell voicings are the structural backbone of O'Rourke's solo-guitar comping vocabulary. Chapter 5, pp. 145-147; Chapter 8, p. 280.

O'Rourke's back-cycling rule licenses inserting additional minor chords from the circle of fourths before the target chord: 'Back cycling substitution rule -- you can add chords to the chord progression of a song based on the "back cycle", i.e. the circle of fourths.' This applies universally including to minor chord slots. Chapter 7, p. 243.

O'Rourke's Tritone Substitution Rule applies universally to any chord: 'You can replace any chord with another whose root is a tritone away from the root of the original chord.' This includes min7 chords in the ii position of the ii-V-I, where a tritone-root replacement can produce interesting reharmonization color. Chapter 7, p. 220.

O'Rourke's melodic common-tone substitution rule applies to min7 chords: 'Substitute any chord for another chord, as long as the new chord has a note in common with it that you use as the melody note on top.' This is the rule that produces modern Rosenwinkel/Kreisberg-style colors and applies to any chord quality in the arrangement. Chapter 7, p. 247.

O'Rourke classifies min7b5 within the Minor harmonic family as the 'm7b5 sub-family' (distinct from the m7 sub-family): '"m7b5" sub-family -- e.g. Cm7b5, Cm11b5.' It functions as the ii chord in a minor ii-V-i cadence, and this sub-family distinction is what drives selection of minor-cadence voicings (with b5 and b9 alterations) over major-cadence voicings. Chapter 2, pp. 33-34.

O'Rourke prescribes selecting min7b5 voicings from the Minor ii-V-i chord collections (string set 4321 and string set 5432), which carry the b5 and b9 alterations characteristic of the minor cadence. The minor sub-family distinction specifically determines that the minor dictionary section -- not the major dictionary section -- is consulted. Chapter 2, pp. 34; Chapter 8, pp. 272-275.

For min7b5 voicings, O'Rourke prescribes the universal omittable-notes priority: 5th (already altered to b5), root, 11th, 9th first -- with 3rd and 7th as last-resort omissions in complex voicings. Chapter 2, p. 79.

O'Rourke classifies dom7 (and its extensions C9, C13) within the Dominant harmonic family, specifically the 'natural dominant' or '7' sub-family (as distinct from the altered '7alt' sub-family): '"7" or "natural dominant" sub-family -- e.g. C7, C9, C13.' The dominant family is the V chord in the ii-V-I progression. Chapter 2, pp. 33-34.

O'Rourke prescribes dominant chords as the primary target for adding extensions and tensions to produce the 'jazzy' sound in arrangements: 'The jazzy sound in arrangements usually comes from adding extensions and tensions to voicings -- particularly to dominant chords.' The chord dictionary dedicates a separate section to tensions and extensions on dominants as the method's color resource. Chapter 4, p. 127; Chapter 8, p. 278.

O'Rourke prescribes tritone substitution as the canonical dominant-chord reharmonization: 'Tritone substitution is the process of substituting one chord for another a tritone away,' justified because C7 and F#7 share guide tones -- 'The guide tones have essentially swapped places between these two chords.' This is called 'the most useful jazz substitution.' Chapter 7, pp. 214-220.

O'Rourke prescribes substituting the iim7 from the dominant's 5th in place of the dominant itself: 'You can use a minor 7 chord from the 5th of any dominant chord (which is like using the iim7 that belongs to the dominant chord). For example: an F7 chord's 5th interval is C. So you could play Cm7 over F7 to get an interesting sound.' Drawn from Pat Martino's minor conversion concept. Chapter 7, p. 230.

O'Rourke's back-cycling rule licenses adding dominant chords before the target chord by moving backward through the circle of fourths: 'Back cycling substitution rule -- you can add chords to the chord progression of a song based on the "back cycle", i.e. the circle of fourths.' Root movement by a 4th is described as 'the most common root movement in Western music.' Chapter 7, pp. 237-243.

For dominant voicings, O'Rourke prescribes the universal omittable-notes priority: 5th first, then root, 11th, 9th, with 3rd and 7th (the guide tones) as last-resort omissions only in complex voicings where their absence is contextually safe. Chapter 2, p. 79.

For solo-guitar arranging, O'Rourke prescribes the shell voicing as the irreducible minimum for dominant chords: root, 3rd, and 7th only, built on the 6th string root, derived from bar chords by dropping the 5th first. The 6th can substitute for the 7th for a warmer, more resolved color. Extensions are stacked from the shell voicing extensions catalog. Chapter 5, pp. 145-147; Chapter 8, pp. 280-281.

O'Rourke imposes an explicit restraint rule on all dominant substitutions: 'Keeping things simple most of the time and just adding a substitution occasionally to brighten up the arrangement is the approach I find works best -- a good arrangement is all about subtlety!' Substitutions are for occasional color, not density. Chapter 7, p. 222.

O'Rourke prescribes selecting natural dominant voicings from the Major ii-V-I chord collections (string sets 4321 and 5432), indexed by melody string, chord type (dominant), and melody-note interval relative to that chord. The natural dominant sub-family determines the major-cadence collection is the correct lookup source -- not the minor-cadence collection. Chapter 2, pp. 34-35; Chapter 8, pp. 266-269.

O'Rourke classifies altered dominants as the '7alt' sub-family within the Dominant harmonic family: '"7alt" or "altered dominant" sub-family -- e.g. C7(b9), C7(b13b9), C7(b5), C7alt.' The altered sub-family distinction specifically drives selection of minor-cadence ii-V-i voicings (with b5 and b9 alterations) rather than major-cadence voicings. Chapter 2, pp. 33-34.

O'Rourke prescribes that altered dominant voicings are drawn from the dedicated 'Tensions and Extensions on Dominant Chords' section of the chord dictionary (Chapter 8, p. 278) -- a separate catalog from the natural dominant voicings -- and from the minor ii-V-i collections on string sets 4321 and 5432, which carry the b5 and b9 alterations characteristic of altered dominants in minor cadences. Chapter 8, pp. 272-278.

O'Rourke identifies altered/extended dominants as the method's primary color resource: 'The jazzy sound in arrangements usually comes from adding extensions and tensions to voicings -- particularly to dominant chords.' Alterations such as b9, b13, and b5 are the specific tools for this color. The chapter-8 tensions-and-extensions dictionary section is the authorized lookup for these voicings. Chapter 4, p. 127; Chapter 8, p. 278.

O'Rourke includes dom7(b9) explicitly within the altered dominant sub-family: 'C7(b9)' is given as a canonical example of the '7alt' sub-family. Its selection from the minor ii-V-i dictionary sections (with the b9 alteration characteristic of minor cadences) distinguishes it from natural dominant voicings. Chapter 2, p. 34.

O'Rourke prescribes drawing dom7(b9) voicings from the Minor ii-V-i chord collections (string sets 4321 and 5432), which encode the b9 alteration characteristic of minor cadence dominants. The minor collection sections in Chapter 8 (pp. 272-275) are the authorized lookup source for this chord type. Chapter 8, pp. 272-275.

O'Rourke's Three Harmonic Families taxonomy places min-maj7 within the Minor family by chord quality. While not named explicitly as a named example in the taxonomy listing (p. 33), the minor sub-family structure (m7 and m7b5) and the minor ii-V-i collections accommodate it as part of the minor harmonic family context. O'Rourke does not address min-maj7 as a distinct chord type beyond this family placement. Chapter 2, pp. 33-34.

Baker places maj7 within the major-mode substitution family. Chapter 3 (p.9) states: 'any chord on a major mode can be used in place of the major triad,' explicitly listing Cma7 alongside Cma6 and Cma9 as interchangeable tonic-side options.

Baker teaches that Gma7 and Bmi7 are 'such close relatives that one can be used for the other at any time' (Chapter 10, p.41). Separately, Gma6 = Emi7 and Ama6 = Fmi7 are presented as the same chord shape under two names (Chapter 7, p.19); the student must 'learn both names of these chords in all keys.'

Cma7 is the prescribed tonic arrival chord in Cycle No. 1 (Chapter 7, p.26): the reharmonized progression lands on 'Cma7 Ebmi7' rather than a plain C major, establishing maj7 as the minimum tonic color in Baker's modern vocabulary.

Chapter 10 (p.34) states that 'Emi7 and Gma6 are the same (relatives), so it can be used as a major run. The same rule that applies to chords applies to runs.' A Bmi7 run substitutes freely for Gma7 in the final two bars of a blues head (Chapter 10, p.41).

Baker places min7 within the minor-mode substitution family. Chapter 3 (p.9) specifies: 'any minor chord can be used on the minor mode — Dmi6, Dmi7 and Dmi9 are adaptable, because they are all on the same mode.'

Chapter 4 (p.12) lays down the core rule: 'if you have a dominant 7 chord you can substitute its relative minor which is the 5th of the chord.' G7 is replaced by Dmi7; D7 is replaced by Ami7. Baker calls this the dominant-to-relative-minor substitution and it is the most frequently applied move in the book.

In Cycle No. 1 (Chapter 7, p.26) Baker prescribes pairing min7 with min6 in a descending two-chord cell: 'Replace C7 with Gmi7-Gmi6; Replace G7 with Dmi7-G13b9.' The min7 always precedes either a min6 resolution or a dom13b9 resolution.

Chapter 10 (p.34) prescribes min7 runs specifically at bars 9-10 of a blues: 'we use the V7 for one bar (D7) and the IV7 for one bar (C7), this allows you to use an Ami7 run for one bar and a Gmi7 run for one bar.' The min7 substitution applies equally to chord voicings and melodic runs.

Chapter 7 (p.19) establishes that Gma6 and Emi7 are the same chord shape — 'the same chord has a different name.' The student is instructed to 'learn both names of these chords in all keys,' making min7 identity context-dependent: the same voicing functions as either a minor ii chord or a major tonic surrogate.

Chapter 10 (p.34) prescribes a specific voice-leading chain: 'Whenever you have one or two bars of D7 going into G major, you may use an Ami7 run to a Cmi7 run which will blend right into a G major run.' The min7 (Ami7) initiates the chain, a b7-minor7 (Cmi7) passes through, and G major arrives — always altered at the V.

Chapter 5 (p.15) identifies the dominant as 'leading chord' for all connections, but min7 substitutes for it in dominant-to-minor and dominant-to-major contexts. Chapter 4 (p.12) confirms: 'most of the time when we have a seventh chord, we substitute minor chords in their place... Dmi7 to Dmi6, or Dmi7 to G13.'

Baker declares in Chapter 3 (p.9): 'With dominant chords there is no limit to what can be done.' The plain dom7 is the minimum entry point for an open-ended menu of substitutions and alterations; using an unadorned dom7 is acceptable only as a baseline, not as a destination.

Chapter 3 (p.9) enumerates the full substitution menu for any dom7: 'G13, G9, G7#5+9, G13#5+9, G7b5, G11, G13b9 and so on.' The student may choose any of these in place of a plain G7 depending on progression context.

Chapter 4 (p.12) states: 'The fifth of any dominant chord can be substituted in place of the Dominant itself.' For G7, the fifth is D, so Dmi7 (or Dmi7-Dmi6) replaces G7. Chapter 11 (p.42) reaffirms: 'The 5th of a dominant chord can be substituted in the dominant place, because they are closely related.'

Chapter 5 (p.15) calls the dominant 'the key to all of the other lessons' and 'the best possible way to connect one chord to another using the dominant as leading chord.' Baker categorizes all dominant usage into three connection types: dominant-to-dominant, dominant-to-minor, and dominant-to-major.

Chapter 3 (p.9) explicitly condemns the plain major triad as lacking 'enough color' and sounding 'corny.' By extension, an unaltered dom7 in a progression heading to a tonic is insufficient — Baker's standard requires at minimum an extension (9, 11, 13) or alteration (#5, b5, b9) to 'add color.'

Chapter 3 (p.9) warns: 'It all depends on how the chords are progressing. You just can't throw these chords in any place, they have to be part of some kind of progression.' Dominant substitutions from the extended menu are context-sensitive, not free-floating.

Chapter 10 (p.34) prescribes: 'when connecting a dominant chord to a major the dominant in most of the time altered, (G7#5+9 to Cma or G13b5+9 to Cma). By altering chords like this they blend together perfectly. This same thing applies to solo work.' G7#5+9 and G13b5+9 are the two canonical altered forms before a major tonic.

Chapter 7 (p.19) provides the diagram annotation: 'G7#5 Db9b5 - Root omitted Root omitted,' establishing that these two root-omitted shapes are identical. The student may label the same fingering as either G7#5 or Db9b5 depending on harmonic context, giving dom7alt a built-in tritone substitution identity.

Chapter 10 (p.34) explicitly extends the altered-dominant rule to solo work: 'This same thing applies to solo work.' Baker treats G7#5+9 and G13b5+9 as mandatory before tonic arrival regardless of whether the guitarist is comping or playing chord-melody.

Chapter 7 (p.26) places G13b9 as the resolution target in Cycle No. 1: 'Replace G7 with Dmi7-G13b9.' The b9 alteration is built into the prescribed ii-V cell — G13b9 is the specific dom7b9 form Baker recommends at the V before I in this cycle.

Chapter 3 (p.9) lists G13b9 within the extended dominant substitution menu alongside G13, G9, G7#5+9, G13#5+9, G7b5, and G11. G13b9 is available as a drop-in replacement for any plain G7 chord within an appropriate progression.

Chapter 7 (p.26) shows the aug7 (G+7) appearing in the 'Standard' progression (C7 / Fmi / G7 / G+7 / C) but being fully replaced in the 'New' version by a Dmi7-Dmi6 cell. Baker's prescription eliminates aug7 from modern usage in favor of the relative-minor substitution pair.

Baker includes a diminished run in the Chapter 9 exercise vocabulary (Lessons 27-31), grouping it with scale, minor, and dominant runs as a foundational solo building block; the run is transposed chromatically up and down the neck using identical fingering (p.30).

Chapter 3 (p.9) lists G13 as the first item in the extended dominant substitution menu: 'you could use G13, G9, G7#5+9...' G13 is Baker's go-to dominant extension — the least altered form in the menu and a direct substitute for any plain dom7.

Chapter 4 (p.12) shows G13 as an explicit resolution target within the ii-V cell: 'I may use Dmi7 to Dmi6, or Dmi7 to G13, or something like that.' G13 (unaltered) and G13b9 (altered) are both available endpoints for the Dmi7 lead-in depending on context.

Chapter 7 (p.26) shows 'G13b5b9' in the Cycle No. 1 reharmonization as a root-omitted dominant form. Baker's tritone equivalence principle (Chapter 7, p.19) applies to these 13-chord shapes as well, enabling the same root-omitted voicing to serve as either G13b5b9 or the enharmonic tritone substitute.

Chapter 3 (p.9) lists G9 as the second item in the extended dominant substitution menu: 'you could use G13, G9, G7#5+9...' G9 is available as a drop-in for any plain dom7 within an appropriate progression, representing the unaltered ninth extension of the dominant.

Chapter 3 (p.9) includes G11 in the extended dominant substitution menu: 'G13, G9, G7#5+9, G13#5+9, G7b5, G11, G13b9 and so on.' G11 is listed as one of the available dominant substitutes, though Baker offers no further specification of its voice-leading or placement within the excerpted material.

Chapter 3 (p.9) lists G7b5 within the extended dominant substitution menu. Chapter 7 (p.19) further identifies Db9b5 as the root-omitted tritone equivalent of G7#5 ('G7#5 Db9b5 - Root omitted Root omitted'), establishing dom7b5 as both a direct dominant substitute and a tritone substitution form.

Chapter 7 (p.26) shows 'Gmi7 C7b5' as a voice-leading pass within the Cycle No. 1 reharmonization of the Fmi bar. C7b5 (dom7b5) appears as a chromatic passing dominant resolving to Fmi7, distinct from its role as a tritone substitute, demonstrating dom7b5 in an inner-voice passing function.

Chapter 7 (p.19) establishes: 'When we are in one key a chord may be Gma7 while still in another key — the same chord has a different name, Emi7.' The specific two-name pairs given are Gma6 = Emi7 and Ama6 = Fmi7. The student must 'learn both names of these chords in all keys,' making maj6 a dual-identity voicing.

Chapter 3 (p.9) places Cma6 within the major-mode substitution family alongside Cma7 and Cma9: 'any chord on a major mode can be used in place of the major triad.' Chapter 10 (p.34) further confirms: 'Emi7 and Gma6 are the same (relatives), so it can be used as a major run.'

Chapter 3 (p.9) lists Cma9 as one of the three primary major-mode substitutes: 'any chord on a major mode can be used in place of the major triad,' explicitly naming Cma7, Cma6, and Cma9 as interchangeable tonic options. Cma9 is the most coloristically rich of the three.

Chapter 3 (p.9) includes Dmi9 in the minor-mode substitution family alongside Dmi6 and Dmi7: 'Dmi6, Dmi7 and Dmi9 are adaptable, because they are all on the same mode.' Dmi9 is available as a drop-in replacement for any minor chord in the appropriate modal context.

Chapter 7 (p.26) prescribes min6 as the second chord in the relative-minor substitution cell: 'Replace C7 with Gmi7-Gmi6; Replace G7 with Dmi7-G13b9.' The min7-to-min6 descent within the cell provides voice-leading motion (the seventh steps down to the sixth) before resolving to the next harmony.

Chapter 3 (p.9) places Dmi6 within the minor-mode substitution family: 'Dmi6, Dmi7 and Dmi9 are adaptable, because they are all on the same mode.' Chapter 4 (p.12) confirms: 'I may use Dmi7 to Dmi6,' showing min6 as the preferred minor resolution within the Dmi7 cell.

Van Eps establishes that all chords are frozen arpeggios: 'Arpeggios are broken chords--chords are frozen arpeggios.' (p.11, Chapter 1). The student must internalize each triad inversion as the residue of moving voices, not as a static grip.

For first inversion major triads, Van Eps prescribes that the middle note may be deleted without spoiling the chordal result: 'The upper and lower notes of first inversion triads are major and minor sixth intervals apart. The sixth makes a very powerful two note chord and because of this power, the middle notes can be deleted without spoiling the chordal result.' (p.19, Chapter 2). The two-note sixth frame alone carries the harmonic identity.

Van Eps defines first inversion with explicit voice placement: 'In the 1st inversion the tonic is on top... in the 2nd inversion the tonic is second... in the root voicing the tonic is the lowest note.' (p.23, Chapter 2). The student must track tonic position across all three inversions as the primary organizational principle.

When working with sixth intervals derived from triads, Van Eps prescribes: 'When working with sixths it is very important to identify the related first or second inversion triad.' (p.115, Chapter 5). Every sixth double-stop must be mentally anchored to its parent triad inversion.

Van Eps prescribes that the first inversion triad is harmonically present even when the middle voice is absent: 'A first inversion triad is inferred with the middle note deleted in the first half of each station, and a root position triad is present in arpeggio form in the middle to last half of each station.' (p.115, Chapter 5). The student should treat the suggested tone as harmonically real.

For any major triad inversion, Van Eps prescribes the super/sub voice-movement system: 'When any one of the voices in a triad is raised one step of the scale it is placed in super position. When it is lowered one step of the scale it is placed in sub position.' (p.160, Chapter 8). The named inversion is the origin; raising the middle voice of a first inversion major triad automatically produces a second inversion member.

Van Eps prescribes keeping the named inversion mentally active at all times during super/sub work: 'When working with the super and sub principle it is necessary to keep the named inversion in mind at all times because it is the origin; it is the original voicing that is going to produce others.' (p.160, Chapter 8). Losing the origin causes harmonic disorientation.

Van Eps prescribes treating every triad inversion as a generative center: 'SUPER AND SUB CONCEPT - All chords are centers - When voices in a chord are moved one step up or down in any scale the resulting change becomes another center.' (p.161, Chapter 8). Moving voices of a major triad by diatonic step produces new harmonic centers rather than mere embellishments.

Van Eps draws an explicit equivalence for first inversion major triads: 'First inversion triads with the upper voice motion sub are the exact same notation as root triads with the upper voice motion super.' (p.175, Chapter 9). The student should exploit this identity to navigate between inversion families without shifting position.

Van Eps prescribes including all root position voicings regardless of reach difficulty: 'In root triads most of the reaches are quite great. However, these voicings must be included no matter how impractical they may appear, because by design they belong to the family of basic triads.' (p.239, Chapter 10). No inversion may be omitted for convenience.

Van Eps prescribes that when the sustained notation cannot be fully fretted, compromise fingerings are acceptable only when the moving voice is detached: 'The difference between an original notation and a compromise fingering is noticeable harmonically when the tones are sustained, but when the moving voice is detached and sounded separately there is no notation difference.' (p.239, Chapter 10).

When two voices move over a sustained third in a major triad context, Van Eps prescribes sustaining the half note full value, but permits releasing it if the reach is too great: 'If at first some of the reaches are too great, it is permissible to treat the half note as though it were a quarter note--to let go of the half note after sounding the triad. However, endeavor to sustain the half note full value.' (p.249, Chapter 11).

Van Eps prescribes cycling all three major triad inversions in a fixed repeat order over an independent bass in blockout studies: 'When the three triad inversions are placed in a fixed uniform group that appears in exactly the same order over and over again, forming a pattern each measure or so thru the cycle, it is quite naturally termed a repeat order.' (p.290, Chapter 14). This systematizes voice-leading across the cycle of fifths.

Van Eps prescribes treating the bass line as entirely separate from the triad: 'Always think of the triad and bass as being separate isolated lines in an overall four note harmonic group of tones.' (p.273, Chapter 13). The major triad is a three-voice unit; the bass is a fourth independent voice that may contradict or color the triad's harmonic identity.

Van Eps prescribes practicing all triad inversion studies through the descending cycle of fifths rather than chromatically: 'Most of the studies in these books go through the keys employing the descending cycle of fifths (up a fourth or down a fifth) in preference to changing keys chromatically.' (p.18, Chapter 2). This is the master organizational principle for all inversion drilling.

Van Eps prescribes using implied tones to reduce voicing density while preserving harmonic identity: 'A very useful tool in harmonic voicing (for all instruments) is: the hint/suggestion of a tone. A note can be inferred but not actually sounded, yet its presence is felt to the point where it is almost heard.' (p.20, Chapter 2). Major triad voicings may omit inner voices when the outer frame and overtones supply the missing information.

When a major triad contains more notes than can be sounded simultaneously, Van Eps prescribes arpeggiating with delayed coupling: 'Another effective method to Experiment with in the illusionary art of compounding triads or any chords that contain more notes than can be sounded Simultaneously is by a delayed type of coupling--The ear will remember the first notes sounded and automatically couple them to the next notes thus forming an overall harmonic picture.' (p.21, Chapter 2).

Van Eps prescribes giving inner voices room to be heard within a major triad texture: 'Moving lines must have space. In order for an inner voice to be able to stand out in any harmonic situation it must be given room to be heard.' (p.17, Chapter 1). Voice density must be managed so that moving lines are not masked by sustained outer voices.

Van Eps prescribes a specific scale assignment per voice when voicing minor triads through inversions: 'Triads - 1st - 2nd And Root - Melodic minor up, middle voice - harmonic minor down, lower voice.' (p.66, Chapter 3). The upper moving line uses melodic minor ascending; the lower moving line uses harmonic minor descending.

Van Eps prescribes recognizing that minor mode inversion patterns cannot be directly mapped from major: 'The Minor Modes Can't Parallel the Major because of the Minor third interval--it is shortened by one semitone.' (p.159, Chapter 7). Minor triad inversions require independent study; the major inversion shapes do not transfer.

Van Eps prescribes employing all three minor triad inversions in blockout studies alongside major inversions: 'Triads, both major and minor are employed in the following blockouts; root, first and second inversions are used.' (p.288, Chapter 14). No inversion of the minor triad is optional; all must appear in the repeat-order cycling.

The super/sub principle applies equally to minor triads: Van Eps states 'Place in all keys - Major and both Minors - sustain the middle voice - reverse the direction of voice motion = open to closed.' (p.253, Chapter 11). Minor triad inversions must be drilled with the same super and sub voice movements as major triads, in both melodic and harmonic minor.

As with major triads, Van Eps prescribes treating the bass as a fourth independent voice beneath minor triads: 'The bass lines are completely independent of the triads. The bass line is an independent fourth voice.' (p.273, Chapter 13). A minor triad placed over an unrelated bass note is a legitimate four-voice harmonic unit, not an error.

Van Eps's fatigue-factor rule applies equally to minor triad voicings: 'Don't depress more strings than are being used because of the fatigue factor.' (p.8, Chapter 1). For minor triad inversions with wide string-set skips, only the active strings should be fretted.

Van Eps's prescription to explore nontraditional configurations applies to minor triads as well: 'Traditional configurations are well known; nontraditional configurations must be found, explored, analyzed, and well practiced.' (p.269, Chapter 13). Minor triad inversions in unconventional positions and string sets must be systematically located and practiced.

Van Eps prescribes using chromatic exercises through all four triad qualities as a scale-construction tool: 'By using these chromatic exercises in all their various forms, positions, and combinations, all scales Maj., Min., Dim., Aug. may be constructed.' (p.149, Chapter 7). The diminished triad is drilled as one of four chromatic exercise types, not merely as a passing sonority.

Van Eps prescribes the augmented triad as one of four chromatic exercise types for constructing all scales: 'By using these chromatic exercises in all their various forms, positions, and combinations, all scales Maj., Min., Dim., Aug. may be constructed.' (p.149, Chapter 7). Like the diminished triad, the augmented is treated as a structural building block of the chromatic vocabulary, not an ornamental chord.

Van Eps prescribes reading dominant 7th chord symbols as context-dependent rather than fixed: 'The G47 degrees 35 above is also an E diminished 9th--in other words the symbol for a chord depends on its use--its place in a progression etc.' (p.141, Chapter 7). A G dominant 7th voicing may be reinterpreted as an E diminished 9th depending on harmonic context; the student must be fluent in both readings.

Van Eps prescribes treating all small chords including dominant 7th configurations as harmonically multivalent: 'All small chords have second, third, fourth (etc) callings under varied harmonic conditions, positions and situations.' (p.276, Chapter 13). A dom7 voicing is not bound to its primary label; it must be learned in all its harmonic roles.

Van Eps prescribes deriving min7 chords from pure major triads via the major-makes-minor identity: 'The minor seventh chord has to contain the notes (open or closed) of one of the three pure major triads.' (p.276, Chapter 13). To voice a min7, locate the major triad embedded within it and treat that triad as the structural core; do not approach min7 as a four-note block independent of triad thinking.

Van Eps explicitly prescribes the major-makes-minor / minor-makes-major identity as the gateway to 7th chord voicing: 'The major seventh chord has to contain the notes of one of the pure minor triads--in other words, major makes minor, and minor makes major.' (p.276, Chapter 13). For min7, the student should identify which major triad (notes open or closed) supplies the chord's harmonic content.

Van Eps prescribes learning the diminished 9th (dim7 with added 9th) as an enharmonic reinterpretation of a dominant 7th voicing: 'The G47 degrees 35 above is also an E diminished 9th--in other words the symbol for a chord depends on its use--its place in a progression etc.' (p.141, Chapter 7). The same voicing that functions as G dominant 7 can be relabeled E diminished 9th; the student must know both names for the same fingerboard shape.

Van Eps prescribes the sixth interval as the primary two-note harmonic unit extracted from first inversion triads: 'The upper and lower notes of first inversion triads are major and minor sixth intervals apart. The sixth makes a very powerful two note chord and because of this power, the middle notes can be deleted without spoiling the chordal result.' (p.19, Chapter 2). Sixth chord voicings for guitar should be understood as first inversion triads with the middle voice omitted, not as independent four-note chords.

Van Eps prescribes expanding sixth intervals to tenths as a specific voice-leading move in upper-line motion studies: '6ths with upper line motion = 1-5-3-1--S-1-3-5- / Sixths opening up to tenths.' (p.115, Chapter 5). The sixth double-stop opens outward to a tenth by moving the upper voice up one diatonic step, generating a wider but harmonically related voicing.

Van Eps proscribes fretting strings not in use: 'Don't depress more strings than are being used because of the fatigue factor.' (p.8, Chapter 1). When voicing any major triad inversion, the fretting hand should contact only the strings that are sounding; extra pressure on muted strings creates physical tension that degrades multi-voice control.

Van Eps proscribes pre-placing fingers before the attack in articulated triad passages: 'Do not place fingers in position in advance--left and right hand attack must be together for best results in articulated situations.' (p.133, Chapter 6). For articulated major triad inversion lines, each finger lands precisely with the pick attack; anticipatory fretting destroys the clarity of voice separation.

Van Eps proscribes allowing notes to ring over each other in sixths-derived triad studies: 'the tones in each station must not be allowed to ring over each other, except when indicated by the ties.' (p.115, Chapter 5). In sixth-interval passages built from first inversion major triads, each station must be cleanly separated unless a tie is written; the harp-like ringing effect is explicitly rejected.

Van Eps proscribes four-note ringing in double-stop triad lines: 'the two notes in the moving line must not be heard ringing together, they must be very closely linked but not ring over each other. When properly executed just a trio of tones is heard, never four, unless a hold-over effect is desired.' (p.185, Chapter 9). The student must mute the previous note of the moving line before sounding the next, so that only three voices are audible at any moment.

Van Eps proscribes accepting wrong notes in triad inversion practice: 'Every wrong note plants the germ of a bad habit because the ear retains the sound of the mistake.' (p.163, Chapter 8). Accuracy in inversion drilling is non-negotiable; a single wrong pitch in a super/sub exercise corrupts the ear's map of the triad structure.

Van Eps prescribes actively searching for non-standard triad configurations rather than relying on familiar shapes: 'Traditional configurations are well known; nontraditional configurations must be found, explored, analyzed, and well practiced.' (p.269, Chapter 13). The major triad's full fingerboard vocabulary requires systematic exploration of unconventional inversion placements and string sets.

Van Eps prescribes treating a cycle-of-fifths bass line as harmonically neutral until triads are added: 'A bass line descending through the cycle of fifths is neutral--neither major or minor--until other voices are introduced.' (p.277, Chapter 13). When placing major triad inversions over a cycle-of-fifths bass, the student is making the quality determination; the bass itself implies nothing.

Van Eps prescribes accepting harmonic clashes as productive when major and minor triad inversions cycle independently over an unrelated bass: 'Blockouts by their very nature will of course contain harmonic clashes and dissonances of many kinds because of the recurring chord and bass misalignment, but these dissonances are very helpful and necessary at times.' (p.288, Chapter 14). The student must not resolve or avoid blockout dissonances; they are the point of the exercise.

Van Eps prescribes grouping certain key cycles by major thirds for concentrated inversion study: 'For example the keys of: C-Ab-E-Major-(only for the first cycle of course) / They are major thirds apart descending.' (p.293, Chapter 14). Major triad inversions in keys a major third apart share fingerboard geography and should be studied as a group.

Van Eps prescribes that the major seventh chord contains a pure minor triad as its structural content: 'The major seventh chord has to contain the notes of one of the pure minor triads--in other words, major makes minor, and minor makes major.' (p.276, Chapter 13). To voice a maj7, locate the minor triad embedded within it; the triad is the voicing's core.

The 4th scale degree on dominant 7th chords carries strong tension and must not be used as a phrase-ending note. Chapter 2 p.6 states: 'The 4th tone of major and dominant 7th chord/scales contains much tension and thus usually isn't emphasized. The 4th is usually treated as a passing tone between the 3rd and 5th scale tones. When in major or dominant keys don't end a phrase on the 4th.'

Although the 4th is forbidden as a phrase-ending note on dominant 7th, it is permissible as a passing tone in motion. Chapter 16 p.54 reiterates: 'Be careful how you treat the 4th tone. Use it as a passing tone.' Chapter 19 p.65 confirms: 'Be careful when playing the 4th note of major or dominant scales. Treat it as a passing tone.'

The preferred color tones that give the dominant 7th chord its characteristic brightness and interest are the 6th, major 7th, 9th, and raised 4th. Chapter 7 p.25 states: 'The pretty notes for major and dominant 7th chords/scales are the 6, 7, 9, and #4.'
