Strong beats should carry structurally important chord tones on dominant 7th chords. Chapter 8 p.28 specifies: 'Beats 1 and 3 seem to want roots, 3rd's, 5th's, 7th's and 9th's (b9's on dom.7th chords that resolve up a perfect fourth).'

The bebop dominant scale adds a chromatic passing tone (major 7th / B natural on C7) to the standard Mixolydian scale to create an 8-note pattern that aligns chord tones to strong beats. Chapter 8 p.28 defines it: 'The bebop scale contains one added tone to each of the four most used scales. Dominant 7th, C7 = C D E F G A Bb B C (The underlined tone is the added tone.)' Chapter 16 p.54 reinforces: 'BEBOP = C7 = C D E F G A Bb B C.'

The added chromatic tone (B natural) in the dominant bebop scale must never fall on a downbeat. Chapter 8 p.28 is explicit: 'Don't allow the B natural (added tone) to fall on a downbeat. The added tone must always come on the upbeat in order to give it the jazz sound we are used to hearing.' Chapter 16 p.54 echoes: 'Play B natural as a passing tone. It should always appear on an upbeat, never on the downbeat.'

The dominant bebop scale can function as a substitute for the minor ii chord in a ii-V progression, allowing one scale to cover both chords. Chapter 8 p.28 states: 'The dom.7th bebop scale can act as a substitute for the minor ii chord. Example: C7 bebop scale (C D E F G A Bb B C) could also be played over the G- chord and vice versa. The chords are interchangeable over the scale.'

When first learning to improvise over dominant 7th chords, target the 3rd and 7th as primary melodic destinations to internalize the harmony. Chapter 11 p.38 instructs: 'Improvise on the 3rd or 7th of each chord in order to get the sound and feel of the harmony in your mind.' Chapter 19 p.65 affirms: 'Emphasize 3rds and 7ths. They are the important notes in the dominant 7th scale/chord.'

Approaching the 3rd or 7th of a dominant chord by half step reinforces harmonic clarity and idiomatic bebop voice-leading. Chapter 11 p.39 prescribes: 'Lead into the 3rd or 7th by half step. This strengthens the harmony.'

The dominant 7th chord has a natural gravitational pull toward the chord a perfect fourth above, and improvised lines should reflect this tendency. Chapter 16 p.54 states: 'Dominants typically want to resolve to a chord up a perfect 4th (C7 wants to resolve to F, F-, F7 etc.).' Altered tones on dominant chords 'usually resolve by half-step to a scale or chord tone' of the target (chapter 16 p.54).

Chapter 16 p.54 lays out seven distinct scale options available over a dominant 7th chord, forming a complete palette from basic to highly altered: the basic Dominant 7th (Mixolydian), Bebop, Lydian Dominant (C7#4), Whole-Tone (C7+), Diminished (C7b9), Diminished Whole-Tone (C7+9), and Spanish/Jewish scale. Aebersold prescribes experimenting with all of them over the cycle-of-dominant-7ths track: 'The proper use of these various scales is part of what makes jazz so appealing.'

The Lydian Dominant scale (Mixolydian with a raised 4th) is a favored color option for dominant 7th chords. Chapter 16 p.54 specifies: 'LYDIAN DOM. = C7#4 = C D E F# G A Bb C The #4 was/is a favorite note.' The #4 also appears on the color-tone list: 'The pretty notes for major and dominant 7th chords/scales are the 6, 7, 9, and #4' (chapter 7 p.25).

The whole-tone scale is a six-note symmetrical option for augmented dominant chords (C7+). Chapter 16 p.54 describes: 'WHOLE-TONE = C7+ = C D E F# G# Bb C This scale only has 6 tones. It is a symmetrical scale used often in cartoon music and by DeBussy and Ravel.' Chapter 18 p.61 notes only two whole-tone scales exist, covering C7, E7, F7, G7, A7, and B7.

When a dominant 7th chord appears in a minor-key context, the Spanish or Jewish scale (equivalent to the harmonic minor built on the 4th) provides an idiomatic color option. Chapter 16 p.54 states: 'SPANISH or JEWISH SCALE = C7(b9) = C Db E F G Ab Bb C This scale is used often when playing in a minor key. It's the same as F harmonic minor.'

Aebersold mandates the Dorian mode as the default minor scale throughout the book. Chapter 2 p.7 states: 'Every minor scale employed on the record and in the musical examples is in the Dorian mode.' Chapter 15 p.53 further ranks the order of preference: 'I have found the order of preference to be Dorian, Bebop, Melodic, Blues, Pentatonic, and then any of the remaining Minor scale choices,' placing Dorian first and pure minor last.

Understanding the Dorian mode through its relationship to the major scale aids internalization and allows reuse of known fingerings. Chapter 2 p.7 explains: 'The minor scale (dorian) is really the same as a major scale whose root lies a whole step below the root of the dorian minor. Example: F- is the same as Eb major (3 flats).'

The tension-generating color tones most characteristic of minor chords/scales are the 4th, 6th, major 7th, and 9th. Chapter 7 p.25 specifies: 'The pretty notes for minor chords/scales are 4, 6, 7, and 9th. These notes create tension and should be used in the over-all tension-release process.'

The minor pentatonic scale rooted on the chord root is a direct and idiomatic scale choice for minor 7th chords. Chapter 10 p.32 instructs: 'Use the pentatonic scale (minor pentatonic) that corresponds to the root of the minor scale/chord. The first choice pentatonic scale for eight measures of F minor would be the F minor pentatonic scale.'

For minor 7th chords, targeting the 3rd and 7th of the chord is the foundational approach for conveying harmonic identity. Chapter 11 p.38 prescribes: 'Improvise on the 3rd or 7th of each chord in order to get the sound and feel of the harmony in your mind.'

The blues scale may be used over a minor 7th chord when that chord is sustained for two or more measures, providing a soulful alternative to the Dorian mode. Chapter 12 p.41 states: 'The blues scale can also be used over minor chords when the minor chord is sounded for 2, 4, 8, or 16 measures or longer.'

For extended minor sections, alternating between Dorian and the blues scale (both sharing the same root) is the recommended strategy for maintaining musical variety. Chapter 12 p.41 advises: 'When playing in minor tonalities you may choose to alternate between the dorian minor and the blues scale, both having the same root tone.'

The pure natural minor (Aeolian) scale is explicitly ranked last in preference among minor scale options and is rarely used. Chapter 15 p.53 states: 'In category #3, MINOR SCALE CHOICES, the PURE MINOR scale choice is not used very often. I have found the order of preference to be Dorian, Bebop, Melodic, Blues, Pentatonic, and then any of the remaining Minor scale choices.'

The minor ii chord and the dominant 7th bebop scale share enough common tones that they can substitute for each other in a ii-V context. Chapter 8 p.28 notes: 'The dom.7th bebop scale can act as a substitute for the minor ii chord.'

The 4th scale degree on major chords is a tension point that should not anchor phrase endings. Chapter 2 p.6 states: 'The 4th tone of major and dominant 7th chord/scales contains much tension and thus usually isn't emphasized. When in major or dominant keys don't end a phrase on the 4th.'

The most characteristic and beautiful color tones for major chords are the 6th, major 7th, 9th, and raised 4th (#4). Chapter 7 p.25 states: 'The pretty notes for major and dominant 7th chords/scales are the 6, 7, 9, and #4.'

The major bebop scale adds a chromatic passing tone (raised 5th / G# on C major) between the 5th and 6th degrees, creating an 8-note pattern that aligns chord tones to strong beats. Chapter 8 p.28 gives the formula: 'MAJOR = C D E F G G# A B C,' where G# is the added bebop chromatic tone.

The Lydian scale (major scale with a raised 4th) is a 'beautiful' and widely used alternative for major chord contexts. Chapter 10 p.32 describes: 'The scale on the third line contains a raised 4th (#4 = F#). This scale is the first cousin to a major scale and is called lydian; C D E F# G A B C. It's a beautiful sound and much used.'

Unlike major and dominant chords where the 4th must be avoided, on half-diminished chords the 4th may be freely emphasized. Chapter 2 p.6 explicitly contrasts: 'It's okay to emphasize the 4th when in minor or half-dim.'

A dedicated bebop half-diminished scale exists for this chord quality, with an added chromatic passing tone. Chapter 8 p.28 provides the formula: 'HALF-DIMINISHED = C Db Eb F Gb G Ab Bb C,' where the added tone (G natural) creates the 8-note bebop pattern.

Half-diminished 7th chords arise naturally within the minor scale context as one of its four diatonic seventh-chord types. Chapter 12 p.41 identifies: 'Major 7th, Minor 7th, Dominant 7th, and Half-Diminished 7th,' confirming the min7b5 as a native chord built on the sixth degree of the Dorian minor.

The dom7b9 chord symbol implies far more than a single alteration; the underlying diminished scale carries three altered tones. Chapter 15 p.53 clarifies: 'C7b9 appears to have only one altered tone (b9) but actually has three: b9, +9 and +4. The entire scale looks like this: Root, b9, +9, 3rd, +4, 5th, 6th, b7 & root (C, Db, D#, E, F#, G, A, Bb, C). This is called a Diminished scale.' Chapter 16 p.54 adds it has 8 tones and is symmetrical.

The flat-9 is specifically appropriate on strong beats (1 and 3) when the dominant 7th chord is resolving up a perfect fourth. Chapter 8 p.28 notes that strong beats want 'b9's on dom.7th chords that resolve up a perfect fourth.'

The dom7alt chord (C7+9) uses the Diminished Whole-Tone scale, also called Super Locrian or Altered Scale, which contains four altered tones creating maximum tension. Chapter 15 p.53 states: 'My chord symbol abbreviation is C7+9 and the name of this scale is Diminished Whole Tone sometimes called Super Locrian or Altered Scale.' Chapter 16 p.54 confirms: 'DIM. WHOLE-TONE = C7+9 = C Db Eb E F# G# Bb C This scale has four altered tones which help create tension.'

The chord symbol C7+9 implies only a raised 9th but the full altered scale contains b9, +4, and +5 as additional alterations. Chapter 15 p.53 states: 'Even though a C7+9 would appear to have only a raised 9th, it also has a b9, +4 & +5. The entire C7+9 scale would look like: Root, b9, +9, 3rd, +4, +5, b7 & root (C, Db, D#, E, F#, G#, Bb, C).'

The defining characteristic of the altered dominant scale is the presence of four altered tones (b9, +9, +4, +5) that collectively generate high harmonic tension. Chapter 16 p.54 states: 'DIM. WHOLE-TONE = C7+9 = C Db Eb E F# G# Bb C This scale has four altered tones which help create tension.'

The blues scale has a fixed six-note formula applicable to any root. Chapter 12 p.41 defines it: 'The blues scale consists of the following: Root, b3rd, 4th, #4th, 5th and b7th. EXAMPLE: F blues Scale F, Ab, Bb, B, C, Eb, F.'

The blues scale should be deployed as fragments and licks rather than played straight up or down as a scalar run. Chapter 12 p.41 states: 'This scale sounds strange when played straight up or down. Jazz players usually play bits and pieces of the scale or make up licks utilizing certain notes of the scale.'

The blues scale is a powerful color device but must not be overused; it should be balanced against regular scale usage. Chapter 12 p.41 explicitly warns: 'Don't run it in the ground by overuse!' Chapter 19 p.65 echoes: 'Experiment with playing the corresponding blues scale. This will give a down-home bluesy sound but may become tiring if you don't also use the regular scales for variety.'

The blues scale's characteristic clash with the underlying harmony is not a flaw but the source of its idiomatic sound. Chapter 11 p.39 explains: 'The notes of the blues scale often clash with the given harmony, but that is what makes it sound like the blues!'

The blues scale carries a specific and bounded expressive character: funky, earthy, soulful. Chapter 12 p.41 states: 'The blues scale is used to convey a Funky, Down-Home, Earthy or Blusey sound/feel.'

Once the core six-note blues scale is mastered, additional tones may be incorporated to expand its harmonic variety. Chapter 12 p.41 advises: 'After you become familiar with the blues scale as I have it listed, you may want to add tones to the scale which give the scale sound more variety.'

The blues scale functions as a horizontal color overlay applicable across both dominant 7th and minor 7th chords rather than being locked to a single chord quality. Chapter 11 p.39 states it 'can, of course, be played at any time during the chorus,' and chapter 12 p.41 specifies it 'can also be used over minor chords when the minor chord is sounded for 2, 4, 8, or 16 measures or longer.'

Baker treats the dominant 7th as the most active chord of the tonality — 'the V of a chord demands resolution, the I is final' — and as the gravitational center to which all chord cycles must eventually arrive before resolving to I. Chapter 8, p. 11.

notes.narrative: Baker prescribes treating dom7 as the floor of a range of Upper Partial alterations: 'The dominant chord can be the dominant 7th, 9th, 11th, aug. 11th or 13th. The 5th or the 9th can be Flatted, nevertheless, these are still the Upper Partials of the dominant chord.' All extended dominant forms share the resolution function of the plain dom7. Chapter 10, p. 14.

references.source: Baker, Mickey - Complete Course in Jazz Guitar, Book 2

notes.narrative: Baker prescribes Forced Harmony — 'adding chords via progressions that move away from, then lead back into the tonic' — as the technique for keeping dom7 contexts active rather than static. When a passage would sit on a dominant chord as written, insert progressions that depart and return rather than sustaining the chord unchanged. Chapter 10, p. 14.

references.source: Baker, Mickey - Complete Course in Jazz Guitar, Book 2

notes.narrative: Baker establishes that 'the II chord can be readily substituted for the V,' permitting the supertonic chord to replace the dominant in a cycle provided the substituted chord still ultimately resolves to tonic. This makes dom7's substitution role bidirectional: it can receive the II or be displaced by it. Chapter 10, p. 14; Chapter 9, p. 12.

references.source: Baker, Mickey - Complete Course in Jazz Guitar, Book 2
Baker, Mickey - Complete Course in Jazz Guitar, Book 2

notes.narrative: Baker prescribes using the dominant as the structural pivot of the Authentic Cadence: introductions stop on V before approaching the song's first chord, while endings 'approach the V and move on to the I, which is the final statement.' The dom7 is thus the obligatory penultimate chord in both cadential contexts. Chapter 12, p. 20.

references.source: Baker, Mickey - Complete Course in Jazz Guitar, Book 2

notes.narrative: Baker classifies dom9 as an Upper Partial form of the dominant — one of the extensions produced by building above the 7th — with the same tonic-resolution function as plain dom7. The 9th may be natural or flatted (dom7b9); both remain members of the Upper Partials family and resolve to I. Chapter 10, p. 14.

references.source: Baker, Mickey - Complete Course in Jazz Guitar, Book 2

notes.narrative: Baker enumerates the 11th and augmented 11th as explicit members of the dominant's Upper Partials family: 'The dominant chord can be the dominant 7th, 9th, 11th, aug. 11th or 13th.' Dom11 and dom7#11 share the same resolution function and are treated as color variants, not structural departures. Chapter 10, p. 14.

references.source: Baker, Mickey - Complete Course in Jazz Guitar, Book 2

notes.narrative: Baker lists the 13th as the outermost Upper Partial of the dominant chord. G13b9 appears by name in the performance solo 'Just Bobi' (Chapter 29) and as the chord played over a G pedal in C Major at the Cadence Break (Chapter 22, p. 37: 'a Dm9 and a G13b9 chord play'). It resolves to the tonic on the same functional basis as all other dominant extensions. Chapter 10, p. 14; Chapter 22, p. 37.

references.source: Baker, Mickey - Complete Course in Jazz Guitar, Book 2
Baker, Mickey - Complete Course in Jazz Guitar, Book 2

notes.narrative: Baker teaches that 'they aren't diminished chords at all when used in this respect — they are the Upper tones to a diminished or flatted 9th chord.' A G7b9 with root omitted is presented side-by-side with B diminished (Exercises 51a and 51b) to prove harmonic equivalence: the dom7b9 shell is the conceptual parent, and the dim7 is its rootless upper structure. Chapter 21, p. 34.

references.source: Baker, Mickey - Complete Course in Jazz Guitar, Book 2

notes.narrative: Baker prescribes G13b9 as one of the specific chord variations played above a G pedal tone in the key of C Major: 'In exercise 56 … a Dm9 and a G13b9 chord play. This is the most popular form of Pedal Point.' The b9 coloring is explicitly named as the preferred upper-voice quality in this context. Chapter 22, p. 37.

references.source: Baker, Mickey - Complete Course in Jazz Guitar, Book 2

notes.narrative: Baker prescribes the minor 9th as the starting point of the method's core modern voice-leading move: 'Each chord is moving from a minor ninth to a minor sixth chord, via passing tones.' The min9 is the departure chord; the min6 is the goal. Both the minor and major forms share this resolution structure, with mode as their only difference. Chapter 4, p. 7; Chapter 5, p. 8.

references.source: Baker, Mickey - Complete Course in Jazz Guitar, Book 2
Baker, Mickey - Complete Course in Jazz Guitar, Book 2

notes.narrative: Baker prescribes opening chord-and-song-form exercises with the minor 9th and closing with the minor 6th: 'In both cases you are starting with the major or minor 9th and closing with the major or minor 6th.' The min9 is the structural opener; students practice this motion applied to well-known standard tunes. Chapter 7, p. 10.

references.source: Baker, Mickey - Complete Course in Jazz Guitar, Book 2

notes.narrative: Baker names Dm9 as one of the two specific chord variations played over a G pedal in C Major: 'In exercise 56 … a Dm9 and a G13b9 chord play. This is the most popular form of Pedal Point.' The min9 thus functions as the predominant color voice above the pedal fifth. Chapter 22, p. 37.

references.source: Baker, Mickey - Complete Course in Jazz Guitar, Book 2

notes.narrative: Baker prescribes the minor 6th as the resolution target of the minor ninth via passing tones — 'chord 1, through use of passing tones, resolves into chord 15 … moving from a minor ninth to a minor sixth chord, via passing tones.' The passing tones (marked 'P' in diagrams) are the voice-leading mechanism, and min6 is the harmonic goal of the minor-mode modern progression. Chapter 4, p. 7.

references.source: Baker, Mickey - Complete Course in Jazz Guitar, Book 2

notes.narrative: Baker prescribes the minor 6th as the closing chord in song-form exercises: 'you are starting with the major or minor 9th and closing with the major or minor 6th.' The min6 provides the point of rest after the min9 departure. Chapter 7, p. 10.

references.source: Baker, Mickey - Complete Course in Jazz Guitar, Book 2

notes.narrative: Baker treats the major 9th as the parallel major-mode departure chord: 'Chords 3 and 4 are resolving into chords 16 and 17. Each chord is moving from a major ninth via passing tones, to a major sixth. The only difference in these two forms is the mode.' The maj9 opens the major-mode modern progression exactly as min9 opens its minor counterpart. Chapter 4, p. 7.

references.source: Baker, Mickey - Complete Course in Jazz Guitar, Book 2

notes.narrative: Baker prescribes the major 9th as the opening chord in major-mode song-form exercises, with the major 6th as its resolution: 'In both cases you are starting with the major or minor 9th and closing with the major or minor 6th.' Applied to standard tunes in Chapter 7, p. 10.

references.source: Baker, Mickey - Complete Course in Jazz Guitar, Book 2

notes.narrative: Baker prescribes the major 6th as the tonic resolution of the major ninth in modern progressions. It is the harmonic goal reached via passing tones from maj9, replacing the simpler dominant-to-tonic arrival of standard progressions: 'moving from a major ninth via passing tones, to a major sixth.' Chapter 4, p. 7; Chapter 5, p. 8.

notes.narrative: Baker establishes that 'the C6 chord and the Am7 chord have the same tones. They are called relatives for this reason.' The major 6th chord is thus enharmonically equivalent to the minor 7th built on its 6th degree — a relative substitution that underpins the method's chord-substitution vocabulary. Chapter 9, p. 12.

references.source: Baker, Mickey - Complete Course in Jazz Guitar, Book 2

notes.narrative: Baker teaches that Am7 and C6 share identical tones — 'They are called relatives for this reason' — making min7 a direct substitute for its relative major 6th. Baker also notes that 'the three tones that form the Dm chord are the upper three tones of the G9 chord,' extending the relative-chord concept to upper-voice extraction from dominant extensions. Chapter 9, p. 12.

references.source: Baker, Mickey - Complete Course in Jazz Guitar, Book 2

notes.narrative: Baker prescribes the minor II chord as the preparatory chord before V in the I-II-V-I cycle, the progression 'in which we are most interested.' The II chord may be inserted before any dominant-to-tonic movement: 'it is possible to use the II chord instead of the V and resolve into the V from the II.' Min7 built on the second degree is the standard color for this role. Chapter 8, p. 11; Chapter 9, p. 12.

references.source: Baker, Mickey - Complete Course in Jazz Guitar, Book 2
Baker, Mickey - Complete Course in Jazz Guitar, Book 2

notes.narrative: Baker prescribes that the II chord — like the dominant — carries its own Upper Partials: 'With the II chord of the scale the same principal applies, you have the 6th, 7th, 9th, 11th, and 13th. Any of these forms of the II chord can be used to resolve into the V which in turn resolves into the tonic.' The min7 is the base; min9, min11, min13, and min6 are all valid superstructures for the II-chord role. Chapter 10, p. 14.

references.source: Baker, Mickey - Complete Course in Jazz Guitar, Book 2

notes.narrative: Baker teaches that diminished 7th chords functioning as dominants 'aren't diminished chords at all … they are the Upper tones to a diminished or flatted 9th chord.' He presents G7b9 with root omitted (Ex. 51a) beside B diminished (Ex. 51b) and instructs students to 'analyze the two chords' — proving that the dim7 is a rootless dom7b9. Chapter 21, p. 34.

references.source: Baker, Mickey - Complete Course in Jazz Guitar, Book 2

notes.narrative: Baker prescribes that the diminished chord may replace the dominant in a V-I resolution: 'notice how the diminished chord instead of the dominant, resolves into the tonic. This is another form of the Altered chord.' Exercise 52 demonstrates the move extracted from a prior exercise, and the caption in Exercise 51 labels it 'the equivalent to the V - I Resolution.' Chapter 21, p. 34-35.

references.source: Baker, Mickey - Complete Course in Jazz Guitar, Book 2

notes.narrative: Baker designates the diminished 7th as the emblematic vehicle of Symmetric Harmony: 'a diminished 7th chord which moves freely up and down the finger board in minor thirds … A diminished chord is built on a succession of minor thirds … each tone in the chord is actually the root or the tonic.' Because all four inversions share the same pitch classes, the dim7 is the purest expression of the 4-tonic symmetric division. Chapter 13, p. 21.

references.source: Baker, Mickey - Complete Course in Jazz Guitar, Book 2

notes.narrative: Baker prescribes moving the diminished 7th chord shape up or down the fingerboard in minor thirds as the fundamental Symmetric Cycle motion: 'if you play a diminished chord on the guitar and move it up a minor third, the same tones will appear but in a different arrangement.' The T1-T4 notation system labels each position. Chapter 13, p. 21; Chapter 14, p. 22.

Baker, Mickey - Complete Course in Jazz Guitar, Book 2

notes.narrative: Baker prescribes the diminished chord fragment — glissandoing in minor thirds — as a viable Symmetric Cycle ending device: 'go back to lesson 11, exercise 25A. In the second bar the last two beats are diminished, notice this chord glissandos up in minor thirds.' Partial chord fragments of dim7 execute the same directional motion as full voicings. Chapter 15, p. 24.

references.source: Baker, Mickey - Complete Course in Jazz Guitar, Book 2

notes.narrative: Baker notes that in chord-melody arranging, non-standard diminished fingerings are legitimate: 'in the 5th bar of exercise 49, there is a D Diminished chord which is not a standard fingering. However, it does fit well into the pattern used.' Students must invent dim7 voicings that fit the melodic line even when no familiar shape is available. Chapter 20, p. 33.

notes.narrative: Baker teaches that augmented chords 'may be used in a similar manner' to diminished 7th substitutes for the dominant: 'Augmented chords may be used in a similar manner. See Exercise 53.' Exercise 53 demonstrates the augmented chord resolving directly to the tonic as a V-I equivalent — a parallel to the dim7 substitution established earlier in Chapter 21. Chapter 21, p. 34.

references.source: Baker, Mickey - Complete Course in Jazz Guitar, Book 2

notes.narrative: Baker defines the aug7 by extending the augmented triad: 'By adding a 7th to the Augmented chord you get still another sound (See Exercise 43).' He prescribes its use as a color device: 'many chords are used that don't appear in the original chord structure of a song. They are used to add color and originality.' Chapter 18, p. 27.

notes.narrative: Baker prescribes the augmented triad (and by extension aug7) as the vehicle for Augmented Cycles: 'Divide the 12 tone scale in three equal parts and you get three tonics, T. 1, 2, and 3. Exercise 40 demonstrates the Augmented chord in a Symetric Cycle.' Major-third transposition of aug7 reproduces the same pitch-class set, making it the 3-tonic symmetric analog to the dim7's 4-tonic cycle. Chapter 17, p. 26.

references.source: Baker, Mickey - Complete Course in Jazz Guitar, Book 2

notes.narrative: Baker establishes the governing rule for all substitution and elaboration work: 'no matter how many chords you add to the cycle, they should eventually reach the dominant and from there resolve into the tonic.' The dom7 (V) is the mandatory penultimate target regardless of how many chords are inserted into the cycle. Chapter 9, p. 13.

references.source: Baker, Mickey - Complete Course in Jazz Guitar, Book 2

notes.narrative: Baker uses the major 6th as a practical tonic-I chord form throughout the method: the I-V-I skeleton has 'one bar of C, two bars of G7, and one bar of C' elaborated by substitution, and the C major tonal center typically manifests as a 6th or 9th chord in modern voice-leading rather than as a plain triad. The maj6 is the resting-point arrival after V resolves. Chapter 9, p. 12; Chapter 7, p. 10.

Baker, Mickey - Complete Course in Jazz Guitar, Book 2

notes.narrative: Baker treats the minor 6th as the parallel resting point for minor-mode tonic arrival — the destination after min9 resolves via passing tones. The two forms (min6 and maj6) are the modern tonic-I sonorities that replace the plain triad in upper-partial playing. Chapter 4, p. 7; Chapter 5, p. 8.

Baker, Mickey - Complete Course in Jazz Guitar, Book 2

notes.narrative: Baker grants the player explicit license to replace written dom7 changes with altered or extended dominant substitutes when building chord-melody solos: 'you use the ideas and musical sounds that sound best to you rather than the ideas and chord cycles that were originally written for the song.' The player's ear, not the chart, governs which dominant form is used. Chapter 10, p. 14.

references.source: Baker, Mickey - Complete Course in Jazz Guitar, Book 2

notes.narrative: Baker prescribes that introductions stop on the dominant without resolving: 'the introduction stops on the V (Example 29). From this point you approach the first chord of the song.' The dom7 is left hanging as a springboard into the song's first chord, while endings push through V to I. Chapter 12, p. 20.

references.source: Baker, Mickey - Complete Course in Jazz Guitar, Book 2

notes.narrative: Baker prescribes that any chord — including min9 — can be placed into a Symmetric Cycle: 'Any chord can be played in a Symetric Cycle. Take any of your favorite chords, start them in a low position on your guitar and move them up in minor thirds.' The min9 shapes from the chord-form vocabulary are explicitly offered as candidates for symmetric transposition. Chapter 14, p. 22.

references.source: Baker, Mickey - Complete Course in Jazz Guitar, Book 2

notes.narrative: Baker specifies G13b9 by name as the dominant-quality chord played above the G pedal tone in C Major: 'a Dm9 and a G13b9 chord play. This is the most popular form of Pedal Point.' The dom13 with b9 alteration is the preferred dominant color above a pedal fifth in this configuration. Chapter 22, p. 37.

references.source: Baker, Mickey - Complete Course in Jazz Guitar, Book 2

notes.narrative: Cmaj7 appears by name in the chord symbols of the closing solo 'Just Bobi' (Chapter 29), alongside Cmaj6 and Cmaj9, as a tonic-I voicing in chord-melody performance context. Baker's use of maj7 alongside the 6th and 9th forms demonstrates that all three are interchangeable tonic colors in an Upper Partial arrangement. Chapter 29 (performance solo).

references.source: Baker, Mickey - Complete Course in Jazz Guitar, Book 2

notes.narrative: Cmaj9 appears by name in 'Just Bobi' (Chapter 29) as a tonic-I color alongside Cmaj7 and Cmaj6, demonstrating that the maj9 is a valid tonic arrival voicing in Baker's chord-melody vocabulary — consistent with the maj9-to-maj6 voice-leading rule taught throughout the method. Chapter 29 (performance solo).

references.source: Baker, Mickey - Complete Course in Jazz Guitar, Book 2

notes.narrative: Gm6 appears by name in 'Just Bobi' (Chapter 29) as a minor-color tonic or subdominant voicing in chord-melody context. Baker's inclusion of the min6 in performance solos confirms it as a usable Upper Partial form in arrangement, not merely a resolution target in exercises. Chapter 29 (performance solo).

references.source: Baker, Mickey - Complete Course in Jazz Guitar, Book 2

notes.narrative: Fm9 appears by name in 'Just Bobi' (Chapter 29), demonstrating that the min9 is used as an active harmonic color in chord-melody performance — not only as a departure point in voice-leading exercises but as a sustained voicing in arrangement. Chapter 29 (performance solo).

references.source: Baker, Mickey - Complete Course in Jazz Guitar, Book 2

notes.narrative: Baker mandates retrograde practice of all Symmetric Cycle exercises: 'Play the exercises below backwards, starting with T1 then 4, 3, 2 and back to the 1.' The dim7 symmetric cycle must be mastered in both ascending and descending directions to build complete fingerboard facility. Chapter 14, p. 23.

references.source: Baker, Mickey - Complete Course in Jazz Guitar, Book 2

notes.narrative: Baker prescribes a concrete directional rule for dim7 glissando endings: 'If the last chord ends high on the finger board, move it down in minor thirds, if it ends low, move it up.' This direction-from-register rule applies when replacing a final chord with a Symmetric Cycle in introductions and endings. Chapter 15, p. 24.

references.source: Baker, Mickey - Complete Course in Jazz Guitar, Book 2

notes.narrative: Baker prescribes that the Cadence Break — 'the music relaxes for one or two bars' at phrase endings — may be filled with Symmetric Cycles, Pedal Point, or original chord progressions. Dominant-quality chords (such as G13b9 over a G pedal) are the canonical harmonization above the pedal fifth at these structural pauses. Chapter 22, pp. 36-37.

references.source: Baker, Mickey - Complete Course in Jazz Guitar, Book 2

notes.narrative: Baker establishes that even the tonic major 6th chord must be subordinated or omitted when it conflicts with the melody in chord-melody arranging: 'pay strict attention to how chords are forced against the melody and, at some points, even dropped for a better melodic line.' Melody priority overrides harmonic completeness for all chord qualities including the tonic. Chapter 26, p. 42.

references.source: Baker, Mickey - Complete Course in Jazz Guitar, Book 2

notes.narrative: Baker prescribes that when a dominant voicing is physically awkward in its notated position, the player should 'move them up to a higher chord' rather than force the fingering. This position-flexibility rule applies to all chord forms including dominant voicings and reflects the method's pragmatic fingering philosophy. Chapter 1, p. 4.

references.source: Baker, Mickey - Complete Course in Jazz Guitar, Book 2

notes.narrative: Baker prescribes passing tones as the obligatory mechanism for moving from min9 to min6: '"R" is for Root, "P" is for Passing tone.' Chord diagrams throughout Chapters 4 and 5 mark each passing-tone note explicitly, and students are instructed to identify root vs. passing-tone status for every note in every voicing as the core analytical exercise. Chapter 4, p. 7.

references.source: Baker, Mickey - Complete Course in Jazz Guitar, Book 2

notes.narrative: Baker prescribes extracting only the first (lowest) note of each arpeggiated maj9 or similar chord to form an independent counter-melody: 'in exercise 49 all the chords are played arpeggio but the first note of each chord is the most important. It forms a melodic line at the base of the chord and gives the whole example originality.' Chapter 20, p. 33.

references.source: Baker, Mickey - Complete Course in Jazz Guitar, Book 2

notes.narrative: Baker prescribes the minor II chord (min7) as part of the rhythmic chord-and-melody background texture in small-combo settings: 'This is Rhythmic Chord and Melody Playing. It deals with background rather than melody … The guitar plays fill-ins and fragments of melody in the background.' Min7 shapes cycle through the II role while a vocalist or solo instrument carries the melody. Chapter 19, p. 28.

references.source: Baker, Mickey - Complete Course in Jazz Guitar, Book 2

notes.narrative: Baker establishes that in Symmetric Harmony 'every chord you play is, in actuality, the tonic. There can be as many tonics as you desire.' This principle applies to dom7b9 and all other chord qualities used in symmetric contexts — none has a fixed dominant or subdominant role; each is treated as a temporary tonic. Chapter 13, p. 21.

references.source: Baker, Mickey - Complete Course in Jazz Guitar, Book 2

notes.narrative: Baker prescribes expanding the 3-tonic Augmented Cycle to six tonics by inserting intermediate chords: 'exercise 41 is similar to exercise 40, however, now we have six tonics, the additional tonics having been forced into the cycle.' The aug7 framework can thus accommodate up to 12 tonics via full Symmetric Harmony with parallel motion. Chapter 17, p. 26.

references.source: Baker, Mickey - Complete Course in Jazz Guitar, Book 2

notes.narrative: Baker prescribes that in ensemble Pedal Point settings the guitar (or piano) carries dominant-quality chord variations above the bass's sustained pedal tone: 'the bass plays the Pedal Point while the piano or guitar plays the chord variations.' The dom7/dom13 family supplies the upper chord voices in this three-layer texture. Chapter 24, p. 40.

references.source: Baker, Mickey - Complete Course in Jazz Guitar, Book 2

notes.narrative: Baker prescribes that the minor II chord's Upper Partials — including the min9 extension — are all valid choices for resolving into V: 'you have the 6th, 7th, 9th, 11th, and 13th. Any of these forms of the II chord can be used to resolve into the V.' Min9 is the most frequently cited II-chord quality in exercises. Chapter 10, p. 14.

references.source: Baker, Mickey - Complete Course in Jazz Guitar, Book 2

notes.narrative: Benson assigns maj7 (and its enharmonic companions Em7 and Am7) to the Root/Tonic region -- the region of rest -- in major keys. "Root Region Chords (Tonic): Cmaj7 (I), Em7 (IIIm), Am7 (VIm)." Any maj7 chord may therefore be freely substituted by any other Root-region chord. Chapter 1, p. 1.

Benson catalogues the full palette of available voicing tensions over a major 7th chord: Cmaj7, Cmaj7(9), C6, C6(9), Cmaj7(#11), C6(#11), C6(9)#11, Cmaj7(6), Cmaj7(6)9. The player should select among these colours according to what the melody permits during comping. Chapter 1, p. 2.

Over a Cmaj7 chord (or any chord belonging to the major scale), Benson prescribes using G major pentatonic quartal voicings, C major pentatonic quartal voicings, or a mixture of both. The F major pentatonic is excluded because it contains the avoid note F. Chapter 6, p. 210.

For a lydian colour over Cmaj7, Benson prescribes borrowing quartal chords from B minor pentatonic or D major pentatonic via modal interchange. "To create a lydian sound over Cmaj7 chord for example, we use quartal chords belonging to 'B' minor pentatonic scale, or 'D' major pentatonic scale." Chapter 6, p. 263.

When comping over a maj7 chord, Benson rules that "the most important thing when comping is to follow the melody, which will 'tell' us what the best chord options are." When improvising, however, the player may freely choose among all learned colour extensions. Chapter 1, p. 4.

Benson places min7 chords across multiple harmonic regions. In major keys, Em7 (IIIm) and Am7 (VIm) are Root/Tonic-region members; Dm7 (IIm) is a major Subdominant-region member. In minor keys, Cm7 (I) is the tonic. Same-region interchangeability governs all substitutions. Chapter 1, pp. 1 and 4.

Benson lists the full tension palette for minor 7th chords: Cm7, Cm7(9), Cm7(11), Cm7(9)11, Cm(maj7)9, Cm6, Cm6(9). The melody always determines which of these is usable when comping; all are available when improvising. Chapter 1, p. 2.

Benson teaches that the IIm7 chord replaces IVmaj7 as the standard subdominant partner in the II/V/I cadence because both belong to the same Subdominant region. "Notice that we had to replace the IVth degree by the IIm, which belongs to the same region." This is the foundational rationale for the II/V/I itself. Chapter 1, p. 3.

Benson prescribes dorian quartal voicings primarily for static-harmony contexts. "Usually the dorian chords are related to static harmonies. However, they can be a tremendous asset when used over non traditional harmonic situations, giving a dorian modal vibe to the chord." Chapter 7, p. 279.

When a tritone substitution is applied over the IIm7 in a major II/V/I (e.g., Gm7 | C7(9) | Fmaj7 -> Gm7(11) | Gb7(#11) | Fmaj7), Benson requires adjusting the IIm7 voicing as well. "We should also change the voicing from the 1st chord as well. Therefore, we would have: || Gm7(11) | Gb7(#11) | Fmaj7 ||." Chapter 1, p. 14.

Benson includes Cm(maj7)9 in the tension palette for minor 7th chords (listed under minor 7th voicing possibilities). In minor II/V/I contexts, the tonic minor chord may be voiced as min(maj7) with the 9th added. Chapter 1, p. 2.

In the F melodic minor quartal family over Dø, Benson notes that the first degree chord Fm(maj7)add4 "sometimes can be replaced by a chord not belonging to that family: D#/E, which is actually a F#7(13)b9 over E. This is not a rule, it is just a chord voicing that works well with the other voicings even though it does not belong to this chord family." Chapter 7, p. 277.

Benson places the half-diminished chord (Bø / Dø) in the Dominant region as the VII degree: "Dominant Region Chords: G7 (V), Bø (VII)." In minor keys, Dø also serves as the II degree in the Subdominant region. Chapter 1, pp. 1 and 4.

Benson lists the tension palette for half-diminished chords: Dø, Dø(9), Dø(11), Dø(9)11, Dm7(b6). The Dm7(b6) variant is the enharmonic of the half-diminished and underscores the locrian-major-2nd reading. Chapter 1, p. 2.

In a minor II/V/I (e.g., Dø/G7/Cm7), Benson prescribes treating Dø as the VI degree of F melodic minor (locrian major 2nd). This dual membership unlocks F melodic minor's entire chord family as a substitution resource over the IIø without altering cadential function. "If we consider Dø chord as being locrian major 2nd we will have the VIth degree of F melodic minor." Chapter 3, p. 47.

Benson specifies three quartal chord families usable over a half-diminished chord: one derived from Eb major (gives locrian sound), one from Db major (re-frames the chord as D7(#9) via tritone substitution logic, giving blues vibe), and one from F melodic minor (because Dø is the VI degree of that scale). Chapter 7, p. 275.

Benson prescribes a specific transformation for the Db major quartal family over Dø: "we transformed the Dø into D7(#9) chord, giving it a blues vibe. Then using the tritone substitution for D7(#9), we can find Ab7(13), that we can consider mixolydian. Therefore, having this mixolydian chord, we can find the 'Db' major scale quartal chord voicings." Chapter 7, p. 275.

Benson demonstrates analytically that the major II (Dm7 / dorian) and the minor II (Bø) are "the same" because the third inversion of Dm6 is Bø: "the third inversion of Dm6 is Bø which is the II degree from the Am cadence. So we conclude that both II degree are the same." Chapter 1, p. 6.

Benson assigns dom7 (G7, V degree) to the Dominant region, whose function is "the sense of tension and instability, and wants to resolve to the tonic." Dominant and subdominant region chords are also declared interchangeable for purposes of delay and color. Chapter 1, pp. 1 and 8.

For the V7 chord leading to a major tonic, Benson catalogues the full tension palette: G7, G7(9), G7(b9), G7(#9), G7(13), G7(b13), G7(b9)b13, G7(#9)b13, G7(9)13, G7(b9)13, G7(#11), G7(b9)#11, Gsus9, Gsus13, Gsus(b9). Melody determines which tension is appropriate when comping. Chapter 1, p. 2.

Benson defines tritone substitution as replacing any dom7 with the dom7 a tritone away from its root: "if the chord is G7, the replacement will be Db7. The reason we can do this exchange is that both have the same tritone." The substituted chord shares the original tritone and is therefore functionally equivalent. Chapter 1, p. 13.

When a tritone substitution sounds poor with its original tension, Benson prescribes adjusting both the tritone chord's extension and the preceding IIm7 voicing together. Example: C7(9) -> Gb7(b13) fails; use Gb7(#11) instead, and change the preceding Gm7 to Gm7(11): "|| Gm7(11) | Gb7(#11) | Fmaj7 ||." Chapter 1, p. 14.

Benson prescribes secondary dominants as dom7 chords that resolve to non-tonic scale degrees, assigned solely by their resolution target: "secondary dominants are dominant chords that resolve to the other harmonic field degrees. They don't belong to the harmonic field and have nothing to do with it, except for the chord that they were assigned to resolve to." Chapter 1, p. 7.

Benson prescribes substituting VII7 for V7 on the basis of chromatic voice-leading: "all the notes of B7 can work as leading tones to the notes of C6, because they are half step from each other, creating a sensation of tension and resolution." The V/I motion (G7, C6) may be replaced by VII7/I (B7, C6). Chapter 2, p. 20.

In blues and Brazilian music contexts, Benson prescribes converting every chord in a turnaround to dominant 7th: "all the chords of the turnaround become dominant with different voicings. Each dominant chord is leading to the next chord until it finally leads to the tonic key (I)." Chapter 4, p. 83.

Benson notes that in a minor II/V/I (e.g., Aø | D7(b9) | Gm7), applying a tritone substitution over the dominant yields Ab7(#11), and "the voicings work perfect and we do not have to change anything." This contrasts with major II/V/I where tensions in the tritone sub are optional. Chapter 2, p. 17.

Benson corrects his own pedagogical simplification (altering only dominant chords leading to minor degrees) and states the real rule: "we can use any alteration to any dominant chord leading to major or minor. However, we must make sure the altered notes we choose can be applied over the song we are playing, because the melody will always determine what we can and can not use." Chapter 1, p. 10.

Benson prescribes that a Fake Diminished chord -- an inverted dom7(b9) with the root removed -- can substitute directly for the V7 chord. For example, an A7(b9) yields four diminished inversions (C#°, E°, G°, Bb°) each usable as a dominant substitute. "This type of diminished chord can be analyzed as an inverted dominant 7th (b9) chord." Chapter 2, p. 19.

Benson prescribes that the V7 chord in a minor cadence almost always takes altered tensions: "the dominant seventh chords almost always use altered tensions such as: b9, #9, #11, b13. The major 13th can be used with some regularity in the chords, but it is still an exception. In the key of Cm we can have the cadence: G7(b9)13 leading to Cm7 for example." Chapter 1, p. 4.

Benson identifies dom7(b9) chords (7, b9, 3 intervals from low to high without the root) as the structural basis of Fake Diminished chords. "Notice that dominant 7th chords such as 7(b9), 7(#9), and 7(b13), can be considered as being the same, therefore they have the same function." Chapter 1, p. 14.

In a minor II/V/I (Dø/G7/Cm7), Benson prescribes treating G7 as an altered chord -- "the VIIth degree of Ab melodic minor" -- which unlocks the entire Ab melodic minor chord family as a substitution resource over the dominant. Chapter 3, p. 47.

Benson prescribes treating a dom7alt chord as locrian (its arpeggio is half-diminished) to unlock the major scale a half-step above as a quartal voicing source: "the scale arpeggio of a dominant 7th altered chord is half diminished, we can consider it for a while as being locrian, which allows us to use all the chords built from the major scale that generates it. In the case of 'G' locrian, we could use all the chords built from the 'Ab' major scale over it." Chapter 6, p. 254.

Over dom7alt (Locrian) quartal voicings, Benson warns that the minor pentatonic fails because "the perfect 5th of the scale does not belong to this mode." The fix: use the minor blues scale instead, emphasizing the #4. Chapter 6, p. 226.

Unlike the minor pentatonic (which fails over Locrian quartal voicings due to the perfect 5th), the minor blues scale with emphasis on #4 may be used over dom7alt Locrian voicings without modal conflict. "In order to solve this problem, we can play the Minor Blues scale over Locrian chord voicings emphasizing the #4." Chapter 6, p. 226.

Any dom7 that is neither the V degree nor a tritone substitution is classified as lydian dominant and must be tensioned with 9, 13, or #11: "Dominant 7th chords that are not the Vth degree or a tritone substitution, are always considered lydian dominant. In other words, we can use the following tensions on them: 9, 13, or #11." Chapter 1, p. 2.

Benson places a strict restriction on lydian dominant (mixolydian #4) quartal voicings: "It can only be used over dominant 7th chords that are not leading to any other chord. The only exception is when we have a sequence of many dominant 7th chords one after another." Chapter 7, p. 279.

Unlike the general ban on lydian dominant quartal voicings over resolving dominants, when every chord in a progression is dominant one after another, lydian dominant quartal voicings may be used throughout the chain. "The only exception is when we have a sequence of many dominant 7th chords one after another." Chapter 7, p. 279.

Benson restricts mixolydian quartal voicings on the V chord to major-resolving contexts only: "on the Vth degree of a minor cadence, we can use all the possibilities we have learned for dominant 7th chords, except with the mixolydian chord voicings, which can only be used when they are leading to major chords." Chapter 7, p. 279.

Benson prohibits using the V degree of a melodic minor scale as a substitute for the dominant when it shares the root of the tonic: "we could not use the C7(9/b13){V degree of F melodic minor} to replace G7, because it has the same root note as the key (Cmaj7), and the cadence would disappear: Dm7, C7(9/b13), Cmaj7." Chapter 2, p. 40.

Benson prescribes using the melodic minor chord family as a resource to substitute for dominant region chords (major or minor subdominant region equivalents): "the chords derived from the melodic minor scale can replace the dominant region chords with the subdominant region chords (major or minor), it means that we can use the melodic minor chord family to replace the dominant region chords." The V degree exception is noted separately. Chapter 2, p. 40.

Benson prescribes replacing a V7 chord with a tonic-root diminished chord in a bass pedal context: the bass stays on the tonic while the chord moves, yielding C° resolving to C6 instead of G7 | C6. "The bass stays the same and the chords move around. Therefore we have: C° resolving to C6." Chapter 2, p. 21.

Benson organizes diminished chords into two functional categories: Fake Diminished (inverted dom7(b9) functioning as a V7 substitute) and Hybrid Diminished (usable as either a connecting chord or a direct V7 substitute in a cadence). Both are dominant-region substitutes. Chapter 2, pp. 19--20.

Benson prescribes exploiting diminished symmetry for substitution: "Diminished Chords have an interesting characteristic, they repeat themselves every minor 3rd. In other words, for every diminished chord, we will always have four options. Example: 'C°' can be replaced by 'Eb°', 'Gb°' or 'A°', because they contain the same notes, therefore are the same chord." Chapter 2, p. 19.

Benson prescribes the Fake Diminished as an inverted dom7(b9) with the root omitted: "This type of diminished chord can be analyzed as an inverted dominant 7th (b9) chord." The root (e.g., A) is removed, leaving the upper structure (b7, b9, 3) which maps to four equivalent diminished voicings, each a usable V7 replacement. Chapter 2, p. 19.

Benson prescribes the Hybrid Diminished chord in two roles: as a connecting chord (passing between chords) or as a substitute for V7 in a cadence. "This type of diminished chord can be analyzed in two different ways: First as a connecting chord, and second as a substitute chord for the V7 degree of a cadence." Chapter 2, p. 20.

Benson includes sus voicings in the dominant tension palette for V7 leading to major: Gsus9, Gsus13, and Gsus(b9) appear alongside standard dom7 tensions. Sus voicings are available dominant-region colour options governed by melody when comping. Chapter 1, p. 2.

Benson prescribes that quartal dom7 voicings for comping should start from the 3rd, 4th, or 5th strings: "we most often use the chords starting from the 3rd, 4th and 5th strings, because the chords rooted from the 6th string might not work. Sometimes, even the chords starting from the 5th string might not work if used in low areas of the instrument." Chapter 6, p. 204.

When dom7 quartal tetrad voicings sound muddy on lower strings, Benson prescribes dropping the lowest note: "some chords on the lower strings might not sound desirable, in these cases we can take out the lower note and play a 3 note quartal voicing." Chapter 7, p. 276. He also notes: "Be careful of the lower notes. They can make the chord sound undesirable." Chapter 7, p. 275.

Benson prescribes memorizing block chord examples rather than constructing them analytically in performance: "they should be memorized and not just analyzed in order to become natural and easy to play." Chord ideas and groove (rhythmic) ideas are treated as independently interchangeable variables. Chapter 7, p. 290.

Benson requires every maj7 voicing concept to be internalized from both the 5th-string root and the 6th-string root: "on the guitar we must learn things considering the 5th string as the root and also the 6th string as the root. Therefore, below we have examples in the keys of 'Cm' (root on the 5th string) and 'Gm' (root on the 6th string)." Chapter 1, p. 11.

As with all chord qualities in this method, Benson prescribes learning minor 7th voicings from both 5th-string and 6th-string root positions, illustrating this with minor key examples in Cm (5th string root) and Gm (6th string root). Chapter 1, p. 11.

Benson prescribes memorizing all dom7 voicing patterns from both 5th-string and 6th-string root positions throughout the chapter exercises. This guitar-specific positional rule is stated as a universal requirement: "on the guitar we must learn things considering the 5th string as the root and also the 6th string as the root." Chapter 1, p. 11.

Benson prescribes that at the I degree (maj7 tonic), only chords from the 1st, 3rd, or 6th columns of the modal interchange table may be substituted: "in every I degree we can use chords belonging from the 1st, 3rd or 6th columns." Chapter 2, p. 29.

At the II degree (IIm7), Benson permits substitutions from the 2nd, 4th, 5th, or 7th columns of the modal interchange table: "in every II degree we can use chords belonging from the 2nd, 4th, 5th or 7th columns." The same columns apply to the IV degree. Chapter 2, p. 29.

At the V degree (dom7), Benson permits substitutions from the 5th, 7th, 2nd, or 4th columns of the modal interchange table: "in every V degree we can use chords belonging from the 5th, 7th, 2nd or 4th columns." Chapter 2, p. 29.

In parallel-mode exercises, Benson requires that the first chord always be drawn from the major key: "the first chord of the sequence will always be from the major key, and all the other chords will be the degrees belonging to the parallel minor key." This rule gives the modal interchange colour its characteristic major-to-minor shift. Chapter 2, p. 33.

When harmonizing a passage over a half-diminished chord using the minor blues scale quartal shape (1, 4, b7), Benson prescribes placing scale notes always in the top voice: "the scale notes will always be on the top voice of each chord. By doing this, we give strength to the chord melody, since they sound like 'power chords' as they contain intervals of a 5th and 4th between each note." Non-scale notes are permitted in inner voices. Chapter 6, p. 244.

Benson prescribes learning all quartal tetrad voicings from every string as a fretboard visualization exercise, not for immediate comping deployment: "Knowing all the possibilities of quartal tetrads starting from each string is part of the fretboard visualization process that we must improve on everyday if we want to improvise and harmonize better." Chapter 6, p. 208.

Benson prescribes modal quartal voicings primarily for static-harmony contexts: "This concept is very useful when we play single chord songs such as 'Impressions', the first part of 'Take Five', 'So What' and 'A Love Supreme'." Over chord progressions, each chord may receive a separate modal quartal treatment, though the major-scale quartal family cannot cover all chord types. Chapter 6, p. 216.

Benson prescribes using bass-note selection to determine modal identity over a fixed quartal chord sequence: "if we play the bass note 'E' continuously over the sequence of chords above, we would have a 'E' Phrygian chord sequence. If we play the bass note 'D' continuously, we would have a 'D' Dorian chord sequence, and so on." Chapter 6, p. 216.

Benson prescribes three practice rules for internalizing quartal triads: (1) never lose the guide chords from view, visualizing each chord by its root note; (2) lower-voiced chords may not work as comping chords; (3) chord symbols for inverted quartal chords use simple letter names. Chapter 6, p. 217.

Benson prescribes the melodic pedal point technique for quartal dom7 voicings: the top voice is held fixed while lower voices shift. "Melodic pedal point is a concept where the lowest voicings of the chords move, but the top voice remains the same." These patterns can be played over any mode from the generating scale. Chapter 6, p. 227.

Benson prescribes memorizing the foundational open-string chord vocabulary before advancing in Chapter 5: "The following chords are considered the most common using open strings. Memorize them and keep following the explanations." Open-string maj7 shapes are among the first-tier vocabulary. Chapter 5, p. 114.

Benson prescribes applying open-string dom7 voicings and pedal-point chords in short harmonic sequences such as I/IVm, I/VI/IIm/V, IV/IVm/I, and I/V: "The best way to use the pedal point chords or any open string chord, is to apply them as much as you can in every situation that is possible. It is advisable to apply them using simple and short sequences." Chapter 5, p. 169.

When an open-string dom7 chord shape is difficult to fret, Benson permits omitting notes to accommodate hand size without destroying harmonic function: "depending on the size of our hand, some chords might be very difficult to play in determined keys. So in order to solve this problem, sometimes we can omit some notes." Chapter 5, p. 112.

When transposing any open-string dom7 shape to other frets, Benson warns that chord quality can shift fundamentally -- a dom7 shape may become another quality entirely: "some chords do not change their characteristics, but others can change completely, going from a major chord to a minor chord at times." The player must verify quality at each fret position. Chapter 5, p. 112.

Benson prescribes that the blues, in its simple form, is harmonically based on dominant 7th chords: "Harmonically, in its simple form, it is based on dominant 7th chords." The blues scale summarizes all the chords in the form. Two forms exist: Major Blues and Minor Blues. Chapter 5, p. 91 (Chapter 4 section).

Benson prescribes a specific method for internalizing blues form dom7 progressions: "Snap your fingers on beats 2 and 4, similar to what the drummer plays on the hi hat, then sing the degrees of each one of the shown blues forms. This is a very important step because we must know these forms inside and out without having to think about them." Chapter 4, p. 91.

Benson prescribes a specific quartal practice protocol for dom7 voicings: study in one key thoroughly before transposing, and memorize only the voicing colours preferred rather than all possibilities: "We strongly recommend to study in one key for sometime, then after visualizing the possibilities in the key you have chosen, go ahead with other keys. Remember that we do not have to memorize all the possibilities presented in this book. Memorize the ones you like." Chapter 6, p. 259.

For Cmaj7 (Imaj7), Benson prescribes descending 'Major 7th Scale Arpeggios' -- Cmaj7 arpeggios with added color tones transcribed from Benson's own solos -- organized zone-by-zone across the fretboard, to sidestep the perfect 4th avoid note. 'We will create melodies for Cmaj7 that can fit over Ionian or Lydian chords.' These are descending arpeggios with added notes, each zone providing a 'guide idea starting from the highest note and ending in the lowest note.' Chapter 7, p. 269.

The perfect 4th is an avoid note over Cmaj7 (Imaj7) and must not be used as a default melodic choice. 'The avoid note (perfect 4th) can create some melodic problems, especially over the root chord and the relative minor chord (Cmaj7 and Am7 in the key of C).' Exceptions exist: 'there are always exceptions and at times the avoid note works fine depending on the situation.' Chapter 6, p. 244; Chapter 7, p. 269.

Although the perfect 4th is proscribed over Cmaj7 by default, Benson explicitly acknowledges contextual exceptions: 'there are always exceptions and at times the avoid note works fine depending on the situation.' The player must judge the musical context. Chapter 6, p. 244.

For Cmaj7, Benson prescribes superimposing a Gmaj7 arpeggio over it to produce a Lydian sound: 'If we play Gmaj7 (G, B, D, F#) over the Cmaj7, we would have a C Lydian sound melodically.' On guitar this must be arpeggiated in sequence rather than voiced simultaneously as on piano. Chapter 7, p. 275.

Benson proscribes relying on scales alone over Cmaj7: 'it is not enough to only use the scales of the chords to create melodies, we must add stronger melodic structures to them such as triads and tetrads.' Scale lines over Imaj7 must be reinforced with arpeggio structures for melodic substance. Chapter 7, p. 269.

For Am7 (VIm7), Benson prescribes descending 'Minor 7th Scale Arpeggios' -- Am7 arpeggios with added color tones derived from Benson solos -- to create melodies 'that can fit over Dorian or Aeolian chords' while avoiding the flat 6th. Each fretboard zone has a 'guide idea starting from the highest note and ending in the lowest note.' Chapter 7, p. 269.

The flat 6th is an avoid note over Am7 (VIm7/Aeolian) and must not be used as a default melodic choice. 'Be careful with the avoid notes of both scales (perfect 4th in the Ionian mode, and flat 6th in the Aeolian mode), because they can clash with the melody note.' Contextual exceptions apply. Chapter 6, p. 244.

Although the flat 6th is proscribed over Am7 (VIm7/Aeolian) by default, Benson allows exceptions: 'there are always exceptions and at times the avoid note works fine depending on the situation.' The player must judge the musical context. Chapter 6, p. 244.

For min7 chords belonging to the minor chord family (natural minor harmonic field), Benson prescribes deploying lick lines built purely from the minor pentatonic scale without mixture of the major pentatonic: 'our preference is to use the lines over minor chords or chord sequences belonging to the minor chord family.' This preference is not an absolute rule. Chapter 5, p. 210.

Benson explicitly notes that unmixed minor pentatonic lines are not restricted to minor chords: 'This is not a rule. Melodic lines using only the minor pentatonic scale will often work perfectly over major chords such as C6, Cmaj7 and of course C7.' The minor-family preference is a tendency, not a law. Chapter 5, p. 210.

For dominant 7th chords in a blues context, Benson prescribes using the minor blues scale in combination with the major blues scale -- not summarizing all chords into one scale. 'When we mix the major blues scale with the minor blues scale, we cannot summarize all the chords into one scale anymore, we must follow the harmony. In other words, the combination of both blues scales will work for each dominant 7th chord individually.' Chapter 4, p. 151.

When applying the minor blues scale over a dominant 7th chord, Benson warns that the major 3rd must be played quickly within the phrase: 'when mixed with the major blues scale in the same key, we can use it over any dominant 7th chord, bringing a blues vibe to it. (Make sure to play the major 3rd quickly in the phrase, otherwise the melody can sound wrong).' Chapter 4, p. 141.

For dominant 7th chords, Benson prescribes the major blues scale as applicable: 'The major blues scale can be played over any individual major chord, including the major 7th and dominant 7th chords. However, this scale can sound not bluesy, so the trick is to mix it with the minor blues scale in the same key, reaching a bluesy sound and vibe.' Chapter 4, p. 141.

Benson proscribes relying on any single blues scale over all dominant 7th chord changes: 'Be careful not to rely on this technique. It will make you sound like a lazy improviser. Your lines will lack variation and will sound stagnant.' The blues scale may summarize all blues chords at once, but doing so is a failure mode. Chapter 4, p. 140.

Benson proscribes applying the same-key minor+major blues combination rule over minor blues form dominants: 'This will not work for minor blues form.' In minor tonality, the C minor blues scale pairs with the Eb major blues scale, not the C major blues scale. Chapter 4, p. 151.

Benson explicitly notes that unmixed minor pentatonic lick lines also work over dominant 7th chords: 'Melodic lines using only the minor pentatonic scale will often work perfectly over major chords such as C6, Cmaj7 and of course C7.' This applies even without mixture from the major pentatonic. Chapter 5, p. 210.

Benson prescribes that dominant 7th chords within the harmonic field (G7/Mixolydian in the key of C) tolerate the natural major scale's perfect 4th avoid note, unlike the Imaj7 and VIm7 chords. 'This scale works perfectly when played over... G7 (Mixolydian), even while using the avoid note. We must be careful with our note choices.' Chapter 7, p. 269.

For Dm7 (Dorian) within the C harmonic field, Benson prescribes that the natural major scale -- including the perfect 4th avoid note -- works without restriction. 'This scale works perfectly when played over Dm7 (Dorian)... even while using the avoid note. We must be careful with our note choices.' The avoid-note proscription applies specifically to the Imaj7 and VIm7 chords. Chapter 7, p. 269.

For Bm7b5 (Locrian) within the C harmonic field, Benson prescribes that the natural major scale including the perfect 4th avoid note works freely. 'This scale works perfectly when played over... Locrian, even while using the avoid note. We must be careful with our note choices.' Chapter 7, p. 269.

For Fmaj7 (Lydian) within the C harmonic field, Benson prescribes that the natural major scale including the perfect 4th works freely: 'This scale works perfectly when played over... Fmaj7 (Lydian), even while using the avoid note.' The avoid-note prohibition is specific to the Imaj7 and VIm7 chords, not all major 7th chord instances. Chapter 7, p. 269.

Benson prescribes the major blues scale as playable over any individual major chord including major 7ths: 'The major blues scale can be played over any individual major chord, including the major 7th and dominant 7th chords. However, this scale can sound not bluesy, so the trick is to mix it with the minor blues scale in the same key.' Chapter 4, p. 141.

For Cmaj7, Benson prescribes using the Cmaj7 chord shape as the navigational anchor for Ionian-side fretboard zones in the five-zone system. 'Each zone will be related with a chord shape (Cmaj7 or Am7). The chords will guide us better than just single notes... Make sure to use the root of each chord to guide you in each zone.' These are navigational tools, not harmonic instructions. Chapter 6, p. 246.

For Am7, Benson prescribes using the Am7 chord shape as the navigational anchor for Aeolian-side fretboard zones. 'Each zone will be related with a chord shape (Cmaj7 or Am7).' The Am7 shape serves as a positional memory aid for the relative minor zones, guiding the player horizontally across the fretboard -- 'we visualize vertically but play horizontally most of the time.' Chapter 6, p. 246.

Benson prescribes understanding that the minor pentatonic scale creates a min7 chord (A, C, E, G = Am7), and that C6 and Am7 share the same notes: 'C6 is an inverted Am7 (1st inversion).' These scales must nevertheless be visualized separately for the five-zone fretboard system to function -- 'it is extremely important to visualize them separately.' Chapter 3, p. 108.

For minor 7th chords in a minor blues context, Benson prescribes memorizing substitution tricks before understanding their theory: 'the minor blues form has two different types of chords (minor and dominant), so we must learn some substitution tricks before we start.' And: 'it is not necessary to understand the theory behind it, just memorize them.' The student must treat these as vocabulary items, not derivable rules. Chapter 5, p. 195.

For Cmaj7 scale arpeggios, Benson prescribes awareness that descending arpeggios span two fretboard zones while ascending arpeggios define a single zone: 'Notice that the ascending arpeggios will define the fretboard zones, because the descending arpeggios will almost always use two zones, because we play descending arpeggios vertically.' Ascending forms orient position; descending forms are the primary melodic vehicle over Imaj7. Chapter 7, p. 275.

For Am7 scale arpeggios, Benson prescribes the same zone-spanning rule as for Cmaj7: ascending Am7 arpeggios define the fretboard zone, while descending Am7 arpeggios with added notes span two zones. 'The ascending arpeggios will define the fretboard zones, because the descending arpeggios will almost always use two zones.' The descending form is the primary melodic vehicle over VIm7. Chapter 7, p. 275.

Benson proscribes mechanically relying on intervallic pattern exercises over Cmaj7: 'In the beginning we will learn some simple intervallic patterns that will help us get familiar with the two scales... But DO NOT rely on these. They are exercises and can begin to sound very predictable and extremely boring.' Patterns are scaffolding only; every pattern must be offset with rhythmic displacement to become musical. Chapter 7, p. 270.

The same anti-pattern prescription applies to Am7 intervallic exercises: 'DO NOT rely on these. They are exercises and can begin to sound very predictable and extremely boring.' Every intervallic pattern over VIm7 must be made musical via rhythmic displacement: 'Every intervallic pattern should be applied using them... what we call rhythmic displacement.' Chapter 7, p. 270.

Benson instructs that existing Cmaj7 and Fmaj7 arpeggio lines can be directly recycled as D Dorian vocabulary: 'by combining Cmaj7 lines with Fmaj7 lines, we can build a beautiful D dorian line. So, it means that we already have thousands of dorian lines just adapting the major 7th lines to minor chords' (Chapter 2, p. 145).

In Chapter 3, the Ionian (#5) scale -- the relative major of harmonic minor -- anchors the five-zone fretboard system via the Eb+(maj7) guide chord shape. Benson writes: 'Guide Chords => Harmonic Minor & Ionian (#5) = Cm(maj7) & Ebmaj7(#5)' (Chapter 3, p. 238).

Benson establishes that the Dorian scale is a 'static scale, which means that it does not have any avoid note. Therefore, we can play all the tetrads and triads from the harmonic field over a dorian chord' -- listing all seven diatonic tetrads and triads of the parent key (Chapter 2, p. 144).

Benson prescribes adding the major 7th to the Dorian scale as a leading tone: 'we can add the major 7th to the dorian scale, in order to make it more melodic. The reason we can do this, is because the major 7th works as a leading tone to the root of the scale, thus creating the illusion of a dominant 7th chord leading to a minor chord' (Chapter 2, p. 144).

Benson distinguishes two tiers: 'We can use dorian ideas over any minor chord as a possibility of color. However, when we have minor chords that do not belong to the harmonic field, there is no other option than using dorian ideas, otherwise the melody will sound wrong' (Chapter 2, p. 144). Dorian is optional over diatonic minor chords but mandatory over non-diatonic ones.

Benson generalizes: 'all the melodic lines in this chapter can be used over any chord derived from C major scale: Dm7 (Dorian), Em7 or Esus(b9) (Phrygian), Fmaj7 (Lydian), G7 (Mixolydian), Am7 (Aeolian), Bm7b5 (Locrian)' (Chapter 2, p. 180).

Benson states that when playing Dorian ideas over a standalone G7, 'we must be careful with the avoid note C, because it can make your melody sound weird or even incorrect... we definitely can use D dorian ideas over G7, but without forgetting to emphasize the B note instead the C note' (Chapter 2, p. 144).

Benson provides a concrete editing rule: 'it is very important to remember that all the lines ending on the C note have to be modified when played over G7 because the C note is an avoid note for that chord' (Chapter 2, p. 146).

Benson frames the harmonic minor scale as reserved specifically for dominant-function contexts: 'we will use its melodies over harmonic situations where we have tension & resolution' (Chapter 3, p. 235). He lists six valid cadential contexts including bare G7 | Cm7, Fm7 G7 | Cm7, and Dm7b5 G7 | Cm7.

Benson warns against landing on the tonic root when superimposing the harmonic minor chord family over G7: 'be careful when using the root of the Cm(maj7), because it can sound weird, making the whole line sound incorrect. So the best thing to do is to forget the root for now' (Chapter 3, p. 308).

Benson instructs that the VII diminished of C harmonic minor (B dim) and its three enharmonic equivalents (D dim, F dim, Ab dim) are all valid superimpositions over G7, because 'all of them are what we call fake diminished chords, because they are G7(b9) [V7] without the root note' (Chapter 3, p. 246).

Benson explicitly prohibits consecutive use of augmented shapes over a dominant: 'Remember that these augmented chords are not to be played consecutively, they are just small melodic cells to help us build melodies using the harmonic minor scale' (Chapter 3, p. 284).

Benson supplies a degree-by-degree substitution table: 'Second degree = Dm7b5: can be replaced by D dim; Fourth degree = Fm7: can be replaced by F dim or Fm7b5; Fifth degree = G7: can be replaced by G+7; Sixth degree = Abmaj7: can be replaced by Abm(maj7) or Ab dim(maj7)' (Chapter 3, p. 335).

Benson establishes that 'B dim will provide us three more equal chords: D dim, F dim and Ab dim. However, all of them are what we call fake diminished chords, because they are G7(b9) [V7] without the root note' (Chapter 3, p. 246). The accompanying table maps each note to its G7(b9) function.

Benson prescribes ascending-only chromatic approach notes when building the chromatic illusion over diminished arpeggios: 'Most often we will only use simple ascending chromatic approaches over the diminished arpeggios. Descending chromatic approaches work differently and we will cover them next' (Chapter 3, p. 260).

Benson rejects a rigid rule for which diminished fingering shape to choose: 'there is no rule about what shape is the best, because it will depend on what comes next in terms of melody. Therefore, the best thing to do is to memorize many single line ideas using the diminished chord' (Chapter 3, p. 248).

Benson carves out an explicit exception to the avoid-note rule for the 4th over a dominant: 'The only exception is when the chord is a Gsus, so the C note will work with this chord as a starting note or even an ending note' (Chapter 2, p. 144).

Benson anchors the entire five-zone harmonic minor fretboard system to two guide chord shapes, the first of which is Cm(maj7): 'Guide Chords => Harmonic Minor & Ionian (#5) = Cm(maj7) & Ebmaj7(#5). 1st Zone: Cm(maj7), 2nd Zone: Eb+(maj7), 3rd Zone: Cm(maj7)...' (Chapter 3, p. 238).

Benson establishes that the ending note must always fit the tonic chord: 'always pay attention to the resolution note because we must always respect the ending chord, which in this case is Cm7, a non C harmonic minor scale chord. Actually, most of the time, the ending chord of a cadence V7/I will not be derived from the harmonic minor scale' (Chapter 3, p. 235).

Benson explicitly prohibits applying harmonic minor lines to the IIm7 chord in a full major cadence: 'when we have a complete C major cadence such as Dm7 / G7 / Cmaj7, we cannot use C harmonic minor ideas over the Dm7, it would not work' (Chapter 3, p. 236).

Benson forbids the natural 6th (A natural in C minor) in any line played over a V7-Im cadence: 'If we have the cadence G7, Cm7, we cannot use the A note (major 6th) to build single lines, because this note is derived from the dorian scale and cannot be played over any cadence' (Chapter 3, p. 261).

Benson mandates a specific technique for descending augmented arpeggios: 'the descending augmented chord shapes will be played horizontally, and for this reason we will have only one shape possibility per string... the George Benson picking technique works much better when we play horizontal ideas' (Chapter 3, p. 284).

Benson maps the three augmented rotations derivable from C harmonic minor to their G7 functions: 'G+: G, B, D# -- (Root, major 3rd, augmented 5th of G); B+: B, D#, G -- (major 3rd, augmented 5th, Root of G); D#+: Eb, G, B -- (minor 6th, Root, major 3rd of G)' (Chapter 3, p. 281).

Benson instructs that all four enharmonic diminished spellings over G7b9 are interchangeable because 'B dim will provide us three more equal chords: D dim, F dim and Ab dim. However, all of them are what we call fake diminished chords, because they are G7(b9) [V7] without the root note' (Chapter 3, p. 246).

Benson restricts chromatic approach direction when decorating diminished arpeggios: 'Most often we will only use simple ascending chromatic approaches over the diminished arpeggios. Descending chromatic approaches work differently and we will cover them next' (Chapter 3, p. 260).

Benson designates Dm7b5 (along with Fm7 and Abmaj7) as passing material only during the G7-Cm7 cadence because it contains the tonic C note: 'We can use the triads and tetrads that contain the C note (Dm7b5, Fm7, Abmaj7) only as passing chords in a melody going from G7 leading to Cm7' (Chapter 3, p. 308).

Benson allows replacing the Dm7b5 (second degree of C harmonic minor) with D dim when superimposing over G7, explicitly to avoid the problematic tonic C note: 'Second degree = Dm7b5: can be replaced by D dim' (Chapter 3, p. 335).

Benson states the anti-scalar principle: 'we use scales only to guide us through the guitar fretboard. When building melodic ideas, we should always mix scales, superimposed arpeggios and chromatic tones, otherwise the improvisation will sound predictable' (Chapter 2, p. 147).
Benson issues a quality-control warning: 'chromatics must be studied very carefully because the borderline between building a beautiful melody or a non-musical melody is very thin' (Chapter 1, p. 5).

Benson specifies how to derive harmonic minor arpeggios from familiar shapes: 'we will use the same scale arpeggios we learned for major 7th and minor 7th chords, but in the major scale arpeggio we will replace the perfect 5th with the #5th, and in the minor scale arpeggio we will replace the minor 7th with the major 7th' (Chapter 3, p. 243).

Benson permits adding the b7 (minor 7th) to harmonic minor lines even though it is not a scale degree: 'we can also use the minor 7th, which is a note that is not derived from this scale but sounds great. The reason we can use both 7ths is because the harmonic minor came from the aeolian scale and both have the same harmonic function' (Chapter 3, p. 235).

Benson's foundational rule: 'we can only use chord tones or chord tension notes as target tones, but not avoid notes. The only exception would be when the avoid note becomes part of the chord' (Chapter 1, p. 1). This constrains what may function as a structural melodic note over any chord quality.

For Gsus(b9), Benson prescribes deriving single lines from the melodic minor scale a whole step below the sus root: 'Over a Gsus(b9) we would visualize the single lines as being derived from "F" melodic minor because the Gsus(b9) chord is the IInd degree of the F melodic minor scale.' The player locates the sus(b9) chord as degree II of the parent melodic minor, then uses that parent scale as the improvisation source. Chapter 5, p. 15.

For C#7alt, Benson prescribes visualizing single lines from the melodic minor scale a half step above the altered dominant root: 'Over a C#7alt we would visualize the single lines as being derived from "D" melodic minor because the C# altered is the VIIth degree of the D melodic minor scale.' The altered dominant is located as degree VII of the parent melodic minor, and that scale governs improvisation. Chapter 5, p. 15.
