For C+maj7 (augmented major seventh), Benson prescribes deriving lines from either A melodic minor or C Ionian(#5): 'Over a C+maj7 we would visualize the single lines as being derived from "A" melodic minor or "C" Ionian (#5) because it is the IIIrd degree (relative) of A melodic minor.' The aug-maj7 chord sits at degree III, and the Lydian(#5)/melodic minor pairing is the characteristic scale resource. Chapter 5, p. 15.

For Am(maj7) -- the tonic minor-major seventh -- Benson prescribes using it as one of the two master guide chord shapes anchoring all five fretboard zones: 'we can use the same 5 vertical zones exactly as we did before with Ionian and Aeolian but this time having Cmaj7(#5) and Am(maj7) as guiding chords.' All melodic minor tetrads across the neck must be related back to this shape. Additionally, the full tension set must be known even if not all tensions are voiced: 'we have to know all of them in order to do not make a mistake when harmonizing or improvising.' Chapter 5, p. 15 (guide chord); Chapter 7, pp. 28, 33.

For Cmaj7(#5) -- the Lydian(#5) major seventh sharp-five -- Benson prescribes using it as the alternating guide chord alongside Am(maj7) in the five-zone fretboard system: 'Guide Chords -> Lydian (#5) & Melodic Minor = Cmaj7(#5) & Am(maj7). 1st Zone: Cmaj7(#5). 2nd Zone: Am(maj7). 3rd Zone: Cmaj7(#5).' Every zone on the neck alternates between these two shapes. Chapter 5, p. 15; Chapter 7, p. 33.

For D7(9) -- the dominant ninth used as the primary laboratory chord throughout the volume -- Benson prescribes applying melodic minor Giant Lines to create 'flux and reflux': extended melodic minor lines are run over the static D7(9) vamp to generate harmonic tension and release. The fretboard visualization for extended lines over this chord requires a minimum of two guide chords: 'we must use at least 2 guide chords in order to properly visualize what we are doing.' Chapters 3, 5, 7-9.

Do not attempt to visualize extended melodic minor scale options over a dominant seventh using only a single guide chord -- 'in these cases we must use at least 2 guide chords in order to properly visualize what we are doing.' A single anchor is explicitly ruled insufficient whenever the scale palette goes beyond basic options. Chapter 7, p. 27.

For D7(#11) specifically, Benson warns that its dual identity as both melodic minor IV and a dominant diminished voicing means certain scales and chords cannot safely be used over it: 'we must know that in some cases we cannot use certain types of scales and chords, otherwise we might have a terrible result.' The dual identity constrains the scale options. Chapter 7, p. 28.

For E7(9, b13) and D7(9, #11, 13) -- the melodic minor V and IV dominant chords -- Benson prescribes knowing all tensions completely even when voicing only a subset: 'The chords D7(9,#11,13), E7(9,b13) do not have to contain all the tensions presented. However, we have to know all of them in order to do not make a mistake when harmonizing or improvising.' Chapter 7, p. 28.

For Dm7 (and the Cm7 reference key used to teach it), Benson prescribes learning all melodic minor tetrads and Giant Lines by first anchoring them in the key of Cm: 'we will learn this new scale arpeggios in the key of "Cm" thus helping us to visualize the "Eb" note replacing "E" note.' The minor seventh chord shape serves as the visual anchor for the Eb/E substitution. Chapters 7, 11, 13.

For F#o (half-diminished, the sixth degree of A melodic minor), Benson prescribes deriving improvisation lines from the A melodic minor scale family: 'The next scale arpeggios can be applyed over any chord derived from "A" melodic minor scale: Am(maj7) or Am6, Bsus(b9), Cmaj7(#5), *D7(9,#11,13), *E7(9,b13), F#o, G#7alt.' The half-diminished chord is treated as an integral member of the melodic minor chord family. Chapter 7, pp. 28, 33.

For a D7 chord, Benson prescribes playing small A7 ideas in the middle of the line to create an outside effect -- the First GB Chord Transition technique. The substitution chord is superimposed momentarily within the single-note line, not comped, to generate harmonic color. Chapter 9, p. 26.

Do not stay on the A7 substitution idea too long over D7 -- exceeding the effective threshold destroys the outside effect and tips the line into mere dissonance rather than colorful tension. The outside superimposition is a flash move, not a sustained region. Chapter 9, p. 26.

The Second GB Chord Transition prescribes embedding a mini V7-I cadence within a single-line idea over D7 -- specifically D7 leading to G major -- as an additional outside device distinct from the A7 superimposition. The relative minor (Em for G) then unlocks a further set of dominant scale options for the line. Chapter 9, p. 26.

Any single-line idea -- inside or outside -- constructed over D7 must end on a chord tone of D7. This Ending Note Rule applies universally to all the outside-effect lines in the chapter; harmonic coherence is restored at the conclusion of each line regardless of how far outside it travels. Chapter 9, p. 26.

Because D Mixolydian derives from the Em chord family, Benson prescribes using B7 ideas leading to Em as a 'very beautiful' outside device over a single D7. The justification is modal-family coherence: the Mixolydian mode's parent chord family supplies the secondary dominant that generates the outside color. Chapter 9, p. 31.

For Dm7 in a static (one-chord vamp) context, Benson organizes the melodic vocabulary into both 'inside' and 'outside' categories, presenting worked examples of each as Giant Lines. The student is expected to practice both categories systematically over the sustained Dm7 before moving to active (changing-chord) contexts. Chapter 11, pp. 60-90.

When a dominant 7th (A7) resolves to a minor tonic (Dm7), Benson prescribes using major-7th superimposed ideas over A7 to strengthen the pull toward Dm7. These same major-7th superimposed options over C7 leading to Fmaj7 may sound too tense or even incorrect, and are not recommended in that context. Chapter 13, p. 77.

Do not apply major-7th superimposed ideas over C7 when it leads to Fmaj7 -- these options may sound too tense or even incorrect in that cadential context. The major-7th superimposition is prescribed for dominant-to-minor resolutions (A7 -> Dm7) only, not for dominant-to-major resolutions (C7 -> Fmaj7). Chapter 13, p. 77.

For Dm7 in active (changing-chord) contexts, Benson prescribes mapping single-note melodic fingerings directly onto guide chord shapes as the concrete fretboard method for internalizing Active Giant Lines. The student visualizes the guide chord shape under the fingers while executing the single-line melody. Chapter 13, p. 77.

Over a sustained D7(9) vamp, Benson prescribes constructing Giant Lines that create and release harmonic tension within the line itself -- the Flux and Reflux technique. Chapters 5 and 7 deepen this practice progressively, establishing that tension generation and resolution is a trainable melodic skill. Chapters 5 and 7, pp. 15-37.

Over a D7(9) dominant vamp, begin with Blues Scale ideas as the foundational layer before adding modal or superimposition vocabulary (Chapter 6, p. 27). The Blues Scale is the first of three escalating technique categories, not an advanced option to be skipped.

Over D7(9), layer Mixolydian, Lydian Dominant, and Blues ideas simultaneously as a single combined approach -- not sequentially or in isolation (Chapter 6, p. 31). Hybrid ideas drawn from all three sources at once are the prescribed method.

Over D7(9) or any dominant-7th chord vamp, superimpose major-7th arpeggios while simultaneously drawing on Blues Scale, Mixolydian, and Lydian Dominant scale ideas (Chapter 6, p. 35). This three-layer blend constitutes the most advanced static dominant technique in the book.

Over a dominant-7th chord vamp, the Fmaj7 interchangeable-chord substitution works better at faster tempos (Chapter 7, p. 38). This is one of the book's few explicitly tempo-conditioned substitution rules.

Over any dominant-7th chord, any chord from the same Harmonic Region may be substituted for it as an 'Interchangeable Chord Trick' (Chapter 7, p. 40). The regional relationship -- not voice-leading proximity alone -- licenses the swap.

Even when two scales share enharmonically identical pitch content, they must be visualized differently when the harmonic context changes (Chapter 4, p. 17). For example, G Major Phrygian and C Harmonic Minor are the same pitches but must be mentally pictured as distinct depending on the dominant-chord situation.
Over D7(#9) or any dominant with altered tensions, the IV-degree chord (e.g., C7) may be replaced by its tritone substitute (F#7 or Gb7), crossing into an adjacent dominant region (Chapter 8, p. 44).

Over D7(#9) -- or Bb7 functioning as the subdominant -- substitute Gbmaj7 derived from the Subdominant Minor region (Bbm) of the home key F (Chapter 8, p. 46). The derivation path is: parallel minor of the subdominant -> its relative chords, yielding Gbmaj7.

Emaj7 can replace Bb7 by extending minor-tonality subdominant region rules into major tonalities: treat the home key's parallel minor (Fm), find its relative major (Ab), and extract Minor Subdominant Region chords from Ab -- yielding Emaj7 (Chapter 8, p. 50). This is the book's densest substitution derivation.

Bm7 (a Minor Subdominant Region chord) may replace Bb7 (a Major Subdominant Region chord) over an altered dominant context, applying the regional interchangeability principle across subdominant region types (Chapter 8, p. 52).

Any non-diatonic minor-7th chord used as a substitution (e.g., Bm7 replacing F7) must be treated as Dorian -- not as a diatonic mode of the home key -- because it does not belong to the home key's chord family (Chapter 10, p. 62).

Over non-diatonic minor-7th substitution chords, hybrid ideas (Dorian combined with altered tensions from the target dominant) tend to sound better than strict modal application (Chapter 9, p. 53; Chapter 10, p. 72). The aesthetic prescription is explicit: 'Usually hybrid ideas tend to sound better.'

When a IIm7-V7-I cadence is superimposed over a dominant chord, strip the V7 degree: it loses tension-bearing capacity and collapses into the IIm7 Dorian, leaving only IIm7 and Imaj7 as active functional identities (Chapter 9, p. 53; Chapter 10, p. 69).

A stepwise chain of consecutive minor-7th chords (e.g., Bbm7-Am7-G#m7) may substitute for a single dominant target; play Dorian or hybrid ideas over each member of the chain (Chapter 10, p. 70). G#m7 Dorian over D7 simultaneously produces a combination of D Altered and D Dominant Diminished sound.

When a minor-7th substitution chord contains a note that functions simultaneously at two interval roles, identify those dual-function pitches as primary flavor generators and foreground them in the melodic line (Chapter 12, p. 120).
In superimposed cadences, apply Dorian ideas over the IIm7 degree and Lydian ideas over its relative IV chord (Chapter 9, p. 53). For example, in C major: Dorian over Dm7, Lydian over Fmaj7.

The cadence Ebm7/Ab7 replacing Bb7 should be considered as a single Ebm7 Dorian or Ebm7 hybrid chord derived from the Minor Subdominant Region (Bbm -> Gbmaj7 -> its relative Ebm7) of the home key (Chapter 11, p. 95).

Cm7/F7 may replace A half-diminished because Ao is an inversion of Cm6, which equals F7(9); further, Cm7 Dorian and Ao Locrian share the same notes as both derive from the Bb key (Chapter 12, p. 100).

C#m7/F#7 substituting for C7 should be read as a single C#m7 Dorian, which produces altered tensions (#9, b9, #11, b13) against C7; the note 'B' (minor 7th of C#m, major 7th of C) is the primary color note (Chapter 12, p. 110).

Reading the C#m7/F#7->C7 cadence as a single F#m7 Dorian or F#m7 hybrid produces a sound that combines C7 Dominant Diminished with C7alt; the note 'B' is again the pivotal color note (Chapter 12, p. 115).

Any non-diatonic major-7th chord used as a substitution (e.g., Bmaj7 replacing F7, or Gbmaj7/Emaj7 replacing Bb7) must be treated as Lydian; the Lydian scale over Bmaj7 simultaneously reveals the altered tensions of the target F7 (#9, b9, #11, b13) (Chapter 10, p. 60).
Superimpose major-7th arpeggios over dominant-7th chord contexts, combining them with Blues Scale, Mixolydian, and Lydian Dominant scale vocabulary simultaneously (Chapter 6, p. 35).

In superimposed IIm7-I cadences, the relative major of the IIm7 (i.e., the IV, e.g., Fmaj7 relative to Dm7) and the relative minor of the Imaj7 (e.g., Am7 relative to Cmaj7) are always available as additional color sources (Chapter 9, p. 53).

Bmaj7 substituting for F7 must be treated as Lydian; the note Bb (A#) -- the major 7th of B and the perfect 4th of F -- functions as a special dual-role color note that gives the substitution a distinctive flavor against F7 (Chapter 10, p. 60).

Diminished chords built on the root function as V7 substitutes because their notes lie a half step above the notes of the target dominant, creating multiple simultaneous leading tones (Chapter 8, p. 49).

The leading-tone principle governing diminished-as-V7 substitution extends beyond the half-step: a note may function as a leading tone even if it is a whole step from its resolution target (Chapter 10, p. 63).

Bo (= Fo = E7 with different bass) substitutes for the Subdominant Region chord Bb7 by functioning as C7 (Dominant Region chord) leading to Fmaj7, with all notes of E7 (except the flat 7th) a half step from Fmaj7 tones (Chapter 10, p. 63).
A half-diminished chord (e.g., Ao) may be replaced by a Cm7/F7 cadence collapsed into single Cm7 Dorian identity, because Ao is an inversion of Cm6 = F7(9) (Chapter 12, p. 100).

When the V degree of a superimposed cadence is itself a tritone substitution of a real dominant in the harmony, expand available scale colors beyond Dorian to include Lydian Dominant or Dominant Diminished (Chapter 9, p. 53).

The cadence Ebm7/Ab7 replacing D7 permits Ab7 Lydian Dominant or Ab7 Dominant Diminished because Ab7 is the tritone substitute of D7; alternatively, collapse the cadence to single Ebm7 Dorian or hybrid (Chapter 10, p. 72).
Bm7 Dorian substituting for F7 produces a combination sound between F Dominant Diminished and F Altered Scale, leading naturally toward Bb7 (Chapter 10, p. 62).

During the turnaround bars (last two bars of the blues form), rest rather than play melodic ideas in order to phrase-separate choruses and create breathing space between melodic 'stories' (Chapter 12, p. 98).

The book explicitly states it will not focus on melodic possibilities for the short turnaround cadence -- the student should not treat the turnaround as a primary soloing opportunity but as a breathing space between choruses (Chapter 12, p. 98).

Do not apply strict diatonic modal thinking over non-diatonic minor-7th substitution chords; hybrid ideas (Dorian combined with altered dominant color) tend to sound better than pure modal application (Chapter 9, p. 53).

When superimposing a IIm7-V7-I cadence, do not apply leading dominant 7th scale tensions over the V degree -- the V loses tension-bearing capacity under superimposition and becomes part of the IIm7 Dorian (Chapter 10, p. 69).

Do not become a 'parrot' by memorizing and reciting lines without understanding their underlying harmonic concept; the lines are vehicles for internalizing harmony, not ends in themselves (Chapter 4, p. 21).

Do not study the whole blues form at once; each section and each harmonic possibility must be studied and mastered separately before assembling the full form (Chapter 4, p. 21). 'It is extremely important to understand that we should not study the whole form at once.'

The Fmaj7 interchangeable-chord substitution over a dominant vamp should not be the first-choice option at slower tempos -- the book states it might sound better with faster tempos (Chapter 7, p. 38).

Bergonzi prescribes playing modal scale sequences over a dominant sus4 chord specifically to remove avoid-note constraints, allowing the player to hear the pure sound of the key without harmonic interference. 'In the example below all of the notes are played over a dominant sus 4 chord. This allows you to hear the sound of the key without having to deal with any avoid notes.' Chapter 28, p. 113.

When rhythmizing scale sequences, Bergonzi directs the student to play the pattern starting from every degree of the scale modally over a sus4 chord, making it the recommended harmonic backdrop for systematic modal transposition practice. 'First play the pattern starting from every degree of the scale (in other words modally transposing it). In the example below all of the notes are played over a dominant sus 4 chord.' Chapter 28, p. 113.

For any chord quality approached by consecutive eighth-note groupings, Bergonzi's harmony anticipation rule prescribes that late displacement positions (#6, #7, #8 for a four-note group; #5, #6, #7 for five-note groups) automatically anticipate the next chord — either by approaching its notes, stating it directly, or letting the final eighth note sound the chord. 'For #6, #7, and #8, the harmony can be anticipated. That is, starting on the "and" of three, beat four or the "and" of four, you can anticipate the next chord by either approaching notes of the next chord or by simply sounding the next chord.' Chapter 3, p. 26.

When recasting any eighth-note line into triplet gear over a dominant (or any) context, Bergonzi prescribes leaving off either the first four or the last four notes of an eight-note phrase to make the line fit comfortably in triplet subdivision. 'To make this line feel comfortable in triplet gear you need to leave off the first four or the last four notes. In this case we'll leave off the last four.' Chapter 19, p. 83.

Bergonzi prescribes that in jazz playing, eighth notes over a dominant groove should coexist with the triplet feel rather than literally become triplets — sometimes by laying back or applying a lob. 'One way to improve your feel or placement of eighth notes is to notice how your eighth notes fit with the rhythm section which is often playing off of the triplet... your eighth notes should be able to coexist with the triplet feel... Sometimes this means laying back on the eighth notes or putting some type of lob on the notes.' Chapter 18, p. 77.

Bergonzi explicitly warns against playing eighth notes as literal triplets over a dominant groove: 'This doesn't mean that your eighth notes should be played as triplets like in this example, but rather that your eighth notes should be able to coexist with the triplet feel.' The feel is internalised, not mechanically applied. Chapter 18, p. 77.

Bergonzi prescribes practicing anticipating chord arrivals (including dominant arrivals) at offsets of 1/2 beat, 1 beat, 1½ beats, 2 beats, 2½ beats, and 3 beats as explicit rhythmic grammar rules. 'Anticipate chords by 1/2 beat, by 1 beat, by 1 1/2 beats, by 2 beats, by 2 1/2 beats, by 3 beats.' Chapter 29, p. 116.

Over any chord change (including dominant resolutions), Bergonzi prescribes deliberately delaying resolution by 1 to 4 beats as a rhythmic grammar tool. 'Resolve late by 1 beat, 2 beats, 3 beats, or 4 beats.' Chapter 29, p. 116.

Bergonzi's rhythmic grammar contains an absolute prohibition on starting or ending a phrase on beat one, applicable over all chord qualities. 'Never start on beat one. Never end on beat one.' Chapter 29, p. 116.

Bergonzi prescribes that improvisers must alternate between passages that are predominantly eighth notes and passages that contain no eighth notes at all — avoiding the trap of relentless eighth-note density. 'Play predominantly eighth notes. Play without using eighth notes.' Chapter 29, p. 116; also Chapter 27, p. 110: 'Very often, less is more.'

At fast tempos over any chord, Bergonzi prescribes collapsing the felt pulse to 'two' or 'one' beat per measure to escape the eighth-note trap — the tendency to fill every subdivision. 'But if you want to get out of that zone for contrast try feeling the music in two or one. Try even perceiving a fast tune as a ballad.' Chapter 27, p. 111.

Bergonzi prescribes treating silence and phrase endings as active compositional events over any chord context: 'Leave periods at the ends of sentences and paragraphs. Know when to end your solo. Listen to the rests. The listener will invite your next idea.' Chapter 29, p. 116.

Bergonzi prescribes playing solos using only half notes, quarter notes, and dotted quarters to create breathing room and enable rhythmic dialogue with the rhythm section. 'Try playing solos on any of the tunes using only half notes, quarter notes, and dotted quarters... Playing less notes at times allows the music to breath more. It also gives the rhythm section space for a little interaction and dialogue.' Chapter 27, p. 110.

Bergonzi prescribes first playing only accents through a tune (as if part of a horn section), then slowly filling in around those accents across several choruses. 'Try taking any tune and playing just accents as if you were the saxophone or trumpet section in a big band. After playing through several choruses, slowly fill in around the accents.' Chapter 27, p. 110.

Bergonzi prescribes developing awareness of which rhythms you are using and where you are in the bar, with the explicit rule that more notes per bar is not better than fewer — only different. 'More notes per bar is not better than a few, just different.' Chapter 1, p. 7.

Bergonzi prescribes treating consecutive note groupings as independent of bar lines — playing a fixed number of notes 'within and over the bar, or through the bar.' The groupings need not even be connected; internal mental grouping affects articulation even when invisible to the listener. Chapter 1, p. 9-10.

Bergonzi prescribes that a five-note grouping may be played over 1 beat, 1½ beats, 2 beats, 3 beats, or 4 beats — the same melodic cell flexibly rescaled to any duration over any harmonic context. 'The five notes can be played as 1 beat or 1 1/2 beats. 2 beats, 3 beats, or 4 beats, etc.' Chapter 1, p. 10.

Bergonzi prescribes displacing one-bar rhythms by 1/2 beat, 1½ beats, or 2½ beats to produce perceptually distinct rhythmic patterns over any chord quality. 'Notice that by displacing a rhythm 1/2 of a beat, or 1 1/2 beats, or 2 1/2 beats, you create entirely different sounding rhythms at times.' Chapter 2, p. 16.

Bergonzi prescribes superimposing odd-meter groupings (3/4, 5/4, 7/4, 9/4, 11/4) over a 4/4 foundation as a systematic method for generating rhythmic variety over any harmonic context. The 5/4-over-4/4 cycle aligns on bar 6; the 7/4 cycle aligns on bar 8. 'This is a 3/4 pattern which takes three bars of 4/4 to work out.' Chapter 3, p. 27; alignment rules at Chapter 15, pp. 69, 71.

Bergonzi prescribes playing 3/4 rhythmic phrases over 4/4 tunes (hemiola) to ensure phrases begin from various beats rather than always landing on beat one, developing bar-line independence and horizontal playing. 'Practicing this rhythmic technique helps the improviser to become independent of bar lines and makes one's playing more horizontal... It takes four bars of 3/4 to equal three bars of 4/4.' Chapter 13, p. 63.

Bergonzi prescribes practicing hemiola (3/4 over 4/4) with a play-along while the right foot taps beat one and the left foot taps beat 3, combined with singing, to physically internalize the cross-rhythm. 'Try to practice these rhythms with a play along and also without a play along while your right foot taps beat one and your left foot taps beat 3. Also, try singing.' Chapter 13, p. 63.

Bergonzi prescribes converting consecutive eighth-note exercises into sixteenth-note (double-time) exercises by doubling up; the resulting 2/4 phrase is then repeated twice to fill a 4/4 bar. 'Take the material presented in Chapters 3-8 on consecutive eighth notes and convert them to sixteenth-note exercises by doubling up... repeat the 2/4 phrase twice to make a 4/4 bar.' Chapter 13, p. 62.

Bergonzi prescribes generating a 5/4 mirror rhythm (hemioval) by restating the same rhythm on beat 2-and that was started on beat 1, and a 7/4 mirror rhythm by restating on beat 3-and. 'By starting the same rhythm on beat 2 "and" that was started on beat 1, you get a 5/4 mirror rhythm.' Chapter 16, p. 72.

Bergonzi prescribes practicing explicit triplet rhythms on a tune and then switching to eighth notes on the same tune, in order to internalize the pocket through felt contrast. 'Practicing playing triplets is one way to get more connected to the rhythm section groove and so it can help to improve your placement of eighth notes. Try playing these triplet rhythms on Tune 8 (One Heart) and then play eighth notes to see if you feel a different pocket.' Chapter 18, p. 77.

Bergonzi prescribes expanding vocabulary by adapting any line to five distinct time zones or gears: quarter-note triplet, eighth-note, triplet, sixteenth-note, and sextuplet. These are interchangeable subdivisions deployable over any harmonic context. 'In this chapter we will consider five different time zones or gears to play in... The aim of this chapter is to expand your vocabulary by adapting lines to these varying time zones or gears.' Chapter 19, p. 82.

Bergonzi prescribes setting the metronome between 50 and 60 on the half note and repeating a line until triplets feel natural with eighth-note articulation. 'Set your metronome between 50 and 60 for the half note and play the line in its original form... Continue repeating the line until you are in the groove of triplets and phrasing them as if they were eighth notes.' Chapter 19, p. 83.

Bergonzi prescribes switching between time zones randomly and spontaneously during improvisation rather than programming gear changes, in order to develop transferable fluency. 'Rather than practicing this in a programmed fashion try using this technique randomly.' Chapter 20, p. 86.

Bergonzi prescribes a three-stage zone-mastery sequence: first go through the entire play-along track sticking to one time zone exclusively, master that zone, then master the next, then freely vary between zones. 'First go through the whole play-along track and try sticking to one time zone. Master that one and then go through and master the next, etc. Then try varying the zones moving from one gear to another.' Chapter 21, p. 88.

Bergonzi prescribes composing your own scale and intervallic sequences in a time zone as the benchmark of genuine mastery, not merely executing given exercises. 'Compose many other scale and intervallic sequences to really get the hang of it.' Chapter 21, p. 88; extended to 12 composed modal sequences over backing tracks in Chapter 28, p. 115.

Bergonzi prescribes internalizing 5-against-4 polyrhythm through repetition and articulation variation before moving to construction methods: 'Play this line or a line of your choice over and over again until you can feel the 5 against 4. Try using different articulations to enhance the sound of the line.' Chapter 22, p. 91.

Bergonzi prescribes building 9-against-4 by adding two notes to the end of an eighth-note line: 'Add one note to each bar of eighth notes or simply add two notes at the end of the original line to make nine notes per bar.' Chapter 22, p. 92.

Bergonzi prescribes building 10-against-4 by subtracting six notes from an eighth-note line, and 12-against-4 by subtracting four notes: 'Subtract six notes from the original line to make the ten notes... Subtract four notes from the original line.' Chapter 22, p. 92.

Bergonzi prescribes playing scale sequences in odd groupings of 5, 7, or 9 over any harmonic context: 'Another way to achieve similar results is to try playing scale sequences in 5, 7, or 9.' Nine-note sequences are played over four beats or two beats depending on tempo. Chapter 23, pp. 94-95.

Bergonzi prescribes that septuplets and nonuplets may be deployed over two, three, or four beats, selecting the metric span by context. 'You can try those septuplet rhythms over four beats, three beats, or two beats... Compose other broken nonuplets and play them over two, three, or four beats.' Chapter 23, pp. 102-103.

Bergonzi explicitly frames polyrhythmic mastery as a long-range pursuit, not a weekly drill: 'Becoming adept at playing all of these polyrhythms isn't a weekly pursuit but rather a long-range one.' Chapter 23, p. 100.

Bergonzi prescribes taking any fixed group of notes and reinterpreting it across different beat spans — from one beat through four beats, or compressed into 1½ beats — as a perceptual strategy for dissolving the strangeness of odd tuplets. 'Expand and try playing these five notes over three beats, and then over four beats. Next try playing the same five notes over 1 1/2 beats by contracting them.' Chapter 24, p. 106.

Bergonzi prescribes starting polyrhythmic exercises one beat early or one beat late so that the pattern crosses the 4/4 bar line, building polyrhythmic independence. 'If you need another challenge try moving all of the exercises over and starting them one beat early, or try one beat late, so that the polyrhythm goes over the 4/4 bar line.' Chapter 24, p. 105.

Bergonzi prescribes first isolating downbeat playing, then upbeat playing, then mixing the two on a single tune to develop fluid quarter-note soloing. 'Try playing just downbeats... Mix up downbeats and upbeats on this next tune.' Chapter 25, p. 107.

Bergonzi prescribes generating groups of seven by leaving out one note from two groups of four within a scale sequence. 'Leaving out one note in two groups of four creates groups of seven.' Chapter 28, p. 113.
Bergonzi prescribes adding rests within scale sequences as an active rhythmizing move: 'Leave out some notes and add rests.' Chapter 28, p. 114.

Bergonzi prescribes varying scale sequences by ascending or descending within them, and by skipping to any note in the scale to start the sequence: 'Ascend or descend within the sequence... Skip up or down to any note in the scale to start the sequence.' Chapter 28, p. 114.

Bergonzi prescribes a two-phase methodology for all sequence work: first familiarise yourself thoroughly with the sequence, then work through the possibilities with full creative freedom, composing 12 modal sequences and playing them over backing tracks. 'Start off with familiarizing yourself with the sequence and then work your way through the possibilities taking as many liberties as you'd like. Try composing 12 modal sequences and then playing each of them on one or more of the play along tracks.' Chapter 28, p. 115.

Bergonzi prescribes practicing without a metronome by meditating on a tempo, hearing quarter notes internally, then adding triplets or other rhythms mentally, with relaxation as the cognitive prerequisite. 'Internalize the rhythm section. Try to meditate on a tempo... Notice that when you become tranquil inside you then have a better perception of the time. Relax, above all, relax!' Chapter 27, p. 112.

Bergonzi prescribes varied metronome placements to develop time independence: on 2 and 4, on 1 and 3, on just 3, on just 4, or on the and of 2 and 4. 'Try using the metronome on 2 and 4, or 1 and 3, or just 3, or just 4, or on the and of 2 and 4.' Chapter 27, p. 111.

When practicing two consecutive eighth-note triplet groups, Bergonzi prescribes sounding only four of the six available subdivisions to develop rhythmic precision and selective articulation. 'Each one consists of two groupings of eighth-note triplets, but only four of the six notes are sounded.' Chapter 9, p. 47.

Bergonzi prescribes internalizing triplet groupings by playing a fixed four-note melody starting on different beats within triplet groupings before attempting free triplet improvisation. 'To get used to playing exercise #13, try playing the same four-note melody starting on the different beats.' Chapter 10, p. 49.

Bergonzi prescribes escalating from structured triplet-grouping drills to randomized practice as the final stage of mastery: 'Practice playing these preceding triplet groupings randomly.' Chapter 10, p. 50.

Bergonzi prescribes superimposing 4/4 one-bar rhythms (from the Chapter 2 palette of 22 rhythms) over a 3/4 harmonic context, and combining two 4/4 rhythms into longer polyrhythmic phrases over the 3/4 tune. 'Take any of the 22 one-bar rhythms in Chapter 2 and play them over this 3/4 tune. Next, try combining two of those 4/4 rhythms and play them over this tune.' Chapter 17, p. 74.

Bergonzi prescribes internalizing 3/4-over-4/4 polyrhythm by first practicing 3/4 rhythms exclusively, then combining any two to make a 6/4 cell, then combining four to create longer 3/4 lines over 4/4, and finally playing random 3/4-over-4/4 without any program. 'Try just playing random 3/4 over 4/4 using one 3/4 rhythm, then another and another without any program in mind. This really gets it into your unconscious mind.' Chapter 15, pp. 68-69.

In any major key, exactly two maj7 chords are diatonic: the I and the IV. Carter states: "Two major sevenths I and IV" (Ch12 p.117). This membership defines where maj7 naturally appears without alteration or borrowing in the diatonic seventh-chord taxonomy.

For physical playability on guitar, the third of the maj7 chord is displaced up an octave from its close-position location. Carter explains: "the third of the chord has been moved an octave higher" as a "standard alternate configuration" (Ch12 p.117).

When maj7 chords appear in cycle-of-fifths progressions, Carter prescribes tracking common tones held between adjacent chords while the remaining voices move by half step or whole step. He analyzes V7-to-I motion showing the tritone resolving inward and common tones maintained (Ch16 pp.155-157): "If you think of harmonic movement as several moving voices rather than a glob of dots on a chord box grid, your arrangements and improvisations will be more airy, more interesting and less clunky."

In solo fingerstyle arrangements, maj7 (and all chords) should be voiced as two or three notes so the melody can dominate. Carter states: "Chords, for instance, are most often only two or three notes, and the melody is all-important" (Ch18 p.169).

Exactly one dominant seventh chord is diatonic to any major key: the V. Carter states: "One dominant seventh V" (Ch12 p.117). Its singularity in the key makes it the primary tension chord and the defining element of the II-V-I progression.

In the II-V-I recipe, the dominant seventh is voiced with just root and third. Carter specifies: "dominant seventh defined with just root and third" (Ch13 p.129). This minimal voicing communicates the dom7 function clearly while leaving textural space for the melody above.

The tritone interval embedded in the dom7 resolves inward by half step to the root and third of the target I chord. Carter illustrates: "You can just feel the tug of the unresolved Bb and E (the tritone interval of a'5) being pulled by the A and F in the resolved F chord" (Ch16 p.156).

In modern jazz, Carter prescribes the half-step movement of the dom7 tritone as the primary voice-leading mechanism. He writes: "the half step movement of the tritone interval here on beats one and three is more common than root movement. This is especially true if you are playing with a bass player who covers roots and fifths" (Ch17 p.159).

Any dom7 chord may be replaced by the dominant seventh built a tritone away, since both chords share the same tritone interval. Carter presents tritone substitution as a practical voicing swap in Ch7.

Every introduction must conclude on a dom7 chord (V7 or substitute). Carter states: "The last chord of the intro must be a V7 or V7 substitute in order to move into the first chord of the tune itself" (Ch17 p.160).

In a tag ending, the final tonic chord is replaced by a dom7 (V7 or substitute) to restart harmonic motion. Carter specifies: "the replacement of the usual final I chord -- E, here -- with a V7 (or other substitute) chord is required" (Ch17 p.164).

Modulation to a new key can be executed in as little as two beats by borrowing the V7 of the target key. Carter writes: "You can modulate as fast as two beats...Use the last two beats to borrow V7 (Ab7) from the upcoming new key, Db" (Ch17 p.165).

In ensemble settings with a bassist, the dom7 may be voiced as stacked alternating fourths and tritones with root and fifth omitted. Carter notes: "There is no explicitly stated root or fifth of the chord. If you play in a group, the bassist will cover roots and fifths" (Ch13 p.130).

When comping behind a soloist, Carter prescribes filling the soloist's rests and thinning out when the soloist plays busily: "play more when the soloist is not playing, and play less when he is" (Ch14 p.135).

Three minor seventh chords are diatonic to every major key: the II, III, and VI degrees. Carter states: "Three minor sevenths II, III and VI" (Ch12 p.117). The II is the most load-bearing as the gateway into the II-V-I progression.

In the II-V-I recipe, the minor seventh chord at II is voiced with root and seventh only. Carter specifies: "a minor seventh defined by a root and seventh followed by the dominant seventh defined with just root and third" (Ch13 p.129).

As a self-accompaniment device, Carter prescribes alternating the root and seventh of a min7 chord in the bass. He notes: "Keeping a strict pattern of root/seventh is not as important as long as the effect (low to high alternation) is there" (Ch13 p.124).

Like the dom7, min7 chords may be voiced as stacked fourths and tritones omitting root and fifth in ensemble contexts. Carter's instruction: "There is no explicitly stated root or fifth of the chord. If you play in a group, the bassist will cover roots and fifths" (Ch13 p.130).
Exactly one half-diminished seventh chord is diatonic to each major key: the VII degree. Carter states: "One half-diminished seventh" (Ch12 p.117).

The half-diminished seventh functions as a passing or substitution chord within the cycle-of-fifths voice-leading system. Its diatonic position at VII and its flattened fifth give it a naturally unstable quality suited for chromatic or diatonic passing motion between more stable chords.

The diminished seventh chord functions as a chromatic connector between adjacent diatonic chords. Carter's characterization is definitive: "the diminished seventh chord is the in-between, the hamburger helper of" passing chords (Ch13 p.121).

The dim7 is specifically deployed to create ascending chromatic harmonic movement -- inserted between two diatonic chords a step apart to produce smooth half-step-by-half-step bass motion. Carter demonstrates this ascending chromatic application in Ch13 p.121.

When a chord symbol indicates an altered fifth, Carter prescribes a direct mechanical adjustment: raise the fifth a half step for #5, or lower it for b5. He states: "If the chord is C7#5, raise the fifth a half step, and if it is C7b5, lower the fifth a half step" (Ch7 p.77).

Melody notes are harmonized by adding a diatonic third below, with the interval quality determined by the chord symbol. Carter: "Try putting thirds below each melody note. Follow the chord symbols to check for the correct third, and/or look at the TABLE OF THIRDS on the next page" (Ch9 p.93).

When the diatonic third below a melody note is not a chord tone, Carter's rule is to let the ear decide: "Non-chord tones make for the interesting spice in an otherwise dull chord-tone-only dish. It's your ear and your decision" (Ch9 p.93).

When a melody note is ambiguous between major and minor, the accompaniment must supply the third. Carter states: "The accompaniment needs the major or minor third to clarify the specific harmony of each measure" (Ch7 p.83).

A melody harmonized only in thirds may sustain for a section but not an entire arrangement. Carter prescribes: "Put the bass back in. Even a simple root/root and root/fifth bass can turn the melody with thirds into a full three-part arrangement" (Ch9 p.93).

When harmonizing in sixths, the key note must occupy the upper voice. Carter warns: "If the key note were in the bottom position the ear would perceive the scale as being in a minor key rather than a major key" (Ch11 p.108).

Tenths below a melody note function as independent bass notes with their own rhythmic values. Carter states: "The tenth does often function as a bass note, but only infrequently does it move parallel to the melodic rhythm. More often it has its own independent rhythm" (Ch9 p.98).

Parallel tenths should not run throughout an entire arrangement because doing so locks the bass rhythm into the melody rhythm. Carter: "You probably would not use parallel tenths throughout the arrangement" (Ch9 p.98).

Arpeggio sweeps must never exceed the melody's pitch ceiling. Carter: "watch that your choice of arpeggiation doesn't reach higher than the melody, which might obscure the melody and confuse the listener" (Ch8 p.88).
Carter prescribes using arranging devices sparingly: "So here is a tune that isn't cluttered with every arranging device, but is still totally whole, missing nothing" (Ch11 p.111).

Change-running (chord-arpeggiating) is the foundational device for the II-7 chord: the improviser arpeggiates the minor seventh chord to tune the ear to its structure, learn the progression, provide pickup notes, and clarify harmony. Coker states that a change-running phrase 'does not necessarily begin on the root of the chord, it may omit one or more chord members, and its direction can be ascending or descending or both' (p. 9). Practice across all 12 keys against exercise tracks that move in the cycle of fifths and chromatically.

The b7 of the II-7 chord is the operative pitch in the 7-3 resolution: it resolves down a half-step to the 3rd of the following V7 chord. Coker explains: 'In both situations the seventh (b7) of the first chord resolves to the third (3) of the second chord, hence the 7-3 designation' (p. 20). He further notes that 'Often the 3rd of the minor seventh chord will be pulled into the embellishment (along with the 7th, of course), since both the 3rd and 7th are crucial notes for determining or establishing chord-types' (p. 22).

The dorian bebop scale is the prescribed scale for minor seventh chords: it is the dorian mode with a chromatic note added between the 3rd and 4th degrees. Coker identifies this as 'the perfect anachronism to the chord quality with which it is used; that is, a major third against a minor seventh chord' -- the added major 3rd directly contradicts the chord's minor quality, yet is '99% consistent with what we find in analyzing transcribed solos' (p. 33). Even a 3-4 note fragment containing this chromatic note implies bebop-scale use.

The bebop lick 'is a specific melodic phrase, generally taking place on dominant seventh and minor seventh chords, and closely related to the bebop scale, using a portion of that scale in its structure' (p. 40). Coker prescribes: 'Begin, however, by learning the lick (motive) in its isolated form, against exercise tracks and tunes which have a preponderance of minor seventh chords and dominant seventh chords' (p. 44), then integrate it into longer melodic lines.

Although CESH's canonical setting is a minor chord of long duration, Coker extends its application to II-7 chords: 'the examples from recorded solos will reveal that improvisers will also use CESH on II-7 chords, V7 chords (the minor CESH will actually be built on the fifth of the V7, as in G [minor CESH] on a C7), or the II-V in combination' (p. 74). Students should practice CESH patterns in all keys against appropriate play-along tracks.

The II-7 chord is fully covered by the tonic major scale as an instance of harmonic generalization: 'A D-7 chord (II of C) is usually interpreted with a D dorian scale, which is a C major scale that is re-circulated from D... Hence a progression of D-7, G7, C [major] could be realized by simply playing a C major scale or a pattern on that scale' (p. 45). This is the safest form of generalization, producing no collision tones.

A single C pentatonic scale covers A-7, D-7, and G-7 (among ten chord types total) with no collision tones: 'a C pentatonic scale (C, D, E, G, A) will fit C [major], F [major], Bb [major](+4), A-7, D-7, G-7, C7, G7(sus. 4), D7(sus. 4), and a Gb7 (+5, b9) with not one colliding [pitch]' (p. 45). This makes pentatonic generalization the safest harmonic generalization strategy available.

Coker prescribes a targeted practice approach for 7-3 resolution work centered on the II-7 chord: 'practice them with exercise tracks and tunes on play-alongs that contain a large number of II-V cells' (p. 24). When using stereo play-alongs, he recommends turning off the piano channel to test effectiveness of 7-3 resolutions without chordal accompaniment, eventually practicing with no accompaniment at all.

In Track AA practice contexts, Coker specifies that the half-diminished chord substitutes for the minor seventh: 'the letters of the root sequence for Track AA is the same as that for Track Y (C, F, Bb, Eb, Ab, etc.)' but with half-diminished chords replacing minor sevenths (p. 32). This substitution rule applies specifically to the Track AA exercise context and introduces the minor II chord of the minor II-V progression.

The 3rd of the V7 chord is the resolution target in the 7-3 device: 'the seventh (b7) of the first chord resolves to the third (3) of the second chord, hence the 7-3 designation' (p. 20). Coker grounds this as primarily a voice-leading and melodic device, not a suspension: 'we are now simply concerned with the smooth connection (voice-leading) of two chords, especially with respect to melodic, rather than harmonic, implications.' Two notes thus imply two chords with maximum efficiency.

The 3-b9 device targets the dominant seventh chord exclusively: '3-b9 refers to melodic motion from the 3rd of a dominant seventh chord to the flatted 9th of the same chord, an extremely common occurrence in improvised solos' (p. 26). The motion is bidirectional ('Sometimes the soloist will move from the 3rd up to the b9, sometimes from the 3rd down to the b9') and may be executed by leap or with scalar fill. Coker chains it with 7-3: 'The 7-3 resolution by definition, ends on the 3rd of the dominant chord. Therefore that 3rd could now proceed to the b9' (p. 26).

The 3rd of the V7 chord serves as a pivot note linking two devices: 'The 7-3 resolution and 3-b9 present our first opportunity to observe that potential... The 7-3 resolution by definition, ends on the 3rd of the dominant chord. Therefore that 3rd could now proceed to the b9, causing the two devices to overlap, with the 3rd serving as both the resolution tone of the 7-3 and the beginning of the 3-b9' (p. 26). This chaining creates compound gestures larger than either device alone.

The mixolydian bebop scale is prescribed for dominant seventh chords: the added chromatic note is 'the half-step between the seventh degree and the octave of the first degree' (p. 33). Coker identifies this as 'the perfect anachronism to the chord quality with which it is used; that is... a major seventh against a dominant seventh' -- directly contradicting the chord's b7 quality -- yet it is '99% consistent with what we find in analyzing transcribed solos' (p. 33). Coltrane uses this bebop scale pattern 21 times in an 8-chorus solo on a 16-bar tune.

The bebop lick 'is a specific melodic phrase, generally taking place on dominant seventh and minor seventh chords, and closely related to the bebop scale, using a portion of that scale in its structure' (p. 40). Coker prescribes learning it in isolated form first against tracks with 'a preponderance of minor seventh chords and dominant seventh chords' (p. 44), then weaving it into longer lines. Its application to tritone substitution contexts is a further extension.

Coker extends the bebop lick's application beyond its basic dom7 context: 'Another interesting way to apply the bebop lick against dominant seventh chords is to use it as a means of playing tri-tone substitutions (or altered dominants), an element that will be taken up later in this book' (p. 44). This implies playing the bebop lick starting on the root of the tritone-substituted chord while the underlying chord is the original dominant seventh.

CESH is applicable over V7 chords by constructing the minor CESH on the fifth of the dominant: 'improvisers will also use CESH on... V7 chords (the minor CESH will actually be built on the fifth of the V7, as in G [minor CESH] on a C7)' (p. 74). This extends CESH beyond its canonical minor-chord-of-long-duration context into the II-V motion.

The V7 chord is covered by the tonic major scale under harmonic generalization: 'A G7 chord uses, among other possibilities, a G mixolydian scale, which again, is a C major scale beginning on G. Hence a progression of D-7, G7, C [major] could be realized by simply playing a C major scale or a pattern on that scale' (p. 45). The C pentatonic also covers C7 and G7sus with no collision tones.

Dominant seventh chords are the primary target for tritone substitution: 'Tri-tone substitution is the substituting, especially of dominant seventh chords, with a chord of the same type whose root is a tri-tone (diminished fifth or augmented fourth interval, or simply three whole-steps) away from the given chord, as in substituting an F#7 for a C7' (p. 82). The substitutions sound consonant because 'the listener's ear hears the given precedents for the event, instead of the conflict with the V7.'

The IV-7 to bVII7 back door progression substitutes for V7: 'The I chord, in a given progression, is often preceded by IV-7 to bVII7, instead of the usual V7 chord. This common practice has led to improvisers using that progression (called the back door progression) even when the given chord is V7' (p. 82). Appendix B prescribes playing CMAR or GBNF starting on the 9th of the substitute chord, or the bebop lick on the 4th.

The #II dim7 chord may be used to substitute for V7: 'Like the back door progression, the #II dim7 is often used to precede the I chord (or III-7, a substitute for I) in a given progression, leading to the improvised use of #II dim7 in place of a given V7 chord' (p. 82). Coker explains this works because 'the listener's ear hears the given precedents for the event, instead of the conflict with the V7.'

Coker prescribes specific harmonic contexts for practicing the 3-b9 device against dom7: 'The harmonic settings that are most appropriate are dominant seventh chords, dominant seventh chords moving around the cycle of fifths, II-7 to V7 cells moving downward in whole steps, and II-7 to V7 (alt.) moving downward in whole steps' (p. 31). These four practice contexts systematically cover the most common real-tune dominant-seventh settings.

The Cry Me A River lick starts on the 13th of a dominant seventh chord: the lick 'starts on the: ninth of the -7 chord / thirteenth of the 7 chord / fourth of the [major] chord / augmented ninth of the 7 (+5, +9) chord / major seventh of the [+5 major] chord' (p. 73). Because the lick accommodates five chord types without alteration, its application to dom7 (starting on the 13th) is one of its highest-frequency uses.

Coker defines the altered dominant precisely: 'The altered dominant is a dominant seventh chord which contains, in its complete realization, an augmented fifth (+5), a flatted ninth (b9), an augmented ninth (+9), and an augmented eleventh (+11, or +4). Tri-tone substitutions and altered dominants are nearly identical, as shown below' (p. 82). The structural near-identity to the tritone substitute is the theoretical basis for their interchangeability in improvisation.

The bebop lick can be deployed over dom7 chords to imply altered dominant sounds: 'Another interesting way to apply the bebop lick against dominant seventh chords is to use it as a means of playing tri-tone substitutions (or altered dominants), an element that will be taken up later in this book' (p. 44). This makes the bebop lick a gateway to altered harmony without requiring a full structural understanding of the altered dominant.

The Cry Me A River lick starts on the +9 of the altered dominant: the lick starts on the 'augmented ninth of the 7 (+5, +9) chord' (p. 73). Since the lick accommodates five chord types without alteration, practitioners should identify and memorize the +9 starting tone for each key to deploy the lick fluently over altered dominant chords. The Gone But Not Forgotten lick is prescribed for the same five chord contexts.

Track AA prescribes using altered dominants in place of unaltered dominants as a systematic practice context: 'the letters of the root sequence for Track AA is the same as that for Track Y (C, F, Bb, Eb, Ab, etc.)' but with the altered dominant (and half-diminished for minor seventh) substituting throughout (p. 32). This trains the ear to hear and use altered dominants across the cycle of fifths.

Coker prescribes a specific practice context for the 3-b9 device leading into altered dominant territory: 'II-7 to V7 (alt.) moving downward in whole steps' (p. 31) is one of the four recommended harmonic sequences. This context prepares the improviser for altered dominant usage in real-tune progressions by drilling the II-V motion with the altered dominant as the target chord.

The C pentatonic scale covers the Gb7 altered dominant without collision tones: 'a C pentatonic scale (C, D, E, G, A) will fit... a Gb7 (+5, b9) with not one colliding [pitch]' (p. 45). This is the most harmonically distant of the ten chord types covered by a single pentatonic and demonstrates the device's particular value for handling tritone-substituted altered dominants.

Change-running over the tonic major chord is the most fundamental improvisational device: 'Change is a synonym for chord. Running is a synonym for arpeggiating' (p. 8). Its functions include tuning the improviser's ear to the chord structure, reinforcing form, and providing pickup notes. Structural freedoms apply: the phrase 'does not necessarily begin on the root of the chord, it may omit one or more chord members, and its direction can be ascending or descending or both' (p. 9).

The major bebop scale is prescribed for major tonic chords: 'The added chromatic note in the major scale is the half-step between the fifth and sixth degrees of the scale' (p. 33). Unlike the dorian and mixolydian variants, the added chromatic note in the major bebop scale does not produce an anachronism -- it does not contradict the chord quality. Practitioners need only a 3-4 note fragment containing the chromatic note to imply bebop scale use (p. 45).

The tonic major scale is the simplest and safest harmonic generalization, covering II-7, V7, and I in a single scale: 'a progression of D-7, G7, C [major] could be realized by simply playing a C major scale or a pattern on that scale (especially non-terminal patterns). There won't be any wrong notes' (p. 45). This is Coker's first and most accessible harmonic generalization strategy.

The C pentatonic covers C major and F major (among ten chord types) without collision tones: 'a C pentatonic scale (C, D, E, G, A) will fit C [major], F [major], Bb [major](+4), A-7, D-7, G-7, C7, G7(sus. 4), D7(sus. 4), and a Gb7 (+5, b9) with not one colliding [pitch]' (p. 45). The pentatonic's five-note structure minimizes risk of harmonic conflict across multiple chord qualities.

The Cry Me A River lick starts on the 4th of a major chord: the lick 'starts on the... fourth of the [major] chord' (p. 73). The lick's extraordinary versatility -- 'capable of accommodating five different chord-types without being altered' -- makes the 4th-of-major entry one of five equally valid deployment points, each targeting a different chord quality.

CESH's primary harmonic setting is the minor chord of long duration: 'The supposed harmonic setting for a CESH to take place is a minor chord of long duration' (p. 74). Of the four varieties, 'the most common one by far is [the variety] in minor, with the root in motion, and that is the type upon which we will focus for this segment' (p. 62). Students should anchor CESH learning to familiar standard-repertoire melodies that use this device.

Coker enumerates four CESH varieties: minor and major, each with either root or fifth in motion -- yielding minor/root-in-motion, minor/fifth-in-motion, major/root-in-motion, and major/fifth-in-motion (p. 62). The minor/root-in-motion variety is 'the most common one by far' and is the primary study focus. Real solos frequently present incomplete or embellished CESH forms: 'Sometimes an improviser will render an incomplete CESH... At other times the player will decorate or embellish a CESH to the point that the novice may have difficulty recognizing it' (p. 62).

The harmonic minor scale may be used over minor II-V-I progressions as a generalization despite producing collision tones. Coker justifies this on three grounds: '(1) most II-V-I progressions in minor transpire about twice as quickly (shorter chord durations) as their major counterpart; (2) although each of the three chords requires a different scale, the sum total of the effect on the hearer is a minor key; and (3) most players instinctively avoid the collision tones, perhaps because their ears warn them in advance of the potential danger' (p. 46).

Track AA substitutes the half-diminished chord for the minor seventh as a deliberate practice device: 'the letters of the root sequence for Track AA is the same as that for Track Y (C, F, Bb, Eb, Ab, etc.)' but with half-diminished replacing minor seventh chords (p. 32). This prepares improvisers for the minor II chord in minor II-V-I progressions, where the II chord is typically a half-diminished (min7b5) rather than a plain minor seventh.

The diminished scale can generalize over the minor II (half-diminished) and V together: 'another variation comes about when an improviser combines the II and V chords in a minor key (but not the I chord) under a single diminished scale. Again, there are collision tones present, but it can and does work, especially in the hands of the more capable improviser' (p. 46). This is an advanced extension beyond harmonic minor generalization and requires instinctive avoidance of collision tones.

The #II dim7 chord is prescribed as a V7 substitute in improvisation: 'Like the back door progression, the #II dim7 is often used to precede the I chord (or III-7, a substitute for I) in a given progression, leading to the improvised use of #II dim7 in place of a given V7 chord' (p. 82). This works perceptually because 'the listener's ear hears the given precedents for the event, instead of the conflict with the V7,' with otherwise anachronistic notes like the 4th and major 7th rendered consonant by the ear's precedent memory.

A single C pentatonic scale covers ten chord types without any collision tones: 'a C pentatonic scale (C, D, E, G, A) will fit C [major], F [major], Bb [major](+4), A-7, D-7, G-7, C7, G7(sus. 4), D7(sus. 4), and a Gb7 (+5, b9) with not one colliding [pitch]' (p. 45). Coker frames this as the safest harmonic generalization available: 'This reduces the risk of colliding pitches and opens up the possibility of searching for notes that are common to several successive chords.'

When a Back Door substitution is chosen, Coker prescribes that the improviser may play the Cry Me A River lick or the Gone But Not Forgotten lick starting on the 9th of the BD substitute chord, or alternatively a Bebop Lick starting on the 4th of that chord. The IV-7 chord (e.g., F-7 resolving to bVII7 to I) thus carries specific melodic content: 'Whenever a BD is chosen, CMAR or GBNF may be played, starting on 9th of BD substitute, or a BBL on the 4th' (Chapter 17, p. 119).

Within the Back Door substitution (IV-7 to bVII7 replacing V7), the bVII7 dominant chord is the resolution target of the BD move. Coker's melodic rule for this chord states: 'Whenever a BD is chosen, CMAR or GBNF may be played, starting on 9th of BD substitute, or a BBL on the 4th' (Chapter 17, p. 119). The 'BD substitute' referenced is the bVII7 itself, so the 9th of bVII7 and the 4th of bVII7 are the prescribed melodic starting points.

When a II-V progression occupies a single measure with two beats per chord, Coker prescribes using only one scale for the entire measure rather than switching scales mid-bar: 'Whenever a II-V progression occurs in one measure (2 beats for each chord), only one scale is given for the whole measure, since both chords are accommodated by the same pitches' (Chapter 17, p. 117).

When a II-V progression compresses to two beats per chord in a single measure, Coker prescribes a single dorian/mixolydian scale covering both the -7 and the 7 chord: 'the notes of a Bb dorian scale (for a Bb-7) are identical to the notes of the Eb mixolydian or dominant scale (for an Eb7)' (Chapter 17, p. 117). The dominant 7 chord in this context is subsumed into the shared harmonic generalization.

In the annotated play-along progression 'Urbane Blues,' Coker embeds two 'built-in' examples of tri-tone substitution -- one in measure 4, one in measure 10 -- both flagged with the abbreviation TT/AD (Tri-Tone substitution / Altered Dominant) in the second annotated version (Chapter 17, p. 117). This confirms that the altered dominant chord and its tritone substitute are structurally equivalent in Coker's system.

Coker warns that when all scales are mentally rooted on the chord root, 'the player is more subject to over-using the root, which is a questionable practice, since the root is generally the weakest note of a chord, sounding simplistic and redundant' (Chapter 17, p. 116). The root of any dominant 7 chord is explicitly identified as the weakest tone, and scales in the book sometimes begin off the root to discourage this over-use.

Coker prescribes deriving the major triad by extracting scale degrees 1-3-5 from the major scale of the chord root: 'By extracting tones No. 1-3-5 from the C Major scale, we arrive at the notes forming the C Major Triad' (Chapter 1, p. 1). Students must be able to recite, write, and play major triads in every key before beginning pattern exercises (Chapter 1, p. 3).

Coker prescribes applying the 1-2-3-5 ascending pattern to any chord with a major third -- 'This pattern may be used on any chord with a major third' (Chapter 6, p. 25). This pattern, together with its minor counterpart 1-2-b3-5, is sufficient to cover virtually all chord changes in a standard tune: 'nearly all chords contained in the tune's progression will have either a major triad on the bottom (i.e., 1-2-3-5) or a minor triad' (Chapter 6, p. 29).

Coker prescribes deriving the major sixth chord by extracting scale degrees 1-3-5-6 from the major scale of the chord root: 'Tones No. 1-3-5-6 of the C Major scale form the C Major Sixth Chord' (Chapter 1, p. 1). Because the M6 shares the major scale with the triad, M7, and M9, patterns written under a triad symbol apply equally to CM6 -- 'The use of the triad symbol in the following patterns is merely for convenience, since it would be impossible to determine exactly which chord is being used when the scale is common to all the chords mentioned' (Chapter 4, p. 16).

Coker prescribes deriving the major seventh chord by extracting scale degrees 1-3-5-7 from the major scale of the chord root: 'Tones #1-3-5-7 form the C Major Seventh Chord' (Chapter 1, p. 2). The M7 shares the same parent major scale with the triad, M6, and M9, so a single scale fingering covers all four qualities (Chapter 4, p. 16). Coker also prescribes the heuristic that 'in most instances, the M7 chord is likely to function as IM7 rather than IVM7' (Chapter 16, p. 82), reducing the decision burden when key context is ambiguous.

Coker prescribes treating the IM7 as the resolution target of the IIm7-V7-IM7 group and assigns it the major scale of its root for improvisation. The method extends one-measure IIm7-V7 patterns to accommodate the IM7 resolution by recycling mastered fragments rather than introducing new material: 'Rather than introducing new patterns, we will use four of the patterns previously discussed with the IIm7-V7 progression and extend them to the IM7' (Chapter 17, p. 90). All three chords share a single parent key signature (Chapter 16, p. 83).

Coker prescribes using the two-fragment combination 5-8-6-4 and 2-5-3-1 from the major scale to achieve complete coverage of all four major chord qualities in a single pattern: 'This pattern utilizes two fragments (5-8-6-4 and 2-5-3-1) from the chord scale, which when played simultaneously will sound any of the major forms of the chords expressed (Triad, M6, M7 and M9)' (Chapter 7, p. 27). This is the book's prescribed method for building harmonic completeness without separate patterns for each extension.

Coker prescribes deriving the major ninth chord by extracting scale degrees 1-3-5-7-9 from the major scale of the chord root: 'Tones #1-3-5-7-9 form the C Major Ninth Chord' (Chapter 1, p. 2). The ninth is the same pitch as the second scale degree -- 'the ninth, eleventh and thirteenth are also the second, fourth and sixth tones respectively, as they are the same letter names' (Chapter 1, p. 3). Because M9 shares the same major scale parent as the triad, M6, and M7, no separate scale is needed for improvisation.

Coker prescribes extracting scale degrees 1-3-5-7 from the Mixolydian mode to form the dominant seventh chord: 'By extracting tones No. 1-3-5-7 from the B-Flat Mixolydian mode, we arrive at the notes forming the B-Flat Dominant Seventh Chord' (Chapter 9, p. 50). The student must relate each Mixolydian mode to its parent key before applying formulas or playing improvisation patterns over the chord (Chapter 9, p. 51).

Coker prescribes a firm rule for dominant function: 'the chord retains its dominant function as long as the third is major and the seventh is minor, regardless of the type of ninth used' (Chapter 25, p. 119). This frees the improviser to alter the ninth, fifth, eleventh, and thirteenth freely. The fifth may be perfect, lowered, or raised; the eleventh perfect or augmented; the thirteenth major or (rarely) minor -- all without disturbing dominant function (Chapter 25, p. 121).

Coker prescribes assigning fragment 3-4-5-1 (extracted from the dominant seventh scale) to the V7 chord within a one-measure IIm7-V7: 'The fragment 3-4-5-7 is to be extracted from the scale of the minor 7th chord, and the fragment 3-4-5-1 is to be extracted from the scale of the dominant seventh chord' (Chapter 17, p. 88). An alternate two-measure assignment pairs fragment 1-2-6-5 against the IIm7's 3-4-5-7, with specific attention to the unusual interval between degrees 2 and 6 (Chapter 20, p. 97).

Coker prescribes exploiting the shared parent key of IIm7 and V7 to run a single scalar pattern across both chords without alteration: 'The pattern fits both chords because they both have the same parent key. Consequently, the accidentals in their respective scales are the same' (Chapter 17, p. 95). On a two-measure IIm7-V7, Coker assigns ascending direction to the IIm7 and descending direction to the V7: 'ascending the scale of the minor seventh chord and descending the scale of the dominant seventh chord' (Chapter 17, p. 94).

Coker prescribes using a diminished scale whose root sits one half-step above the dominant seventh chord root to simultaneously supply all four essential color tones: 'the root of the scale is a half-step above the root of the seventh chord (i.e, a C-sharp diminished scale is used with a C7)' (Chapter 27, p. 130). This yields flat-9, +9, +11, and 13 together -- 'all four color tones are common to one another and can be used together to good effect' (Chapter 27, p. 131).

Coker prescribes applying a single diminished scale to four different dominant seventh chords whose roots lie within the same diminished seventh chord: 'a diminished scale on C-sharp, E, G, or A will fit and enhance (because of the color tones provided) a C7, E-flat7, F-sharp7, or A7 chord' (Chapter 27, p. 131). This efficiency principle -- one scale serves four roots -- directly follows from the diminished-fifth substitution rule linking tritone and minor-third-related dominant chords.

Coker prescribes one of two specific Lydian Augmented Scale alignments for dominant seventh flat-5 chords: 'In the case of the dominant 7th, flat 5th (b5), the root of the scale is the seventh of the chord' (Chapter 33, p. 146). This alignment yields an augmented eleventh (flat-5) color tone over the chord. Students must learn all twelve Lydian Augmented scales 'by playing them over and over throughout the range of your instrument' and in intervallic patterns such as thirds (Chapter 33, p. 146).

Coker prescribes a second Lydian Augmented Scale alignment for dominant chords with raised 5th, raised 9th, lowered 9th, and augmented 11th: 'In the case of the dominant 7th, raised 5th, raised 9th, lowered 9th, and augmented 11th, the root of the scale is the third of the chord' (Chapter 33, p. 146). This distinct root placement -- on the chord's third rather than its seventh -- simultaneously yields all four alterations, making it the prescribed scale source for this altered-dominant context.

Coker prescribes that a turnaround (turnback) must end on a V7 chord or a flat-II7/flat-IIM7 dominant substitute: 'most will begin with a tonic chord (but only for about two beats) and will end with either a V7 chord (dominant) or a flat-II7 or flat-IM7 (dominant substitute)' (Chapter 25, p. 118). This gives phrase-endings 'a sense of direction, namely to return gracefully to the beginning of a repeated section' (Chapter 25, p. 118).

Coker prescribes using the same Mixolydian scale for both dominant seventh and dominant ninth chords sharing the same root: 'Note that the same scale is used for dominant seventh and dominant ninth chords having the same root' (Chapter 9, p. 51). No separate scale or fingering is required; the ninth (scale degree 9 = scale degree 2) is already contained in the Mixolydian parent.

Coker prescribes treating the flat-9 (minor ninth) as one of two available altered ninth options on a dominant seventh chord: 'when the ninth is added to the dominant seventh chord (1-3-5-7), it can also be augmented (+9) or minor (flat-9 -- sometimes referred to as a diminished ninth)' (Chapter 25, p. 119). Dominant function is retained as long as the third is major and the seventh is minor, regardless of the ninth's quality (Chapter 25, p. 119). The flat-9 is also one of the four color tones supplied by the diminished scale one half-step above the chord root (Chapter 27, p. 130).

Coker prescribes obtaining flat-9, +9, +11, and 13 simultaneously from the diminished scale positioned one half-step above the dominant seventh root: 'the pattern also yields the color tones of flat-9, +9, +11, and 13... the experienced improviser or arranger knows that all four color tones are common to one another and can be used together to good effect' (Chapter 27, p. 131). This is the book's primary prescription for fully altered dominant improvisation using a symmetrical scale source.

Coker prescribes deploying the Lydian Augmented Scale with its root on the chord's third to supply four simultaneous alterations -- raised 5th, raised 9th, lowered 9th, and augmented 11th -- over a single dominant chord: 'The LYDIAN AUGMENTED SCALE is an extremely useful scale in this respect... the other application supplying an augmented fifth, a flatted ninth, an augmented ninth, and an augmented eleventh' (Chapter 33, p. 145). This is one of only two prescribed scale-to-chord alignments for the Lydian Augmented Scale.

Coker prescribes deriving the minor triad by extracting scale degrees 1-3-5 from the Dorian mode of the chord root: 'By extracting the tones No. 1-3-5 from the B Dorian Mode, we arrive at the notes forming the B Minor Triad' (Chapter 11, p. 62). The student must relate each Dorian mode to its parent major key before applying any formula (Chapter 12, p. 63).

Coker prescribes deriving the minor sixth chord by extracting scale degrees 1-3-5-6 from the Dorian mode: 'Tones No. 1-3-5-6 of the B Dorian Mode form the B Minor Sixth Chord' (Chapter 11, p. 62). All four minor chord types -- minor triad, m6, m7, m9 -- share the same Dorian mode parent and the same underlying triad: 'Note that all four chords contain the same triad, B, D, F-Sharp; and all four chords use the same basic scale, the B Dorian Mode, to establish their sound' (Chapter 12, p. 67).

Coker prescribes treating min7 as the IIm7 in the IIm7-V7-IM7 chord group and deriving its improvisation scale from the Dorian mode: 'the Gm7 uses a Dorian Mode on the note G (which has the parent key of F Major)' (Chapter 16, p. 83). Because IIm7 and V7 share the same parent key, the improviser may run a single Dorian-derived scalar pattern through both chords (Chapter 17, p. 95). The heuristic is: 'the m7 chord functions more commonly as a IIm7 than as a IIIm7 or VIm7' (Chapter 16, p. 82).

Coker prescribes deriving the minor seventh chord by extracting scale degrees 1-3-5-7 from the Dorian mode (Chapter 12, p. 67), and prescribes using the Dorian mode itself as the improvisation scale for all four minor chord qualities. 'The minor triad, m6, m7 and m9 chords all use the same basic scale: a dorian mode on the chord root... The use of the minor seventh chord symbol is merely for convenience, since it would be impossible to determine exactly which chord is being used when the scale is common to all chords mentioned' (Chapter 15, p. 79). Digital patterns are therefore notated with the m7 symbol for the whole minor family.

Coker prescribes extracting the fragment 3-4-5-7 from the minor seventh chord's scale to form the IIm7 portion of the two-fragment IIm7-V7 pattern: 'The fragment 3-4-5-7 is to be extracted from the scale of the minor 7th chord' (Chapter 17, p. 88). In the two-measure version of this pattern, the fragment is extended as 3-4-5-7 9-10-9-8 (Chapter 20, p. 97). The underlying rationale is that both IIm7 and V7 share one parent scale, so fragment continuity is harmonically coherent.

Coker prescribes practicing minor seventh chord arpeggio patterns by reversing their direction on successive repetitions: 'Practice Pattern No. 108 by reversing the direction of the chord tones: descending, ascending, etc.' (Chapter 14, p. 71). Each chord lasts two beats in these exercises: 'Note: Each chord lasts two beats' (Chapter 14, p. 71). This directional reversal is the defining technical move for internalizing the Dorian sound.

Coker prescribes deriving the minor ninth chord by extracting scale degrees 1-3-5-7-9 from the Dorian mode: 'Tones No. 1-3-5-7-9 of the B Dorian Mode form the B Minor Ninth Chord' (Chapter 12, p. 67). The ninth collapses to the second scale degree by the enharmonic equivalence rule. Because m9 shares the Dorian parent with the minor triad, m6, and m7, the same digital patterns cover all four qualities (Chapter 15, p. 79).

Coker prescribes deriving the diminished triad by extracting scale degrees 1-3-5 from the diminished scale on the chord root: 'By extracting tones No. 1-3-5 from any diminished scale, we arrive at the Diminished Triad on that particular root' (Chapter 21, p. 110). The diminished triad and diminished seventh chord share the same underlying diminished scale, so chord symbol choice is a notational convenience only: 'The use of the Diminished Triad symbol in the following patterns is merely for convenience, since it would be impossible to determine exactly which chord is being used when the scale is common to both' (Chapter 22, p. 116).

Coker prescribes deriving the diminished seventh chord by extracting scale degrees 1-3-5-7 from the diminished scale: 'By extracting tones No. 1-3-5-7 from any diminished scale, we arrive at the Diminished Seventh Chord on that particular root' (Chapter 21, p. 110). The diminished scale is symmetrical -- eight alternating whole and half steps -- and has only three distinct pitch collections covering all twelve roots; mastering three scales gives complete coverage (Chapter 27, p. 130).

Coker prescribes practicing diminished scale patterns starting from every root shown in the reference chart (fig. 32), exploiting the four-root symmetry: 'Be sure to practice it using EVERY starting note illustrated on the chart in fig. 32' (Chapter 22, p. 116). Each diminished scale serves four roots -- e.g., the C diminished scale also yields E-flat, G-flat, and A diminished scales with identical tones but different starting pitches (Chapter 21, p. 109). Transposition across all four roots within each collection is non-optional.

Coker prescribes treating dominant seventh chords whose roots lie within the same diminished seventh chord as mutual substitutes: 'chords whose roots are within the same diminished seventh chord are likely substitutes for each other... chords located a diminished fifth apart, especially when they are dominant sevenths, will substitute for each other (i.e., C7 and F-sharp7). Now we see that halfway to each of the diminished fifth intervals... are two more substitute possibilities' (Chapter 27, p. 131). This yields four dominant seventh substitute relationships from a single tritone pair.

Coker prescribes adding chromatic non-harmonic passing tones between the whole-step intervals of a diminished scale pattern to create chromatic density while preserving the diminished character: 'a non-harmonic (non-chord) tone is added chromatically between pairs of tones from the scale -- pairs which are normally a whole-step apart. The result is a chromatic scale, though the scale continues to sound like a diminished scale because of the placement of the non-harmonic tones' (Chapter 27, p. 130). Placement -- not pitch content -- determines whether the diminished sound is preserved.

Coker prescribes extracting scale degrees 1-3-5 from the whole-tone scale to form the augmented triad: 'By extracting the tones No. 1-3-5 from any whole tone scale, we arrive at the Augmented Triad on that particular root' (Chapter 19, p. 106). Students are warned not to miscount the triad as having six tones due to enharmonic respelling in the chart -- 'The correct spelling for the E Augmented Triad should be E-G-sharp-B-sharp' even though B-sharp is notated as C (Chapter 19, p. 107). Only two distinct whole-tone pitch collections exist, so the student needs only two scale fingerings to cover all twelve augmented triad roots (Chapter 18, p. 104).

Coker prescribes extracting scale degrees 1-3-5-6 from the whole-tone scale to form the augmented seventh chord: 'By extracting tones No. 1-3-5-6 from a whole tone scale, we arrive at the Augmented Seventh chord on that particular root' (Chapter 19, p. 107). Both the augmented triad and augmented seventh chord share the same parent triad and parent whole-tone scale, giving a unifying principle for voice-leading and substitution (Chapter 19, p. 107). Enharmonic respelling is permitted freely to maintain correct chord spelling (Chapter 19, p. 106).

Coker prescribes the augmented scale as the primary scale source for the M7+5 chord (major seventh with augmented fifth): 'the augmented scale fits a rarely-used chord, the major seventh chord with an augmented fifth (M7+5)' (Chapter 28, p. 134). The augmented scale, spelled on C as C-D#-E-G-Ab-B, contains two chromatically adjacent augmented triads and has only four distinct transpositions. 'With slightly less effect, the scale can be applied to the major seventh chord (M7)' as a secondary option (Chapter 28, p. 134).
