Coker prescribes beginning a turnaround with a tonic major seventh chord held for only approximately two beats before permuting through other qualities: 'most will begin with a tonic chord (but only for about two beats)' (Chapter 25, p. 118). The root remains stationary while the chord type changes -- 'the root will remain stationary through two or more chords, while the chord type on that same root will change' (Chapter 23, p. 115) -- shifting function and key center through quality variation alone.

Coker prescribes two methods for constructing polychords over dominant seventh chords: use the given chord plus one of its substitutions, or build the upper triad from the ninth, eleventh, or thirteenth of the given chord -- 'proper choice of the added triad is achieved in one of two ways: either by using both the given chord and one of its substitutions; or by locating a second chord whose tones are made up of ninths, elevenths, or thirteenths of the given chord plus, perhaps, a tone or two from the given chord itself' (Chapter 25, p. 121). The added triad must not alter the bottom chord's dominant function (Chapter 25, p. 121).

Coker prescribes that non-keyboard players (such as guitarists) achieve polychord effects through rhythmic alternation rather than simultaneous voicing, beginning with Pattern No. 180: 'a large number of polychordal possibilities are investigated as well as methods for putting polychords together in patterns that will permit a non-keyboard instrument to sound two chords together by alternation' (Chapter 25, p. 121). This is the book's specific technical prescription for implementing bitonal harmony on single-line instruments.

For dom7 chords in baiao, Faria prescribes practicing all patterns against a 'static seventh chord (mixolydian mode)' -- the dom7 is the modal tonic of the style, not a functional dominant. The bass plays a syncopated pedal tone while the upper voices land on the beat, inverting the samba texture. Chapter 5, p. 121.

Faria prescribes applying baiao Variation #1 (cowbell/syncopated bass texture) 'on a typical lydian b7 mode progression,' treating the dom7 with a raised 4th as the primary harmonic color. The open-string berimbau device in Variation #2 is also anchored to this same lydian b7 modal dom7. Chapter 5, p. 122 and p. 124.

For any chord in samba (dom7 chords appear throughout the typical samba turnaround harmonies), Faria prescribes: 'The bass line keeps switching between the root and the fifth of the chord, and it's a better choice to play the fifth below the root. If the bass note is already placed on the 6th string, you may keep the same note for the whole measure.' Chapter 1, p. 25.

In frevo, Faria prescribes treating the bass movement of dom7 and other chord changes like a jazz 'walking bass, playing even quarter notes,' while syncopations are placed exclusively on the top voices of the chord. The harmonies are kept simple -- 'usually turnarounds' -- and the sixth string root is held where possible. Chapter 4, p. 102 and p. 104.

For five-voice chord voicings in bossa nova (maj7 and other extended chords appear in bossa nova harmony), Faria prescribes an explicit right-hand fingering extension: 'To play the five-note chords in this example, you must use right hand fingers 1, 2 and 3' plus additional fingers, applying the five-note technique to dense upper-structure voicings. Chapter 2, p. 66.

For diminished chords in choro accompaniment, Faria prescribes inverted voicings as the default: 'the use of triads, seventh and diminished chords are common, usually in an inverted position.' Root-position dim7 is not the idiomatic choice; the guitarist should reach for an inversion. The bass line movement around the diminished chord is treated as structurally primary. Chapter 3, p. 86.

Do not voice diminished chords in root position in choro accompaniment. Faria states they are used 'usually in an inverted position,' making root-position dim7 a stylistic error in choro context. Chapter 3, p. 86.

When the bass line in samba moves syncopated and independently from the chord, Faria prescribes the thumb for execution; but when the bass occurs in a 'block style' situation, the student must switch to the index finger: 'play the bass line with the thumb when it occurs as an independent line and with the first finger (index) when it occurs in a block style situation.' Chapter 1, p. 30.

For Samba Variation #3, Faria prescribes an unconventional but specific left-hand fingering order for voicing the chord: 'The chords must be fingered (left hand fingers) from top to bottom 3-1-4-2.' This is not left to the student's discretion -- the fingering is load-bearing for clean execution of the variation. Chapter 1, p. 30.

For a Db9 (dominant with extension) voicing in Samba Variation #17, Faria prescribes three alternative left-hand solutions for the wide stretch: 'Either use the thumb over technique or the left hand fingering 4-1-1-3-2 (from top to bottom) or play the Ab and Db notes by pressing your second finger (left hand) in between the 5th and 6th strings.' Chapter 1, p. 47.

For Samba Variation #1, Faria prescribes voicing the chord changes by switching between low and high register positions 'to simulate the agogo (a percussion instrument made of two cowbells -- hi and low pitches held together).' The variation is a mirror-image two-measure form with the register switch as the defining architectural gesture. Chapter 1, p. 26.

For Samba Variation #15 specifically, Faria prescribes a contextual deployment rule: 'Use this pattern to fill in spaces at the singer's pause or at the end of a section.' The student is taught not to apply this variation continuously but to reserve it for these structural slots. Chapter 1, p. 44.

For Bossa Nova Variation #4, Faria prescribes the same contextual restriction as Samba #15: 'This pattern is very useful at the singer's pause or at the end of a section.' An optional 16th-note displacement sub-variant is also available: 'You can also syncopate by a 16th note.' Chapter 2, p. 68.

In Bossa Nova, when a harmony change coincides with a syncopated note, Faria prescribes that the chord change arrives a 16th note before the syncopated rhythmic accent: 'Notice that the harmony changes a 16th note' ahead of the syncopated landing. This precise rhythmic offset is a defining bossa nova detail. Chapter 2, p. 69.

For Frevo Variation #4, Faria prescribes an upbeat-only texture and offers a left-hand muting technique as an alternative execution path: 'You can play this example using straight 8th notes, muting the down beats with your left hand.' The variation is described as 'a good example of a variation playing only the up beats of the measure.' Chapter 4, p. 108.

For Baiao Variation #5, Faria teaches that syncopating the bass line inflects the genre feel: 'Notice the syncopation of the bass line. It gives a salsa flavor on baiao patterns.' The student is taught that bass rhythmic placement is a genre-inflection lever, not merely a technical option. Chapter 5, p. 126.

For Baiao Variation #2, Faria prescribes using an open G string as a drone device: 'This is a typical baiao cliche on the lydian b7 mode, using a G open string simulating a berimbau pattern.' The open string is not merely a convenience fingering but a timbre-simulation prescription. Chapter 5, p. 124.

For Samba Variation #9, Faria prescribes extending the basic samba cell to a four-measure cycle that 'mixes syncopated and non-syncopated rhythms, generating a batucada style pattern.' The mixing of syncopated and non-syncopated rhythms within the cycle is the defining prescription -- it is not an error but the intended character. Chapter 1, p. 39.

Samba Variation #7 is named and prescribed as the 'Partido alto' sub-style: 'This pattern outlines a samba variation known as Partido alto.' The student is directed to learn this pattern as a distinct named genre category within the broader samba family, not merely as a rhythmic exercise. Chapter 1, p. 33.

Samba Variation #6 is defined as 'the result of syncopating every beat in a measure,' and Faria prescribes it explicitly as a counterpoint technique: 'This makes a strong counterpoint between the bass line (on the beat) and the chord changes.' The on-beat bass against off-beat chord changes is the load-bearing prescription. Chapter 1, p. 33.

For bossa nova chord accompaniment built on the clave, Faria prescribes that the clave direction must be fixed for the entire performance: 'The clave can be played as shown above or inverted, but once the' direction is chosen, it cannot be changed. Switching clave direction mid-performance is a stylistic error. Chapter 2, p. 61.

For choro accompaniment, Faria prescribes a formal modulation rule at Section C: 'The choro form is frequently divided in 3 parts -- A, B and C -- with a modulation to the V or IV chord key center in the part C.' The guitarist must navigate this modulation when reaching the C section. Chapter 3, p. 86.

Baiao Variation #4 is specifically designated for the 'broken chords' style: 'This pattern is specifically used in the broken chords style.' Faria treats this as a distinct textural category within baiao guitar accompaniment that the student should deploy as a named option. Chapter 5, p. 125.

In frevo, Faria prescribes anchoring bass notes to the sixth string where possible: 'If the bass note is already placed on the 6th string, you may keep the same note for the whole measure.' This is a voicing-efficiency rule that prevents unnecessary string crossing. Chapter 4, p. 104.

Bossa Nova Variation #3 in its short-note sub-style prescribes staccato articulation and registral reduction of the upper voices: 'It's basically the variation #3, but using short notes, and playing only the' reduced register positions. This modification transforms the texture without changing the rhythmic cell. Chapter 2, p. 67.

For choro, Faria prescribes a two-stage practice method before performing chord accompaniment: first practice with left-hand muting ('practice these patterns and variations muting the strings with your left hand'), then reinforce with body-percussion ('clapping hands in the high voices and tapping the low voices with your foot'). Chapter 3, p. 88.

Choro Variation #5 carries a specific deployment restriction: 'You can use this pattern through the entire song or at the end of a section.' Faria explicitly names the end-of-section as the idiomatic placement. Chapter 3, p. 93.

Frevo Variation #5 is designated for the marcha rancho sub-style: 'This variation is an example of a marcha rancho in 3/4 meter.' Faria prescribes the 3/4 version as a distinct deployable option within the frevo vocabulary. Chapter 4, p. 110.

Before playing the samba syncopation cliche on the guitar, Faria prescribes kinesthetic pre-internalization: 'It's also a good idea to practice away from the guitar, clapping hands on the high voices and tapping the low voices with your foot.' This body-percussion drill must precede instrument execution and applies across all five Brazilian styles. Chapter 1, p. 25.

IMaj7 anchors the tonic family alongside III-7 and VI-7; all three are interchangeable via simple substitution because none contains the fourth scale degree, making them acoustically stable and suited for phrase endings (Chapter 1, p. 6). Any of the three may be chosen as the first chord of a turnaround (Chapter 8, p. 74).

Seventh chords replace bare triads as the baseline vocabulary in jazz chord notation; writing IMaj7 and IVMaj7 instead of I and IV makes harmonic function analytically legible to performers (Chapter 7, p. 65-66).

Chords rooted on III and VI carry tonic function and may substitute for IMaj7 throughout -- in simple substitution, turnarounds, extended endings, and modulatory interludes (Chapter 1, p. 6; Chapter 9, p. 87).

An extended ending must resolve to a final major-seventh chord in a new key via deceptive cadence following the original V7, using motivic melodic material from the song; the target quality is specifically Maj7, not a dominant or minor chord (Chapter 9, p. 86).

IVMaj7 tolerates the #4/tritone in the melody -- unlike its subdominant substitute II-7, which does not -- even though both chords share subdominant function; the presence of a specific melody note can override family-membership substitution permission (Chapter 1, p. 11).

Diatonic tensions 9 and 13 are stylistically implied on Maj7 chords in standard jazz style and should be omitted from the chord symbol; writing them out explicitly is considered overkill and implies instead that a specific voicing is being prescribed (Chapter 7, p. 67).

Line cliches -- chromatic stepwise motion (typically half-steps) between the fifth and root -- are most commonly applied to the tonic (I) chord, which is the normative home of the technique; applying them elsewhere risks causing the listener to hear the embellished chord as a new tonic (Chapter 11, p. 109).

Overly complex slash chord symbols like E-7/C obscure tonic function; the prescription is to simplify to CMaj7 or G7sus4 when these symbols reveal the same vertical pitches more clearly in terms of harmonic function (Chapter 7, p. 70).

bVIIMaj7 is the one nondiatonic chord permitted in diatonic approach technique; it blends smoothly with diatonic choices because it is diatonic to the parallel Dorian scale and produces a rich sound without overpowering other diatonic chords (Chapter 2, p. 22).

In Lydian modal reharmonization, the #11 (the defining Lydian dissonance) requires a tonic pedal to be heard correctly; without the pedal the #11 is likely to be perceived as a structural error rather than a modal color (Chapter 13, p. 123-145).

Third-inversion Maj7 chords (seventh in the bass) require a root-position form of the same chord immediately before them; without this context the third-inversion voicing is heard as an incomplete voicing built on the bass note rather than as an inversion of the intended chord (Chapter 6, p. 55; Chapter 10, p. 101).

III-7 and VI-7 belong to the tonic family and may substitute for IMaj7; II-7 belongs to the subdominant family. All three qualify as valid simple substitutions for their respective family members, subject to the b9 and tritone gate conditions (Chapter 1, p. 6-7).

Avoid using a 13 or b13 in the lead of II-7 chords: the 13 produces a tritone with the chord's third, and reserving that tritone energy for the following V7 produces a more satisfying cadential flow (Chapter 1, p. 11).

The tritone (#4/b11) melody/harmony interval on minor seventh chords is disallowed across all substitution contexts because it destroys the chord's subdominant or tonic function by making it sound like a dominant structure (Chapter 1, p. 11).

The most common interpolated chord in an extended dominant chain is a minor seventh placed between two dominants; this briefly delays resolution and yields a slightly smoother texture than an unbroken chain of dominant sevenths (Chapter 3, p. 31-33).

When a min7 chord with b3 in the melody lead is displaced by a II-V7 pattern a half step higher, the b3 is recontextualized as tension 9 on the II-7 of the newly inserted pattern (Chapter 4, p. 40-41).

When a min7 chord with b5 in the melody lead is displaced by a II-V7 pattern a half step higher, the b5 is recontextualized as tension 11 on the II-7 of the newly inserted pattern (Chapter 4, p. 40-41).

In bass-line reharmonization, bass notes generating minor seventh chords must be treated as chord tones (1, 3, 5, or 7), not extensions (9, 11, 13); treating them as extensions produces hybrid voicings or overly complex chord symbols (Chapter 6, p. 54).

A chromatic II-V7 pattern pairs a minor seventh chord (or min7b5) with a dominant seventh a half step below; the root motion is chromatic and the two chords function as subdominant-to-dominant (Chapter 12, p. 119).

Minor-quality modal interchange chords (such as I-7, IV-, V-7) clash with melodies containing the major third, producing a b9 interval; melody compatibility is the governing constraint (Chapter 5, p. 45-52).

Use no more than three consecutive modal interchange chords before returning to diatonic harmony; exceeding this limit risks creating tonal ambiguity because the listener loses the sense of the home key (Chapter 5, p. 45-52).

In Dorian modal reharmonization, the I-7 chord is placed in strong rhythmic positions and approached by a two-chord cadence specific to Dorian mode (II-7 -> I-7); the modal key must be sustained for at least four bars (Chapter 13, p. 124).

Repeated use of a line cliche on a chord other than the tonic I may cause the listener to hear the embellished chord as a new I chord, weakening the sense of key; overuse on non-tonic minor seventh chords is specifically warned against (Chapter 11, p. 109).
VII-7(b5) belongs to the dominant family alongside V7, because it shares the tritone formed by scale degrees 4 and 7; it may substitute for V7 in dominant-family contexts (Chapter 1, p. 7).
The b5 displacement rule applies specifically to the min7(b5) chord: when b5 is in the lead, displacement by a half-step II-V7 pattern converts the b5 to tension 11 on the II-7 (Chapter 4, p. 41).
A minor 7(b5) may serve as the II chord in a chromatic II-V7 pattern, paired with a dominant seventh a half step below (Chapter 12, p. 119).

Do not use a minor 7(b5) structure as the upper layer of a hybrid voicing; when combined with the bass note, it tends to sound like a more traditional chord voicing rather than producing the characteristic ambiguous altered-dominant texture (Chapter 14, p. 147).

V7 is the primary dominant-family chord; its forward motion derives from the tritone formed between scale degrees 4 and 7. Dominant chords almost always precede phrase endings and typically resolve to a tonic-family chord (Chapter 1, p. 7).
Any dominant seventh chord may be replaced by the dominant seventh a tritone away (the subV7), because both chords share the same tritone interval (Chapter 3, p. 28).
Cadential dominant seventh chords are the preferred targets for displacement because they anchor phrase structure; displacing them creates a noticeable shift in harmonic shape (Chapter 4, p. 37).

Displaced dominant seventh chords may be approached by: a related II-7 forming a II-V7 pattern, another dominant a perfect fifth above, a dominant a half step higher, or any other technique in the book (Chapter 4, p. 37).

Extended dominant chains must not be overused; at medium-to-fast tempos, chords should appear only on strong beats (1 and 3) to maintain the extended-dominant sound while preventing hyperactive harmonic rhythm (Chapter 3, p. 30-32).

Altered tensions (b9, #9, b5, b13) on dominant seventh chords have most often been resolved downward in pop and jazz performance practice; upward motion is possible but must be contextually justified (Chapter 3, p. 29-30).

Extended dominant and extended II-V7 techniques work best when the melody consists mainly of quarter notes, dotted quarter notes, or half notes; with only one or two melody notes per chord, clashes can be quickly resolved (Chapter 3, p. 35).

The fourth and last slot of every turnaround template must carry dominant function, resolving by strong root motion into the first chord of the new phrase; this slot's identity is non-negotiable (Chapter 8, p. 74).

Four dominant seventh chords are related to any given diminished seventh chord; each shares one of the diminished seventh's tritones. Selected by a three-tier hierarchy: shared tritone -> dominant cadence to target -> maximum shared chord tones (Chapter 12, p. 113-119).

When root motion moves by perfect fourth or perfect fifth (as in II-V-I), resolve chord tone 3 of the dominant to chord tone 7 of the next chord, and chord tone 7 to chord tone 3 of the next (Chapter 10, p. 96).

Any substitution that creates a b9 (minor ninth) interval between the melody and any chord tone of a dominant seventh is disallowed; only V7(b9) resolving conventionally to I is exempt (Chapter 1, p. 10; Chapter 2, p. 23).

In extended dominant chains, dominant seventh chords falling on strong beats may be converted to minor seventh chords to yield a slightly smoother texture; this generates extended II-V7 patterns from extended dominant patterns (Chapter 3, p. 33).

Third-inversion dominant seventh chords (seventh in the bass) require a root-position form immediately before them; without this preceding context the chord will be heard as a type of chord built on the bass note (Chapter 6, p. 55-56).

V7(b9) is the only common exception to the universal rule against b9 melody/harmony intervals; it is acceptable because the b9 is combined with the tritone interval, and both follow established melodic resolution paths into the tonic chord (Chapter 1, p. 10).

Hybrid chord voicings produce an altered dominant sound derived from the altered dominant scale (1, b9, #9, 3, #4/b5, b6, b7, 1); the upper-layer triad or seventh chord above the bass root is the compositional mechanism (Chapter 14, p. 147).

Hybrid voicings producing an altered dominant texture lose their effectiveness when the melody contains a major or minor third above the bass note; this interval destroys the characteristic ambiguous texture (Chapter 14, p. 149).

Hybrid voicings producing altered dominant texture work most effectively at phrase endpoints rather than throughout an entire passage; they function best as deliberate tonal tools deployed for contrast (Chapter 14, p. 149).

V7sus4 belongs to both the subdominant and dominant families depending on context: subdominant because the suspended fourth eliminates the tritone, but dominant when it resolves directly to IMaj7 (Chapter 1, p. 7).
When displacement creates a melody/harmony clash because the melody contains a fourth, adjust the dominant chord's quality to sus4 to accommodate the fourth (Chapter 4, p. 39).
Slash chord symbols like D-7/G may be rewritten as G7sus4 when the latter more clearly reveals the chord's harmonic function (Chapter 7, p. 70).
Diminished seventh chords are reharmonized by replacing them with one of four related dominant seventh chords, each sharing one of the diminished seventh's two tritones (Chapter 12, p. 113-115).

Diminished seventh chords that move up by half step to a chord in root position are most often reharmonized with dominant sevenths a perfect fifth above or a minor second above the target (Chapter 12, p. 116-117).

When no obvious dominant cadence leads from the related dominant seventh into the target chord, choose the dominant that shares the greatest number of chord tones with the original diminished seventh (Chapter 12, p. 117-119).
Any diminished seventh can be expressed as four enharmonically equal chord symbols; context and harmonic function determine the correct one (Chapter 7, p. 68-69).

Two signals indicate that a line cliche is hidden inside a progression as a series of diminished seventh chords: (1) presence of a secondary dominant chord with an augmented quality, and (2) a diminished seventh that does not resolve by step (Chapter 7, p. 69).

Do not use a diminished structure as the upper layer of a hybrid voicing; it tends to sound like a traditional chord voicing rather than the intended ambiguous altered-dominant texture (Chapter 14, p. 147).

Do not use an augmented triad as the upper layer of a hybrid voicing; augmented structures in the upper layer combine with the bass note to produce sounds resembling traditional chord voicings (Chapter 14, p. 147).

I-(Maj7) is one of the twelve common modal interchange chords available for substitution in a major key, drawn from parallel harmonic minor; it introduces color via new chord tones (Chapter 5, p. 45-52).
Bare triadic chord symbols are inappropriate and stylistically incorrect for jazz standards; seventh chords are the minimum baseline vocabulary (Chapter 7, p. 65).

Fisher prescribes using the major scale for improvisation over Maj7 chords, noting that harmonizing any major scale produces two Maj7 chords (I and IV), giving the player two parent-scale choices. As stated in Chapter 5 (p. 77): 'Every Maj7 chord has two major scale choices to use for improvising.' The example given in Chapter 4 (p. 56) is CMaj7 as part of the diatonic progression CMaj7-Amin7-FMaj7-G7, over which 'you could improvise over this with the C Major scale because all of these chords are natural to the key of C.'

Fisher prescribes retaining the 3rd and 7th in any Maj7 voicing. Chapter 3 (p. 46) states: 'it is generally not a good idea to drop 3rds and 7ths because these are the tones that define major, minor and dominant chords.' Roots, 5ths, and 9ths may be dropped in combinations from a Maj7 voicing without losing harmonic identity, but the 3rd (which distinguishes major from minor) and the 7th (which distinguishes Maj7 from a plain triad) must be preserved.

Fisher defines the Maj7 construction formula explicitly in Chapter 3 (p. 30): 'The formula for Maj7 chords is: Root-3-5-7. This means that we combine the root, 3rd, 5th and 7th degrees of the major scale to build the chord. Notice that what we have actually done is add the 7th degree to a major triad.' The student is prescribed to derive all Maj7 chord fingerings from this additive triad-plus-7th rule.

Fisher defines the Maj6 formula in Chapter 3 (p. 33) as Root-3-5-6, with concrete examples: 'In the key of F this would be F, A, C and D. In the key of C it would be C, E, G and A.' The student is prescribed to build Maj6 by substituting a major 6th degree for the 7th, treated as an alternate tonic-quality chord alongside Maj7.

As with all chord qualities, Fisher prescribes retaining the 3rd in any Maj6 voicing because, per Chapter 3 (p. 46), the 3rd is one of 'the tones that define major, minor and dominant chords.' The 6th itself is an extension that may be omitted if necessary, as it falls in the droppable category alongside 9ths (though Fisher does not discuss Maj6 omission specifically, the general rule covers it).

Fisher prescribes three parent-scale improvisation choices for min7 chords, as codified in Chapter 5 (p. 77): 'Every min7 chord has three major scale choices to use for improvising.' This is because harmonizing any major scale produces three min7 chords (ii, iii, and vi), meaning a Dmin7, for instance, can be approached as ii of C, vi of F, or iii of Bb. The mode corresponding to the specific diatonic degree (e.g., Dorian for ii) is the primary choice per the mode-to-chord rule at p. 69: 'The D Dorian mode would be used over Dmin7, the ii chord.'

Fisher prescribes retaining the 3rd and 7th in min7 voicings. Chapter 3 (p. 46) is explicit: 'it is generally not a good idea to drop 3rds and 7ths because these are the tones that define major, minor and dominant chords.' The minor 3rd defines the chord's minor quality; the minor 7th distinguishes min7 from a plain minor triad. Roots, 5ths, and 9ths may be dropped.

When a min7 chord appears outside the current parent key (i.e., its root does not belong to the key's diatonic set), Fisher prescribes switching from diatonic to modal thinking. Chapter 5 (p. 83) states: 'when you get to a chord that is not natural to the key, switch to the modal approach.' For non-diatonic min7 chords, the student must identify the parent key in which that min7 is a diatonic member and apply the corresponding mode.

Fisher prescribes exactly one parent-scale improvisation choice for dom7 chords, stated definitively in Chapter 5 (p. 77): 'Every dominant 7th chord has one major scale choice.' This is because harmonizing any major scale produces only one dom7 chord (V7), so a G7 is approached exclusively via the C major scale (Mixolydian mode on G). The example given in Chapter 4 (p. 56) places G7 as the V chord in the diatonic progression CMaj7-Amin7-FMaj7-G7, with C major as the single approved scale.

Fisher prescribes retaining the 3rd and 7th in all dom7 voicings. Per Chapter 3 (p. 46): 'it is generally not a good idea to drop 3rds and 7ths because these are the tones that define major, minor and dominant chords.' For dom7 specifically, the major 3rd and minor 7th form the defining tritone that gives the chord its dominant quality and harmonic tension; dropping either destroys the chord's function.

When a dom7 chord appears on a root that is diatonic but whose chord type has been altered from the expected diatonic quality (e.g., a chord that 'should be min7, but now it's 7'), Fisher prescribes indicating the deviation in Roman numerals and switching to modal thinking. Chapter 5 (p. 71) gives the example: 'in C: Emin7=iii, E7=III7. Or, Dmin7=ii, D7=II7.' The student must identify the new parent key implied by this secondary dominant and apply its corresponding Mixolydian mode for improvisation.

Fisher prescribes exactly one parent-scale improvisation choice for min7b5 chords, per Chapter 5 (p. 77): 'Every min7b5 chord has one major scale choice.' This is because harmonizing any major scale produces only one min7b5 chord (vii), so the student identifies the single parent major scale of which this chord is the seventh degree and applies the Locrian mode.

Fisher's general voicing rule in Chapter 3 (p. 46) applies to min7b5: 'it is generally not a good idea to drop 3rds and 7ths because these are the tones that define major, minor and dominant chords.' For min7b5, the minor 3rd and minor 7th define its half-diminished quality; the b5 is an alteration of the 5th (a normally droppable tone) but in this chord functions as the defining alteration.

Fisher prescribes the Ionian mode (the major scale itself, starting from its root) as the improvisation scale over a IMaj7 chord in a diatonic context. Chapter 5 (p. 69) states: 'The C Ionian mode is used to improvise over CMaj7, the I chord.' This is the parallel-approach formulation of the mode-to-chord correspondence rule; the derivative approach yields the same scale but conceptualizes it as the parent major scale.

Fisher prescribes the Dorian mode as the primary improvisation scale over the ii min7 chord in a diatonic context. Chapter 5 (p. 69) is explicit: 'The D Dorian mode would be used over Dmin7, the ii chord.' In the derivative approach, Dorian is simply the parent major scale played from its second degree; in the parallel approach it is a distinct fingering memorized independently.

Fisher issues an implicit proscription against using multiple parent-scale options for dom7: because harmonizing any major scale produces only one dom7 (V7), there is only one legal parent-scale choice. Chapter 5 (p. 77) makes this absolute: 'Every dominant 7th chord has one major scale choice.' Unlike min7 (three choices) or Maj7 (two choices), the student may not substitute an alternate parent scale over a dom7 without violating the diatonic system.

Like dom7, Fisher proscribes multiple parent-scale options for min7b5: 'Every min7b5 chord has one major scale choice' (Chapter 5, p. 77). This stands in contrast to the three choices available for min7, and is a hard constraint -- the student must identify the single parent major scale of which the min7b5 is the seventh degree.

Fisher explicitly proscribes dropping the 3rd or 7th from Maj7 voicings. Chapter 3 (p. 46): 'it is generally not a good idea to drop 3rds and 7ths because these are the tones that define major, minor and dominant chords.' While roots, 5ths, and 9ths may be omitted freely, removing the 3rd collapses the chord to ambiguous (no major/minor distinction) and removing the 7th collapses it to a major triad, destroying the Maj7 harmonic meaning.

Fisher proscribes dropping the 3rd or 7th from min7 voicings, per Chapter 3 (p. 46): 'it is generally not a good idea to drop 3rds and 7ths because these are the tones that define major, minor and dominant chords.' For min7, the minor 3rd is what marks it as minor rather than major or dominant, and the 7th distinguishes it from a plain minor triad.

Fisher proscribes dropping the 3rd or 7th from dom7 voicings, per Chapter 3 (p. 46): 'it is generally not a good idea to drop 3rds and 7ths because these are the tones that define major, minor and dominant chords.' For dom7, the major 3rd and minor 7th form the tritone interval that is the chord's defining acoustic signature; removing either tone destroys the dominant quality and its voice-leading tension.

Fisher proscribes applying diatonic major-scale thinking over a dom7 chord whose root is non-diatonic to the current key. Chapter 5 (p. 83): 'when you get to a chord that is not natural to the key, switch to the modal approach.' A secondary dominant (e.g., E7 in the key of C) must trigger a modal-thinking switch -- not be treated as belonging to the C major scale -- since its altered tones (here, G# on E7) are outside the diatonic set.

Fisher prescribes combining locked-position (vertical) and open-position (horizontal) thinking when comping or improvising over any chord including Maj7. Chapter 6 (p. 90) warns: 'when you use it [locked position] to the exclusion of horizontal thinking... it can severely limit your improvisational ideas.' The student must not default to a single positional box over static Maj7 vamps but actively move between string-crossing patterns and along-string horizontal lines.

Fisher prescribes voicing the ii chord (e.g., Dmin9) as a rootless chord on each of the three string sets (6-5-4-3, 5-4-3-2, 4-3-2-1): 'Note that the roots have been omitted from both the Dmin9 and G9 voicings. This is to allow the use of more interesting chords.' The essential 3rd and 7th must be retained; root and 5th are expendable. Chapter 3, p.56.

Fisher prescribes learning sample licks over minor chords, transposing them to all twelve keys, and inserting them into solos immediately: 'Here are some sample licks to use over minor chords. Once again, learn, transpose and insert these into your solos as soon as possible!' Begin each lick phrase on a chord tone, preferring 3rds and 7ths as target notes. Chapter 4, p.64.

Fisher introduces the min7b5 (half-diminished) chord as a specific lick target requiring dedicated ear familiarization: 'There are many ways to improvise over min7b5 (half-diminished) chords. Here are just a few licks to help you get used to the sound.' The prescription is to learn the provided licks as an entry point into the unfamiliar sound of the chord before attempting broader substitution strategies. Chapter 4, p.72.

Fisher prescribes playing a Major 7th arpeggio rooted on the flat-7 of the V7 chord to voice its upper extensions: 'Simply play the notes of a major 7th arpeggio rooted on the b7 degree of the V7 chord in any ii-V7-I progression. For example, if the V7 chord is G7, you can play an FMaj7 arpeggio because F is the b7 of the G7. Notice that this technique works nicely because you are actually just playing the upper extensions of the G7 chord: A is the 9th, C is the 11th and E is the 13th.' The arpeggio need not start on its own root. Chapter 3, p.49.

Fisher prescribes substituting a diminished triad from the 3rd, 5th, or 7th of the V7 chord to produce altered extensions that resolve into the I chord: 'Play a diminished triad starting at the 3rd, 5th or 7th degree of the V7 chord in any ii-V7-I progression. For instance, if the V7 chord is G7, you can play a Bdim arpeggio, a Ddim arpeggio or an Fdim arpeggio. These tones will resolve nicely into the I chord.' The alteration produces a b9 and a b11 (enharmonic 10) among the extensions. Chapter 3, p.51.

Fisher prescribes playing ascending scale-wise lines beginning on a chord tone of the V7, and alternating these with descending patterns for contour variety: 'Simply play ascending scale-wise patterns starting from chord tones' and 'Alternating ascending and descending patterns will give your line a more interesting contour.' The ascent must be anchored to a chord tone at its start. Chapter 3, p.53-55.

Fisher prescribes learning dominant licks over unaltered V7 chords and extending their application to 9th, 11th, and 13th voicings: 'Here are some licks that will work well over unaltered dominant chords. Try using them over dominant 9th, 11th and 13th chords as well. Transpose them and apply them to your solos.' The prescription demands immediate transposition to all twelve keys. Chapter 4, p.68.

Fisher identifies the dom7b5 as 'an extremely important sound in jazz' built from the formula Root-3-b5-b7 (e.g., C-E-Gb-Bb in C). It is described as the familiar V7 chord with a lowered 5th. Fisher's substitution constraint applies: 'context is everything. Just because a substitution is theoretically correct doesn't mean it sounds good in every instance.' Chapter 2, p.18 and p.34.

Fisher prescribes the rootless dom7b9 as a symmetric voicing that can be moved at minor-third intervals around the fingerboard without changing chord quality: 'when you drop the root, you can move the same fingering around the fingerboard at intervals of a minor 3rd without changing the chord's quality.' The formula is Root-3-5-b7-b9 (e.g., E-G#-B-D-F in E). Fisher establishes this minor-third symmetry as a practical fingerboard shortcut. Chapter 2, p.24.

Fisher identifies the dom7#5 as 'another very common sound in jazz' that is 'immediately recognizable,' built from the formula Root-3-#5-b7 (e.g., G-B-D#-F in G). It appears under multiple symbols including 7+, 7aug, and 7b13; adding the 9th yields 9#5 or 9+. Fisher's ear-and-context substitution constraint governs its deployment: theoretical correctness alone does not justify its use. Chapter 2, p.21 and p.34.

Fisher prescribes the maj7 as the tonic resolution target of the ii-V7-I, with the major scale of the I chord governing diatonic improvisation: 'use the major scale of the I chord. If the progression is Gmin7-C7-FMaj7, improvise using the F Major scale.' The maj7 chord's 3rd and 7th must be retained in any voicing; root and 5th may be omitted. Chapter 1, p.8 and Chapter 2, p.17.

Fisher prescribes learning eight sample licks over major-type chords, immediately transposing them to all twelve keys, and inserting them into real songs: 'These licks are labeled with major 7th chords but will work equally well with major 6th, major 9th and major 13th chords. Experiment and let your ear be your guide.' The lick family is explicitly extended to major 6th, 9th, and 13th voicings. Chapter 4, p.60.

Fisher proscribes applying the I-chord major scale rule when the maj7 (or any chord in the ii-V7-I) contains altered tones outside that scale: 'all chords with a raised or lowered 5th, 9th or 11th would make this rule inapplicable, because these altered tones are not diatonic.' When alteration is present, the player must find a scale that accommodates those altered tones rather than defaulting to the major scale. Chapter 1, p.8.

Fisher proscribes applying any chord substitution -- including theoretically valid ones -- without testing it against musical context and ear: 'Remember that when enhancing or substituting chords, context is everything. Just because a substitution is theoretically correct doesn't mean it sounds good in every instance. Experimentation is the way we find out what works.' This applies specifically to all V7 substitution moves including 7b5, 7#5, 7b9, and diminished triad substitutions. Chapter 2, p.34.

Fisher proscribes altering any chord degree other than the 5th, 9th, or 11th: 'the only notes that can be altered in any chord are the 5th, 9th and the 11th.' This boundary applies across all dominant variants (dom7b5, dom7#5, dom7b9) and governs what extensions are permissible in any ii-V7-I chord. Chapter 2, p.17.

Fisher proscribes simultaneous free comping by both guitarist and keyboardist: 'When playing with a keyboard player, it is preferable to take turns comping behind the soloist. If both the guitarist and the keyboard player comp freely at the same time the tune will become like a harmonic can of worms.' The prescription is to alternate the comping role and always listen carefully to what is happening around you. Chapter 3, p.47.

Fisher prescribes down strokes on downbeats and up strokes on upbeats for swing comping, with string damping during rests: 'It's a good idea to strum down on the downbeats and to strum up on the upbeats. This will help you keep your place in the measure. Also, try to damp the strings so that the chords don't sustain during the rests.' Damping is achieved by releasing left-hand pressure or stopping strings with the right-hand palm or wrist. Chapter 3, p.47.

Fisher prescribes an improvisatory approach to swing comping where rhythm is implied rather than stated mechanically: 'Unlike rock, pop and country music, the rhythm in a swing feel is implied. The beat is often suggested by the guitarist. Predictable rhythm parts are considered to be trite, so the guitarist is left to accent various parts of each measure, usually with an element of surprise and with a spirit of improvisation.' The comping guitarist must vary accents unpredictably across the measure. Chapter 3, p.47.

Fisher prescribes organizing V7 chord voicings (e.g., G9) across the three string sets (6-5-4-3, 5-4-3-2, 4-3-2-1) as rootless chords to permit more extensions: 'Playing rootless chords often permits the use of more extensions in chord voicings. The various voices can actually imply the sound of the root. Try to hear the root in your head when playing these chords.' In ensemble contexts the bass player provides the root. Chapter 3, p.56.

Fisher prescribes using the major 7th chord as a melodic device over dominant function, specifically playing a Maj7 arpeggio rooted on the b7 of the V7 chord to imply upper extensions (9th, 11th, 13th). The arpeggio need not begin on its own root: 'Notice that you don't have to start the major 7th arpeggio on the root of the Maj7 chord.' This is the primary technique for adding color to V7 lines. Chapter 3, p.49.

Fisher prescribes three interchangeable scalar tools for soloing over dominant 7th chords in blues contexts -- the minor pentatonic scale, blues scale, and Mixolydian mode: 'This lesson begins with a review of the minor pentatonic scale, blues scale and Mixolydian mode fingerings.' These are presented in C and must be transposed. Mature application combines these tools fluidly across the entire fingerboard rather than staying in a single position. Chapter 5, p.78-79.

Fisher prescribes creating and memorizing transposable licks specifically for V7 chords within turnaround contexts: 'Obviously, if turnarounds are common, you will need to know how to improvise your way through them. Create licks that you know will work over various turnarounds. This will help you make melodically smoother transitions back to the beginnings of your tunes. Memorize and transpose the ones you like.' Chapter 8, p.88.

Fisher prescribes using the I chord as the anchor and goal of turnaround progressions, directing the guitarist to choose among many available turnaround types and lead the ensemble: 'Generally, the guitarist can choose to play any one of the many kinds of turnarounds possible and it's up to the other players to react. For variety's sake, it pays to know a lot of different turnarounds.' When playing four-measure turnarounds, chord durations from two-measure equivalents are simply doubled. Chapter 7, p.86.

Fisher prescribes beginning each improvised phrase on a chord tone of the V7 (or any chord being soloed over), with 3rds and 7ths preferred: 'begin each phrase you play with a note of the chord that you are improvising over. This is called spelling out the changes, targeting chord tones, or using target notes... Improvisors tend to use 3rds and 7ths the most, because these notes are what give a chord its distinctive quality.' Chapter 2, p.26.

Fisher prescribes approaching target chord tones on the V7 with neighbor tones a half step or whole step above or below: 'By far, the most common neighbor tones are the notes one half step below and above the chord tone. Neighbor tones a whole step below and above are common too.' Half-step neighbors are the primary approach device; whole-step neighbors are secondary. Chapter 2, p.31.

Fisher proscribes confining scale-based improvisation to organized fingerboard positions: 'At first, we tend to organize them into patterns in different areas of the fingerboard. In actual practice, we usually combine the various tools and utilize the entire fingerboard. This is because the ideas we hear in our heads don't always conform to organized fingering patterns.' The prescription is to combine all scalar tools across the full neck to follow internally heard ideas. Chapter 5, p.79.

When arranging chord melody, find voicings that place the melody note on top of the major chord. It is often necessary to raise the melody one octave to accommodate larger major chord voicings on the fingerboard (Chapter 2, p. 9). Explore the melody in single notes across every octave before selecting a major voicing.

references.source: Fisher, Jody - Jazz Guitar Method, Vol 3 (Mastering Chord Melody)

notes.narrative: Within the major chord family, all members--Major 6th, Major 7th, Major 9th--are functionally interchangeable; adding extensions or alterations to a basic major chord constitutes enhancement, not substitution (Chapter 2, p. 12). Context and taste should guide how much enrichment is applied, since not everything needs to be enhanced.

references.source: Fisher, Jody - Jazz Guitar Method, Vol 3 (Mastering Chord Melody)

notes.narrative: Not every major chord needs harmonic enrichment; context is everything and taste should be the primary concern when deciding whether to add extensions to a major chord (Chapter 2, p. 12). Enriching indiscriminately undermines the musical impact of enhancement.

references.source: Fisher, Jody - Jazz Guitar Method, Vol 3 (Mastering Chord Melody)

notes.narrative: When approaching a major I chord, it may be preceded by a IV chord--a major chord whose root is a perfect 4th higher--to handle both non-chord tones and chord tones as passing harmonization (Chapter 4, p. 39). This technique creates smooth voice-leading into the major tonic.

references.source: Fisher, Jody - Jazz Guitar Method, Vol 3 (Mastering Chord Melody)

notes.narrative: A major chord may be embellished by using another major chord a half step above or below as a passing chord, applying the same quality as the chord being approached (Chapter 4, p. 38). This like-quality passing technique is a fundamental method for chord embellishment.

references.source: Fisher, Jody - Jazz Guitar Method, Vol 3 (Mastering Chord Melody)

notes.narrative: All chords within the minor family are functionally interchangeable; minor 7th, minor 9th, and minor 6th chords may be substituted for one another as enhancements without changing harmonic function (Chapter 2, p. 12). This enables flexible voicing selection when harmonizing a melody note over a minor chord.

references.source: Fisher, Jody - Jazz Guitar Method, Vol 3 (Mastering Chord Melody)

notes.narrative: When approaching a minor chord, a minor chord a half step above or below may serve as a passing chord of the same quality, creating smooth chromatic voice-leading into the target minor harmony (Chapter 4, p. 38).

references.source: Fisher, Jody - Jazz Guitar Method, Vol 3 (Mastering Chord Melody)

notes.narrative: The minor ii chord is a load-bearing element of the ii-V7-I progression, which defines or establishes a key through characteristic movement of roots, 3rds, and 7ths (Chapter 4, p. 40). Backcycling extends this by preceding the ii chord with its own ii-V7, repeating the fourth-movement pattern systematically.

references.source: Fisher, Jody - Jazz Guitar Method, Vol 3 (Mastering Chord Melody)

notes.narrative: A dominant seventh chord--altered or unaltered--whose root is a half step higher or lower than the target chord functions as a passing chord to smooth transitions; these chords may be non-diatonic (Chapter 3, p. 23). This is one of the most common applications of passing chords in chord-melody arranging.

references.source: Fisher, Jody - Jazz Guitar Method, Vol 3 (Mastering Chord Melody)

notes.narrative: When a progression moves from V7 to I, the V7 may be replaced by a dominant chord whose root is a tritone (diminished 5th / augmented 4th, equal to three whole steps) away, while maintaining harmonic function (Chapter 4, p. 45). This technique also applies to secondary dominant chords within a progression.

references.source: Fisher, Jody - Jazz Guitar Method, Vol 3 (Mastering Chord Melody)

notes.narrative: Any chord may be approached by another chord whose root is a tritone away from the destination chord's root--this is distinct from the V7-based tritone substitution because the substitute is deduced from the destination root rather than the V7 root (Chapter 5, p. 48). This root-distance approach broadens tritone substitution beyond dominant function.

references.source: Fisher, Jody - Jazz Guitar Method, Vol 3 (Mastering Chord Melody)

notes.narrative: Any chord in a progression may be treated as a temporary I chord and preceded by its own V7 (secondary dominant), enhanced or altered as desired (Chapter 4, p. 39). This generalizes the V7-I principle across the entire progression, expanding the dominant's harmonic reach.

references.source: Fisher, Jody - Jazz Guitar Method, Vol 3 (Mastering Chord Melody)

notes.narrative: Dominant chord voicings that include 9ths and altered 5ths may be transposed by whole steps and still retain their dominant function, enabling harmonic color variety without changing chord quality (Chapter 6, p. 60). This symmetrical movement is a primary tool for discovering new dominant voicings from familiar shapes.

references.source: Fisher, Jody - Jazz Guitar Method, Vol 3 (Mastering Chord Melody)

notes.narrative: The 3rd and 7th of the dominant chord are the most important tones for defining its quality and for effective voice leading, since they differentiate dominant from major and minor chords (Chapter 3, p. 22). Arrange voicings so these anchor tones move in whole and half steps between chord changes.

references.source: Fisher, Jody - Jazz Guitar Method, Vol 3 (Mastering Chord Melody)

notes.narrative: A diminished chord positioned a half step below the target chord's root serves as a common substitute for the V7, because the two chords share three notes in common and both resolve similarly to the I chord (Chapter 3, p. 30). This makes the diminished a practical drop-in replacement for the dominant in chord-melody arrangements.

references.source: Fisher, Jody - Jazz Guitar Method, Vol 3 (Mastering Chord Melody)

notes.narrative: Diminished chords repeat themselves every three frets on the fingerboard, so many possible voicing locations are available for any given diminished chord (Chapter 3, p. 28). This symmetry allows the arranger to choose the most ergonomic or voice-leading-friendly position when using a diminished as a passing or substitute chord.

references.source: Fisher, Jody - Jazz Guitar Method, Vol 3 (Mastering Chord Melody)

notes.narrative: Place a diminished chord a half step below the target chord to create a smooth passing harmony that pulls convincingly toward the destination, functioning equivalently to the dominant seventh's resolution (Chapter 3, p. 30). This is a foundational move for harmonizing both chord tones and non-chord tones as passing material.

references.source: Fisher, Jody - Jazz Guitar Method, Vol 3 (Mastering Chord Melody)

notes.narrative: Chords constructed by stacking 4ths rather than 3rds (quartal harmony) offer an alternative harmonic color for harmonizing non-chord tones and chord tones alike in a chord-melody arrangement (Chapter 3, p. 33). Quartal voicings provide a distinct sound that contrasts with conventional tertian harmony.

references.source: Fisher, Jody - Jazz Guitar Method, Vol 3 (Mastering Chord Melody)

notes.narrative: Always arrange a song with basic chords first; only after the basic arrangement is solid should harmonies be dressed up with passing chords, substitutions, and harmonizations (Chapter 2, p. 11). Applying enrichment before the structural foundation is established undermines the arrangement's coherence.

references.source: Fisher, Jody - Jazz Guitar Method, Vol 3 (Mastering Chord Melody)

notes.narrative: Do not enrich or substitute chords before the skeletal arrangement is firmly in hand; building complexity on an unstable foundation prevents confident improvised harmonization (Chapter 2, p. 11). The procedural sequence--basic chords first, then passing chords and substitutions--is non-negotiable.

references.source: Fisher, Jody - Jazz Guitar Method, Vol 3 (Mastering Chord Melody)

notes.narrative: Do not carve arrangements or chord changes in stone; treat them as skeletal frameworks from which to improvise melodically, harmonically, and rhythmically (Chapter 2, p. 11). Flexibility and playfulness in performance are the goal, not fixed execution of a written score.

references.source: Fisher, Jody - Jazz Guitar Method, Vol 3 (Mastering Chord Melody)

notes.narrative: Non-chord tones appearing in the melody may be harmonized by adding them directly to the underlying chord as extensions or alterations, effectively renaming the chord while enhancing it (Chapter 3, p. 19). This is a primary method for generating chord enhancements organically from the melody.

references.source: Fisher, Jody - Jazz Guitar Method, Vol 3 (Mastering Chord Melody)

notes.narrative: Both chord tones and non-chord tones may be harmonized with diads (double-stops), with 3rds and 6ths being the most common intervals (Chapter 3, p. 18). Any interval is possible but 3rds and 6ths produce the most idiomatic results in chord-melody and melodic contexts.

references.source: Fisher, Jody - Jazz Guitar Method, Vol 3 (Mastering Chord Melody)

notes.narrative: Doubling melody notes in octaves creates a stronger effect than single notes, and is appropriate when melodic emphasis is desired--Wes Montgomery and George Benson are cited as authoritative models (Chapter 3, p. 36). This technique applies across all chord qualities as a melodic emphasis device.

references.source: Fisher, Jody - Jazz Guitar Method, Vol 3 (Mastering Chord Melody)

notes.narrative: Good voice leading requires that individual voices travel in whole and half steps between chord changes; prioritize the 3rd and 7th of each chord as they define quality and anchor stepwise motion (Chapter 3, pp. 21-22). Smooth voice movement is the primary criterion when selecting voicings for a chord-melody arrangement.

references.source: Fisher, Jody - Jazz Guitar Method, Vol 3 (Mastering Chord Melody)

notes.narrative: Memorize chord changes and voicings in multiple areas of the fingerboard, learning them systematically in all twelve keys before applying bass-line approaches (Chapters 2 and 5, pp. 11, 50). Fingerboard flexibility across positions is essential for real-time improvised harmonization.

references.source: Fisher, Jody - Jazz Guitar Method, Vol 3 (Mastering Chord Melody)

notes.narrative: Finger voicings with as few fingers as possible--often two--to keep additional fingers free for playing melodies and improvising (Chapter 5, p. 50). Economy of left-hand fingering is especially critical in two-part bass-line arrangements where melody must be added over chord and bass.

references.source: Fisher, Jody - Jazz Guitar Method, Vol 3 (Mastering Chord Melody)

notes.narrative: Discover new voicings by moving individual voices of familiar chord shapes to higher or lower octaves; many sounds are waiting to be discovered within shapes already known (Chapter 6, p. 60). This technique applies across all chord qualities and is the primary method for expanding voicing vocabulary without learning new shapes.

references.source: Fisher, Jody - Jazz Guitar Method, Vol 3 (Mastering Chord Melody)

notes.narrative: Knowing hundreds of chord voicings and techniques is not as important as finding your artistic voice and expressing it; how you use what you know matters more than how much you know (Chapter 6, p. 63). Voicing and technique accumulation is a means to flexibility, not the end goal.

references.source: Fisher, Jody - Jazz Guitar Method, Vol 3 (Mastering Chord Melody)

notes.narrative: Reharmonize sections of a tune by composing a new bass line and letting that bass line guide and drive harmonic choices (Chapter 6, p. 62). This compositional approach treats the bass line as the primary harmonic generator rather than a consequence of pre-selected chord changes.

references.source: Fisher, Jody - Jazz Guitar Method, Vol 3 (Mastering Chord Melody)

notes.narrative: In two-part bass-line arrangements, put a bass note on every beat and have chords appear as accented punches; maintain a realistic volume balance between bass notes and chords as if a bass player and guitarist were playing together (Chapter 5, p. 51). The two parts must remain dynamically and rhythmically distinct.

references.source: Fisher, Jody - Jazz Guitar Method, Vol 3 (Mastering Chord Melody)

notes.narrative: Achieve rhythmic separation in two-part arrangements by playing the bass note on the downbeat and delaying the triad chord slightly after--but within the same beat--to break up quarter-note monotony and simulate two separate instruments (Chapter 5, p. 54).

references.source: Fisher, Jody - Jazz Guitar Method, Vol 3 (Mastering Chord Melody)

notes.narrative: Whenever possible, let two notes of the triad ring while moving to the next bass note to sustain harmonic continuity across the bass-line movement (Chapter 5, p. 55). Practice this slowly to master the physical mechanics before applying it at tempo.

references.source: Fisher, Jody - Jazz Guitar Method, Vol 3 (Mastering Chord Melody)

notes.narrative: Connect triad voicings in a bass-line arrangement by using tones of the scale that the chord is built from as connective bass notes between chord positions (Chapter 5, p. 51). Scale-tone connections give the bass line melodic logic and walking-bass realism.

references.source: Fisher, Jody - Jazz Guitar Method, Vol 3 (Mastering Chord Melody)

notes.narrative: Approach any chord voicing from a note a half step above or below the lowest voice in the triad--a fundamental feature of walking bass lines that adds chromatic movement and realism to chord-melody arrangements (Chapter 5, p. 53).

references.source: Fisher, Jody - Jazz Guitar Method, Vol 3 (Mastering Chord Melody)

notes.narrative: In Chapter 2, Greenan establishes that the major 7th chord is the tonic chord of the Major Diatonic Series and functions as the resolution point of ii-V-I progressions. Its formula is Root-3-5-7, and the 3rd and 7th are the defining guide tones that must be targeted during improvisation.

In Chapter 4, Greenan states the formula for a major 7 chord is 'Root-3rd-5th-7th' and instructs the student that the 3rd and 7th are the guide tones -- the most important chord tones to use as melodic anchors over any maj7 chord. 'Continue to let the 3rds and 7ths of each chord be your guide.'

In Chapter 8, when moving from Cmaj7 to Cmin7, Greenan instructs the student to adjust only the b3 and b7 -- 'The only difference between a major 7 chord and a minor 7 chord is the minor has a b3 and a b7. Make this adjustment and you are good to go!' All other tones remain stable.

In Chapter 11, the Note Choice Map assigns Ionian (the parent major scale, formula 1-2-3-4-5-6-7) as the prescribed pitch collection over maj7 chords functioning as tonic. For example, EbMAJ7 maps to Ionian and BbMAJ7 maps to Ionian in the Stella by Starlight analysis.

In Chapter 8, Greenan presents the bIImaj7 chord as a tritone substitution variant and chromatic passing chord replacing the V7 in a ii-V-I. 'The easiest way to think of this chord is a substitute for the V chord... bars 5-7 are a ii-V-I with a replacement for the V chord.' The bIImaj7 itself carries major quality, distinguishing it from a standard dominant tritone sub.

In Chapter 2, the minor 7th chord is established as the ii chord of jazz's most essential progression: 'there is no more important chord progression to know than the ii-V-I.' The formula is Root-b3-5-b7, and its 3rd and 7th are guide tones that resolve to the 3rd of the V7 chord via stepwise motion.

In Chapter 10, Greenan states a generalized rule: 'Where there is a V chord, you can almost always add a ii in front of it.' This means any min7 chord can be inserted before its companion dom7 to expand a V-I into a ii-V-I, and the student should deploy this expansion actively when navigating standards.

In Chapters 2 and 6, Greenan instructs that diatonic minor chords can and should be converted to dominant 7ths in jazz contexts. 'It is entirely normal and acceptable to turn minor chords in the diatonic series into dominant 7th chords.' The vi minor is the most frequently cited target for this conversion, generating secondary-dominant chains (VI7).

In Chapter 7, Greenan establishes that when a min7 chord functions as the ii chord or as a modal tonic (as in 'So What'), the Dorian mode (formula 1-2-b3-4-5-6-b7) is the prescribed pitch collection. D Dorian and Eb Dorian are the two operative modes for the entire tune. The student is instructed to treat Dorian not as a scale to run but as a 'note choice' inventory.

In Chapter 7, Greenan explicitly instructs the student to abandon guide-tone technique over modal min7 chords: 'Because So What is based on modal harmony, there is no need to identify the guide tones. This is because there is little to no harmonic movement actually happening.' Instead, modes serve as pitch collections and diatonic arpeggios connected by nearest chord tone replace guide-tone voice leading.

In Chapter 5, the min7 chord in the iv position (borrowed from parallel minor) is prescribed as a quick pivot into parallel minor tonality. Greenan offers concrete voicing options: 'The most basic way to approach it is with a V chord (Bb7) leading into the I. But often times, musicians will play an Abmin6, which functions as the minor IV chord... You can also turn that Abmin6 into a ii-V (Abmin7-Db7), or you can even just play a Db7.'

In Chapter 4, Greenan issues a direct avoidance rule for iv minor chords: 'Don't get too hung up on the iv minor chord. In your improvisation, you will simply want to consider the difference in the chord quality. Don't be playing major thirds or major 7ths!' The student must exclude natural 3 and natural 7 when improvising over any chord with minor quality.

In Chapter 11, Greenan names the backdoor ii-V pattern where a min7 chord precedes the bVII7 backdoor dominant: 'The ii chord is being added in front of the backdoor dominant. Therefore, the Bbmin7-Eb7 is really acting as a backdoor ii-V into the Fmaj7.' The student should recognize and deploy this min7 as the ii of the backdoor key area, not as a diatonic ii of the parent key.

In Chapter 2, Greenan establishes that the V chord 'is always dominant' -- both in major and minor diatonic series -- and that the ii-V-I is 'jazz's most essential harmonic pattern.' The dominant 7th formula is Root-3-5-b7, and its 3rd and 7th are guide tones that voice-lead to the resolution chord. 'The 7th of each chord resolves to the 3rd of the next chord.'

In Chapter 4, Greenan defines secondary dominants as 'dominant 7 chords that act as a V chord of a diatonic chord other than the tonic,' naming the process 'tonicization.' The student must read any dom7 appearing outside normal V function as a secondary dominant targeting the chord a fourth above it, and treat it with the same guide-tone and chord-tone tools used on the primary V.

In Chapters 2 and 6, Greenan instructs that a diatonic vi minor chord can be raised to a VI dominant 7th to generate cycling-fourths dominant chains. In 'Sweet Georgia Brown,' 'the vi minor is converted into a VI dominant,' and 'bars 1-13 are just a long cycle of dominant 7th chords resolving to the I chord.' The student should treat this conversion as idiomatic and unremarkable.

In Chapter 6, Greenan prescribes the Mixolydian scale as 'the primary melodic resource over dominant 7 chords.' 'The easiest way to think of a Mixolydian scale is a major scale with a b7. Formula: 1-2-3-4-5-6-b7.' The student is instructed to use it as a 'pitch collection' -- not a scale to run in order -- to generate melodic lines over any dom7 chord.

In Chapter 6, Greenan prescribes a specific chord-tone pattern exercise over cycling dominant 7th chords: 'The first and last lines begin with quarter note chord tones moving in ascending order: R-3rd-5th-b7. The second line descends in this order: R-b7-5th-3rd.' Each bar begins on a different chord tone to ensure the student can approach the arpeggio from any starting point.

In Chapter 10, Greenan instructs that any V7 chord is 'your secret weapon for resolving to a new key center': 'The V chord is always your secret weapon for resolving to a new key center.' When navigating multi-key standards, the student should insert or recognize a V7 at every tonal seam and use it as the modulatory fulcrum.

In Chapter 6, Greenan identifies a descending chromatic dominant approach as a reusable compositional device: 'We are just dealing with a series of chromatically descending dominant 7th chords that are targeting the VI7 chord.' The student should recognize this as a directed approach -- not random chromaticism -- and improvise with awareness of its resolution target.

In Chapter 11, Greenan formally defines the backdoor dominant as 'a dominant 7th chord that substitutes the V7 chord for a bVII7 chord approaching the I chord by a whole step. This works because the bVII7 has a lot of notes in common with an altered V7 chord. Example: Bb7-Cmaj7.' Mixolydian (the standard dom7 pitch collection) still applies, as it maps directly onto the bVII7's note content.

In Chapter 11, the Note Choice Map for 'Stella by Starlight' prescribes Mixolydian over multiple dom7 chords in their straightforward dominant function (e.g., F7 maps to Mixolydian, Bb7 maps to Mixolydian, Ab7 maps to Mixolydian, Eb7 maps to Mixolydian). This confirms the default rule: unaltered dominant 7 = Mixolydian pitch collection.

In Chapter 6, Greenan warns against treating scales as mechanical exercises over dominant chords: 'The best way to think about the use of scales is "pitch collections." They aren't notes that are meant to be played in order, nor are they to be used solely to improvise.' The Mixolydian scale over dom7 is a note-choice map, not a fingering pattern to be played up and down.

In Chapter 9, Greenan teaches that a dominant 7(b9) chord can be represented by a rootless diminished seventh chord built on its 3rd: 'You can think of the F#dim7 as a rootless D7(b9).' The student should recognize that any dom7b9 shares four of its five chord tones with the diminished 7th built a major third above its root, making the substitution directly verifiable by ear.

In Chapter 11, the Note Choice Map prescribes the Altered Scale over dom7(b9) chords in contexts of tension and chromatic approach (e.g., A7(b9) maps to Altered in the Stella analysis). Greenan introduces the Altered Scale as one of 'the ones you haven't seen before in this book' but confirms it as essential for Stella's chromatic harmonic landscape.

In Chapter 9, when improvising over the diminished passing chord that substitutes a VI7b9, Greenan instructs: 'Remember that it is being substituted for the VI7b9 chord, so any of those chord tones will serve you well.' The student should use the chord tones of the underlying dom7b9 (not just the diminished chord's own tones) as their primary note source.

In Chapter 11, Greenan introduces the Altered Scale as a required pitch collection for altered dominant contexts in 'Stella by Starlight,' flagging it as new vocabulary not seen in prior chapters. The Note Choice Map pairs Altered Scale with A7 chords in altered function throughout the form. The student must study this scale before attempting the Note Choice Map exercise.

In Chapter 11, Greenan introduces the Lydian Dominant as a new pitch collection essential for Stella's chromatic harmonic landscape alongside the Altered Scale. It is prescribed for dominant chords where the #11 (raised fourth / Lydian character) is implied or explicit. The student must learn it from the Note Choice Map before attempting the quarter-note solo exercise.

In Chapter 5, Greenan presents the half-diminished chord (min7b5) as the ii chord of the minor ii-V-I: 'If we look at a Gmin7(b5) and a C7(b9) as separate chords, they are confusing. But if we look at them as resolving to an Fmin7, then we have something functional to understand.' Formula: Root-b3-b5-b7. The student must always read min7b5 relationally -- through its resolution target -- rather than in isolation.

In Chapter 5, Greenan teaches a dual-analysis framework: the Gmin7(b5) in a ii-V of ii can simultaneously be read as 'the iiib5 (adding a b5 to the iii minor)' within the parent key, alongside VI7. 'A iiib5 is odd, but again, if we combine this understanding with the ii-V of ii concept everything ties together.' The student should maintain both readings simultaneously.

In Chapter 11, the Note Choice Map for 'Stella by Starlight' assigns Locrian (formula 1-b2-b3-4-b5-b6-b7) as the prescribed pitch collection over every min7b5 chord in the form -- EMIN7(b5), and AMIN7(b5) all map to Locrian. This confirms Locrian as the default modal assignment for half-diminished chords.

In Chapter 11, Greenan defines the hybrid ii-V-I as using a min7b5 borrowed from the parallel minor: 'A hybrid ii-V-I is when a minor ii-V-i is mixed with a major ii-V-I. The ii and V are borrowed from the minor key, but they resolve to the major I. Example: Dmin7(b5)-G7(b9)-Cmaj7.' The student must recognize the minor-quality ii as the trigger for the surprise major resolution.

In Chapter 9, Greenan establishes the core rule for diminished 7th chords: 'F#dim7 chord is a substitute for the dominant VI7 chord... You can think of the F#dim7 as a rootless D7(b9).' The four chord tones of F#dim7 (F#-A-C-Eb) are identical to the upper four tones of D7(b9) (D-F#-A-C-Eb). The student should always reinterpret a dim7 as a rootless altered dominant one minor third below.

In Chapter 9, Greenan describes a dual function for the diminished passing chord: 'On a compositional level the F#dim7 is functioning as more than just a substitution. It's also creating a chromatic passing note, in this case the bass note, to connect the I chord with the ii chord.' The student should hear dim7 chords as performing simultaneous harmonic substitution and bass-line voice-leading duties.

In Chapter 9, Greenan prescribes the whole-half diminished scale as the pitch collection over diminished 7th chords: 'The intervallic formula for this scale is: W-H-W-H-W-H-W. The scale is based on alternating whole steps and half steps.' However, he cautions: 'I don't want you to play this scale verbatim when you are improvising... just playing the music rather than spending too much time getting bogged down in theory is more helpful.'

In Chapter 9, Greenan explicitly warns against running the whole-half diminished scale mechanically over dim7 chords: 'Of course, I don't want you to play this scale verbatim when you are improvising. That's why I think the best way to help you navigate these changes is to give you some musical ideas as a reference. In my experience, just playing the music rather than spending too much time getting bogged down in theory is more helpful.'

In Chapter 10, Greenan distinguishes the passing diminished (biii dim) from the substitution diminished: 'In this case, the biii diminished isn't necessarily replacing anything. Its primary job is to connect the iii chord to the ii chord chromatically.' The student must identify which role a dim7 plays -- substitution or connection -- before selecting note choices.

In Chapter 9, Greenan reveals that the bridge of 'Have You Met Miss Jones' is 'a series of ii-V-Is which our ears recognize. But the key centers are moving in a particular order. They are moving in 3rds. Bb to Gb is a descending major 3rd... Gb to D is a descending major 3rd... D to Gb is an ascending major 3rd.' The diminished logic that governs the A-section passes into a thirds-cycle architecture for the bridge.

In Chapter 5, Greenan offers the min6 chord as the primary voicing option for the minor iv function: 'often times, musicians will play an Abmin6, which functions as the minor IV chord.' The min6 is the first-choice voicing before the student considers expanding to a full ii-V (Abmin7-Db7) or simplifying to just the Db7.

The major 7th chord belongs to the Major family, derived from the foundational major chord. Greene states 'The MAJOR, MINOR, and DOMINANT 7TH chords are the 'fathers' of the 3 families, and all the other chords, with a few exceptions, are derived from them.' (Ch5 p.10)

In five-note major 7th voicings, the root or 5th may be omitted. Greene writes 'in any chord with 5 tones in the formula, the root OR 5th is often omitted and possibly one of the remaining tones DOUBLED.' (Ch5 p.10). The 5th is the preferred omission since it is not essential when unaltered.

Greene notes 'if you lower ONE root in a major chord that has TWO roots, you will get a major 7th chord,' showing that doubling roots is the natural precursor to omitting one. (Ch13 p.73). Leaving out the 5th in a I maj7 chord is explicitly called 'acceptable.' (Ch13 p.69)

Greene prescribes that 'the 3rd of the V7 chord moves up to the root of the I chord in each example; this is common procedure for V7 to I,' making the major 7th chord the resolution target of this half-step voice leading motion. (Ch13 p.69)

Greene specifies that 'Major 7ths and major 9ths that have the root on top or 7th in the bass can be used as good passing chords to a major type chord a 4th higher.' (Ch11 p.63). This gives maj7 a specific half-step approach function in progressions.

Greene notes that 'Try leaving out the 3rd in major type chords for a different type of sound (especially if you replace the 3rd with a 2nd),' indicating that the major 7th chord's 3rd is optional and a sus2 color can substitute. (Ch11 p.63)

In chord melody contexts, the melody must sit above the maj7 voicing: 'the melody is always played ABOVE the chord, not in the middle or in the bass.' (Ch14 p.76). Chords are typically placed on 'the 1ST NOTE IN EACH MEASURE,' not every melody note.

Greene prescribes a specific learning order: 'Learn the major and minor chords first, then the major 6th and minor 6th, then the major 7th, minor 7th, and dominant 7th, etc.' (Ch7 p.13). The maj7 is the third tier of major-family study.

Greene emphasizes exploiting chord synonyms for substitution discovery: 'The main benefit of knowing chord synonyms is that you can use them to come up with substitute chords you wouldn't have come up with otherwise.' (Ch8 p.17). Maj7 chords frequently share notes with min7 chords whose roots are a minor 3rd lower.

Major 7th and major 9th voicings with root on top or 7th in bass are 'good passing chords to a major type chord a 4th higher' (Ch11 p.63), making maj7 a natural IV approach chord in major-key progressions.

The maj7#11 belongs to the major family as an extension. Greene states '#11 is usually put above the 5th in a chord (assuming there is a 5th being played) as in chords like the +11, 13+11, etc.' (Ch5 p.10)

The minor 7th chord belongs to the Minor family. Greene identifies the minor chord as one of the three 'fathers' and notes that 'the major and major 7th chords are closely related, and also the minor and minor 7th chords.' (Ch9 p.55)

Greene establishes the IIm7-V7 relationship as foundational: 'Quite often following a minor 7th type chord a dominant chord whose root is a 4th higher will be used.' (Ch13 p.71). Furthermore, 'IF YOU HEAR IIm TO I, YOU MAY THINK IIm V7 TO I INSTEAD.' (Ch15 p.80)

The min7 chord follows the same omission policy as all five-note chords: 'in any chord with 5 tones in the formula, the root OR 5th is often omitted and possibly one of the remaining tones DOUBLED.' (Ch5 p.10). The 5th is the preferred candidate since it is unaltered.

When moving from m(maj7) to m7 on the same root, Greene prescribes: 'when using m(maj7) type chords with m7 type chords of the same root, the 7 TONE SHOULD MOVE UP 1 FRET or DOWN 1 FRET INTO A ROOT OR b7 TONE.' (Ch14 p.75). This half-step motion is the defining voice-leading event.

The min7 is the standard II chord in back-cycling: 'a smooth transition can be achieved if the new key is preceded by a IIm7 V7 progression OF THAT NEW KEY.' (Ch12 p.66). Back-cycling preceding any target chord with its IIm7-V7 creates forward momentum.

For dominant 7th chord substitution, Greene prescribes: 'you may play a m7 type chord whose root is a 5th higher than the root of the dominant chord, but you do not only play this m7 type chord; you play it for part of the duration of the dominant chord and then play the dominant chord (or extension).' (Ch10 p.58)

Greene places min7 in the third tier of the prescribed learning order: 'Learn the major and minor chords first, then the major 6th and minor 6th, then the major 7th, minor 7th, and dominant 7th, etc.' (Ch7 p.13)

Greene establishes modal equivalence: 'The notes and chords of these scales are the same: C major = G mixolydian = A natural minor = D dorian minor.' (Ch17 p.88). The min7 is the characteristic chord of the dorian mode, which shares its harmonic content with the relative major.

In blues progressions, Greene prescribes: 'The IIIm7 and/or III7 chord are used often in place of the I chord in measure 7 of blues progressions.' (Ch19 p.101). The min7 variant of the III chord provides a softer, jazzier color at the measure-7 position.

The m7b5 (half-diminished) belongs to the minor family as the only widely used altered minor type. Greene states: 'The only altered minor chord that is widely used is the m7b5 type.' (Ch11 p.61). It appears naturally as the VII chord of the harmonic minor scale.

As an altered minor chord, the b5th of m7b5 must be retained in any voicing. Greene is explicit: 'if the 5th is altered, that is, sharped or flatted, you may not leave it out as it is essential to the chord. You could still leave out the root though.' (Ch5 p.10)

Greene lists Im7b5 as a diatonic chord in specific modal scale contexts, noting the harmonized scale produces 'I+ m7 IIm7 IV# V7 VIm7 VII Im7b5 VIII#.' (Ch16 p.87). This confirms m7b5 as a structural diatonic chord, not merely a passing color.

The dominant 7th is one of the three foundational chord 'fathers': 'The MAJOR, MINOR, and DOMINANT 7TH chords are the 'fathers' of the 3 families.' Greene also notes 'There are more dominant chords, by far, than major or minor types.' (Ch5 p.10, Ch8 p.17)

Greene states 'When a 7th chord triad is desired, it is usually best to leave out the root or 5th.' (Ch16 p.84). The 3rd and b7th form the essential tritone shell; the root and 5th are the standard omission candidates for dom7 voicings.

Greene establishes the tritone substitution framework: 'all dominant chords a 5th apart are related.' (Ch11 p.61). 'You can also use chords a b5th higher than those in the cycle if you like the sound.' (Ch15 p.81). This means any dom7 may be replaced by the dom7 a tritone away.

In chord melody contexts, dominant 7th chords are typically placed on 'the 1ST NOTE IN EACH MEASURE' rather than on every melody note. (Ch14 p.77). Greene emphasizes that 'chords are generally played every few notes, not on every note.' (Ch14 p.76)
