Greene defines back-cycling using dom7: 'this technique of putting in V chords right before another chord will be called back-cycling.' For dominant chains: 'For a dominant type chord, you may play another dominant type chord whose root is a 5th higher.' (Ch14 p.79, Ch10 p.60)

Greene declares: 'the blues sound is usually associated with the dominant 7th family.' (Ch18 p.93). In blues, dominant chords appear on I, IV, and V, and 'in 99.9999% of all cases, some form of I chord will be in bar 1 to start the progression, and some form of a IV chord will be in bar 5.' (Ch18 p.93)

Greene prescribes that 'for a rock sound, quite often for a major chord you can substitute the dominant 7th and its extensions.' (Ch20 p.110). This establishes a blanket major-to-dom7 substitution specifically for rock contexts.

Greene describes a chromatic voice-leading technique: 'if you take any 7th chord and lower the 3rd and 7th 1 fret each, you will get a 9th chord built on the IV.' (Ch20 p.105). 'In any progression that has a series of dominant chords based on the cycle, you may progressively lower the 3rd and b7th, one fret at a time.' (Ch20 p.106)

Greene mandates that 'The last chord of a turnaround is almost always a V7 type or its b5 (b11).' (Ch19 p.99). The dom7 (or its tritone sub) is the required final chord in any turnaround, regardless of the starting chord.

Greene states: 'Whenever a major or minor type chord is followed by a major, minor, or dominant type chord whose root is a 4th higher, you may divide the duration of the 1st chord in 1/2 and play a dominant chord with the same root for the 2nd 1/2 of the allotted time.' (Ch10 p.59). This creates secondary dominant motion on any chord.

Greene prescribes that 'Almost any dominant type chord can be moved in intervals of 3 frets as long as the LAST chord resolves into wherever you are going next.' (Ch12 p.65). Free chromatic movement of dominant chords is permitted so long as the final chord resolves correctly.

In chord melody, Greene emphasizes listening for top notes: 'When choosing the inversions, pay particular attention to the melody note (the highest pitch — the top note) in each chord.' (Ch18 p.95). For dom7 voicings in chord melody, the inversion is chosen to place the melody note on top.

Greene observes that 'The harmonies of this scale seem to lend themselves towards the blues and rock field more than the other scales' regarding the mixolydian scale (Ch17 p.90), and because 'The notes and chords of these scales are the same: C major = G mixolydian,' the dom7 is the characteristic tonic chord of mixolydian.

Greene prescribes common-tone technique for smooth dominant progressions: 'COMMON TONES on the top notes of the chords will sometimes help smooth out the transitions' and 'Notice the use of common tones on top of some of these chords. This is one aid to smooth chord resolutions.' (Ch12 p.68, Ch11 p.62)

Greene notes that the III7 chord substitutes for the I chord at measure 7: 'The IIIm7 and/or III7 chord are used often in place of the I chord in measure 7 of blues progressions.' (Ch19 p.101). The dom7 quality of the III gives a brighter, more aggressive substitute.

Greene describes a rock-specific rhythmic cell: 'each measure the IV chord of each basic chord is sandwiched between two I chords' (Ch20 p.110). In a rock I7 context, the IV7 is inserted mid-measure creating a rhythmic I7-IV7-I7 sandwich pattern.

Greene prescribes that altered dominants are contextually restricted: 'Dominant chords with altered tones (b5th, #5th, both, #9th) can be used effectively for dominant chords when the next chord is: 1-one whose root is a 4th higher, 2-one whose root is a 1/2 step lower, and 3-a minor type chord with the same root.' (Ch10 p.58)

Greene restricts altered dominants from opening a song: 'One important point is that you couldn't always replace a I7 at the beginning of a song with an altered chord (except for a 7#9); you might first play the I7 (or extension) and then you could play the altered chord.' (Ch10 p.59)

Altered 5ths are non-negotiable: 'if the 5th is altered, that is, sharped or flatted, you may not leave it out as it is essential to the chord. You could still leave out the root though.' (Ch5 p.10). For dom7alt voicings, the altered tone is the most structurally critical note.

Greene specifies the voicing priority: 'The most critical factor in an altered tone is often its top note (highest pitch).' (Ch10 p.59). When building altered dominant voicings, the altered tone should be placed on top to project its color.

Greene prescribes specific intervallic movement for altered dominants: 'Dominant chords that have b5ths and/or #5ths may be used in 2 FRET INTERVALS effectively, still being careful to resolve nicely.' (Ch12 p.66). This is distinct from the 3-fret diminished movement.

Greene defines the b9 altered dominant explicitly: 'a C7b9b5 would be a C7 chord with the 5th flatted and a b9th added — in other words the formula would be 1,3,b5,b7,b9.' (Ch6 p.12). The b9 is treated as an additive extension on the dom7 structure.

Greene notes that common tones aid smooth resolution: 'Notice the use of common tones on top of some of these chords. This is one aid to smooth chord resolutions.' (Ch11 p.62). For dom7b9, smooth voice leading into the target I chord is the primary concern.

Greene specifies the internal voicing order: 'when using the #9, it is usually put above the 3rd in a chord, not below (such as in chords like 7#9, 7#9#5, etc.).' (Ch5 p.10). The #9 must sit higher than the 3rd in the voicing stack.

Unlike other altered dominants, Greene grants the 7#9 an exception: 'the 7#9 chord can also be used as a direct replacement for the 7th chord in other cases too, when a 'bluesy' sound is desired' and it is the only altered chord that may replace a I7 at the start of a song. (Ch10 p.58-59)

The augmented 11th dominant belongs to the dominant family. Greene states: 'Augmented 11th type chords can be used in place of dominant chords that are followed by a chord a 4th higher (just like other altered dominants).' (Ch11 p.61). It is classified as an altered dominant.

Greene explicitly restricts +11 from tonic function: 'the +11 does not assume a tonic function; that is, you wouldn't REPLACE a I7 at the beginning of a song with it.' (Ch11 p.61). This chord is V7 function only.

Greene prescribes the internal register of the #11: 'the +11 is usually put above the 5th in a chord (assuming there is a 5th being played) as in chords like the +11, 13+11, etc.' (Ch5 p.10). The 5th must be present if the #11 is to be placed above it.

Greene notes a preference hierarchy among related chord types: 'It is actually more common to play a 9b5 than a +11.' (Ch11 p.61). The 9b5 is described as having 'a less muddy sound and are more easily used.' (Ch8 p.52). The +11 is the more complex alternative.

Greene notes that 'The diminished and augmented chords do not really fit in any of the families but they are most like the dominant chords in the way that they are used.' (Ch6 p.12). Functionally, dim7 behaves as an altered dominant despite its structural independence.

Greene establishes the symmetry rule: 'any form of the diminished chord repeats itself every 3 frets.' (Ch11 p.62). This means any dim7 voicing can be moved in 3-fret intervals without changing chord identity, enabling fluid passing motion anywhere on the neck.

Greene prescribes the primary role explicitly: 'Diminished chords are used as 'passing' chords usually; that is, they go IN BETWEEN other chords.' (Ch11 p.62). A specific passing use: '#IVo is used as a passing chord following a IV or IV7 type chord and then leading to a I or I7 type chord.' (Ch19 p.98)

Greene articulates the dim7-as-dom7b9 relationship: 'a VII diminished triad sounds like a dominant 7th chord whose root is 2 whole steps lower.' (Ch16 p.86). More precisely, 'For an interesting sounding resolution of V7 to I, you may try putting together any 3 notes of a diminished 7th chord whose root is one fret higher than the root of the V7 chord, with the root of the I chord.' (Ch20 p.106)

Greene introduces the 'resolving diminished chord' concept: 'This chord will now replace the V7 chord, and will be called a RESOLVING DIMINISHED CHORD.' (Ch20 p.106). 'Resolving diminished chords also work well in place of m(maj7) type of chords, as long as the 7th tone of the m(maj7) is in the resolving dim chord.' (Ch20 p.107)

Because dim7 repeats every 3 frets, Greene notes via the synonyms chapter that 'There are some chords with different names but the same notes, and they may be used in place of each other.' (Ch8 p.17). Each dim7 chord has four enharmonic names, quadrupling its substitution potential.

Greene specifically identifies '#IVo is used as a passing chord following a IV or IV7 type chord and then leading to a I or I7 type chord' (Ch19 p.98) as a standard blues-form passing motion. This chromatic diminished passing move is a defining blues-harmony idiom.

The m(maj7) chord belongs to the minor family as a chromatic color variant. Greene notes it as one of the chord types that 'almost necessitate the use of voice leading principles,' signaling its inherently transitional character. (Ch13 p.73)

Greene is explicit: 'when using m(maj7) type chords with m7 type chords of the same root, the 7 TONE SHOULD MOVE UP 1 FRET or DOWN 1 FRET INTO A ROOT OR b7 TONE.' (Ch14 p.75). This half-step resolution of the major 7th to the root or b7 is the defining voice-leading rule for this chord.

Greene allows m(maj7) as a dom7 substitute in specific contexts: 'm(maj7) type chords can be used in place of dominant chords whose roots are 1 fret lower (like Cm(maj7)/9 for B7). This will only work if the dominant chord is being used as a V7 or V7 function.' (Ch12 p.66)

In harmonic minor contexts, Greene provides a relaxation option: 'When using chord progressions with the harmonic minor scale, you may substitute a plain minor for the Im(maj7).' (Ch17 p.88). This makes m(maj7) the default Im chord in harmonic minor, with plain minor as the simplified alternative.

Greene connects m(maj7) directly to the resolving diminished technique: 'Resolving diminished chords also work well in place of m(maj7) type of chords, as long as the 7th tone of the m(maj7) is in the resolving dim chord.' (Ch20 p.107). The shared major-7th tone is the functional link.
Greene defines the suspended chord categorically: 'any chord that has the 3RD replaced by a 4TH is called a SUSPENDED chord.' (Ch5 p.10). The 3rd is not added to but fully displaced by the 4th.

Greene restricts sus4 primarily to dominant preparation: 'Dominant suspended chords are usually used as partial replacements for dominant 7th chords.' (Ch11 p.62). They precede the resolved dom7 but do not typically replace it outright.

Greene allows for unresolved sus4 usage: 'Sometimes suspended chords are left unresolved; in other words, they may directly replace the dominant 7th chord.' (Ch11 p.62). This is the exception rather than the norm, and context determines acceptability.

Greene notes that when the 3rd is omitted from the 9th chord, 'this chord is also called a 9 suspended.' (Ch8 p.17). This establishes a synonym bridge between 9sus4 and dom9-no-3 voicings, enabling cross-substitution.

The sus4's resolution to the 3rd is the normative voice-leading destination: 'Dominant suspended chords are usually used as partial replacements for dominant 7th chords' (Ch11 p.62), implying the 4th resolves down a semitone to the 3rd of the following dom7, providing smooth stepwise motion.

Greene prescribes omitting the 3rd in 11th chords: 'In chords that have the 11th tone, the 3rd is often omitted, particularly in the 11th chord itself.' (Ch5 p.10). The 3rd clashes with the 11th, making this omission structural rather than optional.

Greene highlights the expressive power of 11th chords: 'The dominant 11th chords (especially with no 3rd) are some of the prettiest chords when used properly.' (Ch11 p.61). Proper use requires avoiding the 3rd to prevent the clash that destroys the chord's characteristic openness.

Greene explicitly restricts the 11b9 chord to authentic V7 function: 'The 11b9 chords are usually used for the V7 chord of a key, but not often for others.' (Ch12 p.64). This chord's strong tension profile limits it to the primary dominant in a key.

Greene specifies flexible omission for the 13b9: 'Sometimes 13b9 chords are played with no b7 or no 3rd - not both.' (Ch8 p.17). Either the b7 or the 3rd may be dropped, but never simultaneously, as both are critical to the chord's identity.

Greene places augmented chords outside the three main families: 'The diminished and augmented chords do not really fit in any of the families but they are most like the dominant chords in the way that they are used.' (Ch6 p.12). Functionally treated as altered dominants.

Greene establishes the symmetry rule for augmented chords: 'Augmented chords repeat every 4 frets' (Ch8 p.52) and reconfirms in Ch12: 'Augmented chords repeat themselves every 4 frets the same way diminished chords repeat every 3 frets.' (Ch12 p.63). Any aug voicing shifted 4 frets is enharmonically equivalent.

Greene advises thinking of the augmented chord reductively: 'It is wise to think of the + chord as a 7+ with no b7.' (Ch12 p.63). This framing makes the augmented triad a shell of the dominant 7#5, with the b7 as the only missing element.

As a chord with an altered (#5) tone, the augmented chord's raised 5th may never be omitted. Greene states: 'if the 5th is altered, that is, sharped or flatted, you may not leave it out as it is essential to the chord.' (Ch5 p.10). The root could still be dropped.

Greene prefers the 9b5 over the +11 for practical use: '9b5's have a less muddy sound and are more easily used.' (Ch8 p.52). The 9b5 and +11 differ only in that the +11 retains the 5th while the 9b5 omits it: 'the only difference is that the 5th and the +11th (b5th) are in the +11 chord while just the +11th (b5th) is in the 9b5.' (Ch8 p.52)

Dom7b5 participates in tritone substitution at the chord level: 'Almost any dominant type chord can be moved in intervals of 3 frets as long as the LAST chord resolves into wherever you are going next.' (Ch12 p.63). The b5 chord is also the direct tritone sub of the plain dominant.

Greene imposes a hard restriction: 'Minor 6th type chords usually should not be used for a minor chord that is followed by a dominant chord a 4th higher, because the m6 type chord will sound too much like the next dominant chord.' (Ch11 p.61). The m6 contains tones of the approaching dom7, creating premature resolution.

The min9 chord follows the five-tone omission policy: 'in any chord with 5 tones in the formula, the root OR 5th is often omitted and possibly one of the remaining tones DOUBLED.' (Ch5 p.10). The unaltered 5th is the standard omission candidate, leaving root, m3, b7, and 9.

Greene notes the expressive impact of 9th chords in blues: 'This progression has a much bluesier sound to most ears due to the abundance of 9th chords.' (Ch18 p.95). Dominant 9th chords are the primary upgrade from plain dom7 for achieving a more sophisticated blues sound.

Greene shows how dom9 arises from dom7 through voice leading: 'if you take any 7th chord and lower the 3rd and 7th 1 fret each, you will get a 9th chord built on the IV.' (Ch20 p.106). This creates a stepwise chromatic motion that generates the IV9 naturally from any I7.

Greene flags a structural constraint unique to this chord: 'There seems to be only one inversion of this amazing chord [9#5b5].' (Ch8 p.52). Its intervallic density makes it one of the most voicing-restricted chords in the book.

For major triads used as 4-note chords, Greene specifies: 'To make triads into 4 note chords, you may double a root, 3rd, or 5th.' (Ch16 p.85). In open triad voicings: 'WHEN USING OPEN TRIADS, THE ROOT IS USUALLY PUT IN THE BASS FOR THE LAST CHORD IN A PHRASE.' (Ch16 p.85)

Greene recommends experimenting with 3rd omission: 'Try leaving out the 3rd in major type chords for a different type of sound (especially if you replace the 3rd with a 2nd).' (Ch11 p.62). The sus2 substitution of the 3rd is highlighted as a particularly effective major color.

Greene prescribes the Picardy third technique in chord melody: 'Ending on a major is an often used technique in minor songs.' (Ch14 p.77). A minor song's final chord is replaced by the parallel major for a brightened cadential effect.

Greene notes: 'The technique of substituting the relative minor is often used on the IV chord of a key.' (Ch16 p.84). The relative minor shares most tones and provides a darker color alternative to the diatonic IV.

Greene allows plain minor as a simplification in harmonic minor contexts: 'When using chord progressions with the harmonic minor scale, you may substitute a plain minor for the Im(maj7).' (Ch17 p.88). This reduces the complexity while maintaining minor tonality.

Greene distinguishes triads as the harmonic currency of Baroque practice versus 7ths and extensions in modern playing (Ch.4, p.15). When triads do appear in modern contexts, he prescribes that register determines viability: 'let your ears be the guide in determining how low to take any progression,' making register judgment the key execution rule for major and minor triads.

Greene specifies that 1st-inversion chord scales carry a special value unavailable to root-position or 2nd-inversion forms: 'there is a certain magic in 1st inversion chord scales...more frequently than root position or 2nd inversion brothers, but this is only true as far as 4-note triads go' (Ch.5, p.17). The prescription is to favor 1st inversion over other inversions when running diatonic chord scales.

Greene introduces the Van Eps 'team concept' as a method for decorating triads in chord-scale passages: 'finding two interesting intervals in a chord and alternating them' (Ch.5, p.21). This positions the major triad not as a static block but as a launching pad for melodic inner-voice motion via note delays and diatonic moving lines.

Greene's 1st-inversion preference applies equally to minor 4-note triads in diatonic chord-scale passages: 'there is a certain magic in 1st inversion chord scales...more frequently than root position or 2nd inversion brothers, but this is only true as far as 4-note triads go' (Ch.5, p.17).

Like major triads, minor triads belong to Baroque practice rather than modern harmony per Greene's taxonomy (Ch.4, p.15). When used, the register rule applies: 'let your ears be the guide in determining how low to take any progression,' with the prescription to avoid muddy low voicings.

Greene establishes maj7 as the I chord in modern major-key harmony, listing the full extension family in Chapter 4 (p.15): C, C△, C6, C/9, C6/9, C2, C4/5, with parenthetical extensions C△/6 and Csus. Use any of these on the I chord according to context, treating the bare triad as the minimal option.

Greene states the missing-tones rule explicitly: 'missing tones are either the 5th or the root' (Ch.4, p.15). For maj7 voicings, the 5th is the preferred omission, and the root may be dropped in extended or upper-structure voicings.

Greene's register prescription applies to all I-chord voicings including maj7: 'some chords, especially some very modern voicings coming up later, sound pretty terrible in low registers (that is, on the lower frets) so let your ears be the guide in determining how low to take any progression' (Ch.4, p.15). There is no prescribed lowest fret; register is an editorial decision.

In the diatonic 7th-chord cycle in C (Ch.8, p.49), C△ and F△ anchor the I and IV positions in the sequence 'C△ F△ Bm7b5 Em7 Am7 Dm7 G7 C△ F△.' Practice cycle-of-4ths diatonic movement with maj7 as the resolution target after the full cycle.

Greene frames the maj7 I chord as the recurring resolution target throughout. Ch.9 (p.61): 'Remember to resolve the V7's to I's occasionally'; Ch.11 (p.79): 'Don't forget to occasionally try resolving the V7's to I's.' Periodic resolution to the I maj7 is a standing functional-harmonic rule.

Greene identifies min7 as the quality of the ii, iii, and vi chords in the diatonic 7th-chord cycle in C: Em7 (iii), Am7 (vi), Dm7 (ii). Lowercase (vi7) for diatonic minor 7th vs uppercase (VI7) for chromatic dominant (Ch.9, p.59).

Greene's substitution rule in Ch.9 (p.59) is categorical: 'ANY m7 TYPE CHORD MAY BE REPLACED WITH A DOMINANT 7th TYPE CHORD, ACCORDING TO PERSONAL TASTE.' Every diatonic min7 (ii7, iii7, vi7) has the option to be recast as a dominant 7th chord.

Greene states in Ch.5 (p.17): 'ii can substitute for IV because they are virtually the same chord — like F#m7 = A6 (the homonym concept).' The diatonic ii min7 is interchangeable with the IV chord when shared tones allow.

Greene prescribes that diatonic chord scales be built by stepwise voice motion: each voice moves 'up to the next note in the major scale which has the same name as the chord' (Ch.5, p.17). Each min7 chord in the scale should be run in 1st inversion in chord-scale passages.

Greene prescribes in Ch.10 (p.74): 'raise the 3rd (one fret higher) in the ii7 types, thereby making them II7's.' Refinement: 'try raising the 3rd that is the lower in pitch of the two...this will create a II7#9 chord in many cases.' This is the procedural bridge from min7 to dom7 in the iii7-vi7-II7-V7 formula.

Greene's Ch.11 (p.78) substitution rule runs both directions: 'try using iii7 types in place of III7 types, or vi7 types in place of VI7 types.' Min7 is always available as a diatonic softening substitute for its chromatic dominant counterpart in III7-VI7-II7-V7.

Greene recommends grouping progressions by starting chord (Ch.9, p.61): 'first make a list of all the different starting chords given in these iii (I) VI ii V's, and then group your favorites accordingly.' Collect all favorite iii7-vi7-ii7-V7 voicing sequences beginning on iii7 or ii7 into distinct practice groups.

Greene places min7b5 (half-diminished) on the vii° degree of the diatonic cycle in C, showing it as Bm7b5 in 'C△ F△ Bm7b5 Em7 Am7 Dm7 G7 C△ F△' (Ch.8, p.49). The label 'vii°' in 'I IV vii° iii vi ii V I' maps to this chord quality.

Greene demonstrates in Ch.3 (p.13) that a single voicing reads as Em6 = C#m7b5 = A9 depending on harmonic context. A min7b5 voicing is simultaneously a major 6th chord and an unresolved dominant 9th chord. Exploit these three-way enharmonic readings when selecting substitute chords.

Greene frames V7-I resolution as a standing cadential rule across Chs.7-11. Ch.7 (p.26): 'You should always try resolving the V to I.' Chs.9, 10, 11 repeat: 'Remember to resolve the V7's to I's occasionally.' Resolution is the baseline functional-harmonic obligation.

Ch.9 (p.59) is categorical: 'ANY m7 TYPE CHORD MAY BE REPLACED WITH A DOMINANT 7th TYPE CHORD, ACCORDING TO PERSONAL TASTE.' Procedural implementation: 'raise the 3rd (one fret higher) in the ii7 types, thereby making them II7's' (Ch.10, p.74).

Greene explains VI7 (chromatic A7 in C major) can be derived from vi7 (diatonic Am7) by raising the third, with an important exception: 'most of them were derived in other ways, specifically to produce more desirable sounds' (Ch.10, p.74). VI7 voicings should be treated as independent chord choices rather than automatic raise-the-third results.

Ch.9 (p.59) states the governing principle for altered tones on dominants: 'VI7 sounds good with any altered tone when used in smooth connection with the chords that precede or follow it.' Any alteration (b9, #9, b5, #5) is acceptable as long as smooth voice-leading is maintained.

In the full cycle of 4ths (Ch.8, p.49) 'I IV vii° iii vi ii V I,' G7 is the only diatonic dominant 7th. This is the vehicle for practicing all seven diatonic 7th qualities, with G7 as the sole dom7 and structural tension chord before resolution to C△.

Greene presents the I-vi-ii-V formula in Ch.7 (p.26) as the foundational 4-chord loop: 'Another important diatonic harmonic formula is I vi ii V...especially common to find this progression used as an opener.' V is always dom7; play 'in order by melody/shape,' treating the V chord as the tension-generating chord demanding resolution.

Greene classifies dom7b9 as an 'altered dominant' — 'those with #9's, b9's, #5's, and b5's,' calling them 'very spicy chords' (Ch.11, p.78). For III7-VI7-II7-V7 progressions, use altered dominants including dom7b9 on any position to create chromatic intensity.

Ch.11 (p.78) prescribes that altered chords like dom7b9 be prepared with diatonic material: 'the ear will accept altered chords more easily in most cases if they are prepared with sounds of a more normal, diatonic major scaley nature first.' Sequencing rule: diatonic first, then dom7b9.

Highly specific substitution directive in Ch.11 (p.82): 'TRY THIS CHORD IN PLACE OF A7b5 WHENEVER A7b5 PROGRESSES TO D7b9b5.' Chord-specific substitution rule involving dom7b9b5 as replacement for a preceding dom7b5 in the III7-VI7-II7-V7 context.

Ch.11 (p.78) defines altered dominants as 'those with #9's, b9's, #5's, and b5's,' calling them 'very spicy chords.' Any combination qualifies as dom7alt in his taxonomy. Use them freely in the III7-VI7-II7-V7 formula.

Ch.11 (p.78) substitution rule runs both directions: where a III7 or VI7 altered dominant appears, one may substitute the diatonic version — 'try using iii7 types in place of III7 types, or vi7 types in place of VI7 types.' Dom7alt is not mandatory; diatonic min7 substitution always available as softening option.

Greene's key constraint on dom7alt: 'VI7 sounds good with any altered tone when used in smooth connection with the chords that precede or follow it' (Ch.9, p.59). Altered tones are free choices conditioned on smooth melodic movement — spice without voice-leading disruption.

Ch.11 (p.79) prescribes combining dom7alt progressions with normal diatonic progressions for contrast: 'combining the consonant and dissonant types of progressions is also fun for your ear because of the contrast; and it is good for you because it will get you into the spirit of combining shorter progressions in order to make longer progressions.' Altered dominants are a compositional ingredient, not wall-to-wall texture.

Ch.10 (p.74) prescribes: 'try raising the 3rd that is the lower in pitch of the two...this will create a II7#9 chord in many cases.' When a min7 voicing contains two thirds (open voicing), raising the lower yields dom7#9 without disturbing the higher third.

Greene limits the raise-the-third operation: 'If you are dealing with a iim7/11 with its 11th in the soprano (highest pitch) then none of these ideas will work very well' (Ch.10, p.74). When the 11th sits in the soprano, the dom7#9 derivation procedure is inapplicable.

Greene lists C6 as a standard I-chord extension alongside C, C△, C/9, C6/9, C2, C4/5 (Ch.4, p.15). C6 is interchangeable with these other I-chord forms, constrained only by the missing-tones rule: 'missing tones are either the 5th or the root.'

Ch.3 (p.13) homonym principle: Em6 = C#m7b5 = A9 from a single voicing. A maj6 chord shares an identical voicing with a min7b5 and an unresolved dominant 9th. Exploit this three-way equivalence when selecting substitute chords.
F6 appears as a standard IV-chord extension in Ch.4 (p.15) alongside F, F△, F/9, F6/9, F9, F4/3, F/9+11, F6/9+11, F7+11, F9+11. Maj6 is equally available on IV as on I, same missing-tones rule.

Ch.5 (p.17) ii-for-IV substitution relies on F#m7 = A6: 'ii can substitute for IV because they are virtually the same chord.' An A6 voicing is identical to F#m7; any maj6 chord is simultaneously a min7 a minor third below.
Ch.4 (p.15) lists C6/9 as a primary I-chord extension, in the core list alongside C△, C6, C/9, C2, C4/5. Maj6/9 is prescribed as a richer-color option for I, still governed by missing-tones rule.

F6/9 and F6/9+11 appear in IV-chord extension list (Ch.4, p.15). F6/9+11 extends maj6/9 with a #11, producing a Lydian-flavored IV chord. The +11 combinations are advanced options signaled by their absence from the I-chord list.

Ch.4 (p.15) lists C/9 (add9) as a standard I-chord extension in the core group alongside C△, C6, C6/9, C2, C4/5. The slash-9 notation signals an added 9th without the 7th — a direct color choice for I.
Ch.4 (p.15) lists F/9 as a standard IV-chord extension alongside F, F△, F6, F6/9, F9, F4/3. The add9 form is available on both I and IV chords as a broadly applicable non-7th color option.

Csus appears in the parenthetical (advanced) section of I-chord extensions at Ch.4 (p.15): '(C△/6, Csus, C/9sus).' The parenthetical signals sus4 on I is less common, more specialized — available but not a default extension choice.

Ch.2 (p.10) foundational definition: 'sus. is an abbreviation for the word suspended which means that the 3rd has been replaced with the 4th.' The 4th replaces (does not add to) the 3rd — governs all sus4 chord readings throughout the book.

Ch.10 (p.74) specific voicing-operation exception: 'If you are dealing with a iim7/11 with its 11th in the soprano (highest pitch) then none of these ideas will work very well.' The raise-the-third procedure for converting min7 to dom7 or dom7#9 is blocked when the 11th is the top voice.

Ch.4 (p.15) lists F/9+11, F6/9+11, F7+11, F9+11 as IV-chord extension options. The #11 (raised 11th / Lydian color) appears specifically on IV, not I — IV accepts this Lydian alteration as a distinct color unavailable as a default I-chord option.

Greene's missing-tones rule for IV-chord extensions — 'missing tones are either the 5th or the root' (Ch.4, p.15) — applies to maj7#11 voicings. With root, 3rd, 5th, 7th, #11, the 5th is the preferred omission since the #11 and 5th create a tritone conflict.

Major 7th chords belong to Greene's 'major Group 1' family. Their formula is 1, 3, 5, 7 derived from the major scale: 'major 7th chords have the following formula: 1, 3, 5, 7... the chord tones of an A Major 7th chord would be the 1st, 3rd, 5th and 7th tones of the A Major scale.' Chapter 1, p. 9.

Group 1 major chords — including maj7 — take either the major scale or the Lydian scale: 'group 1 major chords most commonly take one of two scales, either the MAJOR or the LYDIAN. As to which of the two to use, it is almost always a matter of personal preference... they both sound good in most cases.' Chapter 1, p. 10.

When using the Lydian scale over a major Group 1 chord, the #4 (raised fourth) is the sole distinguishing tone from the plain major scale: 'the Lydian's, it is simply a Major scale with a #4th instead of the regular 4th.' This raised fourth provides the 'hippest' color of the two options. Chapter 1, p. 10.

Major 7th chord formulas extend upward via the upper-partial system: when the formula expands to 1, 3, 5, 7, 9 it becomes a ninth chord; to 1, 3, 5, 7, 9, 11 an eleventh; to 1, 3, 5, 7, 9, 11, 13 a thirteenth. 'The 11th is the same letter name as the 4th, and the 13th tone is the same letter name as the 6th.' Chapter 1, p. 10.

Over major Group 1 chords, the player should combine major and Lydian scale knowledge within a 5-6 fret fingerboard area: 'you will want to know separate scales for the different chords in the song, but if you know enough positions of each scale, you will be able to stay in one little 5 or 6 fret area and play through the whole song.' Chapter 4, p. 60.

Soloing over major Group 1 chords demands active fingerboard visualization, not rote pattern recall: 'Remember to VISUALIZE the notes on the fingerboard as discussed earlier; at the risk of boring you, let me say it again: THIS IS VERY IMPORTANT! It is one of the best things you can do for yourself.' Chapter 4, p. 67.

The major (and Lydian) scale runs learned over major chords can be applied in 3/4 time: '3/4 time can be very attractive in jazz, creating the feel known as "Jazz Waltz". You may find it highly stimulating for variety's sake, to make up some runs in 3/4 time... or even just using the Major (or Lydian) scale.' Chapter 4, p. 71.

The minor 7th chord formula is 1, b3, 5, b7 derived from the major scale: 'Minor 7th chord has the following formula: 1, b3, 5, b7... a C Minor 7th chord would contain the following tones: 1C, b3Eb, 5G and b7Bb, which are the 1st, flatted 3rd, 5th and flatted 7th tones of the C Major scale.' Chapter 1, p. 9.

The Minor 7th scale — a major scale with lowered 3rd and 7th — is the prescribed scale for minor 7th chords: 'The Minor 7th scale is simply a Major Scale with LOWERED 3rd (b3) and LOWERED 7th (b7) tones.' Chapter 4, p. 66.

Do not think of the minor 7th scale as a relative major scale starting a whole step lower: 'You will probably notice that each m7 scale has the same notes as a major scale whose root is a whole step lower. But, as cautioned before on dom. 7 scales, for your own good, don't think of the m7 scale in this way now.' Chapter 4, p. 69.

Minor 7th chord runs should be learned and practiced within the ii-V-I progression context: 'This particular series of sounds is one of the most common in jazz (it is known as "ii-V-I" if that means anything to you now)... and is a practical way, at this stage of the game, for you to become acquainted with m7 runs.' Chapter 4, p. 67.

Minor 7th scale runs should be combined with other scales (Major, Dominant 7th) within a single 5-6 fret fingerboard position, so the player can navigate the full ii-V-I without shifting. Chapter 4 explicitly names 'Combining Scales in One Position' as a technique for multi-chord soloing. Chapter 4, p. 60.

The Dominant 7th scale — a major scale with a lowered 7th — is the prescribed scale for dominant 7th chords: 'The Dominant 7th scale is simply a Major scale with a lowered 7th tone.' Any chord built from some combination of (and only) these scale tones can take this scale. Chapter 3, p. 41.

Do not treat the Dominant 7th scale as a major scale starting a 4th above: 'Don't fall for the "oh, dom. 7th scales, they're really just major scales up a 4th-trap" — it will only tend to make things harder later if you do.' Dominant 7th must be internalized from its own root. Chapter 3, p. 43.

For Group-1 dominants (chords without the 11th), select runs that contain the 3rd: 'for maximum synchronization of runs and chords, you could generalize and say that if a run contains the 3rd, use it over any of the group-1 dominants.' Runs with both or neither the 3rd and 11th work over either group. Chapter 4, p. 59.

For Group-2 dominants (chords that include the 11th), select runs that contain the 11th: 'if a run contains the 11th, use it over any of the group-2 dominants. And if a run contains both (or neither) the 3rd and 11th, use it over any chord in either group of chords. But watch out for ending or lingering tones.' Chapter 4, p. 59.

The perceptual weight of b7 and 9 over dominant 7th chords is determined by register, not merely note choice: 'b7 and 9 really start to come alive in this "higher" register (it's still a fairly low register, but high enough so that these two tones don't sound like big, weighty bass tones, but rather, more like spicy lower mid-range notes).' Chapter 4, p. 58.

Dominant 7th scale runs can be applied in 3/4 time for jazz waltz feel: 'You may find it highly stimulating for variety's sake, to make up some runs in 3/4 time... or even just using... the Dom. 7 scale.' This applies across Group-1 and Group-2 dominant contexts. Chapter 4, p. 71.

The scale-to-chord compatibility rule applies directly to dominant 7th chords: 'Any chord containing some combination of any of (but only) these chord tones, can take the Dominant 7th scale.' Chords that include non-scale tones fall outside this pairing. Chapter 3, p. 41.

Major and Dominant 7th scales should be combined within a single position to allow seamless soloing across I to V chord changes: 'you will see examples of runs that combine the Major and Dom. 7th scales, in one position at a time... you will be able to stay in one little 5 or 6 fret area and play through the whole song.' Chapter 4, p. 60.

When running dominant 7th type arpeggios, arpeggio tones need not be confined to the highest strings: 'These notes may be played on other strings too (5th & 4th strings).' This extends positional reach within the fingerboard area. Chapter 6, p. 107.

Dominant chords built from the Overtone Dominant scale — which adds a #4 (#11) to the Dominant 7th scale — belong to Group 3 dominants: 'The Overtone Dominant scale is simply a Dominant 7th scale with a #4th tone instead of the regular 4th.' Chapter 4, p. 82.

Group 3 dominant chords (with #11) take the Overtone Dominant scale (also called the Lydian Dominant scale): 'Because it contains the #4th (#11th), the Overtone Dominant scale is also called the LYDIAN Dominant scale.' The #11 is its single distinguishing feature from the plain Dominant 7th scale. Chapter 5, p. 83.

Do not classify the Overtone Dominant / dom7#11 as an altered dominant chord: 'The Overtone Dominant scale is not considered to be an altered dominant scale — that #11 is not really a b5th, even though we may call it that — check the Overtone Series diagram again if you are in doubt.' The #11 reflects the overtone series, not chromatic alteration. Chapter 5, p. 94.

Over a dom7#11 chord using the Lydian Dominant scale, the three 'hippest' notes — the 9, #11, and 13 — form a major triad rooted a whole step above the chord root: 'the 9, #11 and 13 form a major triad whose root is a whole step above the root of the scale.' This is the device of POLYTONALITY, treated as a full chapter subject in Volume II. Chapter 5, p. 83.

Before attempting to play Overtone Dominant / Group 3 runs, the player must be able to visualize the Group 3 chord forms in that position: 'If you have trouble visualizing any of these runs, then please, for your own good, go back and learn the chord forms (group 4) for this position. This should straighten it out.' Chapter 5, p. 99.

An altered dominant chord is any dominant 7th type chord containing one or more of: b9, #9, b5, or #5 (b13): 'Any Dom. 7th type chord that contains any one or more of the four altered tones (b9, #9, b5 and #5 or b13) will be considered as being part of what we call the GROUP 4 DOMINANT CHORDS.' Chapter 5, p. 94.

Group 4 altered dominant chords take one of three Altered Dominant scale types. All three types are presented in the same fingerboard position simultaneously: 'the three types of A.D. scales are all so similar that your brain, while noting the differences, can absorb them all in a kind of "package deal", one position at a time.' Chapter 5, p. 96.

The three altered dominant scale types should be learned side by side in the same position to develop color sensitivity: 'because they are all juxtaposed in the same position, the subtle differences between them will be more evident to you, thereby increasing your sensitivity to these slightly different colors, and helping you to learn the sounds faster.' Chapter 5, p. 96.

When runs in altered dominant positions are hard to visualize, the player must return to the Group 4 chord forms before proceeding: 'If you have trouble visualizing any of these runs, then please, for your own good, go back and learn the chord forms (group 4) for this position.' Chapter 5, p. 99.

A dominant chord containing b9 qualifies as a Group 4 altered dominant chord: 'any dominant 7th scale with one or more of the following tones: b9, #9, b5 or #5 (b13)' defines the altered dominant family. The b9 tone is one of the four defining altered tones. Chapter 5, p. 94.

A dominant chord containing #9 qualifies as a Group 4 altered dominant chord. The #9 is one of the four altered tones: 'Any Dom. 7th type chord that contains any one or more of the four altered tones (b9, #9, b5 and #5 or b13) will be considered as being part of what we call the GROUP 4 DOMINANT CHORDS.' Chapter 5, p. 94.

In altered dominant contexts, the #9 may substitute for or be played alongside the natural 9: 'INSTEAD OF OR IN ADDITION TO THE #9.' This substitution rule applies across altered dominant exercises in Chapter 7. Chapter 7, p. 131.

Over Type 3 altered dominant exercises, A7+ (augmented 7th) may be substituted for A7#9+ as a chord choice: 'As before, and on all Type 3 altered dominant pages coming up, you may wish to try A7+ for A7#9+.' This substitution allowance applies as a standing rule across all subsequent Type 3 pages. Chapter 6, p. 105.

A dominant chord containing b5 qualifies as a Group 4 altered dominant chord. The b5 is one of the four defining altered tones listed in the altered dominant definition: 'any dominant 7th scale with one or more of the following tones: b9, #9, b5 or #5 (b13).' Chapter 5, p. 94.

All chord formulas — for any chord quality — are derived from the major scale: 'All chords have a certain group of tones called a formula, that is derived from the major scale.' The major scale is the universal reference from which every chord type is defined via raising or lowering scale degrees. Chapter 1, p. 9.

The operational pairing concept: 'certain kind of chord "takes" a certain scale, what they mean is that that particular scale sounds good when played with that particular chord.' This governs all chord-scale pairings throughout the book. Chapter 1, p. 10.

Regardless of chord quality, the eighth note is jazz's default rhythmic unit for single-note lines: 'At medium and fast tempos, which most of the runs in this book are intended for, the normal unit of rhythm in jazz is the 8th note. Great players often create a very fluid sound by running long streams of 8th notes together in measure after measure.' Chapter 3, p. 39.

Every 8th-note run, over any chord quality, must be practiced in both swing feel and straight feel: 'all the 8th notes in this book should be played as jazz 8ths and straight 8ths, because both feels are necessary to today's music.' Chapter 3, p. 39.

Swing feel over any chord is produced by interpreting written straight 8ths as triplets with the middle note tied or missing: 'In the swing feel, each group of two 8th notes is actually played as if it were a group of three triplets, with the middle one tied or missing. The ear then only hears two notes, which it interprets as kind of funny 8th notes.' Chapter 3, p. 39.

Double-timing — running 16th notes at medium or fast tempos — is an advanced texture applicable over any chord quality: 'Players who possess great technique often love to break into 16th notes at medium (or even fast!) tempos; this is commonly referred to as double-timing.' Chapter 3, p. 40.

For all chord contexts, cleanliness must precede tempo increases: 'The speed that is required here comes of course, as a result of constantly pushing yourself a little, gradually increasing the tempos on all the runs you are practicing; but also by making sure you are playing cleanly at any tempo before moving on to a faster one.' Chapter 3, p. 40.

The trill, applicable over any chord, decorates a held note rather than replacing it: 'another way to look at this, and a way that I prefer, is that A is not really being replaced, but instead, is just being decorated, you know, like we're kind of playing around with the A note, but not getting rid of it, just enhancing it.' Chapter 3, p. 41.

Trills should be placed predominantly on the strong part of the beat: 'The trill is more commonly used on the strong part of the beat than the weak one, but experiment and see what you like.' Chapter 3, p. 41.

At this stage of study, hammer-on target notes must be found within the currently active scale: 'This higher note, for now, will be found in the scale you are working with at that moment.' Hammer-ons to non-scale tones are outside scope at this level. Chapter 3, p. 41.

Do not use hammer-ons as standalone jazz devices at this stage: 'With the exception of a special usage known as the grace note (to be covered in Volume II), hammer-ons, by themselves, have not been commonly used by most jazz guitarists. But they are commonly used as part of the device known as the trill.' Chapter 3, p. 41.

Every run pattern, over any chord quality, should be tried an octave higher within the same fingerboard position: 'Also try this run an octave higher in the same position.' This is a standing practice rule applied throughout Chapter 7. Chapter 7, p. 120.
Each set of scale runs should also be fingered in at least one alternate position to expand positional fluency: 'Try fingering all these Em9 runs in the 5th position too.' Chapter 6, p. 109.
Left-hand fretting should not be done on the tip of the finger: 'REMINDER: not on tip of finger.' This technique rule applies across all chord contexts and positions. Chapter 6, p. 111.

All scale and chord relationships are described using numeric scale-degree notation derived from the major scale: 'The different notes in a major scale are often referred to by number, for instance, if you see the statement "G is the 4th of D", this means "G is the 4th note in the D major scale." This number business also applies to intervals.' Chapter 1, p. 8.

The symbol 'b7' means the 7th tone is lowered by a half-step, NOT that it always ends up as a flat note in its absolute spelling: 'Notice that the term "b7" means that the 7th tone is lowered one-half-step, NOT that the lowered 7th tone always ends up being a "flat" note.' Chapter 3, p. 41.

The major triad formula is 1, 3, 5 derived from the major scale: 'the Major triad's formula is 1, 3, 5.' It is the most basic major chord type from which maj7 and other extensions are built. Chapter 1, p. 9.
The minor triad formula is 1, b3, 5: 'the Minor triad's is 1, b3, 5.' It establishes the lowered-third characteristic that carries into all minor chord formulas. Chapter 1, p. 9.
The diminished triad formula is 1, b3, b5: 'the Diminished triad's is 1, b3, b5.' Chapter 1, p. 9.
The augmented triad formula is 1, 3, #5: 'the Augmented triad's is 1, 3, #5.' Chapter 1, p. 9.

The dominant 7th chord formula is derived from the major scale with a lowered 7th: the Dominant 7th scale is 'simply a Major scale with a lowered 7th tone.' Any chord built from those tones — 1, 3, 5, b7 — is a dominant 7th type chord that can take that scale. Chapter 3, p. 41.

No Type 3 altered dominant material exists for fingerboard Area 4A on the guitar — this is an instrument-specific structural constraint: 'There won't be any Type 3 - 4A.. it's just the way the instrument works out.' Do not expect or construct such exercises. Chapter 7, p. 118.

Altered dominant arpeggio patterns should be extended into the upper register using the EXTRA ARPEGGIOS FOR HIGHER REGISTER section, supplementing the standard fingering-area exercises: 'EXTRA ARPEGGIOS FOR HIGHER REGISTER' extends the altered dominant patterns upward. Chapter 7, p. 133.

Greene organizes all single-note soloing around three fundamental questions applicable over any chord: what notes sound good, where those notes are on the instrument, and how to play them interestingly — 'playing successions of single notes, which form melodies.' Chapter 1, p. 6.

Major chord arpeggios (chord tones 1, 3, 5, 7 played successively) are prescribed as foundational soloing material over major Group 1 chords, alongside scalar runs. Chapter 2 covers 'Major Chord Forms; Major Chord Runs' and arpeggios as core content. Chapter 2, pp. 11-40.

Dominant 7th type arpeggios are prescribed as core soloing material alongside scalar runs over dominant chords. Chapter 4 dedicates a section to 'Dominant 7th Type Arpeggios and Runs' across multiple fingerboard areas. Chapter 4, pp. 61-85.

Minor 7th type arpeggios are prescribed alongside scalar runs over minor 7th chords. Chapter 5 covers 'Minor 7th Type Arpeggios and Runs' as core material within the ii-V-I context. Chapter 5, pp. 86-105.

Overtone Dominant arpeggios are prescribed as soloing material over Group 3 dominant chords. Chapter 6 covers 'Overtone Dominant Arpeggios and Runs' across fingerboard areas with notes that 'may be played on other strings too (5th & 4th strings).' Chapter 6, pp. 106-120.

Altered Dominant arpeggios are prescribed as soloing material over Group 4 dominant chords. Chapter 7 covers 'Altered Dominant Arpeggios and Runs' across Areas 4A, 5, and 5A, with a supplementary higher-register section. Chapter 7, pp. 121-137.

Across all chord types, the student must be aware of melody notes within the scale runs — Chapter 2 (major), Chapter 4 (dominant), Chapter 5 (minor 7th and altered dominant) all include 'Melody Notes' as a dedicated subsection, indicating that melodic targeting within scales is prescribed at every chord-quality level. Chapter 2-5 passim.

Only chords whose tones are drawn from (and only from) the Dominant 7th scale's chord tones may take that scale. Chords that include tones outside the scale's chord-tone set fall outside the pairing: 'Any chord containing some combination of any of (but only) these chord tones, can take the Dominant 7th scale.' Chapter 3, p. 41.

Heussenstamm prescribes the minor seventh chord as the naturally occurring ii in a major-key ii-V-I, and teaches chord-tone-only arpeggio improvisation through the 9th (e.g., Cm9) as the first melodic approach -- mapping chord members across the fretboard to develop harmonic ear before adding scales. Chapter 2, p. 9 and p. 14.

For improvisation on the ii min7 chord, Heussenstamm prescribes D Dorian as the obvious scale choice (modal sibling of G Mixolydian and C major), and teaches arpeggio construction by extracting the 1st, 3rd, 5th, and 7th of Dorian -- yielding root, 3rd, 5th, b7. He frames this as the scalar foundation before chord-tone exercises. Chapter 2, p. 9 and p. 14.

Heussenstamm prescribes reducing min7 to root, 3rd, and 7th (shell), then dropping the root entirely for compact two-string shapes on the middle strings, to be used alongside a walking bassist. He explicitly warns against mechanically trimming any chord shape to middle strings -- only these specific tones belong there. Chapter 5, p. 48.

Heussenstamm teaches that Dorian (rather than natural minor) is the correct scale for deriving full min7 extensions because natural minor produces a wrong 13th -- the scalar 6th of Dorian becomes the chordal 13th, extending Dm7 to Dm13. This mapping of scale degrees to extension numbers is shown with a diagram in Chapter 6, p. 55.

Heussenstamm prescribes soloing over Dm7 by playing purely within Am9 arpeggio tones (A, C, E, G, B), because from the 5th of Dm13 upward the tones match Am9 exactly -- accessing the upper extensions of the original chord. This chord-within-chord approach is the signature improv move taught in Chapter 6, p. 55.

Heussenstamm prescribes substituting Dm7 ideas over G7sus4 because the sus4 chord is structurally equivalent to a minor seventh built on its 5th -- playing Dm7 or Dm9 over G7sus4 naturally accesses the suspended dominant's upper extensions (G9sus4, G13sus4). Taught in Chapter 6, p. 69.

For the minor ii-V-i, Heussenstamm designates the ii chord as a minor seventh with a flat 5th (half-diminished / min7b5), not a plain min7, and prescribes Locrian as its scale (equivalent to natural minor from the tonic). Chapter 2, p. 10.

Heussenstamm fixes the dominant seventh as the V chord in major-key ii-V-I and teaches G Mixolydian as the default scale, noting that Dorian, Mixolydian, and major are all modal siblings sharing the same tones -- making the distinction between them a matter of harmonic context. Chapter 2, p. 9.

Heussenstamm teaches that when a chord symbol gives only 'F7' or 'Bb7' with no further detail, the most critical interpretive decision is whether to treat it as natural or altered. For V-i motion (dominant resolving to a minor chord), altered is strongly favored; for V-I in major, natural is the default unless the device of switching to altered just before resolution is desired. Chapter 4, p. 30-31.

Heussenstamm prescribes a two-stage scalar move over a resolving dominant: first play from Mixolydian, then switch to super Locrian (altered) immediately before resolution to create urgency -- the distinctive tones of super Locrian (not shared with Mixolydian) mark the pivot. This is demonstrated for both D7 and G7 in Chapter 4, p. 33.

Heussenstamm prescribes replacing a dom7 with another dom7 rooted a tritone away -- the b5 pivot point where both chords are note-for-note the same (enharmonically respelled) -- producing chromatic root motion in place of circle-of-fifths resolution, and effectively converting a natural dominant into a fully altered one. Chapter 3, p. 17.

Over a tritone-substituted dominant, Heussenstamm prescribes descending through scalar tones 5-3-2-1 for each chord, creating an overall down-by-half-steps sound through the progression. Chapter 3, p. 17.

Heussenstamm prescribes extending tritone substitution from single chords to entire ii-V pairs -- a bebop-harmony device where a whole substitute ii-V unit replaces the original ii-V, sometimes with the original pair played first and the subs inserted before resolution. Chapter 3, p. 18.

Heussenstamm prescribes using tritone-substitute dominant chords for turnarounds, resulting in parallel chromatic movement of dominant-13 voicings (e.g., Db13 replacing G7#9). He emphasizes this is not random sliding but logically derived from circle-of-fifths substitution while retaining original harmonic direction. Chapter 3, p. 18.

Heussenstamm prescribes shell voicings for dominant sevenths -- root, 3rd, 7th reduced to two strings, then root dropped -- on the middle strings for mellow midrange comping alongside a bassist. He notes that tritone-substitute dom7 shells share the exact same two-string shape, with 3rd and 7th inverted. Chapter 5, p. 48-49.

Heussenstamm prescribes Lydian dominant (Mixolydian with raised 4th) over a natural unaltered dominant seven as an alternative to plain Mixolydian, because the natural 4th clashes with the chordal 3rd when sustained -- Lydian dominant eliminates that clash while accommodating the #11. Chapter 8, p. 93.

Heussenstamm prescribes the bebop dominant scale (Mixolydian plus the natural/major 7th as a passing tone) as a dominant-seven tool favored by Charlie Parker, to be mastered but not overused. Chapter 10, p. 142.

Heussenstamm prescribes the half-step/whole-step diminished scale over dom7 chords -- constructed from the same scale and therefore applicable to the dominant it generates -- and mandates mastery of this sound for all jazz players, paired with a restraint caveat against overuse. The scale covers four keys via three-fret equivalence. Chapter 10, p. 143; Chapter 11, p. 152.

Heussenstamm proscribes overuse of the diminished scale over dominant chords: 'All jazz musicians need to get command of this sound... Don't overuse this scale, but you should definitely master it.' The restraint rule is paired with a mastery imperative. Chapter 10, p. 143.

Heussenstamm teaches (attributing to Bob Conti) that exactly four tension tones -- b5, #5, b9, #9 -- distinguish altered dominants from the native dominant scale; all other tones are already present in the dominant key. Mastering application of these four tones is the core altered-dominant task. Chapter 11, p. 145.

Heussenstamm prescribes Bb Mixolydian (Bb major scale with b7 instead of natural major 7th) as the starting scale for dominant seven improvisation, and introduces the lead-in tone concept -- a chromatic half-step approach note below the root. Chapter 11, p. 145.

Heussenstamm prescribes two contrasting scale choices over a single dominant seventh chord -- minor pentatonic for a bluesy color and Mixolydian for a jazzy color -- and teaches switching between them mid-passage without a chord change, using A7 as the example. Chapter 10, p. 134.

Heussenstamm prescribes moderate or minimal voicing size (root-3rd-7th small shapes) for straight-4 quarter-note comping in the Freddie Green style, with precise release timing between each chord (not blurred, not too chopped) and low volume -- 'felt more than heard.' Chapter 5, p. 46-47.

Heussenstamm fixes maj7 as the I chord in a major-key ii-V-I, teaches C major scale over Cmaj7, and extends it to maj9 for chord-tone arpeggio exercises. The 7th-to-3rd voice-leading rule (each chord's 7th resolving to the next chord's 3rd) is the governing melodic principle at the I chord arrival. Chapter 2, p. 9.

Heussenstamm teaches that the Lydian scale (major with raised 4th) generates the maj7#11 chord via stacked thirds, making Lydian the correct scale for improvising over maj7#11 -- and prescribes B minor pentatonic (C Lydian minus the tonic and 5th, which can sound dissonant against the chord) as a practical shortcut for soloing over Cmaj7#11. Chapter 6, p. 56-57.

Heussenstamm proscribes sustaining the tonic and 5th of C Lydian in a medium or high register over a Cmaj7#11 chord, because these tones can sound dissonant against parts of the chord -- recommending B minor pentatonic (which omits them) as the practical alternative. Chapter 6, p. 57.

Heussenstamm prescribes approaching a maj7 chord from a maj7 a half step above as an outside device, justified by tritone-substitution logic -- Dbmaj7 standing in for G7 (itself a tritone sub of Db dominant) resolves chromatically into Cmaj7, lending V-I mojo to what sounds like sliding one fret down. Chapter 7, p. 86.

Heussenstamm prescribes an altered dominant (at minimum with a flatted or raised 9th) as the V chord in a minor ii-V-i, stating the tendency is 'strong' for V-i motion to use an altered dominant -- this is the strongest single prescriptive rule in the book for altered dominant choice. Super Locrian is the corresponding scale. Chapter 2, p. 10; Chapter 4, p. 31.

Heussenstamm prescribes super Locrian (seventh mode of melodic minor, built a half step above the altered dominant root) as the master scale capturing all four altered tones (b5, #5, b9, #9) plus root, 3rd, b7 -- forming a dom7 without the perfect 5th. G super Locrian = Ab melodic minor. Chapter 1, p. 6; Chapter 11, p. 160.

Heussenstamm prescribes a two-chord dominant pattern in minor blues: the bVI chord is a natural dominant (e.g., Bb9 or Bb13), which then leads to the V as an altered dominant (e.g., D7#9 or D7b5). This bVI natural / V altered pairing is presented as 'the normal pattern' for minor blues. Chapter 3, p. 21.

Heussenstamm prescribes Bb melodic minor as the common scalar ground unifying multiple chord types that coexist in a progression -- starting from A, it becomes A altered/super Locrian; starting from Bb, it produces Eb Lydian dominant. One parent scale covers the entire altered dominant territory. Chapter 6, p. 62.

Heussenstamm designates the min7b5 (half-diminished) as the ii chord in a minor ii-V-i and prescribes Locrian scale for improvisation over it, noting that Locrian over the half-diminished amounts to the same note set as natural minor from the tonic. Chapter 2, p. 10.

Heussenstamm teaches that a minor melodic shape starting on the 9th of a minor chord simultaneously functions as the #9th of an altered dominant, the 13th of a natural dominant, and the 11th of a min7b5 (half-diminished) -- prescribing awareness of this multi-chord mapping as a versatility tool. Chapter 6, p. 62.

Heussenstamm prescribes the 7sus4 (not plain sus4) as the jazz form of the suspended chord, and teaches that in jazz the chord is more likely than in other styles to remain unresolved -- not reverting to the major 3rd. Players should avoid forcing resolution to the 3rd as would be expected in pop or classical contexts. Chapter 6, p. 66.

Heussenstamm proscribes the default resolution of 7sus4 to the major 3rd in jazz contexts -- unlike in pop or classical, the 7sus4 stays suspended. Resolving it undermines the idiomatic jazz sonority. Chapter 6, p. 66.

Heussenstamm prescribes treating 7sus4 as structurally equivalent to a minor seventh built on its 5th (G7sus4 = Dm7 over G), and derives both voicing and improv from this equivalence: Dm7 or Dm9 ideas fit G7sus4 hand-in-glove, naturally accessing G9sus4 and G13sus4 extensions. Chapter 6, p. 66 and p. 69.

Heussenstamm prescribes Mixolydian for improvisation over 7sus4 but inverts the standard dom7 caution: over plain dom7 the player must avoid the 4th clashing with the 3rd, but over 7sus4 the 4th is welcome while the player must instead be cautious about involving the scalar 3rd. Chapter 6, p. 68.

Heussenstamm prescribes brief sus4 treatment as an inner-voice motion device during comping: move the chordal 3rd up a half step to the 4th and back, creating a momentary 7sus4 sound before returning to the original chord. Applied to both I7 and bVII7 in Chapter 8, p. 90.

Heussenstamm prescribes learning diminished chord shapes in the knowledge that the same voicing repeats every three frets (minor 3rd), meaning one shape covers four keys simultaneously -- e.g., B dim, D dim, F dim, and G# dim are all the same four notes in different inversions. Chapter 11, p. 154.

Heussenstamm prescribes using the harmonic minor scale over diminished chords because a diminished chord (vii dim) occurs naturally within the harmonic minor scale -- the A harmonic minor triad chart places G dim as its seventh degree, justifying A harmonic minor over G diminished. Chapter 11, p. 154.

Heussenstamm teaches that the tonic chord of the melodic minor scale is a min-maj7 (minor chord with major 7th), arising from the harmonized A melodic minor scale: i = Am(maj7). The formula for melodic minor is major scale with flat 3rd (1-2-b3-4-5-6-7), and its harmonization produces min-maj7 at the root. Chapter 11, p. 158.

Heussenstamm prescribes treating dom7#9 and dom7b9 as interchangeable voicings and uses their exchange to create inner-voice melodic motion -- e.g., moving from Bb7#9b5 to Bb7b9#5 produces a half-step melodic line on the high E string between the #9th and b9th. Chapter 8, p. 90.

Heussenstamm identifies the 7th-to-3rd guide-tone resolution as the fundamental voice-leading move between dominant and its resolution chord -- specifically demonstrated as G (7th of Am7b5) leading to F# (3rd of D7b9) -- and prescribes targeting these tones at key moments in melodic lines. Chapter 3, p. 22.

For maj7, Larsen prescribes selecting upper-structure arpeggios by shared tones rather than root movement: over Fmaj7, use Am7 (rooted on the 3rd) because 'Fmaj7 and Am7 have three notes in common.' The arpeggio-on-the-3rd is the primary substitution, yielding the richest overlap. Chapter 1, p. 14.

For tonic maj7, Larsen prescribes playing the minor pentatonic from the 3rd (e.g., E Minor Pentatonic over Cmaj7), reframing the pentatonic notes as a Dm7add11 extended arpeggio to make the harmonic rationale explicit: 'D F G A C / 1 b3 11(or4) 5 b7.' Chapter 1, p. 18.

For tonic major chords, Larsen prescribes: 'Playing the minor pentatonic scale from the 3rd is a great device to use over tonic major chords.' This yields a characteristic coloring via the major 7th, 9th, 3rd, 5th, and 6th/13th. Chapter 4, p. 57.

For min7 functioning as a II chord, Larsen prescribes arpeggios built from the 5th degree: 'Playing the arpeggio from the 5th degree of the minor seventh chord creates a nice sound over a II chord, but you could consider adding the 3rd of the Dm7 chord, since that note is not in the arpeggio. Adding the third helps to clearly define the sound of the underlying chord.' Chapter 2, p. 35.

For min7 in bebop context, Larsen prescribes: 'Playing an arpeggio from the 3rd of a chord is a useful device to produce characteristic bebop lines.' This is a named and endorsed bebop substitution principle. Chapter 2, p. 36.

Over a min7 II chord, Larsen prescribes a chromatic bebop approach to the third: 'Over a II chord, a common bebop device is to approach the third chromatically from a whole step above. In the example below this is the chromatic descent from C to Bb.' Chapter 3, p. 50.

For min7 as II chord, Larsen prescribes arpeggiation from the 5th as a voice-leading device: 'Playing an arpeggio from the 5th of the II chord is a fantastic way to target the third of the V chord that follows it. To the ears, it sounds like a suspended chord, but without moving very far from the key.' Chapter 3, p. 49.

For min7 chord tones, Larsen prescribes: 'the lick played over the Gm7 encloses the chord tone with a diatonic note above and a chromatic note below. The same idea is applied first to the root, then the 3rd.' This two-note enclosure formula is applicable to any chord tone on the min7. Chapter 3, p. 47.

For min7, Larsen prescribes the Coltrane 1-b3-4-5 variant: 'Coltrane patterns (1 2 35 on a major chord, 1 b3 4.5 on a minor chord)' -- on a minor chord use the 1-b3-4-5 grouping to break up scalic lines and create interest over fast-tempo changes. Chapter 1, p. 24.

For min7, Larsen sanctions omitting the 3rd to open the sound: 'I have omitted the 3rd (Bb) of Gm7 which immediately makes the line more open sounding. In isolation, it could sound like a G7sus4 chord, but is fine when we hear it in the context of our key.' The rule is contextual tolerance -- the overall harmonic frame justifies the omission. Chapter 3, p. 52.

For min7 as tonic (Cm7), Larsen prescribes an Ebmaj7 arpeggio inversion-skip: 'the line over Cm7 has an Ebmaj7 arpeggio that begins on the root, but skips down to the G, then ascends the arpeggio ... This type of phrase is very common with George Benson and Grant Green.' Chapter 6, p. 77.

For min7 as tonic (Cm7), Larsen prescribes quintal arpeggios: 'The quintal arpeggio is also a great open sounding structure to apply to a Cm7 chord. Here it is used from the Eb and spells out a Cm11 sound. The quintal arpeggio is preceded by a diatonic enclosure of the Eb.' Chapter 6, p. 78.

For dom7, Larsen's primary prescription is the m7b5-on-the-3rd substitution: 'playing a m7b5 chord on the 3rd of a dominant 7 chord causes us to avoid playing the root (G) and adds the rich-sounding 9th (A) ... It sounds so good that many musicians always use it instead of the original arpeggio.' This is 'one of the most common uses of arpeggios in jazz.' Chapter 1, p. 15.

For dom7, Larsen prescribes a strict hierarchy for upper-structure arpeggio roots: 'Jazz musicians will often play a new arpeggio from any note in the underlying chord ... arpeggios from the third (B) fifth (D) or even the seventh (F).' The 3rd-rooted arpeggio is most versatile; as you move to the 5th and 7th, 'you include fewer notes from the original chord, so you need to be a bit more careful.' Chapter 1, p. 14-15.

For dom7, Larsen warns: 'The only thing to watch for here is to choose carefully when to use the C note. Playing a C over a G7 chord will suggest a G7sus4 sound. This might be desirable in some instances but not in others.' The 11th must be deployed with deliberate intent, not by default. Chapter 1, p. 23.

For dom7, Larsen prescribes using the half-whole diminished scale's four embedded major triads (F, Ab, B, D) as upper-structure melodic material: 'The most common sound associated with this scale is probably the 13b9. Guitarists generally think of this as an upper-structure triad placed above a dominant 7th chord. E.g. F713b9 is a D major triad over an F7 chord.' Chapter 5, p. 66-67.

For dom7, Larsen prescribes the Ab+D major triad pair to express 13b9 color: 'The combination of the Ab and D major triads conveys the sound of an F7 with a #9 (Ab), b9 (Gb) and 13 (D). The melody between the Ab and the D creates a voice leading transition between the two, as the Ab moves to A and the Eb moves to D.' Chapter 5, p. 70.

For dom7, Larsen prescribes omitting the root-position major triad in diminished-scale melodic lines: 'I don't often use the F major triad because it doesn't add any colour.' The four diminished-scale triads over F7 reduce in practice to three (Ab, B, D), with F itself excluded. Chapter 6, p. 74.

For dom7 (F7), Larsen prescribes first-inversion F major and B major triads in combination to highlight #11 and b9 extensions: 'The F7 line uses first inversion F major and B major triads. This combination highlights the #11 and b9 extensions.' Chapter 6, p. 75.

For dom7, Larsen prescribes triplet rhythms on 7th arpeggios as a bebop device: 'Using triplets to play 7th arpeggios is a great bebop trick that works well in a more modern jazz context as well.' Rhythmic variation via eighth-note triplets embellishes arpeggios and implies unwritten passing chords. Chapter 4, p. 56.

For dom7 (Bb7alt), Larsen prescribes implying unwritten passing chords to create forward motion: 'Suggesting passing chords that aren't written is a great way to create motion towards a chord change ... the Gm7 arpeggio ... creates a strong motion from the Fm7 to Bb7alt chords.' Chapter 4, p. 58.

For dom7 as V, Larsen prescribes applying harmonic minor material to create a pull to the next chord: 'Uses the harmonic minor on Bb7 to pull towards the Eb7 (in this case playing the pattern of a Ddim arpeggio).' Harmonic minor over the dominant signals the tonic resolution. Chapter 6, p. 82.

For dom7alt, Larsen's primary prescription is guide-tone arpeggio selection: 'The defining tones of a Bb7alt chord are the 3rd and 7th (F and Ab), so if we use arpeggios from the Bb Altered scale that contain those intervals we can stay close to the dominant sound and introduce some cool altered extensions. Only two chords contain both notes: E7 and G#m7b5.' Chapter 4, p. 54.

For dom7alt, Larsen prescribes G#m7b5 (m7b5 on the 3rd of the tritone sub) as the best arpeggio: 'G#m7b5 is related to E7, as it can be viewed as an arpeggio built on the 3rd of E7. Of the two options, the G#m7b5 arpeggio is probably the best candidate to spell out a Bb7alt sound.' Its interval map over Bb7: b7(G#/Ab), b9(B), 3(D), b13(F#). Chapter 4, p. 54.

For dom7alt, Larsen prescribes framing the altered scale through the tritone substitute relationship: 'The Bb Altered scale is the seventh mode of B Melodic Minor ... E7 is the tritone substitute of Bb7.' This reframing makes arpeggios from B Melodic Minor directly available over Bb7alt. Chapter 4, p. 53-54.

For dom7alt (applied to the preceding tonic Fm7 leading into Bb7alt), Larsen prescribes four-note chromatic enclosure to delay arrival: 'In Example 4o the purpose of the enclosure is to suspend the 3rd of the Fm7 chord until beat 3, before the line continues with an Abmaj7 arpeggio.' The enclosure suspends and then releases the target chord tone. Chapter 4, p. 61.

For dom7alt lines, Larsen explicitly endorses multiple simultaneous valid analyses: 'The F7 altered line can be analysed in two ways: an Ebm7b5 arpeggio over the whole bar, or a Gbm triad for the first half of the bar and an Ebm7b5 arpeggio inversion for the second half.' Students should internalize the system rather than fix on one reading. Chapter 6, p. 82.

For dom7alt (F7alt context), Larsen prescribes B and Ab major triads (both first inversion) to maximize extension color: 'On the F7 chord, the line combines B and Ab major triads. Both are in first inversion and together they add a lot of colour with the b9, #9 and #11.' Chapter 6, p. 77.

For dom7b9 (C7 b9/b13 from harmonic minor context), Larsen prescribes specific arpeggios: 'the ones I have selected below will convey a C7 (b9, b13) sound. The arpeggios I recommend are: Cmaj, Edim, Gdim, Abaug, Bbdim, C7, Edim, Abmaj7#5.' These are drawn from F Harmonic Minor over the V chord. Chapter 3, p. 44.

For dom7b9 lines, Larsen prescribes combining b9 and #9 in the same line: 'The dominant 7th line in this example uses a common "trick" -- which is to add in the #9 as well as the b9. In this instance the #9 is an Eb, which sounds great over the C7 chord. It functions a bit like a chromatic passing note, as it leads nicely to E -- the 3rd of C7.' Chapter 3, p. 47.

For dom7b9 (C7 over F harmonic minor), Larsen prescribes deriving the non-diatonic Bbm7b5 arpeggio by rerooting the scale: 'Bbm7b5 is not a diatonic chord of F Harmonic Minor, but it is possible to construct this arpeggio with notes from the scale ... Using Bbm7b5 over the C7 chord imposes the intervals of the b7, b9, 3 and #5. They sound great!' Chapter 3, p. 50.

For min7b5 functioning as the upper-structure substitute on a dominant's 3rd, Larsen prescribes: G#m7b5 over Bb7alt is 'the best candidate to spell out a Bb7alt sound,' yielding b7, b9, 3, and b13 extensions. The m7b5-on-the-3rd rule -- first stated in Chapter 1 for plain dom7 -- is directly extended here to the altered dominant. Chapter 4, p. 54.

For min7b5 as an F7alt melodic device, Larsen prescribes Ebm7b5 as one of two valid readings: 'an Ebm7b5 arpeggio over the whole bar, or a Gbm triad for the first half of the bar and an Ebm7b5 arpeggio inversion for the second half.' Chapter 6, p. 82.

For dim7 as a structural tool, Larsen prescribes extracting embedded major triads: 'The diminished scale can be viewed as two interlocking diminished 7th chords that repeat symmetrically in minor 3rd intervals. One of the best ways to use a "synthetic" scale like this is to pick out and isolate the triads it contains.' The four major triads (F, Ab, B, D) are the primary melodic material. Chapter 5, p. 63.

For dim7, Larsen prescribes exploiting minor-third symmetry to reduce learning load: 'everything that exists inside the Half Whole Diminished scale can be moved in minor 3rds, so we only have to look at the chords we can build on the first two notes ... and we can find the rest by transposing them in minor 3rd intervals.' Chapter 5, p. 65.

For dim7 as a passing chord, Larsen prescribes restating a preceding melodic phrase with slight alteration: 'This is a very common melodic trick which makes a statement over the Eb7 chord and repeats it over the Edim chord, altering it slightly to fit. The F note in bar 5 is changed to an E in bar 6.' Chapter 6, p. 82.

For aug7 / augmented triad over dominant, Larsen prescribes resolution as a characteristic bop move: 'The resolution of augmented triads is a common bop trait that has carried over into more modern styles.' The augmented triad is deployed over the dominant and then resolved. The C7#5 arpeggio (C7 triad with added augmented 5th) is also available as a non-diatonic but scale-compatible option over C7 from F Harmonic Minor. Chapter 4, p. 60; Chapter 3, p. 52.

Laukens treats maj7 as the resolution target of the ii–V–I progression, one of the five essential chord qualities every beginning jazz guitarist must master. In Chapter 1 (p. 10), maj7 is introduced as a moveable shape anchored by the red-dot root ('the red note tells you what the name of the chord is'), fingered with thumb on bass and fingers 1–3 on upper voices for string-6-root voicings. All five shapes correspond to CAGED positions (Chapter 3, p. 66).

Laukens prescribes the major blues scale (major pentatonic + b3) for soloing over maj7 chords in major-key contexts. In Chapter 4 (p. 83), he demonstrates this over the Am7–D7–Gmaj7–Cmaj7 passage from Autumn Leaves: 'You can use this scale to solo over any progression in a major key...or over individual 7th and maj7 chords. Because there is not 7th in this scale, it can be applied to both G7 and Gmaj7 chords.' The absence of the 7th prevents clash with the chord's major-7th quality.

In Chapter 6 (p. 172), Laukens defines the Bird Blues form by its replacement of the standard I7 tonic with Imaj7: 'A Bird blues starts and ends with an Fmaj7 chord, which is odd for a blues progression.' This makes maj7 the distinguishing tonic quality of bebop blues, contrasted explicitly against the dominant-7 tonic of standard blues.

Laukens treats dom7 as one of the five essential moveable chord shapes (Chapter 1, p. 10), voiced with the red-dot root determining the chord's name. In the ii–V–I context, it occupies the V position. In Chapter 6 (p. 158–159), dom7 is also the normative tonic of standard blues: 'The tonic chord of a blues is a dominant 7 chord...The 3 basic chords of a blues are all dominant 7 chords.' Lead-sheet symbols for dom7 may be embellished with 9ths, 13ths, and 6ths in comping (p. 159).

Laukens prescribes the phrygian dominant scale (fifth mode of harmonic minor) as the first-choice soloing sound over V7 and V7alt in bebop contexts. Chapter 5 (p. 101) states: 'When soloing in the bebop style, the phrygian dominant scale is a first-choice sound when improvising over V7 and V7alt chords in your lines.' This is a rule-level prescription, not merely a suggestion.

Laukens teaches tritone substitution as a modification of any dom7 chord: 'The basic application of a tritone sub is to take any 7th chord you see and play another 7th chord that occurs a tritone (#4 aka b5) away' (Chapter 5, p. 105). The substitution is validated by the shared 3rd and 7th between tritone-related dom7 chords — e.g., C7 and F#7 share E and Bb. In Chapter 6 (p. 169), bar-specific applications are given for jazz blues (e.g., bar 10: 'Bb7 in place of E7, the V7 of Am7').

In Chapter 5 (p. 112), Laukens prescribes the Mixolydian mode as 'the mode most associated with the dominant 7th chord sound' and uses it as the basis for double-stop soloing over a pedal tone: 'This phrase is built from the A mixolydian mode...and uses double stops on top of an A pedal.' This establishes Mixolydian as the default scalar color for dom7 in non-altered, non-V7alt contexts.

Laukens prescribes the strategy of mixing the b3 (from the minor blues scale) with the natural 3 (from Mixolydian) over dominant 7 chords in a jazz blues context. Chapter 6 (p. 182) states: 'The first 8 bars use the F minor pentatonic scale, mixed with the major 3rd (bar 3). Mixing b3 and 3 is often used by jazz musicians to create a bluesy sound. One way to do this is mixing the F minor blues scale with the F Mixolydian scale.'

Laukens prescribes replacing or preceding a dominant chord with its sus version as a comping technique. Chapter 6 (p. 178) states: 'Sus chords are a nice way to delay and bring extra motion to dominant chords.' This is offered as a bar-specific instruction (bar 10 of the blues example) and as a general rule for dom7 comping.

Laukens identifies VI7b9 as a Count Basie innovation in jazz blues harmony. Chapter 6 (p. 164) states: 'You will also see...a VI7b9 chord in bar 8, both now commonly used ideas that were popularized by the Basie Band.' This chord functions as a secondary dominant with added b9 tension preceding the ii chord.

Laukens prescribes harmonic minor as the scale for soloing over dominant 7b9 chords. Chapter 6 (p. 184) demonstrates this directly: 'The classic lick in bar 20 uses the G Harmonic Minor scale over D7, creating a 7b9 sound.' This complements the Chapter 4 (p. 87) teaching that tonic harmonic minor over V7alt 'create[s] a V7(b9,b13) sound' — the harmonic minor generates the b9 alteration as a natural scale degree.

Laukens prescribes tonic harmonic minor (not the chord's own root) for soloing over V7alt in a minor ii–V–I. Chapter 4 (p. 87): 'When soloing over the V7alt chord (the B7alt chord in Autumn Leaves) in a minor ii V I, you use the tonic harmonic minor scale.' The phrygian dominant (fifth mode of harmonic minor) is also the 'first-choice sound' for V7 and V7alt in bebop (Chapter 5, p. 101). Both prescriptions derive from the same harmonic minor source, approached from different modal starting points.

Laukens prescribes the Lydian Dominant scale over the tritone substitute of a dominant chord, equating it to the altered scale of the original: 'Bar 16 uses the B Lydian Dominant scale (= F Altered scale). B7 is the tritone substitute of F7 and creates an altered sound over F' (Chapter 6, p. 183). This makes Lydian Dominant the scale of choice when the tritone sub is played in place of a V7alt.
