Laukens introduces min7 as one of the five essential chord qualities (Chapter 1, p. 10), occupying the ii position in the ii–V–I–vi progression. In the arpeggio chapter (Chapter 3, p. 54–55), Am7 is the anchor example for two arpeggio patterns: Pattern #1 using 5th/4th skips and Pattern #2 using groups of three notes. All min7 arpeggio shapes are moveable (p. 59).

Laukens prescribes melodic minor for soloing over Im7 in a minor ii–V–I: 'The final scale is used to solo over the Im7 chord in a minor ii V I, melodic minor. This scale has a raised 7th interval, which creates tension over m7 chords in your solos' (Chapter 4, p. 89). The raised 7th is treated as a deliberate expressive choice: 'experiment with this scale in your solos to determine where you want to use that raised 7th in your lines' (p. 90).

In Chapter 2 (p. 34), Laukens teaches Maiden Voyage as 'a fun study in modal jazz, Dorian modes, rhythmic control, and key changes.' Minor 7 chords in modal contexts are treated as Dorian tonic centers, each chord requiring its own Dorian scale — a direct application of the chord-specific scale-change rule. The four key-center changes in the 32-bar form mean each m7 chord demands a fresh Dorian assignment.

In Chapter 5 (p. 139), Laukens prescribes three-note-per-string legato lines as a soloing technique over min7 chords, citing Pat Metheny's approach: 'Pat translates these scale shapes to the jazz idiom as he uses hammer-ons per string to build a highly fluid line over a Dm7 chord.' The prescription is to 'add as many slurs per string as you can' to develop fluid phrasing.

Laukens prescribes natural minor (Aeolian mode) for soloing over the half-diminished ii chord in a minor ii–V–I. Chapter 4 (p. 85) uses F#m7b5 from Autumn Leaves as the example: 'The next scale is used to solo over the F#m7b5 chord in Autumn Leaves...This scale is the 6th mode of the major scale, and is also called the Aeolian mode.' The shared-root strategy reduces fingering complexity across the whole minor ii–V–I.

Laukens establishes half-diminished 7 (min7b5) as one of the five essential jazz chord qualities, specifically occupying the ii position in a minor ii–V–I. In Chapter 1 (p. 10), it is introduced as a moveable shape. In Chapter 7 (p. 192), it is notated with a small Roman numeral (vii°/ii°), encoding its minor/diminished quality. The CAGED-correspondent moveable shapes apply (Chapter 3, p. 66).

Laukens identifies #IVdim7 as a Count Basie innovation used as a passing chord in jazz blues: 'One of the innovations Count Basie brought to the blues...is the use of the #IVdim7 chord in bars two and 6 of a jazz blues progression' (Chapter 6, p. 164). This positions dim7 as a chromatic passing substitute between I7 and IV7 rather than as a standalone tonic or dominant replacement.

Laukens prescribes a reduced grip set for dim7 chords due to their symmetry. Chapter 3 (p. 70): 'You only need to learn 2 grips for diminished chords because diminished chords are symmetrical.' The same two-grip rule applies to dim7 arpeggios. This is the only chord quality in the book that receives a memorization-reduction prescription based on structural symmetry.

Laukens prescribes playing a dim7 arpeggio from the 3rd of any 7th chord as an essential bebop device called the '3 to 9 arpeggio': 'When playing a dim7 arpeggio from the 3rd of any 7th chord, you will outline the 3-5-b7-b9 intervals of that chord...This is called a 3 to 9 arpeggio, an essential learning for any bebop guitarist' (Chapter 5, p. 104). This is a substitution technique: the dim7 shape is borrowed to add b9 color to a dom7 context.

In Chapter 6 (p. 178), Laukens demonstrates contrary motion voice leading into a dim7 chord: 'The bass goes from C to C# (upward motion), while the D of C9 goes to the C# (downward motion) of C#°7. Contrary motion in voice leading sounds nice.' The dim7 is positioned after the IV9 chord as a chromatic voice-leading event, with contrary motion explicitly named as the preferred technique.

Laukens introduces maj7 as a foundational chord type in Chapter 2, presented in drop 2 and drop 3 root-position voicings (ch. 2, p. 8). The movable-shape system: a single Cmaj7 fingering transposed two frets up becomes Dmaj7 (ch. 1, p. 7).
For maj7, the shell chord reduces to root/3rd/7th on the lower string sets: 'These three-note chords contain the root, 3rd, 7th (or the 6th) of each chord' (ch. 3, p. 14).

Shell voicings on lower string sets require active tone management in ensemble contexts: 'you need to keep your tone in mind so you don't clash with the bass player.' With soft tone these voicings are 'highly effective when comping in a duo, trio, or larger ensembles' (ch. 3, p. 14).

Any inversion of a maj7 chord symbol — root, 3rd, 5th, or 7th in the bass — may be freely substituted: 'if you see a Cmaj7 chord symbol you can play any inversion of Cmaj7' (ch. 6, p. 45). Ear-based selection: 'each inversion will have a slightly different sound.'

maj6 is its own sub-category within extended chords, distinguished by absence of the 7th: 'Major 6 chords and major 6(9) chords are different from the extended chords that follow because they don't contain a 7' (ch. 4, p. 19). The 6 substitutes for the 7 as the defining interval.

Strict interval-substitution rule: 'In a major 6 chord, the 6 replaces the 7' (ch. 4, p. 19). The 7th must be absent; if both 7 and 6 are present, the chord becomes a major 13. Definitional, not optional.
Laukens groups major 6(9) alongside major 6 as one of two extended chord types that omit the 7th (ch. 4, p. 19). The 6(9) adds the 9th atop the 6-replaces-7 structure.

maj9 is the paradigm example of an extended chord that retains the 7th: 'All the other extended chords (such as maj9), contain the 7th in their construction' (ch. 4, p. 19). The 9 adds color but does not displace the 7.

maj13 distinguished from maj6 by co-presence of 7th and 6th: 'When a 6 and a 7 are both present in a major chord, it becomes a major 13 chord' (ch. 4, p. 19). The 13 is enharmonically the 6; the 7th's presence is the diagnostic criterion.

Guitarists cannot voice all available intervals simultaneously: 'guitarists have to leave some notes out when adding extended notes to their chord shapes. Keep that in mind, and notice which notes are replaced' (ch. 4, p. 19). The 7th and 6/13 must both be retained; other tones (e.g., 5th) are candidates for omission.

min7 introduced in Chapter 2 as foundational, taught in drop 2 and drop 3 root-position voicings alongside maj7 and dom7. Learn one shape per chord type before applying it to a real jazz tune (ch. 2, p. 8).
Shell chord for min7: root/m3/m7 on lower string sets. The minor 3rd and minor 7th are the identity-defining intervals retained (ch. 3, p. 14).

Any inversion of a min7 chord symbol may be freely used. Inversions presented in systematic order: 'Notice that for each group of chords, the root is in the bass for the first chord shape, then the 3rd, 5th, and the 7th after that' (ch. 6, p. 45).

dom7 introduced as core four-note drop 2 / drop 3 type, parent type for all altered dominant extensions in Chapter 5: 'These chords can be used over any dominant 7th chord in your comping to create extra tension' (ch. 5, p. 35).
dom7 shell: root, major 3rd, minor 7th — three-note harmonic floor on lower string sets. The tritone between 3rd and 7th is preserved without the 5th (ch. 3, p. 14).

Altered extensions (#11/b5, b9/#9) are available color tones over any dom7. New players directed to begin in minor key contexts: 'These chords can be used over any dominant 7th chord in your comping to create extra tension' (ch. 5, p. 35).

All four inversions of dom7 presented systematically. Ear-based selection: 'some voicings will work better than others' and 'putting the root or the 3rd in the bass causes the chord to have a slightly different flavor' (ch. 6, p. 45).

dom9#11 belongs to Lydian dominant scale family: 'A C7 with a #11 usually contains a natural 9 (d) because this chord is derived from the Lydian dominant scale (4th mode of the melodic minor scale)' (ch. 5, p. 36). Outside the altered-scale dominant family.
Canonical function: bVII7 resolving to Imaj7. 'A C9#11 often functions as a bVII7 going to Imaj7 (C7#11 to Dmaj7, for example)' (ch. 5, p. 36). Backdoor/Lydian dominant approach, not V7.

The #11 voicing characteristically includes a natural 9 — scale-derived co-requirement that distinguishes this voicing from the b5 family. 'A C7 with a #11 usually contains a natural 9' (ch. 5, p. 36).

dom7b5 from altered scale family: 'A C7 with a b5 contains a b9 or #9 because this chord is derived from the altered scale (7th mode of melodic minor)' (ch. 5, p. 36). b5 and #11 enharmonically identical pitches but signal different scale contexts.
b5 voicing co-occurs with b9 or #9 — not natural 9 — because of altered scale derivation. Natural 9 would signal Lydian dominant (ch. 5, p. 36).

dom7b5 (paired with b9 or #9) functions as V7alt resolving to Im7 or Imaj7. 'A C7(b5,b9) often functions as a V7alt going to Im7 or Imaj7 (C7b5b9 going to Fm7 or Fm9, for example)' (ch. 5, p. 36). Canonical minor ii-V-I dominant function.

Minor ii-V-I is the canonical entry point for altered dominants: 'if you have a minor ii V I chord progression (Dm7b5-G7-Cm7), you can use altered extensions over the G7 chord' (ch. 5, p. 35). New players start here before extending to major-key contexts.
min7b5 (Half-Diminished) — both names interchangeable. Core drop 2/3 voicing type, explicitly named as the ii chord in the minor ii-V-I example (Dm7b5, ch. 5, p. 35; also ch. 2, p. 12).
Players must recognize both names: 'Minor 7b5' label and 'Half-Diminished' symbol (ø) are equivalent — prerequisite for correctly parsing chord charts (ch. 2, p. 12).

Quartal chords are structurally distinct from tertian harmony: 'built by stacking 4th intervals above the lowest note of the chord' (ch. 8, p. 59). Outside the extended-chord taxonomy; characteristically open, modern sound.

Unlike altered dominants or open chords, quartal chords are universally applicable: they 'can be used over any jazz standard in your comping and solos' (ch. 8, p. 59). No harmonic context restriction.

Two fretboard implementations of quartal voicings derived from C Dorian: string set 2-3-4-5 (ch. 8, p. 59) and string set 1-2-3-4 (ch. 8, p. 60). Same harmonic material at different registers via direct position transfer.

Quartal chords prescribed for both comping AND soloing: 'can be used over any jazz standard in your comping and solos' (ch. 8, p. 59). Distinguishes them from shell voicings (ensemble comping focus) and drop 2/3 (comping-primary).
Open chords are structurally distinct: 'Open chords use open strings in their construction' (ch. 7, p. 54). Not transposable by the two-fret rule like other shapes in the dictionary.

Open chords prescribed for specific guitar-friendly key centers only: 'Though they are limited to a few keys, these shapes add new flavor to your comping in particular key centers. Open chords have a specific sound that is unique to the guitar' (ch. 7, p. 54). Unique resonant quality justifies learning them despite key restriction.
Complex open voicings must be readable from multiple harmonic perspectives: 'Bm11(b6) = Gmaj7(add 6)/B' (ch. 7, p. 57). Students must master polychord notation to parse open-chord symbols.
dom7alt = b5/b9 or b5/#9 voicing family from altered scale (7th mode of melodic minor). Categorically separated from the Lydian dominant (#11) family (ch. 5, p. 36).

Canonical context: minor ii-V-I. 'if you have a minor ii V I chord progression (Dm7b5-G7-Cm7), you can use altered extensions over the G7 chord' (ch. 5, p. 35), V7alt resolving to Im7 or Imaj7. New players deploy in minor keys first.
Laukens places maj7 chords in the tonic-major family, the resolution target of ii-V-I progressions in major keys (chapter 3 p. 13; chapter 6 p. 200).
Paradigm minor-triad-over-major: 'You can play a minor triad starting on the 3rd of a major chord. For example: Em over Cmaj7' (chapter 8 p. 289).
'Pattern 72 features an Am7 arpeggio over Cmaj7 and can also be used over Am7' (chapter 7 p. 253) — relative-minor arpeggio produces maj9 colour without root-position shape.
'Major bebop scale = major scale + b6' as the idiomatic scale over maj7 chords; guitar requires slides for chromatic passing tone (chapter 7 p. 243).
Characteristic colour move: chromatic descending line between the 7 and 5 of the major chord (chapter 8 p. 285).
'Pattern 57 starts with a G6 arpeggio and can be used on major or dominant chords' (chapter 6 p. 200).
'Pattern 47 is an extension of pattern 43, but this one can only be used on major chords because it contains the 7th' (chapter 5 p. 150).
min7 chords as ii in major ii-V-I and iv in minor (chapter 4 p. 100; chapter 7 p. 240). Dm7 is the paradigm ii chord throughout Studies 4-8.
Wes Montgomery prescription: 'You can play a major triad or maj7 chord on the third of a major chord. For example: Fmaj7 (or F) over Dm7' (chapter 4 p. 100; chapter 8 p. 280).
'You can play a minor triad starting on the 5th of a minor chord. For example: Am over Dm7' (chapter 8 p. 289).

'Augmented chords are often used to play over minor chords, resulting in a minor/major 7 sound. Over a minor chord you can play an augmented triad or maj7#5 arpeggio, both built on the b3' (chapter 4 p. 100; chapter 7 p. 251).
'Minor bebop scale = Dorian mode + 7' as idiomatic scale over min7; guitar uses slides for chromatic passing tone (chapter 7 p. 242).
'The G dominant bebop scale can be played over: G7, G9, G13; Gsus4; Dm7 (in a II VI in C major)' (chapter 7 p. 240) — covers ii-V pair simultaneously.
'Pattern 42 circles around the b3 of Dm7 and contains a minor 1235 pattern starting on the second note' (chapter 5 p. 150) — circling of b3 distinguishes from major-context counterpart.
'if you play an Am triad over Dm7, you can lower one fret and play Abm over G7' (chapter 8 p. 290) — fingerboard shortcut connecting ii-V triad substitutions.
V chord in both major and minor ii-V-I and the most heavily substituted chord quality in the method (chapter 3 p. 13).
'Playing a half-diminished arpeggio from the 3rd of a dominant chord brings out the 9 sound. For example: Bm7b5 over G7' (chapter 3 p. 13; chapter 6 p. 200) — 'very common substitution.'

'Playing Dm over G7 is a technique Wes Montgomery would often use in his solos' (chapter 3 p. 13). Systematic formulation: 'You can play a minor triad starting on the 5th of a dominant chord. For example: Dm over G7' (chapter 8 p. 290).
'The dominant bebop scale is a Mixolydian mode with a descending chromatic note between the root and the b7' (chapter 7 p. 240-241). Primary scale resource over G7, G9, G13.

'You can play the tonic harmonic minor scale over any dominant chord. For example: C harmonic minor over G7... creates a 7b9, b13 sound... Another name for the harmonic minor scale played over a dominant chord is the Phrygian dominant scale' (chapter 5 p. 150).
'Pattern 82 uses tritone substitution by playing a Bb7 arpeggio over E7' (chapter 8 p. 287) — tritone-sub dominant generates full altered sound via chromatic voice-leading.
'Dominants going to major chords can use the regular 1235 pattern. Dominants going to minor chords require a b9 instead of a 9' (chapter 4 p. 100).
'An augmented 7th arpeggio or triad is a convenient way to bring out an altered sound on dominant chords' (chapter 3 p. 13).

'Pattern 83 starts with the chromatic part of the G (dominant) bebop scale and continues with a G7 arpeggio' (chapter 8 p. 288) — standard bebop construction of chromatic approach leading to arpeggio.
'Pattern 86 combines an Em7 arpeggio with a chromatic line' (chapter 8 p. 293) — Em7 = upper-structure minor 7th from 6th/13th over G7.

'You can also play this pattern over dominant chords by changing the natural 7 to a b7 (the 5th note in the pattern)' (chapter 8 p. 286) — one-pitch change separates maj7 from dom7 pattern application.
Ab minor triad over G7: 'The triad brings out a sus4 sound (C) with the altered tensions b9 (Ab) and b13 (Eb)' (chapter 3 p. 13).
'This last pattern voice leads from 13 to b13 to the 9 of C major' (chapter 8 p. 294) — chromatic descending motion through 13th smooths dominant-to-tonic resolution.
'Notice the voice leading going from the 5th of Dm7, to the b9 of G7, to the 5th of Cmaj7. This is a common voice leading over a II V I' (chapter 7 p. 246).

dom7b9 within altered-dominant family, produced when harmonic minor (Phrygian dominant) played over V7 in minor ii-V-I; 7b9/b13 sound is defining colour of V7 in minor contexts (chapter 3 p. 13; chapter 5 p. 150).

'Diminished arpeggios are a common way to play over dominant chord and produce a 7b9 sound. Playing a diminished arpeggio from the b9, 3, 5, or b7 of a dominant chord brings out the b9 sound. For example: Abdim7 over G7' (chapter 5 p. 150).
'Here, I switch from a Bm7b5 arpeggio to a Bdim7 arpeggio, going from the 9 to the b9' (chapter 6 p. 200) — half-diminished to diminished switch intensifies dominant tension.
'Dominants going to minor chords require a b9 instead of a 9' (chapter 4 p. 100) — single alteration converts major-resolving dominant line into minor-resolving one.
dom7alt = maximally tense V chord with all four altered tones (b9, #9, b5/b13) from altered scale (7th mode of melodic minor); G altered scale = Ab melodic minor from G (chapter 6 p. 200).

'The altered scale contains all four of the common altered notes (b9-#9-b5-b13), which are used to create tension over the underlying chord' (chapter 6 p. 200). Used over dom7 in both major and minor keys.
'One of the arpeggios contained in the altered scale is the Gaug7' (chapter 6 p. 200) — discrete melodic unit extracted rather than running scale stepwise.
'Another useful arpeggio in the altered scale is the Bmaj7#5' (chapter 6 p. 200) — higher-register altered color distinct from Gaug7.
'Another useful arpeggio in the altered scale is the Abm/maj7' (chapter 6 p. 200) — completes the three-arpeggio systematic altered-scale extraction set.
'You can play an m(add9) over altered dominant chords, starting on the b9. For example: Fm(add9) over E7#9' (chapter 4 p. 100) — produces #9 and b13 colors.
'You can play a minor triad starting on the b9 of a dominant chord. For example: Abm over G7' (chapter 8 p. 290) — most altered of minor-triad-over-dominant substitutions.
'This is a typical altered scale run starting on the b13' (chapter 8 p. 281) — b13 immediately projects altered color before descent through remaining tensions.
min7b5 as ii in minor ii-V-I, paired with V7alt or V7b9, resolving to minor tonic. Bm7b5-E7alt-Am is the paradigm (chapter 3 p. 13).
'You can play a maj7 chord over a half-diminished chord, starting on the b5 of that half-diminished chord. For example: Fmaj7 over Bm7b5' (chapter 3 p. 13) — produces #11 color.
'You can play a m(add9) arpeggio over half-diminished chords, starting on the b3. For example: Dm(add9) over Bm7b5' (chapter 4 p. 100).
'The G dominant bebop scale can be played over: ... Bm7b5 (in a II VI in A minor)' (chapter 7 p. 240) — bridges half-dim ii and dominant V in minor ii-V.
'This Cmaj7 arpeggio can be used over Cmaj7, Am7, or F#m7b5' (chapter 5 p. 150) — single arpeggio shape serves three harmonic targets simultaneously.
Within the dominant substitution family — not as independent chords but as arpeggio shapes deployed over dominants to produce b9 coloration (chapter 5 p. 150; chapter 6 p. 200).

'The convenient thing about diminished chords and arpeggios is that their inversions are identical in shape and notes' due to stacked minor thirds — every inversion of Cdim7 uses same fingering (chapter 5 p. 150).

'Playing a diminished arpeggio from the b9, 3, 5, or b7 of a dominant chord brings out the b9 sound. For example: Abdim7 over G7' (chapter 5 p. 150) — all four entry points yield same shape due to symmetry.
Sus4 within dominant family: 'The G dominant bebop scale can be played over: G7, G9, G13; Gsus4; Dm7' (chapter 7 p. 240) — sus4 as dominant color variant, not independent quality.
Ab minor triad over G7 — 'The triad brings out a sus4 sound (C) with the altered tensions b9 (Ab) and b13 (Eb)' (chapter 3 p. 13) — sus4 reachable via b9-rooted minor triad sub.
'One of the arpeggios contained in the altered scale is the Gaug7' (chapter 6 p. 200) — aug7 as superimposition shape over dom7alt, not independent quality.
'its inversions look exactly the same, so you can just slide the same shape 4 frets up or down and essentially get the same chord' (chapter 4 p. 100) — mirrors dim7 symmetry rule.

'Augmented triads can also be used to solo over dominant #11 chords... For example: Db7#11 going to Cmaj7. Because Db7#11 is a substitution for G7alt, you can use a G augmented triad over that chord' (chapter 4 p. 100).
min7 as ii in II-V-I: Dm7 | G7 | CM7. Dm7 occupies the ii slot before the dominant (chapter 1 p.1).
Over ii min7, use Dorian bebop scale (Dorian + chromatic passing tone). 'D Dorian bebop (D-E-F-F#-G-A-B-C)' over Dm7 in Lick #6 measure 1 (chapter 1 p.5).
ii min7 occupies bar 1, voiced with its own arpeggio. 'Bar 1: Dm7 arpeggio (D-F-A-C)' as direct approach (chapter 1 p.2).
dom7 as original V7 targeted by the tritone substitution. G7 is the canonical V7 whose altered extensions are highlighted by the substitute (chapter 1 p.1).

'The basic application of a tritone chord substitution is to take any 7th chord and play another 7th chord that has its root a tritone away from the original' (chapter 1 p.1) — yields Dm7 | Db7 | CM7 in C major.
Over substitute dom7 (Db7), solo with dom7 arpeggio on substitute root: 'Bar 2: Descending Db7 arpeggio (Db-F-A-Cb)'. Root of Db7 highlights #11/b5 of G7 (chapter 1 p.1-2).
'The second option is to play a dominant 9 arpeggio (1-3-5-b7-9)' — add ninth to dom7 arpeggio. Db9 tones map to #11, b7, b9, major third, b13 of G7 (chapter 1 p.1, 3).
'The third option' — major pentatonic (1-2-3-5-6) built on substitute root. Db major pentatonic maps to #11, b13, b7, b9 of G7 yielding 'interesting colors' (chapter 1 p.1, 3).

'The fourth option' — Mixolydian (1-2-3-4-5-6-b7) built on substitute root; shares all tones with major pentatonic plus 4/11 and b7. 'The seventh of Db7 (B) is the third of G7.' Lick #6: 'Db7 mixolydian mode' in measure 2 (chapter 1 p.2, 5).
'The sixth (Bb) of Db7 should be used as an approach note in order to target a chord tone' (chapter 1 p.1) — treat 6th as approach not resting tone in pentatonic/Mixolydian over substitute.

Every tone over substitute dom7 is an altered extension of original V7: 'Db is the #11 of the G7 chord. Eb is the b13 of G7. F is the minor 7th of G7. Ab is the b9 of G7' — substitution systematically highlights b9, #11, b13 alterations (chapter 1 p.1, 3).
Resolve substitute dom7 to tonic via chromaticism: 'Measure 2: Db9 arpeggio (Eb-Cb-Ab-F-Db) and chromaticism to approach the root of CM7' (Lick #5, chapter 1 p.4).
Substitute dom7 occupies bar 2 — all soloing material (arpeggio/pentatonic/modal) assigned to that slot. 'Bar 1: Dm7 arpeggio / Bar 2: Descending Db7 arpeggio / Bar 3: CM7 arpeggio' (chapter 1 p.2).
maj7 as tonic I resolving II-V-I. CM7 = destination in Dm7|Db7|CM7. 'Bar 3: CM7 arpeggio (C-E-G-B)' as resolution statement (chapter 1 p.1-2).
All chromatic/arpeggio motion from substitute dom7 resolves into maj7 tonic in bar 3 — 'chromaticism to approach the root of CM7' is the terminal gesture (chapter 1 p.4).

For minor seventh chords, Martino prescribes identifying the chord's inversion form (1-4) and selecting the corresponding numbered activity: Form 1 maps to Activities 1 and 5, Form 2 to Activity 2, Form 3 to Activity 3, Form 4 to Activity 4. The chord inversion is the operative selector -- melodic choice follows from it rather than from independent judgment. Chapter 1, p. 10.

For minor seventh chords, Martino prescribes determining the key not from the chord name alone but from the position on the neck where the activity form is played: the same activity shape in third position is G minor, in fifth position is A minor, etc. Position is the key selector; the form is key-neutral. Chapter 1, p. 11.

For minor seventh chords encountered after completing all five activity forms, Martino prescribes cycling back to Activity 1 one octave higher rather than stopping -- Activities 1 and 5 share the same chord inversion (Form 1) and the same sixth-string starting note (G), making the system infinitely repeatable up the neck. Chapter 1, p. 15.

For minor seventh chords, Martino prescribes mastering all five activity forms horizontally in all twelve keys before advancing to Phase II (vertical movement). The Phase I completion rule is explicit and non-negotiable: 'Then and only then should you move onto PHASE II.' Chapter 1, p. 16.

For major seventh chords, Martino prescribes substituting the relative minor seventh: Cmaj7 = Am9 (relative minor). This reduction allows the player to apply the minor-based activities system directly to major seventh chords without learning a separate vocabulary. Chapter 3, p. 50.

For major ninth chords, Martino prescribes optionally substituting the secondary relative minor (III chord of the major key): Cmaj9 = Em7. This provides a second substitution path when the primary relative minor (Am7) is harmonically less desirable. Chapter 3, p. 50.

For major sixth chords, Martino prescribes substituting the relative minor seventh: Cmaj6 = Am7. The major sixth and its relative minor share all pitch content; the substitution is direct and requires no additional voice-leading adjustment. Chapter 3, p. 50.

For dominant seventh / ninth chords (treated as quality-equivalent: C7 = C9 = C13), Martino prescribes converting to a minor form rooted a perfect fifth above the dominant root -- e.g., G9 -> Dm6 (up a P5). This closes the three-way substitution loop among m7b5, m6, and dominant ninth. Chapter 4, p. 55.

For altered dominant chords, Martino prescribes moving up one half-step from the dominant root and playing minor -- e.g., for Gb7 altered, play G minor. This single interval-direction instruction replaces the altered chord with a minor form the activities system can handle directly. Chapter 4, p. 57.

For altered dominant chords, Martino prescribes melodic minor over harmonic minor as the scale of choice because only melodic minor contains the b7 -- the 'hot' note of the dominant seventh chord. Harmonic minor supplies b9, #9, b5, and #5 but omits the b7, making it insufficient for fully expressing the altered dominant sound. Chapter 4, p. 57.

Do not substitute harmonic minor over an altered dominant as a first-choice scale: although harmonic minor yields the altered 9ths and 5ths (b9, #9, b5, #5), it lacks the b7, which is the defining tone of a dominant seventh chord. Harmonic minor is a weaker choice; melodic minor is prescribed instead. Chapter 4, p. 57.

For half-diminished (m7b5) chords, Martino prescribes moving up a minor third from the m7b5 root and playing minor -- e.g., Bm7b5 -> Dm6 (up a m3). The rationale is explicit: m7b5 is an incomplete dominant ninth chord and is inversionally equivalent to m6 in third inversion, making the substitution harmonically coherent rather than approximate. Chapter 4, p. 55.

For half-diminished chords, Martino prescribes understanding their inversional equivalence to m6: Bm7b5 is Dm6 in third inversion; conversely, Dm6 is Bm7b5 in first inversion. This bi-directional equivalence is the conceptual foundation for the m7b5-to-minor substitution rule and explains why the same activities apply across both chord types. Chapter 4, p. 55.

For augmented triads, Martino prescribes going up a major sixth from the root and playing melodic or harmonic minor (preferring melodic minor). Because every augmented triad has three enharmonic root names, three distinct minor-maj7 substitutions are available from a single chord -- e.g., F augmented yields Dm(maj7), F#m(maj7), and Bbm(maj7). Martino provides a diagram showing each enharmonic root name and its corresponding minor-maj7 target. Chapter 4, p. 56.

For augmented triads, Martino prescribes treating each of the triad's three notes as a valid root name -- the triad inverts to form two other augmented triads enharmonically, so F aug = A aug = Db aug. This tripling of available root names is the prerequisite step before applying the major-sixth-up minor-maj7 substitution rule. Chapter 4, p. 55.

For major triads appearing as slash chords (major triad over a bass note), Martino prescribes converting the major triad to its relative minor and reinterpreting the bass note as a scale degree of that minor key. For example, C/F# becomes Am with the F# treated as the 6th of A minor. Chapter 4, p. 56.

For major triad slash chords where the primary relative minor clashes with the bass note (e.g., creating a b5 in the bass), Martino prescribes falling back to the secondary relative minor -- the III chord of the major key. For Db/E, Bb minor is rejected because E creates a b5 against it; F minor (III of Db major) is prescribed instead. The F harmonic minor scale is validated by containing all pitch content of the slash chord. Chapter 4, p. 56.

Do not apply the primary relative minor substitution to a major triad slash chord when the bass note creates a b5 against the substitute minor root -- this interval clash is explicitly cited as the disqualifying condition that forces the secondary relative minor fallback. Chapter 4, p. 56.

For minor sixth chords, Martino prescribes understanding their inversional equivalence to m7b5: Dm6 is Bm7b5 in first inversion. The equivalence table in Chapter 3 also shows Cm7b5 = Ebm6, making m6 and m7b5 freely interchangeable within the substitution system. Chapter 3, p. 50; Chapter 4, p. 55.

For minor sixth chords as substitution targets, Martino prescribes using them as the output form of the dominant-ninth reduction: G9 resolves to Dm6 (minor rooted a perfect fifth above G). The m6 form is the preferred minor target -- not plain m7 -- when reducing a dominant ninth. Chapter 4, p. 55.

Martino identifies the dominant 7th chord as the system's most flexible pivot point and structural target: 'The 7th chord having the all important tritone host the largest and most flexible of all the chord types. (7th b5, 7b9, 7th #5, 7th #9, 7th 9s, ren bg bs ect).' The dom7 is the convergence system's primary raw material because its embedded tritone makes it maximally convergent and generates the widest range of alteration options. Chapter 3, p. 8.

Martino prescribes the V chord of the II-V cadence as the exact structural moment where the convergence system is to be deployed: 'It was at this final juncture (II-V) where my convergence system was conceived, noticing all the chord possibilities on the final 5th chord in the cadence.' The student's task is to approach the V chord with the full arsenal of 24 scale colors and their extracted chords. Chapter 3, p. 8.

Martino prescribes applying multiple distinct scale colors to a single dom7 chord -- not merely one scale per chord: 'This, from listening to John Coltrane, Yusef Lateef and others caused me to try using many different scale "color" types on one chord (7th).' The entire 24-scale system exists to supply this variety of approach to the dominant. Chapter 3, p. 8.

For scalar convergence onto a dom7 chord, Martino prescribes targeting the tritone's two defining tones -- the 7th and 3rd of the dominant -- via chromatic resolution: 'It is just a matter of using chromatic tones to resolve the tritone (7th or 3rd) to use those scales against a 7th chord convergingly.' This is the concise rule for all scalar approach to the dominant. Chapter 10, p. 82.

Before deploying any approach scale against a dom7 or any target chord, Martino prescribes internalizing the destination tonality through cadential repetition: 'Before playing each scale in this system, you should brainwash your ear with the tonality (F major in this case) with several cadences into the key. (Ex. G-7-C7 FA) (G#-C 139 FA) I-VI-II-V-T ect.' The ear must know the destination before the approach begins. Chapter 4, p. 32.

While executing an approach scale or chord targeting a dom7 resolution, Martino prescribes simultaneously projecting attention to the destination: 'When converging on a tonality project yourself sound wise to it already having your attention (sound attention) on it and on the chord or scale you are using.' Physical execution and aural anticipation of arrival must occur simultaneously. Chapter 4, p. 34.

Martino prescribes mining every scale for all constituent chords as independent convergent devices targeting the dom7 resolution: 'Extract all possible chords from all scales for resolution purposes.' The student is not to treat scales as melodic entities alone -- every voicing latent in the scale is a valid approach chord. Chapter 4, p. 34.

Martino prescribes dom7b5 chords -- both the V7b5 and its tritone substitute -- as the primary character-chord form for convergence. Chapter 7 demonstrates that 'Bb7b5, C7+5, C7b5, Gb7b5' are all interchangeable because they are tritone-related and resolve to the same FA7 target (see diagram p. 58). The tritone pair shared between Bb7b5 and Gb7b5 makes them fully substitutable as approach chords. Chapter 7, p. 58.

The whole-tone scale (Scale #10) prescribes C7b5 as its primary linking chord: 'The linking chord is the C7b5 which resolves nicely into F major. Other chords which have resolving tendencies are the C+7, C69#11, C7b5.' The dom7b5 is the whole-tone scale's canonical harmonic product for cadential approach. Chapter 4, p. 41.

Scale #23 prescribes a cluster of tritone-resolved dom7b5 voicings: 'Gb7b5, C7b5, C7b9, C7b9b5' are the convergence chords for Scale #23. Both C7b5 and Gb7b5 are present simultaneously, illustrating that the tritone-substitute and original dominant are co-equal approach options. Chapter 8, p. 62.

Martino's personal Scale #11 prescribes the dom7b9 sound as its defining character chord: 'My own personal scale containing an E-Bb tritone & the note Bb9 of which gives the scale a C7b9 sound.' The C7b9 is Scale #11's sonic identity and its convergence vehicle into F major. Chapter 5, p. 28.

Scale #11 prescribes a cluster of tritone-related chords including the dom7b9 as convergent approaches to FA79: 'C7b9, D7b5, Gb, Eb13' all converge on FA79 from Scale #11 (Chapter 7, p. 58). The C7b9 anchors the group; the other chords are interchangeable approach options sharing the same tritone resolution path.

For convergence onto a minor chord, Martino prescribes identifying the specific tritone pair governing the relationship: 'The tritone (G-Db) has a G7 or C7b9 relationship to the F minor chord.' The C7b9 is thus the characteristic dominant approach chord for the F minor convergence, extending the dom7b9's role from major-key to minor-key contexts. Chapter 10, p. 84.

Scale #13 prescribes the full altered dominant family -- C7b9b5, C7b9, C7b5 -- as its native character chords, resolving to the extended tonic FA679 (Chapter 7, p. 59). Scale #6 (Jazz Melodic Minor) also prescribes altered extensions including 'E+A7, Bb7+' as its characteristic chords for convergence (Chapter 7, p. 57). Altered dominants are the direct harmonic product of multiple scales in the system.

Martino prescribes generating altered dominant variants on both the V chord and its tritone substitute as co-equal convergers: for a target of Eb, 'E7b5, E13b5, E9+11, E9, E13 may be used as chord convergers in addition to Bb7.' Altered tensions applied to the tritone-substitute dominant are fully licensed approach chords. Chapter 10, p. 80.

The augmented dominant C7+5 appears as a character chord in multiple scale contexts. Chapter 4 lists it as a product of the whole-tone scale alongside C7b5 (p. 41). Chapter 10 adds 'D7+5 also works beautifully as well as Bo7' as a convergent substitute for the Bb7-to-Eb progression (p. 80). The dom7#5 is thus a licensed augmented-dominant substitute alongside the tritone-substitute and diminished families.

Scale #24 prescribes C7+5 as one of its primary chord targets alongside the minor-major 7th and 13th: 'D-triangle7, C7+5, Gb13' are the tritone-related convergence chords for Scale #24, resolving to FA79 (Chapter 8, p. 62). The augmented dominant is Scale #24's characteristic dominant form.

The maj7 chord (FA7 and its extended forms FA79, FA679) is prescribed as the canonical resolution destination for the entire convergence system. Chapter 7 establishes: 'Bb7b5, C7+5, C7b5, Gb7b5 [resolve to] FA7.' FA79 and FA679 appear throughout Chapters 7-8 as the tonic arrival points toward which all tritone-related approach chords converge. The student's goal is always to make these resolution targets sound inevitable. Chapter 7, p. 58.

Martino prescribes conceptualizing the maj7 tonal center as the target of a 360-degree bombardment by all 24 scales: 'You might call this system the astrological charting of a key center because the 360 degree circle is used & the key center lies at the middle which represents the person or key acted upon. You are bombarding this person, or in this case key center with 24 scales & their constituent chords.' The maj7 resolution is not a passive landing but the active destination of a systematic multi-scale approach. Chapter 5, p. 33.

Martino prescribes a three-step sequence for approaching any maj7 resolution: (1) internalize the destination through cadential repetition ('brainwash your ear with the tonality with several cadences into the key'), (2) execute the approach scale while aurally projecting the resolution, (3) extract all constituent chords from the scale as additional convergent devices. The maj7 landing is prepared, not improvised from ignorance. Chapter 4, pp. 32-34.

Martino identifies the II-V cadence as the convergence system's structural origin point: 'It was at this final juncture (II-V) where my convergence system was conceived.' The min7 (II chord) participates as the cadential setup, with example progressions G-7-C7-FA and I-VI-II-V-I cited as the practice vehicle for ear preparation. Chapter 3, p. 8; Chapter 4, p. 32.

Martino prescribes the Dorian mode as a convergence scale targeting the min7 function within the II-V: 'This scale is simply a dorian mode of the F major scale. It contains C7, G-7, EX. This scale contains the E-Bb tritone which belong to the C7 & F#7 chords which lead to F major.' The G-7 (min7) chord is listed as one of the Dorian scale's extracted character chords. Chapter 6, p. 37.

Scale #24 prescribes D-triangle7 (minor-major 7th) as one of its primary convergence chord targets, appearing alongside C7+5 and Gb13, all resolving to FA79 (Chapter 8, p. 62). The min-maj7 is a co-equal approach chord form in Scale #24's harmonic palette, demonstrating that non-dominant chord types can participate directly in convergent motion.

When converging onto a minor chord using Scale #24 (which contains D-triangle7 as a character chord), Martino prescribes that scales containing major thirds must be applied to embellish the fifth of the minor chord rather than its root: 'Scale #3 has a major 3rd already in it so it has to be used as above to embellish the 5th of the F minor.' The min-maj7 character chord inherits this constraint when the resolution target is minor. Chapter 10, p. 84.

Martino prescribes the diminished seventh chord as a tritone-sharing substitute for the dominant V chord: 'Also the diminish chord D7 has the same tritone as the Bb7 (D-Ab). It smoothly voice leads into the Eb7.' The dim7 joins the tritone-substitute dominant as a licensed approach chord because it shares the critical tritone interval, not merely by convention. Chapter 10, p. 80.

Martino prescribes the diminished scale as a convergence source for both the Fi7 (diminished/half-diminished) and FA7 (major) contexts simultaneously: 'DIMINISH Fi7 / FA7' (Chapter 8, p. 64). This dual applicability -- the dim7 chord serving both diminished-quality and major-quality resolution targets -- reflects the system's principle of symmetrical indifference, where diminished symmetry allows one chord to serve multiple tonal destinations.

Martino prescribes exploiting the diminished scale's symmetrical indifference by starting on different internal notes to serve multiple tonal centers with the same scale form: 'same symmetrical indifference as the #4 scale which permits it to be used (starting on different notes) for converging cadences to several tonalities.' The dim7 chord derived from this scale inherits the same multi-key convergence utility. Chapter 4, p. 36.

Martino prescribes the diminished scale's terminal voice-leading: 'The last note of the scale (the b9th of 7th chord) voice leads smoothly to the note C (the fifth of F major).' The dim7 chord's characteristic endpoint lands on the fifth of the target key, making the fifth -- not the root -- the primary resolution point. Chapter 6, p. 41.

Scale #6 (Jazz Melodic Minor) prescribes E+A7 (augmented major 7th / aug7 variant) as one of its character chords for convergence, appearing in the chord palette alongside Gb7b5 (Chapter 7, p. 57). The aug7 family is a licensed harmonic product of the Jazz Melodic Minor scale within the convergence system.

Martino prescribes reading augmented dominant tones through dual harmonic identity: 'the note Ab which is the minor 3rd of F minor tonality function in an all important way as the +5 of the V chord (C7th +5) making it more tonally palatable. The same note Ab finds its participation as the 3rd of the E7+5 chord produced on this same scale.' A single pitch simultaneously justifies a minor-quality reading and an augmented-dominant reading. Chapter 5, p. 35.

Scale #14 prescribes C7b9sus (suspended dominant with b9) as one of its derived character chords, appearing alongside DbA7b5 and Eb13 (Chapter 7, p. 59). The suspended dominant variant is a licensed approach chord within the convergence system, generated from Scale #14's pentatonic structure mapping to V-chord degrees.

Scale #12 (diminished with minor 3rd and raised 4th) prescribes G-9b5 as one of its character chords alongside Bb7b5 and Db7b5 (Chapter 7, p. 58). The min7b5 (half-diminished) quality is a direct harmonic product of the diminished-family scale within the convergence system, expanding the definition of which chord qualities can function as tritone-related approach chords.

Martino prescribes that when scales containing a major third are used to converge onto a minor chord, they must target the fifth of the minor chord rather than its root: 'Scale #3 has a major 3rd already in it so it has to be used as above to embellish the 5th of the F minor.' This preserves the minor quality of the target and prevents color conflict. Chapter 10, p. 84.

Unlike the general restriction on major-third scales against a minor-chord root, Martino prescribes that scales with major thirds CAN be deployed convergently against a minor chord when aimed specifically at the chord's fifth: 'Scale #3 has a major 3rd already in it so it has to be used as above to embellish the 5th of the F minor.' The fifth-targeting move is the explicitly licensed exception to the root-placement restriction. Chapter 10, p. 84.

Martino prescribes generating the maximum possible palette of approach chords for any single dominant target: 'This yields 21 convergent chord possibilities into Eb7.' For a Bb7-to-Eb convergence, the palette includes Bb7 and all its altered variants, E7 and its tritone-substitute variants with added tensions, the shared-tritone diminished chord D7, the augmented dominant D7+5, and the diminished seventh Bo7. No single approach chord is prescribed as default; the entire palette is available simultaneously. Chapter 10, p. 80.

Martino prescribes organizing all convergent motion toward a tonal center through three interlocking tritone pairs: 'Three tritones (C-F#), (G-Db) & (E-Bb) are involved. Each chord comes from scale (on same line) and either can converge or bombard the F major tonality chord.' Every dominant approach chord in the system belongs to one of these three tritone families; knowing which family a dom7 belongs to determines its convergence destination. Chapter 10, p. 83.

Martino prescribes deploying the full convergence system specifically in turnbacks, cadences, and cycles: 'The usage of these scales in turnbacks, cadences and cycles (which comprise all music) in Jazz yields a wider source of ideas for the improvisor-composer-arranger.' These three structural locations are the designated deployment zones for the system's dominant-chord vocabulary. Chapter 3, p. 4.

Pass identifies the Dominant 7th Chord as the load-bearing gateway to jazz phrasing, explicitly distinguishing it from the major chord: 'Most are based on the Dominant 7th Chord (C7) since many people seem to need guidance in their exploration of its possibilities, especially in distinguishing it from the major chord.' The dom7 family anchors the entire dominant-flexibility system. (Ch. 7, p. 22)

Pass prescribes anchoring the dom7 to the Basic Chord Form and flatting only the seventh tone as the irreducible minimum for improvising on the dominant: 'By constantly using and thinking in terms of the Basic Chord Forms and simply flatting the seventh tone, the number of mistakes made in playing on the Dominant will be greatly reduced.' (Ch. 7, p. 23)

Pass explicitly permits and encourages the alteration of dom7 with b9, +9, b5, or +5 in improvised lines: 'Against almost any Dominant 7th Chord, I will include the b9, +9, b5, or +5 in my lines, which is the Altered Dominant 7th Scale in most cases but the student is cautioned to use his ears.' (Ch. 1, p. 8)

Pass mandates an exclusive pairing: the three diminished scales are played only against Dominant 7th chords - 'There are only three Diminished Scales. The five examples are all to be played against Dominant 7th Chords.' (Ch. 5, p. 20)

In the blues context of Joe's Blues, Pass provides a concrete substitution palette for the tonic dom7: 'The following variants may be used in place of G7: G13, G9, G9(6), G7+9, G7(b9). Db9 in the fourth measure can be played in the same way.' (Ch. 8, p. 24)

Pass imposes a strict density ceiling on all dom7 voicings: 'All changes should be reduced to three- or four-note chords.' Unnecessary doubling or thickness is explicitly rejected regardless of how many extensions are being used. (Ch. 10, p. 30)

Pass prescribes that dom7 voicings must connect to the next chord either through stepwise voice motion or by sharing a common tone: 'for better movement, voicings should lead into one another or have a common tone connecting them.' (Ch. 10, p. 30)

Pass requires that dom7-based jazz licks be memorized and transposed through at least three Chord Forms and all keys, practiced at medium tempo until the student 'can sing them and hear them and feel them.' (Ch. 7, p. 22)

Pass instructs that melodic/scale patterns over dom7 chords must grow out of the chord itself: 'The melodic/scale patterns, in the following examples, grow out of the chords at the beginning of each line, which should be apparent when they are played.' (Ch. 5, p. 21)

Pass states the tritone substitution rule explicitly: 'E7 can be replaced with E+9/Em9/E13/E9 or Bb9/Bb+9/Bbm9/Bb13/Bb9. Bar 9 can be altered in much the same way since these chords are interchangeable.' Any member of the E7 dominant family is interchangeable with any member of the Bb9 dominant family. (Ch. 8, p. 24)

Pass imposes a behavioral check on every dominant-chord harmonic choice during improvisation: 'Students must be able to choose freely from the alternatives available not only in chording but also in solo improvisation. In Joe's Blues the student should check out each phrase against the chord he thinks is being used.' (Ch. 8, p. 24)

Pass specifies that when playing a dom7 chord or scale, one Chord Form must be kept in mind at all times: 'When playing a Dominant 7th Chord or Scale, one Chord Form must be kept in mind.' (Ch. 7, p. 23)

Pass classifies altered dominants (+9, b9, +5, b5 combined) as freely interchangeable members of the dominant family: '+9/b9/13/9(6)/11/-+5/b5 may be substituted for simple Dominants.' (Ch. 10, p. 30)

In the ii-V-I template presented in Alison, Pass requires the dominant to carry at least one altered extension to generate chromatic voice motion toward the tonic: 'Dm7 G7(13) G7(+5) Cmaj7 or Cm9 voice leading.' The alteration is not decorative but structurally necessary. (Ch. 11, p. 31)

Pass directly links the Altered Dominant 7th Scale to the combination of b9, +9, b5, and +5 alterations: 'Against almost any Dominant 7th Chord, I will include the b9, +9, b5, or +5 in my lines, which is the Altered Dominant 7th Scale [See page 10] in most cases.' (Ch. 1, p. 8)
Pass identifies the dom7b9 as a diminished-chord voicing against which a Diminished Scale is employed: 'G7b9 is a diminished chord against which a Diminished Scale can be employed.' (Ch. 1, p. 8)

The b9 alteration activates the Diminished Scale pairing: 'G7b9 is a diminished chord against which a Diminished Scale can be employed.' Pass further notes that 'For improvisation the b9 and +9 go together.' (Ch. 1, p. 8)

In the Joe's Blues palette, G7(b9) is one of five freely available substitutions for the tonic dominant G7: 'variants may be used in place of G7: G13, G9, G9(6), G7+9, G7(b9).' Selection is ear-driven. (Ch. 8, p. 24)

Pass demonstrates compound altered dominant resolution in the Alison voice-leading example B: 'Dm9 C13 G7(+5/b9) - C9(6) (c) Fmaj7 voice leading.' The b9 is compounded with the +5 alteration to maximize chromatic voice movement into the extended tonic C9(6). (Ch. 11, p. 31)

Pass places maj7 (Cmaj7) as the resolution target of the ii-V-I template in Alison: 'Dm7 G7(13) G7(+5) Cmaj7 or Cm9 voice leading.' The tonic maj7 is reached by stepwise or common-tone connection from the altered dominant. (Ch. 11, p. 31)

The economy ceiling applies universally including to maj7 tonic chords: 'All changes should be reduced to three- or four-note chords.' In the Alison examples, Bbmaj7 and Ebmaj7 appear as resolution targets; their voicings conform to the three-or-four-note maximum. (Ch. 10, p. 30; Ch. 11, p. 31)
In Alison, Pass demonstrates Ebmaj7 as a substituted voicing over the underlying Eb backbone chord: '(C7) (F7) (Bbmaj7) (Eb) - F13 Bbm7 Ebmaj7.' (Ch. 11, p. 31)

In Alison voice-leading example B, the extended tonic C9(6) appears as the resolution target of the compound altered dominant: 'G7(+5/b9) - C9(6) (c) Fmaj7 voice leading.' The maj7 tonic is extended to the ninth and sixth to absorb the chromatic voice motion. (Ch. 11, p. 31)

Pass specifies a triplet feel as the governing rhythmic framework for the chord-melody application of Alison, where maj7 voicings (Cmaj7, Bbmaj7, Ebmaj7) appear as resolution targets. All voice-leading moves into maj7 tonic chords in this context are executed within this triplet rhythmic grid. (Ch. 11, p. 31)

Pass uses Dm7 as the canonical ii chord in the ii-V-I template demonstrated in Alison: 'Dm7 G7(13) G7(+5) Cmaj7 or Cm9 voice leading.' The min7 built on the supertonic initiates the voice-leading sequence. (Ch. 11, p. 31)

Pass explicitly names Bm7 as a turnaround pivot in Joe's Blues bar 8: 'In bar 8 Bm7 can be replaced by F13/F9/F+9/Fm9. Bm7 can be changed to a Dominant 7th (B7) or B9/B13.' The min7 functions as a harmonically flexible pivot whose specific quality can be abandoned mid-bar. (Ch. 8, p. 24)

In the ii-V-I template, Dm7 and Dm9 appear as the initiating ii chord requiring smooth connection to the dominant: 'Dm9 C13 G7(+5/b9) - C9(6).' The min7/min9 must lead into the following dominant through stepwise motion or a common tone. (Ch. 11, p. 31; Ch. 10, p. 30)

In Alison, Bbm7 substitutes over the underlying F7 in the backbone progression: '(C7) (F7) (Bbmaj7) (Eb) - F13 Bbm7 Ebmaj7.' The min7 quality is the specific substituted form selected for the subdominant function. (Ch. 11, p. 31)

Pass classifies dim7 as functionally linked to the dom7b9: 'G7b9 is a diminished chord against which a Diminished Scale can be employed.' The diminished quality in Pass's system is not an independent category but an alteration-state of the dominant, specifically the b9 form. (Ch. 1, p. 8)

The three diminished scales pair exclusively with dominant-related (diminished) chord contexts: 'There are only three Diminished Scales. The five examples are all to be played against Dominant 7th Chords.' Pass's diminished scale is anchored to the dominant/diminished function. (Ch. 5, p. 20)

In the Grete improvisation framework, an Edim passing chord appears directly in the backbone sequence: 'Eb Edim | Dm7 G7.' The diminished chord functions as a chromatic passing chord between Eb and Dm7. (Ch. 12, p. 32)
Pass identifies the 11th as one of the freely substitutable dominant extensions: '+9/b9/13/9(6)/11/-+5/b5 may be substituted for simple Dominants.' (Ch. 10, p. 30)
Pass uses Dm9 in the advanced voice-leading example of Alison: 'Dm9 C13 G7(+5/b9) - C9(6) (c) Fmaj7 voice leading.' The min9 is the extended form of the supertonic ii chord. (Ch. 11, p. 31)

Pass identifies the augmented dominant (dom7+5) as a distinct member of the dominant family linked exclusively to whole-tone scale: 'the chord G7+5 is augmented and can be interpreted linearly by an Augmented Scale.' (Ch. 1, p. 8)
The two whole-tone scales are prescribed exclusively for dom7+5 chords: 'There are but two Whole Tone Scales. They will fit with all Dominant 7+5 Chords.' (Ch. 5, p. 20)

Pass uses G7(+5) as an intermediate altered-dominant voicing within the ii-V-I template, appearing between G7(13) and Cmaj7: 'Dm7 G7(13) G7(+5) Cmaj7.' The +5 form is a chromatic intensifier in the dominant approach. (Ch. 11, p. 31)
Pass treats E+9 (augmented dominant with +9) as interchangeable with the Bb9 tritone family: 'E7 can be replaced with E+9/Em9/E13/E9 or Bb9/Bb+9/Bbm9/Bb13/Bb9.' (Ch. 8, p. 24)

For major triads in harmonized scale study, Van Eps prescribes six distinct fingering forms across defined string sets and key ranges, each practiced independently as long, medium, and condensed variants. 'The first exercise is a harmonized major scale in triads using six different fingerings... the fingerings are different in each one, and should be practiced as separate exercises.' Chapter 2, p. 8.

For major triads in sequence form, Van Eps prescribes the three-steps-up-and-back pattern: 'the major scale (harmonized in common triads) is shown in sequence form, three steps up and return on the first triad, then, on the second triad, etc., ascending; the reverse, descending.' This structural pattern governs traversal through all six forms. Chapter 2, p. 10.

Van Eps proscribes rushing the final note of each measure when playing major triad harmonized scale forms: 'the tendency is to skip over the last note in each measure in order to get to the next position in time.' Notes must be of equal value; legato shift requires a quick, accurate positional change, not an early exit from the preceding note. Chapter 2, p. 9.

When major triad harmonized scale exercises alternate whole-note triads with arpeggio-picked measures, Van Eps prescribes counting four beats for the whole-note measure just as for the arpeggio measure: 'every other measure is in arpeggio picking and the natural tendency is to hurry the whole notes. Count four beats for the first measure just as you would for the second measure.' Chapter 2, p. 11.

For the barre triad in major harmonized scale forms, Van Eps prescribes rotating through all four fingers as the barre finger in turn: 'the second triad should be played not only with a Barre of the fourth finger as marked, but also with Barres of the third, second and first fingers alternately.' Chapter 2, p. 12.

Van Eps prescribes sustaining inner voices for their full written value while the upper melodic line moves: 'The upper (melodic) line is in half notes while the two lower voices are in whole notes. Make sure they sustain their full value.' This voice-independence requirement is stated as the governing purpose of practicing all three forms equally for balanced technique. Chapter 2, p. 14.

Van Eps prescribes the finger-flattening technique for major triad forms where an added note is required: 'you flatten the first joint of the second finger to produce the added note, which brings this principle into the classification of a fifth finger. It is a very difficult maneuver because the finger that is doing the flattening must sustain another note during the process... This flattening principle must be practiced methodically as it must be reliable rhythmically and should be done with a snap.' Chapter 2, p. 15.

At modulation points between major triad forms, Van Eps proscribes sliding the left hand: 'Do not slide the left hand in the modulation. It should be a fast, accurate change. The pressure should be released for just a fraction of a second during the change.' Chapter 2, p. 15.

After all six major triad forms are perfected individually, Van Eps prescribes joining the lower and upper forms without a break: 'After all the forms have been perfected join them up with the harmonized scale an octave higher and practice without a break. You will then be able to run two octaves in the harmonized scale.' Chapter 2, p. 13.

For minor triads in harmonized scale study, Van Eps prescribes the same six-form treatment as for major: arpeggio picking and all-keys transposition are the standard method. 'Give this exercise the same treatment as Ex. 1, such as arpeggio picking, etc. Practice in all keys.' Chapter 3, p. 18.

Legato is prescribed as a constant, non-optional goal across all six minor fingering forms: 'Always bear in mind the legato practice and the use of the six different fingerings. Practice in all keys.' Chapter 3, p. 19.

Van Eps warns that lower minor scale forms contain unconventional but correct fingerings that must not be altered: 'Practice very carefully as some of the fingerings, though correct, are confusing.' The student is explicitly told not to substitute conventional fingerings where the method's fingering is prescribed. Chapter 3, p. 20.

For minor triad harmonized scale exercises using alternate picking, Van Eps prescribes upstrokes specifically on the second and fourth triads in each measure: 'this exercise uses alternate picking, which means that the second and fourth triads in the measure are played with up-strokes.' Chapter 3, p. 25.

Van Eps prescribes a specific harmonic reduction technique for minor scale study -- using only the tonic triad as harmony while each fingering form is practiced with attention to its individual technical hazards: 'The harmonized minor scale built on the tonic chord... using the tonic triad only, as harmony. Practice each form carefully as each fingering presents different hazards. This exercise is to be practiced in all keys.' Chapter 3, p. 22.

Van Eps prescribes applying extra fretting pressure on the bass note to sustain it while other fingers are in motion: 'You may have difficulty in sustaining the bass note while the other fingers are performing. This is overcome by concentration and a little more pressure on that one note. Practice slowly.' Chapter 3, p. 35.

Van Eps prescribes exploiting diminished symmetry -- the property that the chord repeats every four frets -- with fast, slide-free positional jumps using the same fingering transposed: 'the diminished chord repeats itself every four frets. Therefore it is necessary to have a good foundation in order to judge the distance between triads... The jumps should be fast and accurate with the fingers solidly implanted each time. In other words, look out for slides.' Chapter 3, p. 28.

For diminished triad exercises, Van Eps prescribes keeping idle fingers suspended just above the string they are not fretting: 'The first finger should rest just above the fourth string, not riding it, but suspended a little above the string.' In the reverse exercise, the fourth finger performs the same readied suspension above the first string. Both idle fingers must lie in readiness until perfect. Chapter 3, p. 28.

For legato execution of diminished triad sequences, Van Eps prescribes the rocker-arm alternation: 'The first and fourth fingers should alternate like the ends of a rocker arm. In other words the first finger should remain down until the fourth comes down, but make sure there are never four notes sounding not even for a fraction of a second.' Downstrokes are used until the exercise is mastered; alternate picking follows. Chapter 3, p. 28.

Van Eps proscribes allowing all four notes of a diminished rocker-arm sequence to sound simultaneously, even for a fraction of a second: 'make sure there are never four notes sounding not even for a fraction of a second.' The overlapping sound is the diagnostic failure of incorrect rocker-arm technique. Chapter 3, p. 28.

For open-voicing diminished chord exercises, Van Eps prescribes using a fretting finger to simultaneously mute the adjacent string: 'It is necessary to "deaden" a string. This is taken care of by the fingering. For instance, in the first form the D string (IV) is stopped from vibrating with the second finger while that finger is used for the note on the A (V) string.' Chapter 3, p. 31.

In open-voicing diminished exercises where a sustaining voice sits above the target string, Van Eps prescribes a modified pick-return path -- a small arc around the upper string after the downstroke: 'After the down-stroke the pick should travel in a small returning arc around the upper string so you will not touch it and stop its vibration. Then with the descending backward motion the pick will strike the middle note safely. Use a complete wrist action.' Chapter 3, p. 32.

Van Eps proscribes deadening either sustaining voice with the upstroke in open-voicing diminished work: 'Make sure you do not deaden either of the sustaining voices with the up-stroke.' The arc pick-path prescription is the method's specific remedy for this error. Chapter 3, p. 32.

For the chromatic diminished scale form requiring two successive notes from one finger, Van Eps prescribes executing the movement at maximum speed without sliding: 'The difficulty here is in making these two notes sound as though they were fingered with two fingers instead of one. This can be done by making the movement very fast without sliding or slurring. Practice slowly.' Chapter 3, p. 31.

For the diminished exercise introducing an unusual second-finger position, Van Eps prescribes keeping all other fingers arched while the second finger bears the strain: 'Make sure that all the fingers except the second are arched. Don't be alarmed if the first joint of the second finger aches slightly while it is learning to bear the strain.' The fingering remains the same ascending to the octave and reverses descending. Chapter 3, p. 30.

For diminished chord exercises requiring simultaneous two-finger drops, Van Eps prescribes a hammer-fashion snap coordinated with the pick stroke: 'have the fingers formed before the two fingers drop and make sure they come down together firmly. Do not merely lay them down but snap them down hammer-fashion simultaneously with the pick stroke. Give the notes their full value and practice slowly.' Chapter 3, p. 34.

For contrary-motion diminished stretching exercises, Van Eps prescribes sustained practice in both forms across all keys, normalizing the resulting dissonances as structurally correct: 'Contrary motion is introduced in this stretching exercise. This comes more under the heading of hand gymnastics. Constant practice of these two forms will definitely increase the spread of the fingers, particularly in the first form. Though dissonant in spots, it is correct.' Chapter 3, p. 27.

For seventh arpeggio exercises spanning the full fingerboard, Van Eps prescribes a specific truncation rule when the range exceeds the instrument: 'These exercises cannot be played in all the keys in their original form but can be moved up and down the fingerboard by leaving out the first measure when descending (if too low) and leaving out the fifth measure when ascending (if too high).' Chapter 3, p. 24.

For major triad harmonized scale exercises, Van Eps prescribes arpeggio picking as the core right-hand technique: a pulsation in which the pick passes over each string with a slight kick, stopping downstrokes against the next-highest string. 'The pick passes over each string and accents it with a slight kick, which is more of a pulsation... In the down strokes, use the next highest string as a pick stop.' Striking two strings at once is the diagnostic error of incorrect pulsation. Chapter 2, p. 9.

Van Eps proscribes forcibly pushing the pick across strings rather than pulsating: 'you will not strike two strings at once, as you might do if you were just forcibly pushing the pick across the strings.' Striking two strings simultaneously is explicitly named as the indicator that pulsation is absent. Chapter 2, p. 9.

For broken string set exercises, Van Eps prescribes smooth pick-jumping over the skipped string: 'This is the first exercise using a broken set of three strings... Practice in all keys in straight down strokes, then with arpeggio picking. Be careful in the latter as you have to jump over a string with the pick. This must be done smoothly.' Chapter 3, p. 26.

Van Eps prescribes increased fretting pressure when major triad exercises are transposed to lower string sets: 'More pressure has to be applied when playing on the lower strings in order to obtain a clear tone.' This is a universal transposition rule that applies across all chord types. Chapter 3, p. 37.

Van Eps prescribes increased fretting pressure when minor triad exercises are transposed to lower string sets: 'More pressure has to be applied when playing on the lower strings in order to obtain a clear tone. Practice carefully.' This rule is stated as a physical property of string tension and applies across all forms and chord types at lower string registers. Chapter 3, p. 37.

After all minor triad exercises have been learned with downstrokes, Van Eps prescribes a method-wide retrospective revision: 'Go back through the book now, taking all exercises in which down-strokes only were used and practice them using up-strokes. Then practice them using up and down strokes alternately. WARNING: In crossing the strings with the pick, make sure the up-strokes are played just as quickly as the down strokes.' Chapter 3, p. 39.

Van Eps prescribes keeping the fourth finger arched throughout diminished exercises: 'This exercise increases the reach of the fourth finger. This finger will have a tendency to lay flat when it should be arched. This may be a strain at first but it can be developed through work.' Chapter 3, p. 30.

Van Eps proscribes allowing the fourth finger to lay flat in diminished exercises: 'This finger will have a tendency to lay flat when it should be arched.' The flat fourth-finger posture is named as the characteristic failure mode to be actively corrected. Chapter 3, p. 30.

Warnock prescribes Dm7 as the ii chord entry point for all jazz guitar study, introduced as one of four core chord shapes to be memorized over the ii V I progression. Students learn the voicing in isolation first, then with metronome, then over backing track: 'Start by playing these chords on your own, memorize them, and then add in a metronome when ready.' Chapter 1 (book chapter), p. 4.

For min7 in the ii function, Warnock prescribes the Freddie Green rhythm as the first comping approach: one chord per beat in quarter notes, with accents on beats 2 and 4. 'The rhythm is all quarter notes, meaning you play one chord per beat... accent the 2nd and 4th chords/beats in each bar. This imitates the hi-hat and helps you bring a higher level of swing to the rhythm.' Chapter 1, p. 5.

After the Freddie Green rhythm is internalized on Dm7, Warnock prescribes adding the Charleston rhythm -- chord on beat 1 and the & of 2 -- before mixing both patterns freely. 'This rhythm places the first chord on beat 1 of each bar, then the second chord is on the & of 2, between beats 2 and 3 in each bar.' Chapter 1, p. 6.

For min7 as the ii chord, Warnock prescribes chromatic approach chords: take the Dm7 voicing shape and play it one fret above (approach from above) or one fret below (approach from below), then resolve into the target chord. 'Approach chords are where you play a chromatic chord one fret above or below the target chord you're aiming for.' The approach-from-above direction is practiced before below, then both are mixed. Chapter 3, p. 11-12.

Warnock prescribes a bass-first picking pattern for Dm7 (and the full ii V I) when playing solo or without a bassist: separate the bass note from the melody in the picking hand. 'The first picking exercise separates the bass from the melody. This type of comping pattern is helpful when there's no bassist in your group, when you play solo guitar, or for technical development.' Learn bass-first before melody-first. Chapter 2, p. 9.

G7 is introduced as the V chord of the core ii V I vocabulary alongside Dm7 and Cmaj7/Cmaj9. Warnock prescribes learning it as part of the four-chord block -- 'here are four chords that fit over the ii V I progression' -- in the sequence: solo practice, metronome, backing track, rhythmic variation. Chapter 1, p. 4.

For G7 in the V function, Warnock prescribes the same Freddie Green quarter-note comping as the first rhythmic approach: one chord per beat with 2-and-4 accents for swing feel. This is the first named rhythm applied systematically to all chords in the progression before introducing the Charleston or approach-chord techniques. Chapter 1, p. 5.

For G7 as the V chord, Warnock prescribes the same chromatic approach-chord treatment as all chords in the progression: move the voicing shape one fret above or below and resolve into the target. 'Approach chords bring a tension and release sound to your comping, jazzing up your chords along the way.' The dominant function makes this tension-release especially apt. Chapter 3, p. 11.

For soloing over G7 as the V chord of a ii V I, Warnock prescribes using the tonic major scale (C major) rather than a separate dominant scale. 'Because all 3 chords in a ii V I are in the parent key, so Dm7-G7-Cmaj7 are all in C major, you can use the tonic major scale to solo over all of those chords.' No chord-specific scale substitution is taught for dom7 in this method. Chapter 4, p. 14.

For Cmaj7 as the I chord, Warnock prescribes reading the lead-sheet symbol but voicing the richer Cmaj9 color: 'In jazz, you normally see the simplest chord symbol written on a lead sheet, then you as the performer color that chord from there. So, it's good to get used to seeing Cmaj7 but playing the Cmaj9 color as it imitates a real-life musical situation.' Chapter 3, p. 11.

Warnock implicitly proscribes playing the bare Cmaj7 voicing in performance contexts where the lead sheet shows Cmaj7: the convention in jazz is that the written symbol is the minimum, not the target. Playing Cmaj7 without added color (e.g., the 9th) fails to meet real-world performance expectation. 'It's good to get used to seeing Cmaj7 but playing the Cmaj9 color as it imitates a real-life musical situation.' Chapter 3, p. 11.

For Cmaj7/Cmaj9 as the I chord, Warnock prescribes the Freddie Green quarter-note comping as the foundational rhythmic approach -- all four beats, accents on 2 and 4 -- before introducing syncopated or approach-chord treatments. This establishes the harmonic landing point of the progression with maximum metric support. Chapter 1, p. 5.

For Cmaj7 (voiced as Cmaj9) as the I chord, Warnock prescribes approach chords as a comping color device: 'The first exercise features approach chords from above, where you play the same shape one fret higher, then resolve into your target chord from there.' The identical mechanic applies from below. Resolution into the maj7 target is mandatory -- the approach is incomplete without it. Chapter 3, p. 12.

For Cmaj7 and the I chord in chord-melody or chord-soloing contexts, Warnock prescribes the melody-first picking pattern to highlight the top voice: 'Bringing out the melody is useful for comping, chord soloing, and especially chord melody playing.' Learn this after the bass-first pattern. Chapter 2, p. 10.

Warnock prescribes Cmaj9 as the preferred voiced realization of a Cmaj7 lead-sheet symbol, establishing the 9th as the default color tone added by the performer. 'To begin, here are four chords that fit over the ii V I progression, with the Cmaj7 and Cmaj9 being two colors of the Cmaj7 sound.' Cmaj9 is the richer of the two and represents real-life jazz comping practice. Chapter 1, p. 4; Chapter 3, p. 11.

When applying approach chords to the Cmaj9 voicing, Warnock prescribes preserving the entire shape and moving it chromatically as a unit -- the voicing is not rearranged for the approach. 'You play a chromatic chord one fret above or below the target chord you're aiming for' using 'the same shape.' Chapter 3, p. 11-12.

Dunbar prescribes the dominant seventh chord as the primary vehicle for convergence, identifying it as 'the largest and most flexible of all the chord types' due to its tritone. Multiple scale colors (major, minor, augmented, dominant, diminished) are to be rotated over a single dominant seventh chord in varying orders -- 'many different scale color types on one chord (7th)' -- derived from listening to Coltrane and Lateef. The player may combine several scales together 'in several rotas varying their order' for richer harmonic color. Chapter 1, p. 4.

Dunbar prescribes expanding the plain dominant seventh into its alteration variants -- specifically 7b9, 7#5, 7#9, and 7b5 -- as direct applications of the tritone's flexibility. The book states: 'The 7th chord having the all important tritone host the largest and most flexible of all the chord types. (7th bs, 7b 9, 7th #5, 7th #9, 7th 9s).' Each variant is a legitimate convergence chord at the V position of any II-V cadence. Chapter 1, p. 4.

Dunbar explicitly names 7b9 as one of the load-bearing variants hosted by the dominant seventh's tritone: 'The 7th chord having the all important tritone host the largest and most flexible of all the chord types. (7th bs, 7b 9, 7th #5, 7th #9).' The 7b9 voicing is prescribed as a natural expansion of the basic V7 in the convergence system, particularly in II-V cadences and turnbacks where additional color is desired. Chapter 1, p. 4; Chapter 8, p. 69.

Dunbar prescribes altered dominants -- including 7#5 and 7#9 forms -- as direct outgrowths of the convergence system's tritone logic. The tritone within the dominant seventh is identified as the 'mysterious' central interval of the II-V cadence, and chromatic tones are used to resolve it: 'It is just a matter of using chromatic tones to resolve the tritone.' The 7#5 and 7#9 variants are named explicitly alongside 7b9 as members of the dominant seventh family eligible for convergence use. Chapter 1, p. 4; Chapter 8, p. 69.

Dunbar prescribes that any main chord in a tune may be approached by a preceding dominant seventh a tritone away: 'Whatever chord you are leading up to (main chord) is or can be usually preceded by a five chord with a tritone. This interval participates in this five or dominant-seventh chord as well as another seventh chord a flatted 5th from its root.' The Circle of Gravities (Chapter 8) maps these tritone relationships systematically and is the prescribed navigational tool for chord-on-chord motion. Chapter 8, p. 66.

Dunbar's convergence system was explicitly 'conceived at the II-V cadence,' and the II chord -- including the half-diminished (min7b5) quality appropriate to minor II-V progressions -- is a primary application target. Scale #15, described as 'half-diminished / half-whole-tone,' is specifically prescribed for convergence contexts involving half-diminished color: 'The scale has one half of its length yielding diminish color.' Scale #15's E natural leading tone is cited as resolving directly to F (the target tonal destination), making it the prescribed scale approach for minor ii function. Chapter 3, p. 32.

Dunbar prescribes two distinct diminished scale types as convergence vehicles, differentiated by interval structure. Scale #4 uses H-W symmetry (half-whole-half-whole) and Scale #5 uses W-H symmetry (whole-half-whole-half): 'This scale is a second type diminish scale. It has a W,H,W,H,W,H,W,H step symmetry. It permits ascending diminish color to a point of convergence.' Both are prescribed for bombarding a target tonal center with diminished color; the practitioner chooses between H-W and W-H depending on the approach direction and color desired. Chapter 2, pp. 21-22.

Dunbar prescribes Dorian mode as a direct convergence scale over the II (minor seventh) chord: 'This scale is simply a dorian mode of the F major.' Furthermore, G Jazz Melodic Minor -- which shares the same pitch content -- is prescribed as an interchangeable II-convergence substitute: 'the G Jazz melodic minor scale has the same notes as this scale so it may be used as a II convergence scale.' Both are valid because the final tetrachord resolves into the target key. Chapter 4, p. 50.

When a convergence scale contains a major 3rd that conflicts with a minor chord target, Dunbar prescribes redirecting the scale to embellish the fifth of the minor chord rather than its root: 'Scale #3 has a major 3rd already in it so it has to used as above to embellish the 5th of the F minor.' This conflict-redirection rule preserves the minor tonic's harmonic identity while still allowing major-color scales access to convergence function. Chapter 8, p. 70.

Before applying any convergence scale over a dominant seventh (or any target chord), Dunbar prescribes priming the ear first: 'Before playing each scale in this system, you should brainwash your ear with the tonality (F major in this case) with several cadences into the key.' This preparatory step is mandatory in the method -- the ear must already hear the destination before executing the approach. Coupled with sound projection ('project yourself sound wise to it already having your attention on it'), these two steps constitute the prescribed pre-execution ritual for any convergence scale. Chapter 2, pp. 18, 20.

Dunbar prescribes extracting every possible chord from every convergence scale and treating those chords as resolution material: 'Extract all possible chords from all scales for resolution purposes.' The governing rule is that 'Each chord represents a member chord sound of one of the modes of the scale it comes from.' Applied to dominant seventh contexts, this means the practitioner should harvest all modal-member chords from each of the 24 scales and use them as approach/resolution chords over V7. Chapter 2, pp. 17, 20.

Dunbar prescribes a universal voice-leading rule that applies to every scale used over any chord in the system, with the dominant seventh as the primary target: 'The last note of all the scales in this system are only a whole or half step away from the 1st, 3rd, or 5th or root of the desired tonal destination.' This rule functions as the validation criterion for whether a scale qualifies as a convergence scale -- any scale whose final note does not land within a whole or half step of a chord tone of the target is not admissible. Chapter 2, p. 22.

Dunbar prescribes Scale #16 -- a major scale with raised 4th (Lydian-like) -- as a convergence vehicle targeting major tonality.
