The scale 'begins on the 7th of the V chord of F major,' meaning it approaches the major tonic from the leading tone of the dominant, with the raised 4th equaling the major 3rd of the V chord. This construction is prescribed as a major-color convergence scale that satisfies the universal last-note resolution rule while contributing Lydian color to the approach. Chapter 3, p. 33.

Dunbar prescribes Scale #11 -- his personal descending scale built on an E-Bb tritone -- as a distinctive convergence vehicle for dominant seventh contexts. The scale is usable 'from any note within it,' and all scales including this one 'may be connected together in different orders for convergence into a tonal center.' Scale #11's tritone matches the tritone embedded in the V7 chord, making it a natural harmonic fit for approaching the tonal destination through the dominant. Chapter 3, pp. 28, 30.

For maj7 as tonic resolution, Vaartstra prescribes isolating and playing the guide tones (3rd and 7th) in half or quarter notes through the entire song form before attempting melodic improvisation. 'It's a great practice to play them isolated with either half notes or quarter notes through the entire form of a song.' Chapter 2, p. 38.

When navigating I-i minor shifts (e.g., Cmaj7 to Cmin7), Vaartstra prescribes adjusting only the b3 and b7 -- the defining quality intervals -- while keeping all other notes constant. 'The only difference between a major 7 chord and a minor 7 chord is the minor has a b3 and a b7. Make this adjustment and you are good to go!' Chapter 8, p. 122.

Vaartstra explicitly licenses targeting upper extensions (9th, 11th, 13th) over any maj7 chord in improvisation. 'Most chords in jazz are labeled as 7 chords. But this doesn't mean you can't add or target extensions and alterations of these chords. Utilizing the 9th, 11th and 13th can have a powerful effect.' Chapter 8, p. 132.

Vaartstra prescribes recognizing maj7 chords as targets of the backdoor dominant device: the bVII7 approaches the I maj7 by whole step rather than the conventional V7. 'A backdoor dominant is a dominant 7th chord that substitutes the V7 chord for a bVII7 chord approaching the I chord by a whole step. Example: Bb7-Cmaj7.' Chapter 11, p. 177.

For dominant 7 chords in ii-V-I progressions, Vaartstra prescribes voice-leading the 7th of the dom7 to the 3rd of the next chord by stepwise motion. 'Notice how the 7th of each chord resolves to the 3rd of the next chord... the closest step-wise motion you can make from the 7th of a chord in this ii-V-I, is the 3rd of the next. That's voice leading.' Chapter 2, p. 37.

Vaartstra prescribes treating any dom7 that precedes a non-tonic diatonic chord as a secondary dominant (tonicization), and expanding it with a ii chord in front to form a ii-V. 'It's just as easy to add a ii chord in front of it to create a ii-V chord progression. Where there is a V chord, you can almost always add a ii in front of it.' Chapter 5, p. 78; Chapter 10, p. 158.

Vaartstra prescribes freely converting diatonic minor chords to dominant 7ths as a core jazz harmonic practice. 'It is entirely normal and acceptable to turn minor chords in the diatonic series into dominant 7th chords.' This is applied in the analysis of Sweet Georgia Brown's VI7 opener and recurs across multiple standards. Chapter 6, p. 95; also Chapter 2, p. 33.

For improvising over dom7 chords, Vaartstra prescribes the Mixolydian scale as the primary pitch collection: 'The easiest way to think of a Mixolydian scale is a major scale with a b7. Formula: 1-2-3-4-5-6-b7.' Students are told to use it as a pitch collection -- not a linear drill -- and to practice chord-tone patterns starting on different chord tones each bar. Chapter 6, p. 98-99.

Vaartstra prescribes recognizing that any dominant 7 chord may be replaced by the dominant 7 chord whose root lies a tritone away. 'Sometimes this is called a tritone substitution, meaning, a chord is being substituted by another chord with a root a tritone interval away.' He also offers the alternative reading of interpreting the substituting chord as a chromatic passing chord between ii and I. Chapter 8, p. 122.

Vaartstra prescribes the backdoor dominant as a V7 substitute: the bVII7 approaches the tonic by whole step and may be preceded by its own ii chord to form a full backdoor ii-V. 'The Bbmin7-Eb7 is really acting as a backdoor ii-V into the Fmaj7.' Players should also learn the dual interpretation -- the same dom7 chord can be read simultaneously as V7/IV or as a backdoor dominant into I. Chapter 11, p. 177-178.

For min7 in its ii-chord function, Vaartstra prescribes entering the arpeggio on whichever chord tone is nearest to the last note played in the prior chord, not necessarily the root: 'Whatever the last note played in a particular bar was, I move to the nearest chord tone of the next chord.' Regardless of starting tone, arpeggios always proceed in order (Root-3-5-7 or any rotation). Chapter 4, p. 65.

Vaartstra prescribes treating a song-opening vi min7 as the initiator of a diatonic cycle of 4ths rather than as an isolated tonic substitute. 'Notice that it starts with the vi chord. This vi chord starts a long cycle of 4ths all the way through the Dbmaj7 in bar 5. Everything here is diatonically pure to the key center.' Chapter 10, p. 158.

For min7 chords functioning as modal tonics (e.g., D Dorian in So What), Vaartstra prescribes abandoning the guide-tone framework entirely and using the Dorian mode (formula: W-H-W-W-W-H-W; scale tones: 1-2-b3-4-5-6-b7) as the pitch collection. 'There is no need to identify the guide tones... the best way to improvise over modal harmony is by using modes.' Players should use sparse, space-conscious phrasing modeled on Miles Davis. Chapter 7, p. 103-108.

Vaartstra prescribes the minor iv chord (e.g., Abmin6 or Abmin7 functioning as iv in a major key) as a substitute for the plain V7 before the I chord, and further allows expanding it to a full backdoor ii-V (e.g., Abmin7-Db7) or compressing it to a single Db7. 'Musicians will play an Abmin6, which functions as the minor IV chord... You can also turn that Abmin6 into a ii-V (Abmin7-Db7), or you can even just play a Db7.' Chapter 5, p. 80.

Vaartstra proscribes using major 3rds or major 7ths when improvising over the iv minor chord. 'Don't get too hung up on the iv minor chord. In your improvisation, you will simply want to consider the difference in the chord quality. Don't be playing major thirds or major 7ths!' Chapter 4, p. 63.

Vaartstra prescribes distinguishing a closing cycle-of-4ths built from minor ii-Vs from the more common dominant ii-V cycle. 'This cycle of 4ths is different than we have seen before in that they are a series of minor ii-V's.' Scale and note choices must reflect the minor quality. Chapter 11, p. 179.

Vaartstra prescribes treating min7b5 (half-diminished) as the ii chord in minor-key ii-V-i progressions, formula Root-b3-b5-b7, and identifies it as such within the hybrid ii-V-I construction: 'A hybrid ii-V-I is when a minor ii-V-i is mixed with a major ii-V-I. The ii and V are borrowed from the minor key... Example: Dmin7(b5)-G7(b9)-Cmaj7.' Chapter 11, p. 179. For improvisation, target chord tones directly derived from the formula. Chapter 4, p. 64.

Vaartstra prescribes a dual reading of min7b5 in context: the same chord may be analyzed as either a ii7b5 of the secondary key (standard minor ii-V reading) or as the iiib5 within the parent tonal center when the chord pair is reread as iii(b5)-VI7. 'The Gmin7(b5) can also be thought of as the iiib5 (adding a b5 to the iii minor) and a VI7... if we combine this understanding with the ii-V of ii concept everything ties together.' Chapter 5, p. 79.

Vaartstra prescribes interpreting min7b5 in context of its resolution target rather than in isolation: 'If we look at a Gmin7(b5) and a C7(b9) as separate chords, they are confusing. But if we look at them as resolving to an Fmin7, then we have something functional to understand.' Improvisation should reflect that relational function. Chapter 5, p. 79.

Vaartstra prescribes using dom7b9 (e.g., G7b9) as the V chord in the hybrid ii-V-I, borrowed from the parallel minor key while still resolving to the major I: 'A hybrid ii-V-I is when a minor ii-V-i is mixed with a major ii-V-I. The ii and V are borrowed from the minor key, but they resolve to the major I. Example: Dmin7(b5)-G7(b9)-Cmaj7.' Chapter 11, p. 179.

Vaartstra prescribes treating a dom7b9 chord as analytically equivalent to a diminished 7 on its 3rd: 'F#dim7: F#-A-C-Eb / D7(b9): D-F#-A-C-Eb... You can think of the F#dim7 as a rootless D7(b9).' For improvisation, either chord tones of the dim7 or the full dom7b9 pitch set will serve. Chapter 9, p. 141.

Vaartstra prescribes understanding a passing dim7 in two simultaneous ways: as a rootless dominant b9 substitute for the chord a major 2nd below, and as a chromatic passing chord connecting adjacent diatonic chords by bass half-step. 'On a compositional level the F#dim7 is functioning as more than just a substitution. It's also creating a chromatic passing note, in this case the bass note, to connect the I chord with the ii chord.' Chapter 9, p. 142.

For improvisation over passing dim7 chords, Vaartstra prescribes targeting the chord tones of the implied dominant b9 that the dim7 substitutes. 'Remember that it is being substituted for the VI7b9 chord, so any of those chord tones will serve you well.' The Whole-Half diminished scale (W-H-W-H-W-H-W-H) is taught as the theoretical note resource for this context. Chapter 9, p. 145.

Vaartstra prescribes reading a biii diminished 7 chord in a cycle-of-4ths context (e.g., All the Things You Are) as a purely chromatic connector rather than a dominant substitute: 'The biii diminished isn't necessarily replacing anything. Its primary job is to connect the iii chord to the ii chord chromatically.' Improvise through it as a brief chromatic link. Chapter 10, p. 161.

Vaartstra prescribes recognizing the i minor chord substitution on a major-key I chord (e.g., Cmin7 replacing Cmaj7 in bar 3 of On Green Dolphin Street) as a deliberate quality shift, not an error, and adjusting improvisation by altering only the b3 and b7. 'The form starts right on the tonic... until we get to bar 3 where we make a sudden switch to the i minor.' Adjust only the defining 3rd and 7th in melodic lines. Chapter 8, p. 122.

While Vaartstra does not label the So What chord explicitly as 'sus4', he prescribes using D Dorian (W-H-W-W-W-H-W) as the pitch collection over the modal chord structure of So What -- a stacked-4ths voicing implying suspended quality -- and models Miles Davis's approach: 'He generally plays within the Dorian mode, with exceptions of course and occasional chromatic approach notes.' For modal voicings implying sus/quartal quality, guide tones are explicitly not required. Chapter 7, p. 103-114.

Carter prescribes maj7 chords as the I and IV members of the diatonic seventh-chord set ('Two major sevenths I and IV'), voiced in open rather than close position to accommodate finger span: 'the third of the chord has been moved an octave higher, and in the second case both the third and fifth have been moved an octave higher.' For voice-leading into the next chord, the bass note should be selected to continue a chromatic line rather than defaulting to the root. Chapter 9, pp. 117-120; Chapter 10, p. 120.

Carter prescribes open-position voicing as the practical solution for maj7 fingering: close-position seventh chords are defined but immediately redirected -- 'Unless you have long spidery fingers, you are probably more comfortable with these chords in either of the following standard alternate configurations' in which the third is raised an octave, or both third and fifth are raised. Chapter 9, p. 117.

Carter identifies minor sevenths as the II, III, and VI scale degrees in a major key ('Three minor sevenths II, III and VI'). In cycle-of-fifths practice, minor sevenths should be voiced with independent voice motion -- individual voices moving by half or whole step -- rather than root-position parallel block motion: 'If you think of harmonic movement as several moving voices rather than a glob of dots on a chord box grid, your arrangements and improvisations will be more airy, more interesting and less clunky.' Chapter 9, p. 117; Chapter 13, p. 156.

Carter prescribes the II-V7-I progression as 'the most common jazz progression unit' and the most idiomatic modulation bridge. The minor seventh on the II degree serves as the harmonic on-ramp before V7: 'putting a II of the upcoming new key in front of the new key V7' is the preferred jazz-language solution for connecting song sections and keys. Chapter 14, p. 166; Chapter 11, p. 141.

Carter identifies the half-diminished seventh (min7b5) as the VII chord of the major scale -- 'One half-diminished seventh VII' -- and classifies it among the four diatonic seventh-chord types. In ascending chromatic root-movement contexts, Carter prescribes the diminished seventh (dim7) rather than min7b5 as the connector. Chapter 9, p. 117; Chapter 10, p. 120.

Carter prescribes the dominant seventh (V7) as 'the most basic harmonic movement of jazz' and the mandatory gateway chord: 'The last chord of the intro must be a V7 or V7 substitute in order to move into the first chord of the tune itself.' For V7-I resolution, the prescribed voice-leading move is contrary motion: 'As the top note descends by half step the root note has its own opposing pattern, not parallel to the top.' Chapter 13, p. 156; Chapter 14, p. 160.

Carter prescribes V7 as the mandatory substitute for the final I chord when initiating a tag or coda: 'the replacement of the usual final I chord -- E, here -- with a V7 (or other substitute) chord is required.' The trigger is the cue 'Tag!' from the bandleader. Chapter 14, p. 164.

Carter prescribes V7 as the closing chord of every turnaround, treating the turnaround as 'practically another intro': 'Like introductions, turnarounds often start on a I chord and finish on a V7 or V7 substitute chord.' Chapter 14, p. 164.

Carter proscribes elaborate dominant-seventh turnaround elaboration when a singer is holding a note through the final two measures: 'About the only restriction is when you are backing a singer who is holding a note through the last two measures. You should then still be accompanying intelligently and not kicking out the jams.' Chapter 14, p. 164.

Carter prescribes rootless close voicing for dom7 chords in ensemble contexts: 'the accompaniment is voiced so that the harmony moves in alternating pairs of fourths and tritones. The bottom note in each pair alternates between major or minor seventh to major third. There is no explicitly stated root or fifth of the chord. If you play in a group, the bassist will cover roots and fifths.' Chapter 10, p. 129.

In cycle-of-fifths movement, Carter prescribes analyzing dom7-to-dom7 motion voice by voice rather than as root-position block changes. Using C7->F9 as the specimen: 'The middle voice moves by half step from E to Eb. The bottom line travels from C, the root, to A, the third of F9, by Bb, the 7 of the C7 note.' Chapter 13, p. 156.

Carter prescribes borrowing V7 from the destination key as the fastest modulation method -- achievable in as little as two beats: 'Presume you have ended a tune on the standard I chord and have used two beats doing it. You are moving to Db. Use the last two beats to borrow V7 (Ab7) from the upcoming new key, Db.' Chapter 14, p. 165.

Carter prescribes a specific bass-motion pattern for dom7 chords in spread texture: 'The root bass notes alternate in moving up a fourth and then down a fifth. Each new bass note is a tenth interval from the melody note above.' This produces the idiomatic 'spread' arrangement texture. Chapter 13, p. 157.

Carter prescribes a direct alteration rule for aug7 (dom7#5) and dom7b5 bass voicings: the major-scale shortcut for deriving the fifth 'does not automatically work with scales (or chords) that have raised (sharped) or lowered (flatted) fifths.' Instead, read the alteration from the chord name itself. Chapter 5, p. 77.
Carter's rule for aug7 (C7#5) bass voicing: 'If the chord is C7#5, raise the fifth a half step.' The plain major-scale fifth derivation is explicitly forbidden for this chord type. Chapter 5, p. 77.

Carter prescribes the diminished seventh chord as the standard connector for ascending chromatic root movement: 'In many cases the diminished seventh chord is the in-between, the hamburger helper of ascending harmonic movement.' Chapter 10, p. 120.

Carter prescribes chromatic approach chords -- including dim7 in the ascending direction -- as a recognized harmonic device: 'Approaching a chord from a half step above or below is another accepted way of moving the harmony.' Chapter 15, p. 167.

Carter prescribes a specific distributional rule for major triads in solo arrangement: 'when the melody is a major or minor third, the bass note is either a root or fifth, and when the melody is other than a third, the third is used in the bass to harmonically identify the chord.' Chapter 5, p. 83.

Carter's third-supply rule applies identically to minor triads: when the melody contains the minor third of the chord, 'no additional third is required -- the melody notes define the major or minor sound of the harmony.' When the melody does not contain the minor third, place the minor third in the bass to establish the chord's identity. Chapter 5, pp. 79-83.

Carter prescribes free stroke (not rest stroke) as the mandatory technique when harmonizing a major chord's melody with a note a third below, because thirds fall on adjacent strings: 'Since thirds are on adjacent strings, the free stroke must be used.' Chapter 6, p. 91.

Carter prescribes a strict voicing rule for sixth-below harmonization of major chords: 'By convention, scales harmonized in sixths have the key note of each scale on top, with the harmony note a sixth below. If the key note were in the bottom position the ear would perceive the scale as being in a minor key rather than a major key.' Chapter 8, p. 108.

Carter's key-note-on-top rule for sixth-below harmonization applies equally to minor chords. Diatonic sixths may imply minor sevenths or ninths; Carter permits adjusting 'the C to D if you wish to keep the sound to a simple Dm chord' when the extension is unwanted. Chapter 8, pp. 104-108.

Carter prescribes adjusting sixth-below harmonization when it implies an unwanted seventh or ninth extension on a minor chord: 'the sixth below will be the minor seventh interval C, of the Dm7 chord. The chord symbol above it is a simple triad, Dm. You can change the C to D if you wish to keep the sound to a simple Dm chord.' Chapter 8, p. 104.

Carter prescribes chromatic approach notes as the defining characteristic of jazz walking bass over dominant seventh chords. Bass-first conception is mandatory -- 'Think bass-plus-chord, not chord-plus-bass' -- because committing to a chord voicing first severely restricts available approach-note paths. Chapter 10, pp. 124, 141.

Carter prescribes whole-tone scale color as an option for dominant seventh chords specifically in intro construction: the example intro uses 'a little sprinkle of whole-tone scale thrown in at the C+7' before the final resolution. Chapter 14, p. 160.

Carter prescribes three standard ending formulas all resolving to the I (major) chord: 'V7-I, IV-I, and especially II-V7-I are standard.' The IV-I is identified as characteristic of soul and gospel music. Chapter 14, p. 163.

Carter prescribes the root/fifth alternation as the foundational oom-pah bass pattern under major chords: 'a root and a fifth are placed under each chord.' For variety, Carter prescribes mixed-rhythm bass (quarter, half, whole notes in combination) as the technique for 'de-emphasizing the oom-pah accompaniment while still using only root/fifth.' Chapter 5, pp. 76-78.

Carter's root/fifth bass pattern applies to minor chords with the same procedure as major: 'For Am, root/fifth is A, E.' If the chord has an altered fifth, the alteration must be read from the chord symbol and applied directly. Chapter 5, p. 76; Chapter 5, p. 77.

Carter prescribes moving tenths as the signature self-accompaniment device for major chords in stride-inspired solo playing: 'Moving tenths in the left hand was one of the primary accompanying devices of pianists in the swing era. Fats Waller, Willie "The Lion" Smith, Art Tatum, Teddy Wilson, and many others made this the style.' On guitar, Carter prescribes achieving 'at least half notes' for the moving tenths. Chapter 10, p. 127; Chapter 7, p. 98.

Carter prescribes independent rhythmic motion for tenths under dominant seventh chords: 'You probably would not use parallel tenths throughout the arrangement. For one thing, the melody would then have the same rhythm as the bass rhythm. The tenth does often function as a bass note, but only infrequently does it move parallel to the melodic rhythm.' Chapter 7, pp. 98-99.

Carter proscribes using parallel tenths throughout an arrangement: 'You probably would not use parallel tenths throughout the arrangement. For one thing, the melody would then have the same rhythm as the bass rhythm.' The prescription is to give the tenth its own independent rhythmic pattern. Chapter 7, p. 98.

Carter prescribes a bVI chord insertion after diatonic cycle movement as a deceptive cadence and modulation device: 'a bVI (Ab6) of the C scale is inserted. This deceptive cadence opens up several possibilities.' Chapter 15, p. 167.

Carter prescribes two-note inner-voice voicing as sufficient: 'A melody accompanied by two additional notes is often all you need to make an arrangement sound full, whether you are playing by yourself or with a group.' Chapter 10, pp. 125-126.

Carter prescribes back-cycling through the cycle of fifths as a systematic modulation method: 'Using the cycle of fifths as a method of movement, work backwards in the cycle to F7 and then C7.' Chapter 14, p. 166.

Carter prescribes tritone pairs as the primary harmonic accompaniment for sparse, ensemble-friendly solo arrangements: '3 on 4 takes its name from having many three-beat phrases in the context of 4/4 measures. The melodic line is primarily accompanied by tritones.' Chapter 15, p. 179.

Carter defines and prescribes the walkdown as a primary structural device: 'A walkdown is a descending bass line with a common tone on top of a chord stack. This is the device that keeps popping up in this tune along with its hook-like rhythm.' Chapter 15, p. 181.

Carter prescribes a strict ceiling rule for arpeggiated chord accompaniment: 'watch that your choice of arpeggiation doesn't reach higher than the melody, which might obscure the melody and confuse the listener.' Chapter 6, pp. 87-89.

Carter proscribes arpeggiation when the melody moves unpredictably by large leaps: 'If you notice that the melody of the tune you wish to arrange continually leaps up and down wildly, abandon arpeggiation for that particular tune.' Chapter 6, p. 90.

Carter prescribes that thirds harmonization alone is insufficient: 'A melody harmonized only in thirds can progress by itself for a section of a tune, but probably not for the entire song. Put the bass back in.' Chapter 6, p. 92.

Carter proscribes relying on thirds harmonization alone for an entire arrangement: 'A melody harmonized only in thirds can progress by itself for a section of a tune, but probably not for the entire song.' Chapter 6, p. 92.

Carter prescribes the ear as the final arbiter when a third-below harmonization lands on a non-chord tone: 'Non-chord tones make for the interesting spice in an otherwise dull chord-tone-only dish. It's your ear and your decision.' Chapter 6, p. 92.

Carter prescribes voicing all comping chords on the top four or five strings when playing alongside an electric bassist: 'If you play low-pitched, walking four-to-the-bar chords and your partner plays a walking bass line, it results in a muddy tangle of sounds. The solution is simple: play your rhythm part higher on the board on the top four or at most five strings.' Chapter 11, p. 135.

Carter prescribes a density rule for comping behind a soloist: 'play more when the soloist is not playing, and play less when he is. Play more when there are "holes" to be filled, and don't step all over the soloist when he is playing busily.' Chapter 11, p. 135.

Carter proscribes constant doubled bass notes for modern jazz style: 'Today the bass doesn't often play four quarter notes to the bar. Older-style bass playing included much doubling of two same notes per measure. Unless you want to recreate vintage jazz, avoid constant doubling.' Chapter 11, p. 141.

Cma9 appears as the tonic resolution target in the major-sounds progression. Ch.2 p.15: 'The fifth chord is G13b5 (or Db7+9b5) which resolves into Cma9.' The major-ninth voicing is the landing point, not a passing color.

G7 anchors the seventh-sounds section. Ch.2 p.15: 'The first three chords illustrate movement around G7. The next four chords illustrate a substitute turn-around back to G13, followed by a cycle seventh movement.' Dominant sevenths drive both the local turnaround and the extended cycle.

Pass specifies that chord-symbol qualifier order equals voice order bottom-to-top. Ch.2 p.20: 'These chord symbols are written so that the order of appearance of notes coincides with the spelling of the chord symbol. For example, D7+9+5 means D7 with the raised 9th next, and the raised 5th on top.' The altered dominant D7+9+5 exemplifies the convention.

Pass instructs sustaining the lead note from one dominant voicing to the next. Ch.2 p.24: 'NOTE: Try to sustain lead notes from one chord to the next. For example, C9 to F13, sustain the G on top.' The common G is held across the II–V motion rather than re-attacked.

The tritone substitute Db7+9b5 is presented as interchangeable with G13b5. Ch.2 p.15: 'The fifth chord is G13b5 (or Db7+9b5) which resolves into Cma9.' The parenthetical equivalence signals the substitution as a practical re-spelling, not a separate color.

The altered dominant D7+9+5 demonstrates the voicing-layer convention. Ch.2 p.20: 'D7+9+5 means D7 with the raised 9th next, and the raised 5th on top.' Each suffix maps directly to a voice layer ascending from the seventh-chord shell.

Pass treats diminished chords as freely interchangeable approach chords that can resolve to multiple targets. Ch.2 p.15: 'Resolve the last chord in this sequence into any chord. For example: (1) Dm7 — G7 — Cma7, or (2) Em7 — Eb9 — Dm9 — Db9.' The open-resolution prescription underscores diminished's non-committed approach function.

Pass explicitly substitutes diminished chords for 7b9 harmony in a minor-key context. Ch.2 p.15: 'Use of diminished chords for seventh flat ninth chord movement, utilizing the basic pattern of A7 — Dm — G7 — C.' The diminished voicing replaces the A7b9 functional slot while retaining the approach-tone content.

Augmented chords are held as a sustained color before resolving chromatically into a cycle. Ch.2 p.15: 'The first six chords are basically G aug. Movement is used chromatically to get to the basic cycle (A7 — D7 — G).' The prescription is to sustain the augmented sound across multiple voicings rather than move through it quickly.

G aug serves as the final resolution target in the half-diminished-to-augmented passage. Ch.2 p.15: 'A7b9 to Dm7b5 resolving finally to G aug.' The augmented chord receives the cadence rather than a tonic major, functioning as an open, unresolved color endpoint.

Dm7 initiates the minor-seventh-to-seventh passage and resolves via a chromatic intermediate. Ch.2 p.15: 'First four chords illustrate movement in Dm7, resolving into Ab13 to G13.' The chromatic Ab13 is inserted as an approach dominant between the ii-chord and the diatonic V13.

Dm7b5 appears as the ii° chord in a iiø–V7b9 minor cadence and again in a iiø–V aug context. Ch.2 p.15: 'A7b9 to Dm7b5 resolving finally to G aug' and 'Dm7b5 chords to G aug. Notice the chords used to obtain these sounds.' The half-diminished functions as the ii chord in both cadential sequences.

A7b9 precedes Dm7b5 in the iiø–V7b9 passage. Ch.2 p.15: 'A7b9 to Dm7b5 resolving finally to G aug.' The b9 dominant is the V chord in a minor-key iiø–V pairing, with the cadence landing on an augmented rather than a tonic minor chord.

Treat Maj7 (along with C6 and CMaj9) as members of the Major harmonic family when harmonizing melody notes over tonic major chords. Build your chord collection from this family to ensure any melody note above a major root can be harmonized. (Chapter 3, p.22)

Use shell voicings — root, 3rd, and 7th — as the minimum needed to define the Maj7 sound. Drop the 5th entirely; it does not compromise the chord's essential character and frees a voice for melody or extensions. (Chapter 5, p.145)
When voicing Maj7 chords, prioritize omitting the 5th, root, 11th, and 9th (in that order of commonness) to keep voicings lean and playable without losing harmonic identity. (Chapter 4, p.79)

Substitute a Maj7 I chord with the vi minor chord of the same key (e.g., replace CMaj7 with Am7). Use this relative substitution when the melody note is compatible with the vi chord to add color while maintaining tonic function. (Chapter 6, p.224)

Replace a Maj7 chord with chord iii of its key (e.g., replace CMaj7 with Em7) as an alternative reharmonization. This works because chord iii shares strong common tones with the I chord and maintains the major harmonic family sound. (Chapter 6, p.225)

Any chord can substitute for Maj7 provided the substituting chord contains the current melody note on top as a common tone. Always verify this condition before deploying any substitution over a Maj7. (Chapter 7, p.247)

When adding shell voicings over a walking bass on a Maj7 chord, mix placement on the downbeat and on the '& of 1' rather than locking every chord to the beat, in order to create rhythmic variety and a more authentic jazz feel. (Chapter 6, p.186)

Assign min7 voicings to the ii chord in any major-key ii-V-I progression; this is the primary harmonic context where min7 functions, and mastering it here trains the ear to every other minor 7 application. (Chapter 4, p.48)

Treat min7 (along with Cm9 and Cm13, forming the 'm7' sub-family) as the standard minor color; never substitute min7 when the harmonic situation calls for min7b5, as doing so can sound wrong. (Chapter 3, p.23)
Voice min7 at minimum with root, 3rd, and 7th (shell voicing). The 5th is the first candidate for omission and can be dropped without losing the chord's essential character. (Chapter 5, p.145)

Play a min7 chord built on the 5th of any dominant chord as a substitute for that dominant (e.g., Cm7 over F7). This borrows the iim7 that belongs to the dominant's key and produces an interesting, less direct sound. (Chapter 6, p.230)

Following Joe Pass's practice, freely interchange the ii (min7) and V (dom7) chord with one another in a progression; treat them as functionally interchangeable colors that can be swapped to vary the harmony. (Chapter 6, p.230)

When comping min7 shell voicings over a walking bass line, alternate placement between the downbeat and the '& of 1' to create rhythmic variety rather than always landing on beat one. (Chapter 6, p.186)

Use min7b5 exclusively as the ii chord in a minor ii-V-i progression. Study minor ii-V-i progressions as the primary vehicle for learning and internalizing min7b5 voicings in context. (Chapter 4, p.61)

Never substitute plain min7 for min7b5 when the progression demands it — the harmonic situation will sound wrong. Keep min7b5 (and its extension Cm11b5) as a distinct sub-family separate from the 'm7' family. (Chapter 3, p.23)

When you identify a min7b5 chord as the ii of a minor ii-V-i (e.g., Bm7b5 - E7b9 - Am7), you may replace the written melody at that point with a pre-learned minor ii-V-i jazz lick as a melodic substitution device. (Chapter 7, p.250)

Assign min7b5 to the minor harmonic family but treat it as its own 'm7b5' sub-family distinct from 'm7'. Include it in your chord collection for any minor tonic context where the flattened 5th is diatonic. (Chapter 3, p.22-23)

Assign dom7 (natural dominant, including C9 and C13 extensions) to the Dominant harmonic family as the 'natural dominant' sub-family, distinct from altered dominants. Use this sub-family for V chords in major ii-V-I progressions. (Chapter 3, p.23; Chapter 4, p.48)
Add extensions and tensions (9ths, 13ths, etc.) to dom7 voicings whenever possible, as these color tones are the primary source of the jazzy sound in chord-melody arrangements. (Chapter 5, p.127)

Build dom7 shell voicings from the root, 3rd, and 7th; these guide tones are the irreducible core that defines the dominant sound. The 5th can always be dropped first among all omittable tones. (Chapter 5, p.145)

Starting from a basic G7 shape, generate many distinct dom7 voicings by adding or adapting individual notes from that shape rather than learning each voicing in isolation — exploit the template systematically. (Chapter 4, p.87)

Replace any dom7 chord with the dom7 whose root lies a tritone away (e.g., substitute F#7 for C7). This works because the 3rd and 7th (guide tones) of the original chord are enharmonically the same pitches as the 7th and 3rd of the tritone-sub chord, ensuring smooth voice-leading. (Chapter 6, p.220; p.216)

When placing dom7 shell voicings over a walking bass, alternate between the downbeat and the '& of 1' on each bar to introduce rhythmic variety and avoid stiff, on-the-beat chord placement. (Chapter 6, p.186)

To approach a dom7 chord chromatically, play the identical voicing one fret above or below the target position as the approach chord, then resolve to the target voicing. The same shape one fret away is sufficient for the chromatic approach effect. (Chapter 6, p.197)

Do not use a natural dom7 (C7, C9, C13) where the harmonic context demands an altered dominant — substituting the wrong sub-family can sound wrong. Always determine whether the progression calls for natural or altered dominant before choosing a voicing. (Chapter 3, p.23)

Following Joe Pass, treat the V (dom7) as interchangeable with the ii (min7) in a progression; either chord can stand in for the other, giving you a flexible reharmonization option at every dominant. (Chapter 6, p.230)

Extend or reharmonize any dom7 by adding preceding chords based on the back cycle (circle of fourths), inserting new dominant chords that cycle backward to the target. Apply this to build tension before any dominant resolution. (Chapter 7, p.243)

Classify dom7b9 (C7b9, C7b13b9) within the 'altered dominant' sub-family alongside C7b5 and C7alt, distinct from the natural dominant sub-family. Always apply altered dominant voicings when the harmonic context demands alteration. (Chapter 3, p.23)

Use dom7b9 as the V chord in minor ii-V-i progressions (e.g., Bm7b5 - E7b9 - Am7). Study minor ii-V-i progressions specifically to learn dom7b9 voicings in their natural harmonic context. (Chapter 4, p.61)

Never substitute a natural dominant (dom7, dom9, dom13) for dom7b9 when the progression demands altered color — the wrong sub-family will sound wrong. Commit to the altered dominant voicing whenever the harmonic situation specifies it. (Chapter 3, p.23)

When a dom7b9 appears as the V of a minor ii-V-i (e.g., E7b9 in Bm7b5 - E7b9 - Am7), use it as the trigger to substitute an entire pre-learned minor ii-V-i lick in place of the written melody at that point. (Chapter 7, p.250)

As an altered dominant, dom7b9 already carries the primary tension color; further enrich it with additional extensions and alterations (b13, etc.) where the voicing allows, since the jazzy sound in arrangements comes specifically from loading dominant chords with extensions and tensions. (Chapter 5, p.127)

Treat dom7alt (C7alt) as a member of the altered dominant sub-family alongside C7b9 and C7b5, not the natural dominant sub-family. Use it wherever the harmonic situation calls for maximum alteration on the V chord. (Chapter 3, p.23)

Do not replace dom7alt with a natural dominant (dom7, dom9, dom13) — the wrong sub-family will sound wrong in context. Confirm that the progression requires alteration before selecting any altered dominant voicing. (Chapter 3, p.23)

Deploy dom7alt as a valid V-chord voicing choice in minor ii-V-i progressions, interchangeable with dom7b9 within the altered dominant sub-family. Use minor ii-V-i progressions as the primary study context for mastering dom7alt voicings. (Chapter 4, p.61)

Like all dominant chord types, dom7alt must carry its extensions and tensions into chord-melody voicings; the jazzy sound of arrangements depends on loading dominant chords — including fully altered ones — with these color tones. (Chapter 5, p.127)

For maj7 chords (Cmaj7 and Fmaj7 in C major, Abmaj7 in C harmonic minor), Goodrick catalogs both Close and Spread voicings as paired entries across every cycle; practice the same diatonic root-motion sequence in both density positions and observe which voice carries the common tone (the major seventh resolving up by half-step or held). Chapter 1, pp. 12-189.

In Cycle 2 (stepwise root motion), maj7 voicings yield the tightest possible voice-leading motion: each upper voice moves by step, making this the ideal cycle for practicing minimal displacement across Cmaj7 and Fmaj7 in Close voicing. Use the Intervallic layer to confirm that no voice leaps more than a major second. Chapter 1, pp. 12-189.

In Cycle 5 (root motion by fourth/fifth), maj7 chords in C major connect Cmaj7 to Fmaj7 via dominant-resolution-style root motion; the major seventh of each chord resolves or is retained as a common tone in the next voicing. Consult the Functional layer to track how the leading tone function shifts across the cycle. Chapter 1, pp. 12-189.

Apply the M.S.R.P. string to the maj7 catalog entries to choose which chord tone occupies the top voice: the Root, Third, Fifth, or Seventh as soprano produces four distinct voicing shapes for Cmaj7 and Fmaj7. Cycling through all four MSRP positions across Cycles 2-7 generates the complete voice-leading matrix Goodrick encodes in the tables. Chapter 1, pp. 12-189.

Abmaj7 appears as the bVI maj7 chord in C harmonic minor; Goodrick's tables catalog its voice-leading through all six cycles in that context, where it functions as a tonic-substitute or pre-dominant sonority. Use the Functional layer entries for C harmonic minor to distinguish its role from the tonic-function Cmaj7 of C major. Chapter 1, pp. 12-189.

Min7 chords (Dm7, Em7, Am7 in C major) are cataloged in both Close and Spread voicings across all six cycles; in Close voicing the minor seventh collapses the voice-span, while Spread voicing opens the outer-voice interval, making common-tone retention more audible. Compare both density columns for the same cycle to identify which voicing density better sustains legato connections. Chapter 1, pp. 12-189.

Cycle 5 root motion chains min7 chords in a ii-V-like succession (e.g., Dm7 to Gdom7 to Cmaj7 in C major); the Almanac's tables isolate the min7 portion, showing how the flat-seventh of Dm7 descends by step to become the third of G7. Use this cycle's min7 tables as the foundation for constructing ii-V-I voice-leading frameworks. Chapter 1, pp. 12-189.

Cycle 3 (root motion by thirds) connects min7 chords that share common tones: Dm7 and Am7 in C major share C and E, so the Intervallic layer tables for Cycle 3 will show two stationary voices and two moving voices. Use this common-tone richness to practice smooth contrary-motion resolutions between third-related min7 chords. Chapter 1, pp. 12-189.

The four MSRP positions for min7 produce the root-position, first-inversion, second-inversion, and third-inversion voicing shapes; the Seventh-on-top shape places the minor seventh in the soprano, yielding the flattest, most open sound. Goodrick's tables enumerate all four for Dm7, Em7, and Am7 in every cycle and scale environment. Chapter 1, pp. 12-189.

In C melodic minor, the diatonic min7 chords shift in quality relative to C major; Goodrick catalogs these altered diatonic positions so the player can compare how the same physical chord (e.g., Dm7) functions differently depending on its parent-scale context. Cross-reference the Functional layer entries between C major and C melodic minor tables to map common voice-leading pathways. Chapter 1, pp. 12-189.

G7 (dominant 7th) appears in C major, C harmonic minor, and C melodic minor (ascending variants), and Goodrick catalogs it in Close and Spread voicings; Close voicing concentrates the tritone (B-F) within a narrow span, while Spread voicing displaces it by an octave, changing the tension character. Always practice both densities for dom7 to control the intensity of the tritone resolution. Chapter 1, pp. 12-189.

Cycle 5 is the home cycle for dom7: the root-motion-by-fourth paradigm is the dominant-to-tonic resolution engine, and the Almanac's Cycle 5 dom7 tables encode exactly how each voice of G7 resolves into each MSRP position of Cmaj7. Use the Functional layer column to confirm that the tritone always resolves inward (B up to C, F down to E) regardless of voicing inversion. Chapter 1, pp. 12-189.

In Cycle 2 (stepwise root motion), dom7 chords appear consecutively in modes of the parent scale; the Intervallic layer tables show how minimal semitone or whole-tone shifts connect adjacent dom7 voicings, useful for chromatic parallel-dominant passages. This cycle reveals how much of the dom7 structure can be held static while the root descends by step. Chapter 1, pp. 12-189.

The Seventh-on-top MSRP position for G7 places the minor seventh (F) in the soprano, creating a falling-line potential into the third (E) of the resolution chord; the Third-on-top position places B in the soprano, creating a rising half-step resolution to C. Goodrick's tables catalog both soprano-voice scenarios so the guitarist can plan melodic direction through the dominant. Chapter 1, pp. 12-189.

G7 in C harmonic minor is the definitive V7 of a minor key; the Almanac catalogs its voice-leading in this context separately from C major, highlighting that the resolution target is Cmin (or CminMaj7) rather than Cmaj7. Use the harmonic-minor Functional layer entries to track how Ab (the b6 of C harmonic minor) appears in surrounding chords and shapes the approach to G7. Chapter 1, pp. 12-189.

The Functional layer across cycles reveals that dom7 chords with the same tritone (e.g., G7 and Db7) share identical functional voice-leading profiles; Goodrick's exhaustive cycle tables allow direct cross-referencing so the player can substitute tritone-related dom7 voicings without relearning the resolution logic-only the root changes. Chapter 1, pp. 12-189.

Min7b5 (half-diminished) chords-Bm7b5 in C major, Dm7b5 in C melodic and harmonic minor-are cataloged in both Close and Spread voicings; the diminished fifth between root and fifth is the defining interval, and Close voicing keeps it in its most compact, dissonant form. Compare densities to find which placement most clearly exposes the half-diminished color for ii-half-dim to V7 motion. Chapter 1, pp. 12-189.

In Cycle 5, Bm7b5 resolves toward E7 (or Em) by fourth-root motion; the Almanac tables show how the diminished fifth (B-F) is absorbed into the next voicing with minimal displacement, and the Intervallic layer confirms whether the b5 moves up by half-step (to the natural fifth of the target) or held as a common tone. Chapter 1, pp. 12-189.

Dm7b5 occupies a different diatonic position in C melodic minor (IV) than Bm7b5 does in C major (VII); Goodrick catalogs both, enabling the player to see how the same chord quality takes on different functional roles depending on scale context. Cross-reference the Functional layer between the two scale tables to identify shared approach and departure patterns. Chapter 1, pp. 12-189.

The b5-on-top MSRP position for min7b5 places the most dissonant interval in the soprano, maximizing tension before resolution; the Root-on-top position produces the least dissonant soprano line. Use the Almanac's MSRP layer to plan whether the half-diminished chord should peak or sustain the tension arc into the following dominant. Chapter 1, pp. 12-189.

Bdim7 appears as the viio7 chord in C harmonic minor; because dim7 is fully symmetric (all minor thirds), its Close and Spread voicings are inversionally equivalent, and Goodrick's paired catalog entries reveal which voicing position is most fingering-efficient on guitar for each cycle. Use both density columns to build a complete set of enharmonic substitution voicings. Chapter 1, pp. 12-189.

Cycle 3 (third-related root motion) is particularly revealing for dim7 because the chord's symmetry makes every minor-third transposition an enharmonic inversion of itself; Goodrick's Cycle 3 dim7 tables expose how the same four pitches rotate through different voicing positions as the 'root' changes. The Intervallic layer entries confirm that no voice actually moves-only the labeling shifts. Chapter 1, pp. 12-189.

The Functional layer for Bdim7 in C harmonic minor documents its role as a dominant substitute (viio7 = V7b9 without root); cross-reference these entries against the dom7 Cycle 5 tables to find equivalent resolution patterns. Goodrick's exhaustive enumeration makes it possible to swap Bdim7 for G7b9 in any voicing shape and identify the closest common-tone connection. Chapter 1, pp. 12-189.

Bdim7 is exclusively cataloged within C harmonic minor in the Almanac (the only parent scale among the three that generates a diatonic dim7 chord); use this as a filter-whenever you encounter dim7 voice-leading tables in Chapter 1, you are operating in harmonic minor territory. The MSRP layer provides four soprano-position variants, all equally tense due to the chord's symmetry. Chapter 1, pp. 12-189.

CminMaj7 (minor triad with major seventh) appears in both C melodic minor and C harmonic minor as the tonic chord; Goodrick catalogs it in Close and Spread voicings, and the major seventh creates an especially sharp clash against the minor third in Close density. Practice both densities to calibrate how much of the chord's characteristic tension is density-dependent versus inherent to the quality itself. Chapter 1, pp. 12-189.

In Cycle 5, CminMaj7 as tonic receives resolution from G7 (V7 of C harmonic/melodic minor); the Almanac tables show how the major seventh (B natural) of the minMaj7 is approached from the leading tone of G7-they are the same pitch, making it a common-tone arrival. Use the Functional layer to confirm this leading-tone retention as the defining feature of minor-key tonic voice-leading. Chapter 1, pp. 12-189.

The Major-Seventh-on-top MSRP position for CminMaj7 places B natural in the soprano, immediately signaling the raised seventh that distinguishes this chord from a standard min7; this soprano choice creates the most harmonically distinctive sound. Use Goodrick's MSRP tables to plan whether the raised seventh appears as a melodic goal or as an inner voice depending on the cycle context. Chapter 1, pp. 12-189.

In C melodic minor, CminMaj7 is the tonic chord and its voice-leading through all six cycles is cataloged; the Functional layer entries specifically trace how the major seventh (B natural) behaves differently in ascending melodic minor context versus harmonic minor context, since the surrounding scale degrees differ. Compare the C melodic minor and C harmonic minor minMaj7 entries side by side to identify which cycles produce identical voice motions. Chapter 1, pp. 12-189.

EbMaj7#5 (aug-maj7, the III+ chord) is exclusive to C harmonic minor and is cataloged in Close and Spread voicings; the augmented fifth makes this one of the most internally dissonant major-seventh types, and Spread voicing distributes that dissonance across a wider register, making it slightly less abrasive while retaining the augmented color. Chapter 1, pp. 12-189.

The aug-maj7 chord is uniquely generated by the harmonic minor scale (bIIIMaj7#5 = EbMaj7#5 in C harmonic minor); Goodrick's catalog provides voice-leading through all six cycles in this context alone. Use the Intervallic layer to observe how the augmented fifth (B natural, enharmonic Cb) creates oblique or contrary motion in adjacent voices when the root moves. Chapter 1, pp. 12-189.

The Functional layer for aug-maj7 in C harmonic minor shows its relationship to the tonic and mediant functions; because the augmented fifth (B natural) is the same pitch as the major seventh of CminMaj7, cross-reference both chords' functional entries to find common-tone substitution pathways between them. This allows the player to substitute EbMaj7#5 for CminMaj7 without disrupting the soprano line. Chapter 1, pp. 12-189.

Augmented triads arise diatonically from C harmonic minor (III+, Eb+) and C melodic minor; like dim7, they are symmetric (all major thirds), so Close and Spread voicings are inversional equivalents. Goodrick's paired catalog entries expose the three enharmonically equivalent root positions, allowing the guitarist to choose the most ergonomic fingering for each cycle's root-motion context. Chapter 1, pp. 12-189.

Cycle 3 (major-third root motion) maps directly onto the augmented triad's internal structure; Goodrick's tables reveal that in Cycle 3, the aug-triad's voices rotate with zero displacement-each voice becomes the 'next' voice of the same chord. Use this property to practice effortless aug-triad sequences where the hand stays in one position while the functional label of each voice shifts. Chapter 1, pp. 12-189.

In C melodic minor, the augmented triad appears at a different diatonic degree than in C harmonic minor; Goodrick catalogs both occurrences, enabling the player to observe how the same symmetric chord assumes pre-dominant or mediant functional roles depending on the parent scale. Cross-reference the Functional layer between the two scale contexts to identify which cycles produce the smoothest common-tone connections. Chapter 1, pp. 12-189.

Major triads (C, F, G in C major; Ab, Eb in C harmonic minor) are cataloged in both Close and Spread voicings; the triad's three voices produce fewer options than seventh chords, but the MSRP positions (Root, Third, Fifth in soprano) create three distinct color profiles. Use the Almanac's triad tables as foundational voice-leading prototypes before adding seventh-chord extensions. Chapter 1, pp. 12-189.

Cycle 6 (root motion by major sixth, inverse of minor third) connects major triads that share one common tone; Goodrick's tables show that in C major, C major and A minor (relative minor's tonic) are a sixth apart, making this cycle efficient for parallel major-to-relative-minor progression practice. The Intervallic layer confirms which two voices move and which one is retained. Chapter 1, pp. 12-189.

Minor triads (Dm, Em, Am in C major; Cm in C harmonic and melodic minor) are paired in Close and Spread voicing across all six cycles; the minor third as the lowest interval in Close voicing gives a darker, more compact sound compared to Spread. Drill both densities against all six cycle root motions to internalize how minor-triad voice-leading differs from major-triad motion by a single semitone (the third). Chapter 1, pp. 12-189.

Cycle 5 minor-triad motion in C major (Am-Dm-Gm... or Am-Dm-G when diatonic) models the ii-V descent in minor; the Almanac's tables trace how the minor third in each chord migrates through the voicing as the root moves by fourth. Use the Functional layer to flag which minor triads are tonic substitutes versus pre-dominant in the C major context. Chapter 1, pp. 12-189.

Cm as the tonic minor triad in C harmonic minor is cataloged with its six-cycle voice-leading matrix; the tables contrast with C major's Am triad to show how the same minor-triad quality sounds with different surrounding diatonic contexts. Use the Functional layer entries for Cm in C harmonic minor to practice tonic-function arrivals from each of the six cycle root-motion directions. Chapter 1, pp. 12-189.

The diminished triad (Bdim in C major; Ddim and Bdim in C harmonic minor) is cataloged in Close and Spread voicings; in Close voicing the tritone between root and fifth is in its most compressed, tense form, while Spread voicing displaces it by an octave. Goodrick's paired tables let the player choose density based on how much tension they want the diminished triad to project before resolution. Chapter 1, pp. 12-189.

The Functional layer for Bdim in C major documents its dominant-substitute role (rootless G7); cross-reference the dim-triad Cycle 5 entries against the dom7 Cycle 5 tables to find voice positions where the two chords share identical upper-voice motion into the tonic resolution. This substitution is one of the most practically useful cross-references Goodrick's exhaustive catalog enables. Chapter 1, pp. 12-189.

Goodrick treats quartal voicings (3-part and 4-part 4ths) as structurally opposed to tertial chord families: "tertial harmony and quartal harmony are pretty much exact opposites." The primary intervals of a quartal voicing are 4ths and 5ths; 3rds and 6ths are present only as color or secondary intervals, the inverse of triads (Chapter 5, p. 9).

Goodrick prescribes excluding 3rds and 6ths as primary intervals in a quartal voicing context: the interval inventory of a 3-part 4th chord is Two 2nds, Four 4ths, Two 5ths, One 7th — Primary intervals: 4ths and 5ths; Color intervals: 3rds and 6ths (missing) (Chapter 5, p. 10).

The diminished 4th between B and Eb is proscribed in quartal voicing context because it sounds like a major 3rd despite appearing as a 4th on the staff: they don't work very well in a 4th voicings context. A quartal voicing containing B–Eb risks collapsing into a triadic sonority (Chapter 5, p. 9).

Goodrick prescribes tuning the low E string down a whole step to D and using it as a pedal while cycling through all 4th-voicing positions, placing the player in D Dorian where there aren't any avoid notes (Chapter 5, p. 10).

Goodrick prescribes arpeggiation of quartal voicing shapes as a melodic generation tool. The five M-Lode applications (melodies, arpeggios, counterpoint, 3-part chords, 4-part chords) all apply to quartal material (Chapter 5, p. 10; Chapter 6, p. 11).

Goodrick prescribes alternating arpeggio direction across successive M-Lode chord positions: arpeggiate up the first chord, then down the second chord, up the third chord, down the fourth chord, etc. (Chapter 6, p. 11; Chapter 15, p. 20).

Goodrick prescribes analyzing every quartal voicing through a paired Intervallic/Functional Voice-Leading grid. Example for 3-part 4ths Cycle 6 Close: 5→2nd / 2→2nd / 1→2nd intervallic; 5→1 / 2→5 / 1→2 functional (Chapter 19, p. 27).

When traversing quartal positions within a cycle, any voice that does not move is annotated as c.t. (common tone) — a distinct analytical category. Example: 4-part 4ths Cycle 2 (C Major, 4-way close) shows voices 4 and 1 as c.t. while voices 7 and 3 move (Chapter 19, p. 27; Chapter 23, p. 159).

Drop 3 and 4 is only for finger-style guitarists. The Double Drop 2/Drop 4 (octave inserted between the middle two voices of a Drop 2) also favors fingerstyle, which enables partial barres and selective string plucking (Chapter 10, p. 15; Chapter 8, p. 14).

When any voice within a quartal (or any M-Lode) voicing moves by a third between successive positions, fill that interval with a melodic passing tone. Applies to individual melodies, counterpoint, 3-part and 4-part chords (Chapter 13, p. 17-18).

Many spread cluster voicings are difficult to play on the guitar: BE VERY CAREFUL!!! Spread clusters are extremely interesting and mostly unknown but demand careful physical preparation (Chapter 16, p. 22).

Begin all arpeggio and voicing exploration at 4-way close density. Look at all of the 4-way close options within the M-Lode — easiest area to explore that gives the best initial results. Seek open-string voicings (Chapter 15, p. 20; Chapter 16, p. 21).
Prefer C Harmonic Minor as the scale context for quartal and M-Lode voicing exploration: IT JUST SOUNDS BETTER IN HARMONIC MINOR (Chapter 15, p. 20).

Octave insertion places an octave between any two voices within a 3-part or 4-part chord. Applies to quartal voicings as well: all of this applies to the 3-part 4th voicings as well. Named variants include Double Drop 2/Drop 4 and Drop 3 and 4 (Chapter 8-9, p. 14; Chapter 10, p. 15).

Play all 6 possible 2-voice combinations and all 4 possible 3-voice combinations of every 4-part chord. Joe's 2 Plus 2 Thing divides the 4-part chord into two 2-note groupings alternating as call-and-response pairs (Chapter 7, p. 12-13; Chapter 12, p. 16).

Goodrick places triads in the M-Lode as 3-part structures whose interval content consists primarily of 3rds and 6ths with some 4ths and 5ths, but containing no 2nds or 7ths. This interval profile distinguishes them categorically from 3-part 4th voicings. Chapter 4, p. 8.

Interval omission is permitted within the triad family — Goodrick states that 'the omission of interval types only occurs within particular 3-part chord families (triad; 3-part 4th; spread cluster).' Chapter 4, p. 8.

Goodrick teaches that dropping one voice from a 4-part 7th chord produces two possible triadic 3-part types: the 7th chord without its 3rd, or the 7th chord without its 5th. Each resulting 3-part triad type appears across four different 4-part chord families, creating a symmetry the student should exploit for reharmonization. Chapter 5, p. 9.

Goodrick recommends 3-part chords — including triads — over 4-part chords for guitarists: '3-part chords are easier to play than 4-part chords. Also, they often afford more space between the voices for melodic embellishment.' Chapter 11, p. 71.

All twenty foundational 3-part chord types in Chapter 11 — including triads — are derived from three source scales: Major, Melodic Minor, and Harmonic Minor, transposed to the root of C. The student must then transpose to remaining keys independently. Chapter 11, p. 71.

For triads moving through a diatonic scale, Goodrick identifies that Volumes I and II used only three of six possible generic voice-leading patterns. Volume III introduces the remaining alternates; the student should apply all six A-B-C generic patterns to triads. Chapter 10, p. 56.

To learn all inversions of a chord type, Goodrick prescribes the Grip-Slipping technique: cycle through inversions using Drop 3 voicings within a whole-tone (six-tonic) system. May also try Drop 2 and Drop 2&4. This is Specific Chromatic Voice-Leading (SCVL). Chapter 12, p. 161.
Goodrick prescribes splitting 4-part voicings into two-voice duets — top two voices and bottom two voices — and adding passing tones. He notes this is 'NICE in Harmonic minor!' Chapter 10, p. 43.

Because each 3-part chord type appears inside exactly four different 4-part chord families, Goodrick teaches the student to substitute any of the four parent families when harmonizing a given 3-part sonority. Chapter 5, p. 9.

Goodrick classifies stacked-fourth chords (both 3-part and 4-part) as sus4 structures within the M-Lode. He recommends naming them sus4: 'My suggestion for a suitable name for this chord would be: G [sus4]. That means a G Major triad with 4 suspended for 3.' Chapter 2, p. 4.

Goodrick prescribes sus4 notation as the preferred label for all stacked-fourth chords, rejecting more cumbersome alternatives. For 4-part 4ths: 'Sus 4 Chords... I think it's the best way to go.' Chapter 2, pp. 4-5.

3-part 4th voicings (sus4 structures) belong to the family class in which interval omission is permitted, alongside triads and spread clusters. The student may omit interval types within 3-part 4th voicings without leaving the family. Chapter 4, p. 8.
Goodrick defines 3-part 4th voicings as primarily consisting of 4ths and 5ths with some 2nds and 7ths, but containing no 3rds or 6ths — the inverse of the triad's interval profile. Chapter 4, p. 8.

Goodrick uses CMaj7 as the primary worked example for deriving 3-part chords from a 4-part 7th chord, positioning it as structure number 1 in the 35-structure taxonomy. Dropping the 3rd yields a 7th-no-3rd voicing; dropping the 5th yields a 7th-no-5th voicing. Chapter 5, p. 9.

For CMaj7-type 4-part chords, Goodrick teaches the full menu of voicing transformations: 4-way close, Drop 2, Drop 3, Drop 2&3, Drop 2&4, and Double Drop 2 Drop 3, applied across root position, 1st, 2nd, and 3rd inversions. Chapter 5, p. 9; Chapter 11.

Roberts prescribes close voicings as a deliberate textural device — "very effective but not too often used, on the guitar" — deployed specifically as contrast against open voicings: "These can be used as texture contrast to the big sound of open voicings" (chapter 3, p. 12). The implication is sparing use: close voicings land with more impact when they punctuate an otherwise open-voiced texture.

Roberts prescribes converting any close voicing to an open voicing by octave displacement: "Closed voiced chords can be opened up as far as your reach will permit, simply by moving one or more chordal tones up or down an octave" (chapter 2, p. 6). This is the primary mechanism for expanding harmonic texture on guitar.

Roberts explicitly allows both close and open voicings within the block chord device: "This is done by placing a full chord underneath each melody note. The chords can be either close or open voicings" (chapter 2, p. 8). The choice of density is left to the player's ear within the block chord context.

Roberts establishes open voicings as the dominant sound of chord melody on guitar — the "big sound" against which close voicings provide contrast (chapter 3, p. 12). Open voicings are produced by moving one or more tones an octave away from a close position: "Closed voiced chords can be opened up as far as your reach will permit, simply by moving one or more chordal tones up or down an octave" (chapter 2, p. 6).

When sustaining an open voicing through a long melody sequence, Roberts prescribes dropping chord tones as fingering demands while relying on listener memory: "if each chordal tone is sustained for as long as possible, the listener usually remember those notes that have been dropped" (chapter 2, p. 9). The instruction is to sustain each tone as long as physically possible before releasing — delay, not avoidance.

Roberts gives explicit permission to add extensions freely to any voicing: "the addition of the extensions Maj. 7th, 6th, 9th, etc., only affect the color and texture of the chord and do not change its scale function or its role in the progression" (chapter 4, p. 36). The arranger can reach for richer open voicings without disrupting harmonic logic.

Roberts prescribes substituting diminished chords in place of dominant 7b9 chords to inject chromaticism: "The E° and Db° chords are both functioning as A7b9, and are being used to provide some chromatic relief from the monotony of diatonic lines" (chapter 3, p. 13). Any diminished chord whose tones overlap with the dominant 7b9 spelling is a valid substitute.

Roberts demonstrates that a chord symbol may carry dominant 7b9 function even when spelled as a 6th chord: "The G6 in bar 3 is functioning as a dominant chord (Eb + 7b9)" (chapter 3, p. 12). The lesson is that Roman numeral function must be read from the phrase context, not the chord symbol alone — a G6 can be the upper structure of an Eb7b9.

Roberts prescribes using diminished chords (E°, Db°) as substitutes for dominant 7b9 sounds — specifically A7b9 in the cited example — to "provide some chromatic relief from the monotony of diatonic lines" (chapter 3, p. 13). Roberts advises practicing this substitution in all keys with various diatonic melodies as ear training (chapter 3, p. 13).

Beyond its dominant-substitute role, Roberts implies diminished chord shapes function as chromatic passing connective tissue between diatonic progression points — part of the broader family of altered passing chords (alongside m7+5 shapes) enumerated in chapter 3 and demonstrated in the chapter 5 solo. Chapter 3 prescribes studying these substitutions in all keys: "It is good ear training to improvise this sort of thing in all keys, with various diatonic melodies" (p. 13).

Roberts demonstrates a specific minor 7 substitution in a block chord context: "The Gm7 in bar 3 is being used as a substitute for Eb maj 9" (chapter 2, p. 8). The Gm7 supplies three of the Eb maj9's upper extensions (G=3, Bb=5, D=maj7, F=9), making it a viable relative-minor upper-structure substitute in chord melody harmonization.

Roberts explicitly uses Am7 and Bm7 as structural diatonic chords in a passing-chord study: "Example 35 shows the primary progression consisting of G6, Am7, Bm7, Cmaj7 (one chord per bar) being connected by the passing chords G#m7+5, Am7+5" (chapter 3). The min7 chords anchor the diatonic skeleton that the altered passing shapes then connect.

Roberts's universal sustain rule applies to all chord qualities including min7: "Sustain each chordal tone for as long as possible. In general, this means to keep your fingers in place until it's absolutely necessary to move them. This will contribute measurably to the continuity of your chord melody style" (chapter 3, p. 15). For min7, this means the root, minor third, fifth, and seventh should each ring through into the next chord event until finger movement is forced.

Roberts explicitly names the major seventh as the first example of an extension that "only affect the color and texture of the chord and do not change its scale function or its role in the progression" (chapter 4, p. 36). The arranger should therefore feel free to reach for maj7 voicings wherever a major chord appears in the progression without disrupting harmonic identity.

Roberts uses Cmaj7 as one of the four structural diatonic anchor chords in the chapter 3 passing-chord study: "the primary progression consisting of G6, Am7, Bm7, Cmaj7 (one chord per bar) being connected by the passing chords G#m7+5, Am7+5" (chapter 3, p. 11). Cmaj7 sits at the IV position in G major and is treated as a stable harmonic target, not a passing shape.

Roberts explicitly names the sixth as a coloristic extension that does not change a chord's scale function: "the addition of the extensions Maj. 7th, 6th, 9th, etc., only affect the color and texture of the chord" (chapter 4, p. 36). The 6th chord is therefore interchangeable with its triad or maj7 form for purposes of progression logic.

Roberts demonstrates that a 6th chord can carry dominant 7b9 function when read in phrase context: "The G6 in bar 3 is functioning as a dominant chord (Eb + 7b9)" (chapter 3, p. 12). This is a concrete instance of Roberts's principle that functional identity depends on full phrase analysis, not isolated chord spelling.

Roberts uses G6 as the tonic anchor of the chapter 3 diatonic passing-chord example: "the primary progression consisting of G6, Am7, Bm7, Cmaj7 (one chord per bar)" (chapter 3, p. 11). G6 functions as I in G major, confirming the 6th voicing as a fully valid tonic chord quality in Roberts's harmonic vocabulary.

Roberts names the ninth among the extensions that "only affect the color and texture of the chord and do not change its scale function or its role in the progression" (chapter 4, p. 36). The ninth may therefore be added to any chord freely in chord melody arranging without altering the harmonic grammar of the passage.

Roberts prescribes altered minor-seventh chords with raised fifths (m7+5, equivalent to min7b5's enharmonic neighbor) as chromatic passing shapes between diatonic progression points: "the passing chords G#m7+5, Am7+5" connect the primary diatonic chords in Example 35 (chapter 3, p. 11). These altered passing shapes serve as connective tissue even when momentarily dissonant with the underlying harmony.

Roberts's chapter 3 passing-chord study employs m7+5 shapes (minor seventh with augmented fifth) as chromatic connective tissue between diatonic chords, demonstrating that augmented-fifth voicings belong to his palette of altered passing chords (chapter 3, p. 11). The augmented quality is treated not as a harmonic destination but as a linking texture that creates "interesting extensions" from the independence of melody and harmony (chapter 4, p. 40).

Roberts states his universal chord-tone sustain rule across all chord qualities: "Sustain each chordal tone for as long as possible. In general, this means to keep your fingers in place until it's absolutely necessary to move them. This will contribute measurably to the continuity of your chord melody style" (chapter 3, p. 15). The rule is not quality-specific — it applies to every chord the player voices.

Roberts prescribes a permissive rule for harmonizing chromatic melody notes against any chord quality: "Any chromatic note within finger range can always be harmonized with a given chord form, although it may occasionally be dissonant" (chapter 4, p. 38). When melody and harmony move independently, "interesting extensions" emerge from the friction (chapter 4, p. 40).

Roberts states a hard physical constraint applying to all chord qualities: "if the melody note is placed too low on the staff, you will not have enough strings left to form a satisfactory chord beneath it" and the floor is explicit — "as low as the 4th string but no lower" (chapter 4, p. 36). When the melody falls below this floor, Roberts prescribes jumping the melody up an octave rather than compromising the voicing.

Roberts prescribes that in block chord style every melody note must be accompanied by a freshly voiced chord: "it is more desirable to change the voicing or inversion with each new melody note, in order to create the effect of all lines moving at once" (chapter 2, p. 9). Leaving the chord form unchanged while the melody moves "tends to destroy the block chord effect" — a proscriptive corollary.

Roberts explicitly warns against leaving the chord form unchanged when the melody moves in block chord style: "Often the melody can be fingered easily without having to change the chord form, but this tends to destroy the block chord effect" (chapter 2, p. 9). The student must change voicing or inversion with each new melody note even when it is mechanically unnecessary.

Roberts prescribes that short chord punctuations must be "played with authority and appropriately placed within the bar" to maintain harmonic continuity without constant restriking (chapter 2, p. 10). Harmonic continuity can be further reinforced by "choosing melodies which emphasize chordal tones" — the melodic line does harmonic work that the sparse chord cannot do alone.

Roberts prescribes a deliberately modest iterative method for developing chord melody arrangements: "develop chord melody solos for each of these examples, keeping them as simple as possible. Concentrate mainly on finding chord voicings that sound good to you and still permit the melody to be played" (chapter 4, p. 42). Simplicity is the starting constraint, not the final destination — repetition builds instinct toward extemporaneous chord melody (chapter 4, p. 52).

Use medium-heavy strings (.012 minimum first string) and medium-high action to build resistance that develops right-hand accuracy and left-hand strength. Narrow-gauge strings do not return to center fast enough to permit predictable accuracy. (Chapter 1, p. 3)

references.source: Roberts, Howard - Jazz Guitar Technique in 20 Weeks
references.citation: Chapter 1, p. 3: 'Extremely nar-row gauge strings do not create enough resistance or "return" to their center position quickly enough to permit the right hand to develope predictable accuracy, or to strengthen the left hand. So, use a medium-heavy set of strings; nothing smaller than an .012 first string, etc.'

notes.narrative: Use a medium-sized, medium-to-heavy celluloid pick. Avoid very large or oddly shaped picks. Pick thickness and material directly affect tone control and right-hand mechanics. (Chapter 1, p. 4)

references.source: Roberts, Howard - Jazz Guitar Technique in 20 Weeks
references.citation: Chapter 1, p. 4: 'Your pick should be of medium size, and medium to heavy in thickness. Avoid very large or odd shaped picks. Standard celluloid picks are well suited to this purpose.'

notes.narrative: Three non-guitar tools are mandatory: a metronome, a tape recorder (reel-to-reel or cassette), and a timer. These externalize the method's three core feedback loops — time, self-monitoring, and session discipline. (Chapter 1, p. 4)

references.source: Roberts, Howard - Jazz Guitar Technique in 20 Weeks
references.citation: Chapter 1, p. 4: 'Also essential to the studies in this book will be: (1) a metronome, (2) a reel-to-reel or cassette tape recorder, and (3) an alarm clock or timer.'

notes.narrative: After setting up the guitar, verify that every note rings loud and clear across the entire fingerboard — like a grand piano. This is the primary diagnostic criterion for correct setup. (Chapter 1, p. 3)

references.source: Roberts, Howard - Jazz Guitar Technique in 20 Weeks
references.citation: Chapter 1, p. 3: 'After adjusting your guitar, make sure that each note rings loud and clear; just like a grand piano, over the entire range of the fingerboard.'

notes.narrative: Speed is a byproduct of accuracy and is unattainable without it. Every practice decision — tempo targets, equipment choices, session structure — is downstream of this premise. Never chase speed at the expense of precision. (Chapter 1, p. 3)

references.source: Roberts, Howard - Jazz Guitar Technique in 20 Weeks
references.citation: Chapter 1, p. 3: 'Speed comes as a by-product of accuracy. Without accuracy, speed is unattainable.'

notes.narrative: The right hand is the primary limiting factor for most modern guitar improvisers. Once a poor picking style becomes habitual it is extremely difficult to change — complete retraining is often required. Establish correct mechanics from the outset. (Chapter 2, p. 5)

references.source: Roberts, Howard - Jazz Guitar Technique in 20 Weeks
references.citation: Chapter 2, p. 5: 'The right hand seems to be the greatest limiting factor for most modern-day guitar improvisors. It appears that once a style of picking has become habitual, it is very difficult to change, and frequently, total retraining is required.'

notes.narrative: Flexibility — the ability to adapt the right hand to a variety of moves — is the single governing principle of right-hand technique. Adaptability is more important than any fixed system. (Chapter 2, p. 5)

references.source: Roberts, Howard - Jazz Guitar Technique in 20 Weeks
references.citation: Chapter 2, p. 5: 'flexibility-the ability to adapt the right hand to a variety of moves-is the key to longevity.'

notes.narrative: Avoid any fixed anchor system — at the elbow, at the wrist, or grasping the pick-guard with the little finger. Such anchors may serve contextual sounds but create a hard speed ceiling when used as the foundation of overall right-hand technique. (Chapter 2, p. 5)

references.source: Roberts, Howard - Jazz Guitar Technique in 20 Weeks
references.citation: Chapter 2, p. 5: 'The big thing to avoid is any kind of anchor system that inhibits freedom of movement. Observe anchors at the elbow, at the wrist, grasping the pick-guard with the little finger, etc.; all of which may be functional for a specific sound, but should be viewed with caution when considered as the basis of an overall right hand technique.'

notes.narrative: Keep the picking arm loose — any rigidness in the picking leverage system acts like a brick wall at fast tempos. Tension is a hard mechanical speed ceiling. (Chapter 2, p. 5)

references.source: Roberts, Howard - Jazz Guitar Technique in 20 Weeks
references.citation: Chapter 2, p. 5: 'Keep it loose! - like a guy strumming a ukelele in a pineapple field. Tf there is any rigidness in your picking leverage system, it can stop you like a brick wall when the tempos get fast.'

notes.narrative: Left and right hands must attack every note simultaneously — no flams in either direction. If the finger arrives first, two sounds result; if the pick arrives first, two sounds result. Perfect synchronization means a single audible attack. (Chapter 2, p. 5)

references.source: Roberts, Howard - Jazz Guitar Technique in 20 Weeks
references.citation: Chapter 2, p. 5: 'Under any circumstances, the left and right hands must be in perfect synchronization. No Flams! If the finger attacks first and the pick follows, there will be two sounds instead of one. If the pick attacks first and the finger follows, again, two sounds instead of one.'

notes.narrative: To diagnose flams, play notes very slowly at all positions across the full fingerboard. Only slow play reveals the differential of attack. Fast warm-up playing obscures synchronization errors before they become ingrained. (Chapter 2, p. 5)

references.source: Roberts, Howard - Jazz Guitar Technique in 20 Weeks
references.citation: Chapter 2, p. 5: 'To do so, play tones very slowly at all points on the fingerboard. Only in this way can we hear the flam effect. If we play fast in warming up, it becomes more difficult to hear the differential of attack.'

notes.narrative: The left-hand thumb should ride along the approximate center of the back of the neck, enabling the perpendicular finger angle required for accuracy. (Chapter 2, p. 5)

references.source: Roberts, Howard - Jazz Guitar Technique in 20 Weeks
references.citation: Chapter 2, p. 5: 'The thumb of the left hand should ride along the approximate center of the back of the neck.'

notes.narrative: Fret strings with fingers perpendicular to the fingerboard — straight up and down like piano hammers. Angling the finger moves the string from its center position, cutting accuracy and stretching the string out of tune. (Chapter 2, p. 5)

references.source: Roberts, Howard - Jazz Guitar Technique in 20 Weeks
references.citation: Chapter 2, p. 5: 'The fingers should operate straight up and down on the strings, like hammers in a piano, at a right angle to the fingerboard. Attacking the string at an angle will move the string from it's center position, both cutting down on accuracy and also stretching the string to sound out of tune.'

notes.narrative: Lift fingers only high enough off the string to avoid noise when moving — not higher. Excess finger lift is wasted motion that reduces speed. Balance noise control against efficiency. (Chapter 2, p. 5)

references.source: Roberts, Howard - Jazz Guitar Technique in 20 Weeks
references.citation: Chapter 2, p. 5: 'The fingers should be lifted only high enough off the string to avoid string noise when moving, but not so high as to become wasted motion.'

notes.narrative: Keep the left wrist fairly flat. Avoid severe arching, which produces undesirable strains and risks injury. A flat wrist posture supports both consistency and longevity. (Chapter 2, p. 5)

references.source: Roberts, Howard - Jazz Guitar Technique in 20 Weeks
references.citation: Chapter 2, p. 5: 'The wrist should maintain a fairly flat posture. Avoid severe arching of the left wrist as this can produce undesirable strains.'

notes.narrative: Understand chord progressions through key centers — identify which major or minor scale the chords belong to by stacking thirds — rather than treating each chord independently. The dominant seventh chord uniquely identifies a single major key and is the most decisive harmonic landmark. (Chapter 3, pp. 6–7)
