references.source: Roberts, Howard - Jazz Guitar Technique in 20 Weeks
references.citation: Chapter 3, p. 6: 'When a given major or minor scale is stacked upon itself in thirds as shown in Example 1, it creates harmony characteristic of that scale.'

references.source: Roberts, Howard - Jazz Guitar Technique in 20 Weeks
references.citation: Chapter 3, p. 7: 'Eb 7 is a V chord (Dominant 7 type) which only appears once in any given major key, always as the V chord, and therefore, only one possibility, the V of Ab.'

notes.narrative: When a new key center is reached in a progression, immediately move your hand to a convenient fingering pattern for that scale and improvise within that region of the guitar. Use the bracketed key centers as navigation instructions. (Chapter 3, p. 8)

references.source: Roberts, Howard - Jazz Guitar Technique in 20 Weeks
references.citation: Chapter 3, p. 8: 'for each new one, move your hand to a convenient fingering pattern for that particular scale and do your improvising in that region of the guitar.'

notes.narrative: Learn all five movable finger-per-fret scale patterns for any given key. Together they cover the entire fingerboard; mastering all five yields complete neck coverage. Tonics are circled in each pattern for visual targeting. (Chapter 3, pp. 8–9)

references.source: Roberts, Howard - Jazz Guitar Technique in 20 Weeks
references.citation: Chapter 3, p. 8: 'There are five such patterns for any given scale. And each of these five are movable up or down the neck to the selected key or, they may be connected to increase the range.'

references.source: Roberts, Howard - Jazz Guitar Technique in 20 Weeks
references.citation: Chapter 3, p. 9: 'When these patterns are laid end to end, they cover the entire finger-board for any one key.'

notes.narrative: Moving between the five scale patterns is achieved by exactly three techniques: (1) position skips, (2) stretching to the adjacent pattern, or (3) sliding on the half step between patterns. These three moves constitute the complete system for full-neck fluency. (Chapter 3, p. 10)

references.source: Roberts, Howard - Jazz Guitar Technique in 20 Weeks
references.citation: Chapter 3, p. 10: 'There are essentially three "moves" involved in moving from one pattern to another. (1) Position skips ... (2) Stretching from one pattern to the next, ascending or descending; or (3) Sliding on the half steps.'

notes.narrative: Prioritize developing a strong visual imprint of each pattern coupled with its sound. Specific fingerings within a pattern may change during improvisation — the visual/auditory internalization is the durable goal, not mechanical fingering adherence. (Chapter 3, p. 10)

references.source: Roberts, Howard - Jazz Guitar Technique in 20 Weeks
references.citation: Chapter 3, p. 10: 'The most important thing here is to develop a strong visual imprint of the pattern itself, coupled with the tone sequence it produces (the sound) with the view that when improvising, the fingerings may be open to change at any time.'

notes.narrative: The ultimate goal of key-center study is to play changes by ear rather than through intellectual calculation. Analytical key-center identification is the means; ear-based improvisation is the end. (Chapter 3, p. 8)

references.source: Roberts, Howard - Jazz Guitar Technique in 20 Weeks
references.citation: Chapter 3, p. 8: 'the ability to play over changes by ear, can be viewed as the ideal end result.'

notes.narrative: Play arpeggios within the scale pattern corresponding to the key center of the chord, not as isolated chord shapes. For example, a IIIm7–VIm7–IIm7–V7 progression in Bb means selecting one of the five Bb patterns and playing all arpeggios within it. (Chapter 3, p. 9)

references.source: Roberts, Howard - Jazz Guitar Technique in 20 Weeks
references.citation: Chapter 3, p. 9: 'arpeggios will be easier to handle if they are played within a scale pattern that corresponds to the key center from which the chord is derived, e.g. the progression Dm7, Gm7, Cm7, F7 is a III, VI, II, V Progression in the key of Bb. Therefore, one would select one of the five patterns for that key and play the arpeggios in that pattern.'

notes.narrative: Common tones — notes shared between two or more consecutive chords — are a valid and deliberate relief technique. When playing non-stop eighth notes or triplets, the line does not need to keep moving; sustaining a common tone flattens the line and provides relief from excessive vertical movement. (Chapter 4, p. 11)

references.source: Roberts, Howard - Jazz Guitar Technique in 20 Weeks
references.citation: Chapter 4, p. 11: 'A common tone is a note that is common to two or more chords, a very simple technique but not to be overlooked, i.e. when playing non-stop eighth notes, or triplets, etc., it is not necessary to keep the line moving at all times. The line can be flattened out --- a nice relief from excessive vertical movement.'

notes.narrative: Arpeggios outline bar harmony and provide a strong contrast to scale movement. They create smooth rolling lines at steeper melodic angles than scales, and should be used as a distinct color alongside scale passages. (Chapter 4, p. 13)

references.source: Roberts, Howard - Jazz Guitar Technique in 20 Weeks
references.citation: Chapter 4, p. 13: 'Arpeggios are specifically chords, broken up into single notes. They are effective in outlining the bar harmony and offer a nice contrast to scale movement as they create smooth rolling lines, at sharper angles than scales.'

notes.narrative: Use interval skips to create sharp, dramatic lines that break up scale monotony. Large interval skips are a primary antidote to the beginner trap of playing exclusively scalar lines. (Chapter 4, p. 13)

references.source: Roberts, Howard - Jazz Guitar Technique in 20 Weeks
references.citation: Chapter 4, p. 13: 'Interval skips create sharp, dramatic lines. An interval is the distance between any two notes. Large interval skips can be a valuable tool for creating interesting lines and can have a dramatic effect in breaking up the monotomy of excessive scale movement.'

notes.narrative: Derive all interval skips diatonically — respecting the scale's half steps — so that sequences of thirds, sevenths, ninths, etc. produce combinations of major and minor intervals rather than parallel intervals. Parallel interval sequences violate the key's internal structure and destroy tonality. (Chapter 4, p. 13)

references.source: Roberts, Howard - Jazz Guitar Technique in 20 Weeks
references.citation: Chapter 4, p. 13: 'Any sequence of interval skips, 3rds, 7ths, 9ths, etc., can easily be applied to a key center by playing scale intervals that take into account the half steps of the scale, thus, resulting in combinations of major and minor 3rds or major and minor 7ths (not, parallel 3rds, 7ths, etc.)'

notes.narrative: Do not play more than 3–4 consecutive scale tones in the same direction before changing direction or introducing a skip. Exceeding this limit produces lines that sound purely scale-like — the most common beginner flaw. Limiting stepwise runs forces interval skips and melodic variety. (Chapter 4, p. 13)

references.source: Roberts, Howard - Jazz Guitar Technique in 20 Weeks
references.citation: Chapter 4, p. 13: 'A most common complaint of beginning improvisors is that their playing tends to become too scale-like. One solution to this could be to stop playing things that "sound" like scales, for example, as an exercise; don't play more than 3 or 4 scale tones in the same direction.'

notes.narrative: Use the diminished scale (alternating whole steps and half steps, symmetrical) most commonly over dominant 7th chords or diminished chords. (Chapter 4, p. 12)

references.source: Roberts, Howard - Jazz Guitar Technique in 20 Weeks
references.citation: Chapter 4, p. 12: 'The Diminished Scale (symetrical, consecutive whole step and half steps) most commonly used over dominant 7th chords or diminished chords.'

notes.narrative: The whole-tone scale (symmetrical, consecutive whole steps) is most commonly used over dominant 7th chords. Its symmetrical structure means no half steps, and it lacks gravitational pull toward a specific tonic, making it suitable for suspended or floating dominant passages. (Chapter 4, p. 12)

references.source: Roberts, Howard - Jazz Guitar Technique in 20 Weeks
references.citation: Chapter 4, p. 12: 'The Whole Tone Scale (symetrical, consecutive whole steps) most commonly used over dominant 7th chords.'

notes.narrative: The major pentatonic scale (diatonic major with the 4th and 7th — the active tones — omitted) creates inversions of a major 6/9 chord when harmonized. Its removal of half steps gives it little gravitational pull toward any key center, making it usable across multiple harmonic contexts depending on application. (Chapter 4, p. 13)

references.source: Roberts, Howard - Jazz Guitar Technique in 20 Weeks
references.citation: Chapter 4, p. 13: 'The Major Pentatonic Scale (same as diatonic major with the active tones 3rd and 7th left out). When harmonized creates inversions of a Major 6/9 chord, with little gravitational pull toward any key center "depending on the usage".'

notes.narrative: The harmonic minor scale can be derived quickly from the already-learned diatonic major patterns by raising the fifth scale step (equivalent to raising the seventh of the relative minor). This minimizes new memorization by building on existing pattern knowledge. (Chapter 3, p. 9)

references.source: Roberts, Howard - Jazz Guitar Technique in 20 Weeks
references.citation: Chapter 3, p. 9: 'the relative harmonic minor scales can be quickly learned by simply sharping the fifth scale step of the diatonic scales, which is the same as sharping the seventh of the relative minor scales.'

notes.narrative: The melodic minor scale follows ascending/descending rules (half steps at 2nd/3rd and 7th/8th ascending; reverts to natural minor descending), but this rule is a technicality that may be disregarded in favor of the existing bar harmony. Prioritize harmonic context over rote rule-following. (Chapter 4, p. 12)

references.source: Roberts, Howard - Jazz Guitar Technique in 20 Weeks
references.citation: Chapter 4, p. 12: 'The Relative Melodic Minor Scale (with half steps between the 2nd/3rd and 7th/8th scale steps ascending and reverting back to the natural minor descending. NOTE: The ascending and descending rules here are a technicality, which in the final analysis may be disregarded in favor of the existant bar harmony)'

notes.narrative: Use alternate picking exclusively during project lesson sessions — no two consecutive strokes in the same direction. The qualitative standard is dynamic equality: upstrokes must sound as strong as downstrokes. Directional alternation alone is insufficient if the strokes are dynamically unequal. (Chapter 7, p. 19; Chapter 8, p. 19)

references.source: Roberts, Howard - Jazz Guitar Technique in 20 Weeks
references.citation: Chapter 7, p. 19: 'Use Alternate Picking only. No two strokes in the same direction, i.e. strive to make up strokes sound as strong as down strokes.'

references.source: Roberts, Howard - Jazz Guitar Technique in 20-Weeks
references.citation: Chapter 8, p. 19: 'Use Alternate Picking only. No two strokes in the same direction, i.e. strive to make up strokes sound as strong as down strokes.'

notes.narrative: During Weeks 1–13 of the program, play only continuous, uninterrupted eighth notes with no rests, no phrasing, no hammer-ons, no pull-offs, and no other ornamentation. This constraint isolates picking mechanics as the sole variable under development. (Chapter 7, p. 19)

references.source: Roberts, Howard - Jazz Guitar Technique in 20 Weeks
references.citation: Chapter 7, p. 19: 'Play only eighth notes, continuous and uninterrupted. No rests. No phrasing. No hammer-on's. No pull-offts. No other ornamentation. "Nothing" but steady eighth notes.'

notes.narrative: Play legato — hold each note as long as possible. Great attention must be given to holding steady time; never rush or drag the tempo. Note sustain and metronomic steadiness are the two non-negotiable execution quality standards for all project lessons. (Chapter 7, p. 19)

references.source: Roberts, Howard - Jazz Guitar Technique in 20 Weeks
references.citation: Chapter 7, p. 19: 'Play Legato. Hold each note as long as possible. Great attention should be given to holding steady time. Do not rush or drag the tempo.'

notes.narrative: Hammer-ons, pull-offs, and glissandi are introduced only in Weeks 15–17 of the program, not before. Their strategic value is that they allow multiple notes per single pick stroke, producing a dramatic increase in apparent speed without increasing picking effort. (Chapter 5, p. 15)

references.source: Roberts, Howard - Jazz Guitar Technique in 20 Weeks
references.citation: Chapter 5, p. 15: 'Review the project lessons as before using (a) hammer-on's (b) pull-off's (c) glissandi (slides). The introduction of these techniques should cause your technique and speed to increase dramatically in that via these devices several notes can be produced with one picking stroke.'

notes.narrative: Begin every practice session with a 5-minute warm-up playing notes slowly all over the fingerboard — low, high, and medium register. String travel distance varies significantly by register (high-neck notes have much greater travel than low notes) and directly causes left/right-hand synchronization failures if not addressed at the start of each session. (Chapter 6, p. 16)

references.source: Roberts, Howard - Jazz Guitar Technique in 20 Weeks
references.citation: Chapter 6, p. 16: 'At the beginning of each practice session, warm up for 5 minutes by playing notes all over the fingerboard. Play very slowly, low, high, and medium pitches, to develop a feel for string travel at a given picking area. Notes played high up on the neck have a much greater string travel than the low ones and can create coordination problems between the left and right hands.'

notes.narrative: When diagnosing technique flams: first play very slowly listening for uneven attacks; then play using all upstrokes for scales and interval skips; then use consecutive down and up strokes; then reverse the assignment (upstroke on downbeat, downstroke on upbeat). This systematic picking-direction sequence isolates the source of the coordination problem. (Chapter 6, p. 16)

references.source: Roberts, Howard - Jazz Guitar Technique in 20 Weeks
references.citation: Chapter 6, p. 16: 'HANGUPS: Play very slowly and listen carefully for any flams. Use all up strokes. Make each note sound as loud and strong as any other. Now use all up strokes, scales, interval skips. Now use consecutive down and up strokes. Now reverse to all up (on the down beat) and down (on the up beat) strokes.'

notes.narrative: Before attempting any technical fix, correctly identify which hand is at fault. The most common mistake is blaming the left hand when the right hand is the problem, or vice versa. Misattributing the fault causes the student to practice the wrong hand and never resolve the actual issue. (Chapter 6, p. 17; Chapter 7, p. 17)

references.source: Roberts, Howard - Jazz Guitar Technique in 20 Weeks
references.citation: Chapter 6, p. 17: 'A most common mistake is to blame the left hand when the right hand is at fault, or vice versa. Watch out for this.'

references.source: Roberts, Howard - Jazz Guitar Technique in 20 Weeks
references.citation: Chapter 7, p. 17: 'A most common mistake is to blame the left hand when the right hand is at fault, or vice versa. Watch out for this.'

notes.narrative: When a solo line stalls, sketch a simple structural melody over the changes using half notes and quarter notes and let it run mentally as a basic melody. Play fills around it. This scaffolding technique gives the line form and a starting point when improvisation is blocked. (Chapter 6, p. 16)

references.source: Roberts, Howard - Jazz Guitar Technique in 20 Weeks
references.citation: Chapter 6, p. 16: 'Sometimes it's helpful to sketch out a very simple melody line over the changes, i.e. half note, quarter notes, halves, etc. Let this line run through your head as a basic melody and play "fills" around it. This will at least get your line started with some form.'

notes.narrative: Question and answer is a foundational structural form for building a solo line. When the Q/A pattern recurs, it becomes a sequence. Use this form as a primary organizational principle for creating melodically coherent improvised lines. (Chapter 6, p. 16)

references.source: Roberts, Howard - Jazz Guitar Technique in 20 Weeks
references.citation: Chapter 6, p. 16: 'A very common form for building a solo line is: QUESTION AND ANSWER. When this Q/A routine re-occurs, it is generally called a sequence.'

notes.narrative: Sing the solo before playing it. Listen to the pre-recorded changes and vocalize the line you intend to play, internalizing melodic ideas through the ear before the hand executes them. Ear-to-hand development is a core principle of line construction in this method. (Chapter 6, p. 16)

references.source: Roberts, Howard - Jazz Guitar Technique in 20 Weeks
references.citation: Chapter 6, p. 16: 'Listen to the "pre-recorded changes" and sing the solo the way [you want to play it].'

notes.narrative: Recognize repeated licks in real time and actively play something different in the next pass without stopping. Breaking habitual patterns must be done in the flow of playing — stopping to reconsider defeats the purpose of improvisation continuity. (Chapter 6, p. 16)

references.source: Roberts, Howard - Jazz Guitar Technique in 20 Weeks
references.citation: Chapter 6, p. 16: 'In this program you will reach many moments in which you hate that "same old lick" you "always play". Be aware of this point in the tune and the next time around, do something else, no stops.'

notes.narrative: Technique training exists to serve spontaneous invention, not to constrain it. Model solos and project-lesson examples are reference material and source material only — not prescriptive blueprints. When doing project lessons, invent your own original lines. (Chapter 9, p. 27)

references.source: Roberts, Howard - Jazz Guitar Technique in 20 Weeks
references.citation: Chapter 9, p. 27: 'Remember! This example and all other examples for the project lessons are models of the type of sold line to be improvised. The important consideration is the spontaneous invention of your own solo line. The point of the project lessons is to hone your technique to a level that will facilitate and not hinder the immediate reproduction of any and all of your musical ideas. Use the examples as source material and for reference, but when doing the project lessons, it's "every man for himself".'

notes.narrative: Key-center brackets in chord progressions represent one valid analysis — not the only one. Chord substitution and alternative key interpretations are freely available. When two valid analyses exist (e.g., a chord readable as III of one key or II of another), individual preference governs. The ear is the final arbiter: if a substitution is right, it will sound right immediately. (Chapter 7, p. 19; Chapter 8, p. 19)

references.source: Roberts, Howard - Jazz Guitar Technique in 20 Weeks
references.citation: Chapter 7, p. 19: 'The key centers bracketed in the chord progressions represent only one analysis of the progression. Other views may be applied as well ... Feel free to use any harmonic devices at your disposal. If they're right, they will sound right and if they're wrong, you will know it immediately.'

references.source: Roberts, Howard - Jazz Guitar Technique in 20 Weeks
references.citation: Chapter 8, p. 19: 'The key centers bracketed in the chord progressions represent only one analysis of the progression. Other views may be applied as well ... Feel free to use any harmonic devices at your disposal. If they're right, they will sound right and if they're wrong, you will know it immediately.'

notes.narrative: Memorize chord changes and get the progression off the page as soon as possible. Reading notation splits cognitive attention away from real-time musical decision-making. Memorized changes free all attention for what is actually being played. (Chapter 6, p. 17; Chapter 7, p. 17)

references.source: Roberts, Howard - Jazz Guitar Technique in 20 Weeks
references.citation: Chapter 6, p. 17: 'Get the progression off the paper and into your head as soon as possible. Memorizing the chord changes allows you to focus all of your attention on what you are playing rather than reading the music.'

references.source: Roberts, Howard - Jazz Guitar Technique in 20 Weeks
references.citation: Chapter 7, p. 17: 'Get the progression off the paper and into your head as soon as possible. Memorizing the chord changes allows you to focus all of your attention on what you are playing rather than reading the music.'

notes.narrative: The program's objectives are attainable only through exact compliance: no missed days, no shortened sessions, no out-of-sequence technique introductions, no sixteenth notes where eighth notes are called for. Any deviation invalidates the expected results. (Chapter 6, p. 17; Chapter 7, p. 17)

references.source: Roberts, Howard - Jazz Guitar Technique in 20 Weeks
references.citation: Chapter 6, p. 17: 'The objectives put forth in this book are attainable only if the reader follows each step of the program without deviation from the schedule (that means no missed days, hours shortened, time frames disobeyed, key centers missed, introducing hammer-on's, pull-off's, before stated, playing sixteenth notes instead of eighth notes, etc., etc.) If you do it, you get it. If you don't, you don't.'

notes.narrative: Practice six consecutive days with one day off. Never skip a day for any reason — irregular practice is hazardous to progress, not merely suboptimal. Regularity is the essential structural requirement for skill consolidation. (Chapter 8, p. 19)

references.source: Roberts, Howard - Jazz Guitar Technique in 20 Weeks
references.citation: Chapter 8, p. 19: 'Do each project lesson for six consecutive days, with one day off. Avoid skipping a day, for whatever reason. The effect is hazardous to progress. Regularity is essential. Follow the steps faithfully as given.'

notes.narrative: Do not set the metronome to a desired target speed and try to rise to meet it. Use the metronome only to track progress — record daily tempos. Tempo may vary faster or slower from day to day; this is expected and not a failure signal. (Chapter 7, p. 19; Chapter 8, p. 19)

references.source: Roberts, Howard - Jazz Guitar Technique in 20 Weeks
references.citation: Chapter 7, p. 19: 'Do not set your metronome to a desired speed and try to rise to meet it. Rather, use the metronome only to track your progress. Keep a daily record of your tempos in the boxes provided. (NOTE: Your tempo may vary slower or faster from day to day. This is to be expected.)'

references.source: Roberts, Howard - Jazz Guitar Technique in 20 Weeks
references.citation: Chapter 8, p. 19: 'Do not set your metronome to a desired speed and try to rise to meet it. Rather, use the metronome only to track your progress.'

notes.narrative: Never sacrifice accuracy and precision to meet weekly tempo objectives. Tempo goals are targets, not requirements. The tempo objective plan is symmetrical; the learning curve is not — speed will follow accuracy in asymmetric leaps, not at a steady two-metronome-point daily rate. (Chapter 7, p. 19; Chapter 8, p. 19)

references.source: Roberts, Howard - Jazz Guitar Technique in 20 Weeks
references.citation: Chapter 7, p. 19: 'Care should be taken not to sacrifice accuracy and precision in order to meet the tempo goals. These will always come in time. The tempo objective plan is symmetrical, but the learning curve is not.'

references.source: Roberts, Howard - Jazz Guitar Technique in 20 Weeks
references.citation: Chapter 8, p. 19: 'Care should be taken not to sacrifice accuracy and precision in order to meet the tempo goals. These will always come in time. The tempo objective plan is Symmetrical, but the learning curve is not.'

notes.narrative: Once a given tempo level is reached and maintained for approximately 21 consecutive days of daily playing, that ability is permanently imprinted in the nervous system as a motor reflex. After 21 days at tempo, a six-month layoff followed by 2–3 weeks of hard practice will restore the level. (Chapter 7, p. 18)

references.source: Roberts, Howard - Jazz Guitar Technique in 20 Weeks
references.citation: Chapter 7, p. 18: 'once you reach a given level of speed, and maintain playing at that level or faster, for approximately 21 days, on a daily basis, -- the ability acquired during that period of time will be permanently imprinted and assimilated by your nervous system. You could lay off for six months, come back and practice hard for about 2-3 weeks and it will come right back.'

notes.narrative: Certain tempo ranges are structurally uncomfortable for a given rhythmic feel (steady eighths, shuffle, triplet/12-8, etc.) — each feel has its own natural slow, medium, and fast zones; tempos between those zones feel awkward even to experienced players. During speed-building, expect long periods where the tempo feels wrong and occasional points where it feels right. Do not interpret awkward tempos as personal failure. (Chapter 7, p. 18)

references.source: Roberts, Howard - Jazz Guitar Technique in 20 Weeks
references.citation: Chapter 7, p. 18: 'when tunes are played with a specific feel, i.e. steady eighths or dotted eighths, sixteenths (shuffle) or triplets (12/8), etc., they tend to have slow, medium and fast tempos that are just right for that particular rhythm feel and any other tempos inbetween feel awkward and difficult to play on. This applies even to the most experienced players.'

notes.narrative: Before attributing bad-sounding music to technique failure, audit the practice environment for ambient pitch sources (air conditioners, refrigerator motors, traffic). Room sounds can superimpose a subliminal pitch reference that makes an in-tune guitar sound wrong and triggers a reflexive stop-playing response. Eliminate environmental interference before self-blaming. (Chapter 7, p. 18)

references.source: Roberts, Howard - Jazz Guitar Technique in 20 Weeks
references.citation: Chapter 7, p. 18: 'your guitar may sound out of tune, which is certainly possible. However, keep in mind that it may actually be in tune with itself, but out of tune with an air conditioner, refrigerator motor, or traffic noises from outside. When your music sounds bad to you, the natural reflex is to stop playing. So before you blame yourself for a problem, make sure that you have accounted for elements in your environment that may be superimposing a subliminal orchestration over what you are playing.'

notes.narrative: The feeling of getting nowhere — like pulling a train uphill — is the signal of active neurological development. The feeling of great progress and ease signals a rest plateau, during which no new learning is occurring. The subjective experience of progress and the reality of progress are inversely correlated. The only correct response to both states is maintaining the unwavering practice schedule. (Chapter 6, p. 17; Chapter 7, p. 17)

references.source: Roberts, Howard - Jazz Guitar Technique in 20 Weeks
references.citation: Chapter 6, p. 17: 'The overall physical feeling is like pulling a train uphill, and the psychological spin-off is the feeling that we are getting nowhere ... The progress was made during the uphill climb, not during the rest period. So, on and on it goes, but your practice regimen must remain constant.'

references.source: Roberts, Howard - Jazz Guitar Technique in 20 Weeks
references.citation: Chapter 7, p. 17: 'In the Growth Process, we all go through periods in which we are activating new nerve junctures, both in the brain and throughout other parts of the body. This type of growth work draws a tremendous amount of systemic energies.'

notes.narrative: Bio-cycles create natural monthly high and low emotional periods. Low periods bring discouragement but must not interrupt the regularity of practice. Continue the program with controlled discipline regardless of day-to-day emotional state. (Chapter 7, p. 18)

references.source: Roberts, Howard - Jazz Guitar Technique in 20 Weeks
references.citation: Chapter 7, p. 18: 'be aware of your bio-cycles. Every person has natural high and low points running in approximately monthly cycles. During low periods, you may feel very down and disqouraged, but this must not interrupt the regularity of your practice routine ... You must continue to practice with controlled discipline, no matter how you feel about things from day to day.'

notes.narrative: Noodling while doing low-attention activities (e.g., watching television) is a valid and effective learning mode. Count informal practice time as legitimate. Low-pressure, unstructured playing reinforces muscle memory and pattern internalization without the cognitive load of formal sessions. (Chapter 6, p. 16)

references.source: Roberts, Howard - Jazz Guitar Technique in 20 Weeks
references.citation: Chapter 6, p. 16: 'a very effective type of learning takes place while watching television and noodling.'

notes.narrative: Group practice — exchanging solos and comping, trading in sequence with other guitarists — is superior to private study for this program. Ensemble group dynamics are the single fastest accelerator for developing the skills the method builds. (Chapter 7, p. 18)

references.source: Roberts, Howard - Jazz Guitar Technique in 20 Weeks
references.citation: Chapter 7, p. 18: 'An Accelerator -- form a group of other guitar players. Exchange solos and comping. Trade off in sequence. The group dynamics is superior to private study for a program of this sort.'

notes.narrative: The 20-week program is divided into three sequential phases: (1) Weeks 1–6, duple time — eighth notes as primary subdivision; (2) Weeks 8–13, triple time — eighth-note triplets as primary subdivision; (3) Weeks 15–17, tempo solidification with legato techniques. Each phase must be completed before the next begins. (Chapter 5, pp. 14–15)

references.source: Roberts, Howard - Jazz Guitar Technique in 20 Weeks
references.citation: Chapter 5, p. 14: 'The First Six Weeks, Project Lessons 1-A, 1-B, 2-A, 2-B, 3-A, 3-B, focus on the use of eighth notes, as representative of duple time ... Weeks Eight Through Thirteen, Project Lessons 4-A, 4-B, 5-A, 5-B, 6-A, 6-B focus on triple time via eighth note triplets.'

references.source: Roberts, Howard - Jazz Guitar Technique in 20 Weeks
references.citation: Chapter 5, p. 15: 'Review the project lessons as before using (a) hammer-on's (b) pull-off's (c) glissandi (slides). The introduction of these techniques should cause your technique and speed to increase dramatically.'

notes.narrative: Each project lesson session runs 50 minutes per day, six consecutive days per week, with one day off. The overall tempo target to be reached over 20 weeks is ♩ = 126, maintaining precision and accuracy at all times. (Chapter 5, p. 14)

references.source: Roberts, Howard - Jazz Guitar Technique in 20 Weeks
references.citation: Chapter 5, p. 14: 'The Program is made up of a series of project lessons, each lasting 50 minutes per day, running six consecutive days per week, with one day off. The objective is to gradually increase the tempo over the course of 20 weeks to reach a metronome setting of approximately ♩ = 126 (maintaining precision and accuracy at all times).'

notes.narrative: Repeat project-lesson chord progressions in transposed keys. Transposition forces new fingering patterns and stimulates fresh melodic approaches and ideas, preventing mechanical repetition from substituting for genuine improvisation. (Chapter 5, p. 14)

references.source: Roberts, Howard - Jazz Guitar Technique in 20 Weeks
references.citation: Chapter 5, p. 14: 'Project Lesson 1-B uses the same chord progression transposed to another key, thus requiring a change of fingering patterns, licks, etc. This also tends to stimulate fresh approaches and ideas.'

notes.narrative: Chapter 3 (p. 4) and Chapter 2 (p. 4) explicitly prescribe sus4 labeling over shorter notations such as C2 or add-2 on grounds of musician legibility. The author states 'I will grant you that C2 is shorter, but' and recommends 'G [sus4]' as the suitable name. This prescription extends to all inversions of both 3-part and 4-part fourth-based structures.
Chapter 2 (p. 4) extends the sus4 naming convention to all inversions: 'Of course, this applies to all of the inversions as well'. No inversion should revert to C2 or add-2 notation.

Chapter 3 (p. 7) prescribes '7th (no 3rd)' as one of three new 3-part chord types expanding the M-Lode taxonomy. Must be recognized as a distinct 3-part type in the catalog, not collapsed into another category.

Chapter 3 (p. 7) prescribes '7th (no 5th)' as a distinct 3-part chord type within the expanded M-Lode. Arises directly from the voice-omission derivation taught in Chapter 4 (p. 9): removing a single voice from a 4-part 7th chord.

Chapter 3 (p. 7) prescribes '3-part Spread Clusters' as the third new 3-part chord type completing the expanded M-Lode. Must be cataloged as a distinct 3-part chord family alongside 7th (no 3rd) and 7th (no 5th).

Chapter 7 (p. 71) prescribes that 3-part chords take priority over 4-part as the foundational chord literacy on ergonomic grounds: 'As guitarists, we can see that 3-part chords are easier to play than 4-part chords.' The 840-chord catalog (Chapters 6-9) introduces 3-part material before 4-part.

Chapter 4 (p. 9) establishes 4-part chords as the density ceiling: no chord construction exceeds 4 voices, and all 3-part derivation flows downward from 4-part sources by removing exactly one voice. Each 3-part type appears exactly four times — a direct consequence of the four voices available for omission.

Chapter 5 (p. 15) prescribes that passing-tone and melodic-embellishment exercises on 3-part voicings are learned first in C Major (no accidentals): 'All of the material that follows in this next section will be presented in C Major (no accidentals).' The student is then expected to transpose independently to other 7-note scales.

Harris assigns the dominant 7th chord to the major 6 diminished scale family. Every dom7 chord belongs to a family of four related dominants sharing the same diminished triad, built a major 3rd above the dominant note. 'The rule of thumb for finding a related diminished chord is to build it a major 3rd above the dominant note.' Chapter 1, p. 27.

The four dominant 7th chords derived from the same diminished triad are interchangeable when resolving V7-I. Harris illustrates with D7-Gmaj7: F7, Ab7, and B7 are also related to F# diminished and make interesting voicings when played against D in the bass. Chapter 4, p. 83.

When substituting related dominants over a V7-I resolution, Harris prescribes keeping the original dominant root in the bass while shifting the upper voicing to the related dominant chord. The D7-Gmaj7 example shows F7, Ab7, and B7 played against D in the bass, preserving bass-line identity while varying harmonic color. Chapter 4, p. 83.

For the dominant 7th scale, Harris specifies exactly three important arpeggios: on the tonic, the 5th, and the 7th. These are the only arpeggio positions the student prioritizes in practice. Chapter 1, p. 13.

The dominant 7th scale has its own set of scale-degree-specific rules for inserting chromatic half-steps in descending phrases to generate bebop vocabulary. Half-steps typify the language of the bebop player and are an endless source of improvisational ideas. Chapter 1, p. 17.

When applying diminished extensions over dominant 7th chords in minor keys, Harris specifies the diminished chord by key: C7 in F minor uses E-diminished; G7 in C minor uses B-diminished. The related diminished selection is both key- and chord-specific. Chapter 5, p. 93.

Harris assigns the major 6th chord as the primary identity of the major 6 diminished scale family. It is the foundational chord from which all major-function voicings derive via 'a scale for chording, and a method of assigning virtually any chord to one of two scales—the major 6 diminished and the minor 6 diminished.' Chapter 3, p. 66.

The C6 diminished scale—built on the major 6th chord—contains three interlocking diminished chords providing its internal architecture: the C and A belong to one diminished, the E and G to a second, and the B diminished chord provides the other four notes. All voicings within a major-function passage are drawn from this scale. Chapter 3, p. 67.

When moving between major-6-scale voicings, Harris's governing rule applies directly: remember to move each note to the next note of the scale. Each voice in a maj6-family voicing steps to its adjacent neighbor in the major 6 diminished scale, creating smooth voice motion. Chapter 3, p. 71.

Harris collapses the min7 chord into the major 6 diminished scale family by redefining it as an inversion: 'Every minor 7 chord is an inversion of a major 6th chord.' The student should think of any m7 chord not as its own category but as a major 6th chord viewed from a different inversion, unlocking all major-6-diminished voicings for min7 contexts. Chapter 3, p. 69.

Because every min7 chord is an inversion of a major 6th chord, all voicings for a min7 chord are drawn from the major 6 diminished scale of the corresponding major 6th chord. The student assigns the min7 to that scale and applies the standard movable-chord voice-leading rules. Chapter 3, p. 69-71.

Harris names a special role for the min7 chord: 'Important minor is the term given to the chord found on the 5th degree of a dominant 7th scale (5 of 5).' This specific min7—the minor 7th a 5th above the dominant—serves as a reusable harmonic tool in progressions like Rhythm Changes. Chapter 2, p. 46.

Harris collapses the min7b5 (half-diminished) chord into the minor 6 diminished scale family: 'every minor7 flat5 chord is an inversion of a minor 6th chord.' The student should think of any m7b5 as a minor 6th chord in inversion, unlocking all minor-6-diminished voicings for half-diminished contexts. Chapter 3, p. 69.

Because every m7b5 chord is an inversion of a minor 6th chord, all voicings are drawn from the minor 6 diminished scale of the corresponding minor 6th chord. The movable-chord rule applies: move each note to the next note of the minor 6 diminished scale. Chapter 3, p. 69-71.
The minor 6th chord is the foundational identity of the minor 6 diminished scale family, the second of Harris's two universal chording scales. Chapter 3, p. 66.

The minor 6 diminished scale is constructed by fusing the minor 6 chord with its related diminished chord: 'This scale is formed by combining a minor 6 chord with its related diminished chord. The diminished chord is built from a major 3rd above the dominant note of the scale.' Chapter 2, p. 58.

Harris prescribes a specific named voice-leading unit ending on a minor-with-6th-in-bass chord: 'the progression from major to minor to minor with the 6th degree in the bass: (Bb major-G minor-Gm/E).' The min6 position is the cadential arrival of this three-chord formula. Chapter 4, p. 79.

Harris prescribes building the related diminished chord a major 3rd above the dominant note to locate the four interchangeable dominant 7th chords in any key. 'Just go up a major 3rd from the root of the dominant 7th chord.' Chapter 1, p. 27; Chapter 2, p. 42.

Each diminished chord generates exactly four related dominant 7th chords, all interchangeable in cadential contexts. F# diminished generates D7, F7, Ab7, B7. The diminished chord is the organizational hub for a family of four V7 colors. Chapter 4, p. 83.
Within the C6 diminished scale, three interlocking diminished chords provide the scale's internal architecture and serve as symmetric stepping-stones for moving voicings. Chapter 3, p. 67.

In minor key contexts, Harris specifies which diminished chord to apply over each dominant by key: C7 in F minor uses E-diminished; G7 in C minor uses B-diminished. The student selects the related diminished by key signature. Chapter 5, p. 93.

Harris defines the augmented arpeggio as a variant of the major arpeggio with the 5th raised a half-step: 'An Ab augmented arpeggio (the 5th degree is raised a half-step from the major).' It appears in the vocalist's warm-up series as a technical skill prerequisite for improvisation freedom. Chapter 5, p. 95.

Ligon places the ii chord (minor seventh) as the initiating member of the ii-V-I progression, and identifies its third as the single most harmonically specific melodic target. F reveals the minor quality of the chord and is the best choice for harmonically specific counterpoint over the D in the bass; playing just the F over D in the bass sounds like a complete minor chord even though only two notes are being played. The root is omitted because the bass covers it, opening eleven pitch choices while preserving harmonic clarity. Chapter 2, p. 5.

The seventh of the ii chord is the 'restless pointer' that drives melodic momentum. Sevenths resolve downward to the third of the following chord. For the ii min7, the seventh must land on a metrically significant beat, positioned later in the line than the third, so that its downward resolution to the V7's third is perceptible as directed motion. Chapter 2, p. 5-6.

Over the ii min7, Outline No. 1 begins on beat one with the third, descends stepwise through the chord, and delivers the seventh on beat four as the pointer into the V7. Placing the third on beat one and waiting for beat four to play the seventh leaves only two beats to fill, creating a walking quarter-note melody line to counter the walking bass line. Chapter 2, p. 6.

Outline No. 2 treats the ii min7 as an ascending arpeggio 1-3-5-7, where the seventh functions as the restless tone that resolves to the third of the V7 chord. The canonical form begins on the root of the ii chord and spells the arpeggio to the seventh. Fragments that omit the root are fully valid because the bass covers the root. Chapter 2 p. 8; Chapter 5 p. 60, 63.

Outline No. 3 descends the ii min7 as 5-3-1, then adds the seventh below as a pointer tone. The seventh usually occurs on the upbeat; the target third on the strong downbeat. The leap from the third of the ii to the flat-nine of the V creates compound melody as a byproduct. Chapter 2 p. 9; Chapter 6 p. 66.

When using Outline No. 2 over a ii min7, the sixth scale degree (the tone that will become the third of the following V7) must be reserved for the V7 chord and not used as a passing tone on the ii. This tone is the punch line, the denouement of the story, not given away ahead of time as a passing tone. Early arrival of the target tone collapses the harmonic tension the outline is designed to build. Chapter 5 p. 54.

The punch line rule (reserving the target note for the V7) may be broken when the line extends to the ninth of the ii chord, reducing the premature arrival's disruptive effect. The extension contextualizes the early target as an inner passing tone rather than a harmonic spoiler. Chapter 5 p. 58.

Ligon treats the dominant seventh as the resolution target for the ii chord's seventh-as-pointer: the V7's third is the single most important arrival note in the ii-V-I progression. The third of V7 is the downbeat destination that sounds at rest after the restless seventh of ii. All three outlines converge on this arrival point as their primary harmonic goal. Chapter 2 p. 5-6.

Over any dominant seventh functioning as V7 in major, Ligon prescribes borrowing the flat-9, sharp-9, and flat-13 from the parallel minor key. Over G7, the dominant of C major, jazz musicians often use A-flat (b9), B-flat (#9) and E-flat (b13) from the parallel key of C minor. These borrowed tones have greater downward pull than their diatonic counterparts. Chapter 3 p. 16.

C.E.S.H. (Chromatic Elaboration of Static Harmony) is the characteristic chromatic device applied across the ii-V progression, superimposing a descending chromatic line from the root of the ii down to the third of the V7. In the key of C (D minor-G7), the movement is D-C#-C-B. All three outlines support C.E.S.H., and Outline No. 3 has a special affinity for it. Chapter 3 p. 15; Chapter 4 p. 39; Chapter 6 p. 68.

The signature Outline No. 3 move over the V7 is the leap from the third to the flat-nine, which splits the line into a primary melody and a counter-melody. The first and last four notes sound like the primary melody; the middle notes sound like a secondary answer or counter melody. This is the idiomatic octave-displacement move specific to the V7 within Outline No. 3. Chapter 6 p. 66.

Chromatic non-chord tones over the V7 are licensed only when target tones (the third and seventh of the dominant) land on metrically strong beats. All twelve chromatic pitches may be used yet harmonically clear; not random chromaticism. Target notes occur in rhythmically significant spots, non-harmonic chromatic notes resolve when and where expected. Chapter 4 p. 43; Chapter 6 p. 74.

When an ascending scalar passage approaches an upcoming target note on the V7, the scale must skip the target pitch rather than include it as a passing tone. Premature scalar arrival at the target weakens its harmonic impact on the strong beat. Chapter 4 p. 32.

The signature octave displacement move over V7 replaces a descending step from the third to the second with an ascending seventh leap from the third up to the ninth or flat-ninth. The leap must occur after the guide tone, from downbeat to upbeat, and never crosses the barline. Chapter 3 p. 14.

The third of the V7 may be approached by encirclement - diatonic upper neighbor tone followed by chromatic lower neighbor tone, or the reverse - to create tension and momentary ambiguity before resolution. The common practice from Mozart to Charlie Parker uses the diatonic UNT and the chromatic LNT. Chapter 5 p. 52; Chapter 3 p. 11.

Ligon explicitly extends all three outlines to the minor ii-V context, treating the half-diminished chord as a direct functional equivalent of the diatonic ii min7 in terms of outline applicability. All the outlines work as well for half-diminished/V7 in minor as they do in major. The same target-tone logic applies: third of half-dim is the opening melodic goal; its seventh resolves to the third of the V7. Chapter 5 p. 52.

Over the dominant V7 in a minor ii-V-i context, Ligon's parallel-minor borrowing rule carries the same force as in major: the flat-9, sharp-9, and flat-13 are drawn from the parallel minor and prescribed as melodic color tones that resolve with greater downward pull than their diatonic counterparts. Because the minor ii-V already exists in a minor-key harmonic environment, the borrowed tones are particularly idiomatic. Chapter 3 p. 16.

Ligon teaches that dominant sus4 voicings are interchangeable with ii-V7 voicings for outline purposes. Since this sound is essentially the ii and V7 chord together, any of the outlines will work for this harmony. A sus chord is treated not as a separate harmonic category but as a composite of ii and V7 stacked, meaning all three outlines and their embellishment devices apply without modification. Chapter 6 p. 65.

Over a modal ii min7 context (e.g., G Dorian), Ligon prescribes superimposing bebop outlines via leading-tone approach to bring harmonic clarity to an otherwise static harmonic environment. The mechanics demonstrated by Cannonball Adderley include approaching chord tones by their leading tones and using encircling motion; outline no.1 can be clearly heard on the downbeats with leading tones added giving the line more of a sawtooth shape. Chapter 8 p. 78.

In modal blues contexts, the C.E.S.H. version of Outline No. 3 over the dominant functions as a deliberate contrast device against motivic and blues-inflected playing. Cannonball Adderley uses this C.E.S.H. version of outline no.3 several times in the solo to contrast with his modal, motivic, and down-and-dirty blues playing on this modal blues tune. The outline's harmonic specificity stands out precisely because the surrounding context is harmonically vague. Chapter 8 p. 78.

Ligon explicitly states that any chord progression with root motion descending by fifths - not only ii-V-I but secondary dominants, back-cycling progressions, blues turnarounds, and standard-tune sequences - is governed by the same three-outline system. Anytime root movement is down in fifths, any of these outlines will work, regardless of chord quality. The quality of the chords does not restrict outline selection; root motion is the controlling factor. Chapter 4 p. 29.

Outline fragments that omit chord tones from the ii min7 retain full harmonic clarity as long as the target tones are placed and resolved correctly. Parker's technique demonstrates that the seventh of ii resolving to the third of V7 is a sufficient harmonic kernel even without all chord tones present. Morgan's technique shows the only note missing is the third of the half-diminished ii and the line still follows the outline. These omissions are valid because the root of the chord is covered by the bass. Chapter 7 p. 76-77.

Ligon's answer-key appendix codifies rhythmic delay as a device over V7: stop-and-go rhythms delay the resolution of E7 until beat three; arpeggio on E7 (3-5-7-9). The stop-and-go rhythm withholds the target note arrival beyond its expected metric position, extending the tension of the outline across additional beats. The arpeggio formula 3-5-7-9 is the named chord-tone pattern deployed in this context. Chapter 16 p. 145.

The sawtooth embellishment device over V7 combines a leap back to a chord tone with a chromatic leading tone that precedes the target. Leap back to a chord tone creates sawtooth shape, delays resolution of C7; chromatic leading tone (D#) precedes target note (E); leap from third to root of C7. The chromatic leading tone, being a sharped note, follows the upward-tendency rule, pulling directly into the target note on the strong beat. Chapter 16 p. 145; Chapter 3 p. 11.

The target note on the V7 may be surrounded by both its upper and lower neighbor tones in succession before arrival: target note (A) approached from above (C-Bb-A) and below (G-G#-A). Upper approach is diatonic; lower approach is chromatic, consistent with the UNT/LNT convention. Chapter 16 p. 145.
